Sports.title: Leclerc has wrong mentality, says Hamilton: ‘It’s ‘do-or-die, either I win or none of us do” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari would have lost more wins this year if he had the same “kamikaze” mentality as team mate Charles Leclerc.

The seven-times world champion blamed his team mate for costing Ferrari victory in yesterday’s Mexican Grand Prix. Both he and Leclerc went off at turn four while fighting over the lead on lap one.

Hamilton said he’d noticed Leclerc’s battles with his predecessor Carlos Sainz Jnr cost Ferrari points in the past.

“Before I joined this team, when I was at Mercedes, I watched and witnessed the back and forth between Charles and Carlos several races, where they were battling so much that the person ahead just pulled away, and they had the pace to actually win,” he said. “But it is one thing when that’s happening in fourth and fifth, as opposed to first and second, and you lose the win. That’s significant.

“The guy [Leclerc] is 28 years old, so I don’t think it’s an age thing. I think it’s a mentality thing. It’s like, “Do-or-die. Either I win or none of us do,” and it shouldn’t be that. It should be us having, getting that one-two.”

Hamilton pointed out he did not compromise Leclerc’s race when he won at Silverstone earlier this year. “In Silverstone, I could have gone all kamikaze on him and taken him off and lost us the win, but instead the one-two was there.” They finished first and third but were holding the top two positions before Hamilton pitted when the Safety Car was deployed.

“For me, I’m happy for the team to have experienced that, but I’m hopeful we’ll work towards a better working place in the future.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

In remarks similar to those of Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur, Hamilton said the result did not do justice to the effort made by the team.

“I think the core thing to remember, which maybe comes with age, is that every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team,” he said. “So, working as a team is a part of our job and a part of our contract.

“We have to work as a team, which we could have easily done today. So, it’s a shame to see us lose this, as we did. That will just continue unless action is taken, if a real deep, serious conversation is had. So, it shouldn’t happen [again] moving forward.

“Of course, I’ve had close battles with team mates in the past, and you can’t always get it right, but nine times out of ten we should be able to. So, I think we’ll take it offline and we’ll have some good conversations, hopefully. For sure, it won’t be easy, but it must be done.”

However Hamilton admitted he’d experienced tougher situations previously at other teams, such as at Mercedes, where he and team mate Nico Rosberg once took each other out at the start of a race.

“I’ve had way worse times at Mercedes. There were some really bad moments. I don’t really see there being huge differences. I think it was managed well at Mercedes, and I think Fred’s doing his best.

“Fred came and spoke to me before the race, and I think he was nervous. Of course, he wants [his] two drivers to do well.”

He said he would have had to explain his actions had he attacked his team mate from behind the way Leclerc did.

“From my side, if I’m coming from behind and I’m taking all the risk and it ends up that we lose as a team, then I think I have some answering to do, because it impacts a lot of people. But the other way around, I’m in the lead, and it was just unnecessary.

“I think we could have easily had that one-two today, which would have been huge for the team and for everyone back at the factory who’s worked so hard to bring us these upgrades. I don’t really know what will be done because up until now nothing really has been done.”

Sports.title: Antonelli “lost two seconds because I was crying” at end of Mexican GP | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli admitted he was already crying before he took the chequered flag to win the world championship.

The Mercedes driver finished third in Mexico, clinching the title in his second season as a Formula 1 driver. The 20-year-old was so emotional he was struggling to see the track and he lost 1.8 seconds to the leaders on his final lap.

“I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying, basically,” Antonelli admitted. “I couldn’t see clearly ahead.

“I could see two Ferraris, somehow, with the tears. So it was very special.”

Antonelli became the youngest world champion in F1 history, just five years after moving from karts to cars. “A lot of memories went through my mind in that moment,” he said, “all the memories since karting all the way to here.

“It was a very special final lap, and definitely when I crossed the line, I let it all out because it was just achieving one of my biggest dreams. It was very special.”

The championship outcome was a foregone conclusion before the weekend began: Antonelli needed to score only two points to be certain of the title even if his closest rival won all the remaining rounds. Nonetheless he felt the weight of expectation during the weekend.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I knew I was very close. However, I still needed to get the job done, and, of course, you still want to do a good race. You want to do a good performance, so that was the goal.

“But it hasn’t been the easiest weekend either. Physically, I haven’t been in the best shape, but also yesterday we had a bad qualifying execution, and emotions were a bit high overall.

“But I’m really happy that today we did a strong race and really happy that we managed to finish the job. And then now we’ve got a few races to go, and we’re just going to enjoy all the way and try to finish on a high.”

He made a careful start to the race, ceding a position to eventual winner Max Verstappen on the run to turn one. However he decided to risk more at the second standing start following a red flag period.

“At the start I was very cautious, and I gave a lot of room. So I was probably playing it very much on the safe side.

“But then I saw I had the pace, and especially that first stint, I knew we would be in the fight because the pace was very good on used tyres.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Then with the red flag, it kind of all went back to zero. And in that moment I was like, ‘You know what? I’m just going to take more risks.’

“I had the opportunity to gain a few places, and that move on Charles [Leclerc] was crucial to get on the podium. I tried until the end to stay close, and it was very fun, the last stint, because we were all, I think, the three of us within two seconds, and we were all pushing. It was just difficult, of course, to overtake, but it was high intensity, and it was fun.

“Then on the last lap I just backed off because I just couldn’t see the track. I was getting emotional, and I said, ‘I’m just going to back off because otherwise I crash here.’ So it was just good to bring it home.”

Andrea Kimi Antonelli says the post-race photograph of him with two of his fellow world champions deserves a place on his wall.

The new world champion joined the two most successful drivers in Formula 1 today on the podium at the end of yesterday’s Mexican Grand Prix. The trio now have 12 world championships between them – Lewis Hamilton having seven and Max Verstappen four.

“I will definitely frame the picture and put it in my house because it’s just an incredible moment. And as well, to see so much respect from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is truly special, and a moment that will live and will always be remembered.

“So definitely I will frame the picture and put it on the wall of my house so I can see it very well whenever I go in.”

Sports.title: Call this the ‘Maxico’ Grand Prix says Verstappen after sixth Mexican GP win | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen joked Formula 1 should rename Mexico’s round of the world championship after him following his sixth victory in the race.

The Red Bull driver has now scored more wins in Mexico City than he has at any other venue. He became the fourth driver to score more than five wins at the same venue and the first to do so at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez

“They should actually call it the ‘Maxico’ Grand Prix,” said Verstappen. “That would be great.”

His five previous wins at the track came between 2017 and 2023. Verstappen said he saw no obvious reason why he had been particularly successful at this venue.

“I honestly love being here,” he said. “I love the city, I love the environment, I love the fans, but I have no idea why.

“It just happens. Sometimes your car just comes alive and you’ve had good races and not a lot of bad luck sometimes as well. So it’s just always come together for me here and, of course, I happily take that.”

Verstappen said he was surprised to move into a strong position immediately after the start of the race, thanks partly to Ferrari drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton going off at turn four.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The first start already made my race a bit better, getting into turn one, and then, of course, the battle that I saw unfold in turn four put me in a quite nice spot.”

Leclerc received a five-second time penalty for his infringement and Verstappen jumped ahead of him when they pitted on the same lap.

“It was a bit tough, to be honest, I think Charles just pulled away. I could not really stay with him. I did not have the pace to follow him, but at the same time, I was still within that five-second window.

“So, then the team did a really good job to follow him in [to the pits]. It’s always very tough when you have a five-second penalty to actually make it exactly five seconds. So, I jumped him, and honestly, after that, it was quite tough.”

The race winner said he feared for his chances when the Safety Car was deployed following Valtteri Bottas’s crash. The race was stopped and restarted, and Verstappen maintained his lead ahead of Hamilton.

“Kimi [Antonelli] was flying, still, out there on the first set of tyres, and I just did not really have the grip for whatever reason. Charles was very close, but at the same time, it’s very hard to follow around here because everything overheats, and that probably helped me as well because I think at one point Charles had to back off just for cooling, and that was quite nice for me.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“But at the same time, when I saw the Safety Car come out just out of the last corner and I couldn’t box, I was like, ‘There’s no way this is happening now,’ because that was then probably game over for me.

“Then, of course, it ended up being a red flag, so then it reset everything. I was a bit worried because our starts this year have not been amazing, but luckily today, twice, they have actually been good, and that then made my way ’til the end.

“But it was not made easy. I mean, Lewis was in my gearbox, pushing hard. It was basically a qualifying lap ’til the end. Yeah, it was tough out there. It was a tough race to the end, just to not make any mistakes. But, of course, I’m happy to win today.”

Sports.title: Social media: Italian sports newspaper takes swipe at Ferrari as Antonelli claims title | Brief
Sports.content:
The major Italian daily sports newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport delivered a stark verdict on Ferrari’s performance as Andrea Kimi Antonelli clinched the 2026 world championship.

“Kimi Antonelli is a Formula 1 world champion,” read the commentary on the front page of Monday’s edition. “Thanks to his talent, the car and the fact that he isn’t racing for Ferrari.”

Antonelli’s father Marco has previously said Ferrari missed the opportunity to sign his son. He claimed Maurizio Arrivabene, Ferrari team principal from 2014 to 2019, turned him down.

The new world champion joined Mercedes’ young driver programme at the age of 11. Yesterday he scored the eighth drivers’ championship success for a Mercedes driver since 2014. No driver has won the world championship in a Ferrari since Kimi Raikkonen in 2007.

Sports.title: “I’ll stay with number 12” – no number one in 2027 for new champion Antonelli | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli will not use the number one on his car, which is reserved for world champions, next year.

The Mercedes driver succeeded Lando Norris as the reigning world champion with his third-place finish in yesterday’s Mexican Grand Prix. But while Norris swapped his regular number four for the champion’s one, Antonelli will not do the same.

“I’ll stay with number 12 because, obviously, it’s a very special number for me,” he said. “But also it’s a way for me to stay grounded, to stay humble.

“I feel like by keeping number 12 it allows me to have a new point where to start and build on everything again and try to improve.”

Antonelli admitted there is an element of superstition in his preference to stick with his current number.

“Also, to be honest, I’m very superstitious, and number one has never been a good number for me. Whenever I [used] it, it went extremely badly. So that’s one more reason to stay with number 12.”

Prior to racing in F1, Antonelli used number 12 when he won the European and Middle East Formula Regional championship titles in 2023, and the Italian Formula 4 title the year before.

He is the first driver to win the world championship using number 12 since Ayrton Senna in 1988. Both drivers also scored their first grand prix victories with number 12: Antonelli this year, Senna in 1985.

Antonelli is planning a tribute to the Brazilian three-times world champion at this weekend’s Brazilian Grand Prix.

“I will have a special helmet for Brazil, for Ayrton,” he said. “Also because it’s going to be 35 years since he won [while stuck] in sixth gear in his home race.

“I think it’s one of my best helmets that I’ve made, hopefully you guys, everyone, will like it.”

Sports.title: Mercedes fined as Russell skips media duties after power unit frustration | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The stewards fined Mercedes €5,000 (£4,173) after George Russell refused to speak to media following yesterday’s Mexican Grand Prix.

Russell expressed more frustration with his power unit during yesterday’s race after losing three places at the original start. He did not speak to media after the race, in which his team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli clinched the world championship.

The stewards noted Russell “left the circuit without attending the post-race media commitments” and also failed to attend their hearing. “Noting that the stewards can proceed to make a determination in the case of a non attendance at a hearing, a penalty of €5,000 is imposed on the competitor.”

In a statement issued by Mercedes after the race, Russell said: “Unfortunately, it was a very disappointing race on my side.

“I made a good start and was in a strong position, but then we suffered an issue which caused me to not have full deployment down the straight. That cost us a lot of positions and ultimately took us out of contention for a strong result. It’s frustrating to have the race compromised by something outside of my control but that is racing.”

Russell also collected a 10-second time penalty during the race for colliding with Isack Hadjar.

He congratulated Antonelli on “a thoroughly deserved championship” victory. “He has done a fantastic job this season and can be incredibly proud of what he has achieved.”

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said it had been “another race where we didn’t give [Russell] the platform to show what he could do.”

“The deployment issue at the start immediately compromised his afternoon and, although the incident and penalty made his race more difficult, he kept fighting and brought the car home in [sixth],” said Wolff. “There have been too many occasions this season where we have let George down, and he has deserved more from us.

“His contribution to what we have achieved this year has been immense, and we shouldn’t lose sight of that today.”

Sports.title: Revitalization in Riyadh
Sports.content:
Saturday afternoon saw Saul “Canelo” Alvarez (64-3-2, 39 KOs) defeat Christian Mbilli (29-1-1, 24 KOs) by unanimous decision over 12 rounds. For all the talk of Canelo being washed after his dismantling at the hands of Terence “Bud” Crawford last year, Canelo looked quick, efficient, and energized on both offense and defense from beginning to end.

Some major differences in his performance included a low lead hand stance as his primary, with the high guard as a secondary; a return to the head movement that was once touted as among the best in boxing; and the most consistent and effective jab we’ve seen from him in close to a decade. He also threw a hell of a lot of feints and changed up the velocity of his punches rather than throwing everything hard as he has tended to do. This not only helped him conserve energy, but it also deterred Mbilli’s aggressiveness. In a fight that many expected to be a war, Canelo focused on pure boxing and high-level defense to slow the action down and prevent Mbilli from launching an all-out attack in the pocket.

In the early rounds, Canelo played a little rope-a-dope, laying against the ropes while slipping, ducking, and blocking the younger fighter’s shots. When the action made its way back to the center of the ring, Canelo popped Mbilli with sharp, well-timed jabs at mid-range. After four rounds, Mbilli had slowed enough for Canelo to begin finding big, clean counters in exchanges. Six rounds in, Canelo started circling more rather than going to the ropes. At times, he would touch the ropes with his back to bait Mbilli in, and then flurry with rapid combinations as Mbilli stepped in thinking Canelo was going back on defense.

From the seventh round on, it was a basic boxing clinic, with Canelo showing that he can still box his ass off when he isn’t in love with his power. The eleventh and twelfth rounds were competitive as Mbilli tried to finish strong, yet Canelo consistently landed the bigger, cleaner shots, even wobbling Mbilli toward the close of round 12.

Mbilli simply was never able to mount a consistent attack because Canelo had an answer for everything he attempted. Against Terence Crawford, Canelo simply sought to overpower what he perceived as a naturally smaller man, but Crawford was able to blunt everything coming from Canelo with sophisticated defense and control at midrange. When Canelo went back to the drawing board with his team, he must have been kicking himself for never attempting to establish the jab, failing to use his head movement, and allowing Crawford to maintain foot control all night.

When Mayweather dominated Canelo over 12 rounds with superior defense and intelligent punch selection, the takeaway was that brute force isn’t enough to topple the fighters at the top. Somewhere during his 168 lb undisputed run, he lost sight of that and locked into a seek-and-destroy mindset. It seems like the Crawford loss may have initiated a similar reboot, which could carry Canelo into a final run at undisputed before retirement.

One point of concern Saturday night took place outside of the ring, with the commentary team missing as much as Christian Mbilli was. Notably, Todd Grisham seemed intent on dragging Canelo. At one point, he implied that Canelo got the benefit of the doubt against Daniel Jacobs, which was actually a clear and decisive win for Canelo. He also mentioned a fight between Canelo and Derevyanchenko, which does not exist. In the opening rounds, when Mbilli would miss six or seven punch combinations, the commentary team would praise the guy who missed rather than the guy who made him miss.

In round eight, after multiple fouls, when Mbilli drove a palm into the back of Canelo’s head, the referee separated the two and walked Mbilli to the center of the ring. He clearly had Mbilli’s glove in hand, preparing to take a point, when Canelo tapped his shoulder to complain about the fouls as fighters often do. When the referee proceeded to dock the point, Grisham erupted into an accusation that Canelo had forced the referee to penalize Mbilli. The ref was clearly already preparing to take the point, but furthermore, Canelo has zero power to force a referee’s hand. What Canelo apparently stated was that if he was fouled again, he would kick his opponent. He didn’t use his name or influence to sway any decision-making; he simply made a statement out of anger.

Of course, many viewers who aren’t familiar with the intricacies of the sport rely on the commentary team to provide an accurate analysis of the fight. Much of the post-fight narrative following Saturday’s bout has been centered around the perception that Canelo had the referee in his pocket and that the fight was a robbery, simply because the commentators seemed to favor ineffective aggression over defensive prowess.

Outside of whatever bias he has against Alvarez, there wasn’t much technical analysis from Grisham. Sergio Mora, though he has experience as a fighter and sometimes points out strategies or techniques, is often unable to articulate what he sees clearly. Grisham frequently views fights as a casual fan might: “Throw punches = good. Not throw punches = bad. Move forward = good. Block punches = getting hit.” DAZN would do well to bring on an individual who truly understands the nuances of the sport and can convey them effectively to the common fan.

One thing that hasn’t been prevalent in the aftermath of the fight is anyone accusing Canelo of “running,” even though he more or less did to Mbilli what Crawford did to him. People who accuse boxers of running because they do not sit and slug it out at close range are generally uninformed or unwilling to give credit to certain styles of fighters like Crawford, Foster, or Mayweather. Canelo rarely sat still for exchanges, yet he is (rightfully) being praised for his high defensive IQ. Now, what could that double standard possibly be about?

So, what impressions did Saturday’s main event leave on us?

First, Canelo didn’t learn any new tricks; he simply brushed the dust off his old tool bag and returned to the basics. The jab was tweaked, but overall, the head movement, feints, and punch variety are elements fans have been asking him to bring back for years.

Secondly, DAZN needs to step up its commentary game. The broadcast should accommodate the casual viewer while remaining educated and informed enough for die-hard boxing fans. You simply cannot skimp on commentator quality at this level of production.

Lastly, Canelo’s future. Alvarez remains a polarizing figure. But love him or hate him, it is hard to deny that he has been boxing’s biggest star since Mayweather retired. What might his plans be moving forward, and how will the boxing world react? Given the promotional tagline of “Return of the King,” it seems reasonable to assume he will once again seek to become the undisputed champion of the 168 lb division before retiring. Ideally, he would collect all the belts and gain one more signature victory, though that is a steep path for a 36-year-old.

Wherever the future leads him, he has carried the sport at several key points in his career. He is a reminder that greatness and perfection are not one and the same, and are often at odds. Steadfast determination and a true, honest love for boxing have defined Canelo’s persona inside and outside the ring. Despite falling short against generational greats, he remains an example of how passionate dedication to a dream can endure long after achieving everything you set out for.

Sports.title: Andy Cruz Faces Artur Subkhankulov November 27 For IBF Title
Sports.content:
Andy Cruz has found a fresh path to the IBF lightweight crown, even if picking up the belt leaves his loss against Raymond Muratalla unanswered. The Cuban standout meets undefeated Artur Subkhankulov on November 27 in Ufa, Russia, battling for the vacant title now that Muratalla has jumped up in weight.

Ring Magazine broke the news of the matchup, dropping Cruz right into his opponent’s backyard.

Muratalla moving up for 140 pounds without settling things leaves a sour taste, especially when so many ringside observers believed Cruz (7-1, 4 KOs) did enough to earn the decision last January. Walking away with the belt and immediately going to light welterweight lets Muratalla hold onto bragging rights without having to solve Cruz a second time.

That controversial loss against Muratalla basically gave Cruz the best of both worlds. The disputed cards shielded him from the career damage of a decisive defeat, while the sting of leaving with an empty hand shook him out of his amateur habits.

Amateur legends often stay stuck in neutral because their pure boxing ability bails them out. Cruz could have spent years coasting on touch-and-move tricks, flicking jabs, and winning rounds by narrow margins. Instead, that decision forced him to confront the cold reality of professional prize fighting: relying on judges to appreciate finesse will get you robbed.

Shifting toward sitting down on his punches and hunting real damage is the exact adjustment he needed. If he had been given the decision against Muratalla, he probably would have stayed comfortable. Taking the hit turned him into a far more dangerous fighter.

Going into Russia against Subkhankulov with that mean streak makes him a completely different situation. Subkhankulov is walking in prepared for an Olympic stylist. If Cruz shows up planting his heels and looking to take his head off, that wake-up call against Muratalla might end up being the best thing that ever happened to his career.

Cruz, 31, last fought in July, stopping Abraham Montoya in three rounds in his first appearance since losing to Muratalla. The change was dramatic. He fought with greater aggression and looked intent on hurting Montoya rather than allowing his cleaner boxing to carry him through the rounds.

Sports.title: David Nyika Ready To Spoil Usyk Retirement Plans
Sports.content:
Oleksandr Usyk‘s planned farewell tour has hit an unexpected roadblock. David Nyika’s team intends to enforce his mandatory standing with the IBF, putting a wrench in the Ukrainian’s plan to capture another undisputed cruiserweight crown.

Trainer Noel Thornberry confirmed he reached out to Usyk’s management regarding a potential clash. He made it clear that while they want the fight, stepping aside for a different matchup will require serious negotiation. As Thornberry told AAP, everyone would need to sit down to reach a deal.

Usyk’s camp envisions a two-bout cruiserweight run in 2027. Step one involves claiming a vacant belt. Step two targets David Benavidez for all four titles. For that scenario to materialize, Benavidez must defeat WBC titlist Michal Cieslak on December 5 to unify three belts, leaving the IBF strap as the final piece Usyk must supply for the undisputed finale.

Mapping out that schedule on paper is simple enough, but executing it requires cooperation from fighters who have no interest in playing along. Nyika wants to build his own legacy, giving him zero incentive to stand down just to accommodate a heavyweight champion’s retirement timeline.

Ranked as the IBF’s top contender, Nyika sits in prime position. The division remains murky, however, with former champion Jai Opetaia currently contesting the stripping of his belt following his jump to Zuffa Boxing. Opetaia stopped Nyika in January 2025, meaning any legal resolution reinstating Opetaia would shake up Usyk’s options even further.

Thornberry’s approach prepares for either scenario. His team welcomes a direct shot at Usyk, but also acknowledges that a lucrative deal would be required to let an Opetaia bout happen first. While these statements make Nyika’s ambitions obvious, the IBF has yet to issue an official fight order.

Weight presents another major hurdle. Usyk turns 40 in January and hasn’t made 200 pounds since knocking out Tony Bellew in November 2018. While advisor Serhii Lapin maintains Usyk will be at peak form against Benavidez, dropping back down after eight years at heavyweight creates real physical uncertainty.

Thornberry openly questions whether an aging Usyk can handle the cut, stressing that Nyika views the former undisputed ruler as a beatable target rather than an intimidating legend.

Regardless of past victories or legendary status, securing another championship still demands a sanctioning body belt, an eligible challenger, and signed paperwork. Before Usyk can lock in his grand exit, Nyika’s camp plans on forcing its way to the negotiating table.

Sports.title: Jake Paul Opponent set for MVP Christmas Eve Spectacle in Dubai
Sports.content:
Cédric Doumbé will swap MMA for boxing on December 24 when he faces Jake Paul at Coca-Cola Arena in Dubai. The former two-time GLORY welterweight champion has signed for an eight-round cruiserweight bout, giving him his second professional boxing appearance.

Doumbé wasted little time taking aim at his opponent after Most Valuable Promotions announced the Christmas Eve fight.

“Jake Paul calls himself the Problem Child, but he’s never faced a problem like me. He has no idea what a Frenchman is capable of, and on Thursday, December 24 in Dubai, I’m going to eat ‘El Poulet’ for dinner.”

The Cameroon-born French fighter built most of his career in kickboxing, compiling a 75-7-1 record with 45 knockouts. He then moved into MMA, where he stands at 6-1 with six stoppage wins, including his nine-second knockout of Jordan Zebo in Paris in September 2023.

His professional boxing record is 1-0. That leaves a sizeable gap in boxing experience against Paul, who has fought 14 times since turning professional in 2020 and holds a 12-2 record with seven knockouts.

The contest is scheduled at the 200-pound cruiserweight limit with 10-ounce gloves. Broadcast details and the fight-night start time were not included in the announcement.

For Paul, the booking adds another opponent from outside traditional boxing to a record that includes victories over Tyron Woodley, Anderson Silva and Nate Diaz. He also beat former middleweight champion Julio César Chávez Jr. in June 2025 before facing Anthony Joshua that December.

Paul said the challenge from Doumbé had been brewing for two years.

“Cédric Douchebag was calling me out two years ago after knocking some dude out in 9 seconds. Well Douchebag, now you get your chance.”

Their first face-to-face meetings are set for next week, with public press conferences in Paris and Dubai. Paul challenged Doumbé to bring the same talk with him.

“You like to talk a lot, so let’s see what you have to say in person at the press conferences next week in Paris and Dubai.”

The Paris stop takes place at Pavillon Cambon on November 10 at 6 p.m. CET, followed by Dubai on November 12 at 6 p.m. GST. Both events are free and open to fans.

Tickets for the fight go on general sale November 15 at noon GST, or 9 a.m. CET. A registered-fan presale opens November 14, with PFL Dubai ticket purchasers getting access from November 6.

The card marks Paul’s first professional fight in Dubai. MVP has yet to name any undercard fights in the supplied announcement.

Sports.title: Joshua Buatsi Chases Paper Crown Against Willy Hutchinson
Sports.content:
Joshua Buatsi claims he made the right call walking away from Dmitry Bivol. Picking up a vacant strap against Willy Hutchinson will not convince anyone he belongs with the division’s elite.

Taking the long road to a world championship by beating an opponent you already handled proves very little.

Buatsi meets Hutchinson for the vacant WBC light heavyweight belt at Manchester AO Arena on November 7. David Benavidez moved up to cruiserweight, opening up the position. That handed Buatsi a lifeline after Callum Smith battered him. That defeat derailed his standing as a serious threat at 175 pounds.

The brutal three-fight stretch since 2024 has taken plenty out of Buatsi, and walking straight into a rematch with a spiteful puncher like Hutchinson right now is playing with fire.

At 33, Buatsi is not the fresh prospect who could rely on physical superiority to bail him out. The wear and tear is showing.

Buatsi told BoxingScene that the financial terms to face Bivol were unacceptable. He insisted he has zero regrets about passing up the Russian champion.

Boxers can argue over purse splits all day. The reality is that picking up a belt against Hutchinson will never replace the test Bivol presented. It will not recover the years Buatsi wasted playing it safe.

The British bronze medalist is running out of road. Securing a belt gives him leverage at the bargaining table, yet beating Hutchinson does not turn him into an elite light heavyweight.

Hutchinson knows Buatsi looks vulnerable. Buatsi dropped him twice in their first clash, but Smith exposed him soon after. Buatsi also looked ordinary squeaking past Zach Parker in a controversial verdict many observers scored the other way.

Hutchinson has a clear path to victory. He must keep the pressure on. He must stay active every minute of every round. He must stay off the floor.

Buatsi can defend his business decisions. Inside the ring this weekend, he needs a dominant display if he expects fans to take his championship status seriously.

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia Owes Bektemir Melikuziev His Title Shot
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguia owes Bektemir Melikuziev his next title defense, and his narrow escape against Nikita Zon gives the mandatory challenger plenty of confidence. Munguia already received permission to delay that obligation once. Looking elsewhere simply because the required fight feels risky should not be on the table.

Munguia retained his WBA super middleweight belt by unanimous decision against Zon in Riyadh, but a routine showcase quickly turned into survival mode. An uppercut staggered him in the sixth round, leaving an unheralded opponent inches away from wrecking the champion’s plans on the Canelo Alvarez card.

The Ring reports that a deal is set for Munguia to face Melikuziev in early 2027. That ought to settle any debate over what comes next. The WBA granted Munguia an exemption to squeeze in Zon; the man waiting patiently in line deserves his shot.

Diego Pacheco and Jermall Charlo have surfaced as potential backup plans if that agreement hits a snag. Both carry name recognition, but floating them ignores the central issue: the champion already used his free pass.

If talks collapse, context is important. A legitimate injury or an insurmountable contract dispute would need a close look. Sidestepping Melikuziev because the stylistic matchup feels uncomfortable, on the other hand, would look terrible. Sanctioning another detour would demand some serious answers from the sanctioning body.

Zon revealed exactly why the champion’s team might hesitate. Munguia landed heavy blows throughout the night, yet he left wide defensive lanes that nearly cost him everything. His appetite for firefights always delivers excitement, but it invites danger that a veteran titlist should know how to avoid.

Melikuziev brings an even trickier puzzle as a southpaw with serious power in his left hand. Munguia cannot afford to linger in the pocket after unloading combinations, where incoming fire arrives from sharper, unfamiliar angles. Getting caught in the transitions could easily recreate the sixth-round crisis he just barely survived.

A dedicated body attack could prove decisive for the challenger. If Munguia relies on movement to limit the exchanges, steady work to the ribs can take the air out of his legs. If he sits down on his punches, he enters a shootout with a heavy hitter built to exploit porous defense.

Munguia earned respect for weathering that sixth round storm and pulling away once Zon ran out of steam. That resilience won the night, but surviving a scare does not guarantee another puncher will run dry before closing the show.

Melikuziev has every reason to believe he walks away with the title. Munguia brings volume and championship seasoning, but his latest outing makes backing the underdog a very reasonable call. The champion got his delay; the next ring walk must fulfill the order.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley Says Mbilli Blew Golden Chance Against Canelo
Sports.content:
Tim Bradley believes Christian Mbilli let the threat of Canelo Alvarez’s counters strip away his aggression Saturday night. His harshest criticism was that the pressure fighter stopped fighting like himself once he got in front of the Mexican star.

Rather than setting a grueling pace, Mbilli grew tentative. Bradley noticed a fighter second-guessing his offense out of dread for the incoming counters.

“He was scared to get countered. They came in with an entirely different game plan. He lost his identity last night,” Bradley said on his channel about Mbilli. “He lost his identity last night because Nelo was on a whole another level.”

Bradley praised Canelo’s defense for creating that doubt. He highlighted subtle head movement and shoulder rolls that defused punches, robbing Mbilli of the momentum he needed to let his hands go.

“That slowed down the pace. That discouraged that man even more,” Bradley said. “Mbilli didn’t look ferocious like he usually looks ferocious.”

Bradley even noticed shades of Terence Crawford in Canelo’s tactics. He pointed out the snappy combinations and strategic clinches, suggesting Canelo learned a few practical tricks from their meeting.

“You take something from each fight,” Bradley said. “Crawford tied his ass up when he had to, and Nelo finally tied somebody up. I could not believe it. Turned that pitbull into a poodle,” Bradley said.

Whether Mbilli chose to box off the back foot as a deliberate tactic remains an open question. Nothing from his corner confirmed it after the final bell, but the approach looked calculated rather than fearful.

Mbilli did not look terrified of getting hit. Instead, he looked like a fighter saddled with a flawed strategy, trying to outthink a master counterpuncher at his own game. The decision to abandon his trademark swarm left him stranded in no man’s land.

By the time Mbilli finally realized the mistake and started pressing inside, the fight had already slipped away. Giving up the early and middle rounds in a passive posture dug a hole far too deep to climb out of against someone of Canelo’s caliber.

Mbilli left his mark, connecting with shots whenever he actually let his hands go. The official scorecards did not reflect how competitive those exchanges really were.

More importantly, Mbilli exposed Canelo’s current physical limitations. The Mexican star simply cannot fire sustained combinations or maintain an intense pace anymore. Canelo was fighting in brief spurts, resting frequently, and relying on single power shots.

The real tragedy of the night was Mbilli’s failure to exploit those vulnerabilities. With Canelo showing his age and accumulated ring wear, the blueprint was right there: step on the gas, make him work every second of every round, and drown him in volume. Instead, Mbilli gave an aging veteran the exact thing he needed to survive, which was time to breathe.

Sports.title: Chris Billam-Smith Risks World Title Ambitions On Pointless Clarke Revenge Tour
Sports.content:
Even with a world title on his resume, Chris Billam-Smith cannot completely shake his two amateur losses to Cheavon Clarke. On Saturday, November 7, he gets his shot at redemption, though he risks far more than the man who twice got the better of him in the unpaid ranks.

Their 10-round cruiserweight clash tops Zuffa Boxing 12 at London’s Copper Box Arena, broadcast live on Sky Sports and Paramount+. This marks their first meeting as pros, and Billam-Smith admits those past defeats fuel his fire.

“I’ve got a lot of bitterness inside me which I need to unleash on November 7!” Billam-Smith told Sky Sports in October. Clarke’s wins include the 2016 national amateur championship final, which crushed Billam-Smith’s long-standing tournament dream.

That backstory brings real heat to this matchup, but Billam-Smith must keep his emotions in check. A victory maintains his momentum toward another major title run. Chasing payback for a decade-old loss could easily backfire against a dangerous puncher.

Clarke showcased his resilience along with his defensive flaws against Jack Massey in June. He hit the canvas twice before rallying to halt Massey. Billam-Smith competed on that same Bournemouth card, dispatching Ryan Rozicki in seven rounds. Both enter the ring coming off stoppage wins, yet Clarke’s grit under fire stands out as a crucial factor.

Those knockdowns offer Billam-Smith an incentive to test Clarke’s chin early. Still, they serve as a clear warning to remain composed if Clarke gets hurt. Clarke proved that dropping him does not guarantee the win. Rushing in recklessly could leave Billam-Smith wide open to counterpunches.

As a former WBO champion, Billam-Smith owns the far more accomplished professional resume. That pedigree ought to carry more weight than short-format amateur bouts from years ago. Billam-Smith excels in grueling pro championship rounds where physical strength, inside fighting, and pace control reign supreme.

Clarke is 35, entered the pro ranks late, and his absolute ceiling so far has been British and European contention. If Billam-Smith goes out and dominates him over ten rounds, the immediate reaction will simply be that an experienced former world champion beat a novice pro who started his career late. Nobody is awarding Billam-Smith points in the world cruiserweight rankings for beating a domestic contender.

If things go wrong, the fallout is devastating. Clarke can crack, as Jack Massey found out, and Billam-Smith gets hit cleanly in almost every fight he enters. Getting clipped or outpointed by someone who has not even fought for a world title instantly kills Billam-Smith’s chances of getting back in line for the division leaders or securing another massive payday.

Letting amateur grudges dictate matchmaking at this stage of a pro career is purely emotional thinking. It satisfies a personal itch, but in business terms, it is a massive detour that risks throwing away years of hard-earned status over a couple of short-format bouts from 2016.

Ghana News.title: Health expert proposes a One Health approach, towards resolving global health ecosystem challenges
Ghana News.content:
The Head of the Global Health Department of the School of Public Health at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Prof John Humphrey Amuasi, has suggested the One Health approach, for resolving challenges in the rapidly changing global health ecosystem.

According to him, this would ensure a rebuilding approach that would move beyond the formative intentions of the global health ecosystem which is protecting trade and economic interests to protect humans, animals and the environment.

He was addressing the 2026 University of Health and Allied Sciences 2026 Reserch Conference.

“We need to be resilient and yet also be flexible because the ecosystem is changing rapidly. The global health ecosystem was born to protect trade and economic interests.”

“We need to find a way of rebuilding it with the emphasis on protecting people, animals and the environment that we share. This is why I recommend a One Health approach to addressing the challenges that we face in our global health ecosystem”, he said.

He also among other things, advised health practitioners not to rely solely on artificial intelligence (AI) but instead use their acquired knowledge in every situation at hand before seeking an AI intervention

Prof John Humphrey Amuasi also advocated for the inclusion of mental health in primary healthcare ensuring that practitioners are available at the basic level of healthcare delivery.

The Vice Chancellor of the University of Health and Allied Sciences, Prof Lydia Aziato, opined that formulating innovative measures in enhancing healthcare should also focus on emergency and disaster management readiness.

“I think that innovation should not only be technology-driven, should not only be related to advanced equipment or digital AI-driven systems but these should be responsive to emergencies and disaster readiness”

"COVID-19 taught us a lot. If there is COVID-26, are we ready? If COVID-26 is not viral, is not something that we have to protect ourselves from by wearing masks, but it is something different, are we ready?”, she quizzed.

The 2026 edition of the University of Health and Allied Sciences Research Conference had academia, students, and researchers among others, converge at the main campus in Sokode Lokoe.

Themed, Innovating for Resilient Healthcare Delivery in a Changing Global Health Ecosystem, the conference provided a platform to discuss and adopt measures to improve quality healthcare delivery.

Discussions were tailored around universal health coverage, climate change, the increasing threat of communicable diseases, and antimicrobial resistance.

The conference would also serve the purpose of networking and ensure a collective approach towards improving global health.

Ghana News.title: NACOC defends Lebanon cocaine arrest, rejects claims of failed controlled delivery
Ghana News.content:
Drugs seized by the Customs in Beirut's International Airport on Oct. 30, 2026. (Credit: Lebanese Customs)

The Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) has rejected suggestions that its controlled delivery operation involving a 40-kilogramme cocaine shipment from Ghana to Lebanon was unsuccessful.

The Commission's Deputy Director-General in charge of Enforcement, Control and Elimination insists that the arrest of the suspect at Beirut International Airport was consistent with established procedures.

Alexander Twum-Barima explained that the operation was not expected to allow the suspect to leave the airport before being apprehended.

Speaking on JoyFM’s Top Story on Monday, November 2, he explained that the immediate arrest of a courier could help investigators trace other individuals connected to a drug consignment.

He was responding to concerns that Lebanese authorities arrested the Syrian national immediately after he arrived at the Rafic Hariri International Airport, rather than allowing him to proceed to a location where other alleged accomplices could be identified and arrested.

Mr Twum-Barima dismissed that approach, explaining that investigators did not need to allow couriers to leave an airport before acting on intelligence gathered during an operation.

“We never allowed them to go out of the airport and go and chase them outside. It's not done. You put them there, and right from there, his links and information will lead you to the people,” he said.

He added that information obtained from the arrested suspect, together with intelligence shared by other security agencies, could help investigators establish links to other people involved in the operation.

“Most of these couriers that you see, they don't even know the actual owner of the goods. I'm telling you on authority,” he said.

Mr Twum-Barima cited a case involving a British national who is currently in remand custody in Ghana after allegedly arriving from Thailand with drugs.

He said Thai authorities had intelligence that the suspect was travelling with narcotics but did not arrest him before his arrival in Ghana.

According to him, intelligence shared with NACOC enabled the Commission to arrest the suspect and identify two other accomplices.

Mr Twum-Barima also addressed discrepancies in the quantity of suspected cocaine seized in the Lebanon operation.

While NACOC reported approximately 40 kilogrammes, Lebanese security agencies put the quantity at 46.7 kilogrammes.

“If I'm telling you something is about 40, and someone is saying 47, are we not around the same thing? What's the difference? The difference is saying 47, and I'm saying around 40,” he said.

He further highlighted efforts to strengthen cooperation between Ghana and Lebanon in tackling international drug trafficking.

He disclosed that Lebanese authorities visited Ghana in February 2026 to engage NACOC and discuss the signing of a memorandum of understanding to improve cooperation and intelligence-sharing.

He noted that the engagement followed previous cocaine seizures linked to Ghana in Lebanon in July 2024, February 2024 and 2021, when 8.9 kilogrammes were seized.

Mr Twum-Barima said the Lebanese authorities had sought stronger collaboration with Ghana following concerns about the level of cooperation in previous cases.

"They wanted to come and have this MoU sign with us and build some understanding and cooperation so that in the future, after that February, we can be working together well on subsequent cases where we need to share intelligence, we share intelligence.

"And I can tell you that from the night or the dawn of early Saturday night until Sunday, till this evening as I'm talking to you, the Lebanese authorities have been in touch with us too much. They have been in touch with us, sharing information upon information,” he said.

The Syrian national was arrested at Beirut's Rafic Hariri International Airport after allegedly attempting to transport the suspected cocaine shipment from Ghana.

Ghana News.title: VALCO expansion must be backed by Ghana-specific sustainability evidence – Researcher
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian finance professional and researcher, John Akwetey Boafo, has urged the government to back its ambition to increase production at the Volta Aluminium Company Limited (VALCO) to at least 200,000 tonnes annually by the end of 2028 with credible, locally grounded sustainability evidence.

He says Ghana must demonstrate the commercial and environmental advantages of the smelter through verifiable data on its electricity sources, carbon emissions, production efficiency and community impact to strengthen its investment case.

Mr Boafo argues that relying solely on international sustainability benchmarks could overlook Ghana's specific economic, institutional and environmental circumstances, potentially limiting investors' understanding of the project's actual value.

His comments come as the government pursues a strategic partnership to modernise and expand VALCO, with plans to increase annual production from about 40,000 tonnes to at least 200,000 tonnes by the end of 2028.

In January 2026, the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, urged the selected investor to commence modernisation work immediately, while emphasising the importance of securing the investment needed to revive the smelter. The government subsequently inaugurated a negotiating team on August 21 to agree on the definitive terms of the proposed partnership. Republic of Ghana+1

Finance professional and researcher, John Akwetey Boafo

Mr Boafo's concerns are informed by a systematic review of sustainable banking and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) integration research, which he co-authored and published in July 2025 in the Interdisciplinary Journal of Management Sciences.

The study analysed 1,104 Scopus-indexed publications spanning 1933 to 2025 and identified significant gaps in research output from Africa and Latin America.

The review found that Nigeria accounted for 12 publications and South Africa 19, compared with 141 for China and 129 for India within the dataset.

It also identified limitations in the application of sustainability models developed in other markets, particularly where informal economies and state-owned institutions have different operating conditions.

Mr Boafo says these gaps should prompt Ghana to develop its own evidence base as it negotiates the future of one of its strategic industrial assets.

“The counts do not prove a financing penalty by themselves, and they are not a substitute for a Ghana-specific study. They establish something more fundamental: African conditions occupy a small share of the evidence used to refine sustainable-finance practice.

“For a project as distinctive as VALCO, locally grounded evidence is therefore not an academic luxury. It is part of the investment case,” he said.

Electricity and carbon emissions

Mr Boafo identified electricity consumption as one of the critical areas where sustainability evidence could influence the assessment of VALCO's competitiveness and investment potential.

He noted that GIADEC's original vision for VALCO was linked to the use of electricity from the Akosombo Dam to support an integrated aluminium industry.

While hydroelectric power could give the smelter a lower electricity-related carbon footprint compared with facilities relying on coal-generated electricity, he said Ghana would need to establish the actual sources of power supplied to the plant.

According to him, the historical association with hydropower should not be treated as sufficient evidence of the facility's current environmental performance.

He also drew attention to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which entered its definitive phase on January 1, 2026, and covers aluminium imports.

Under the current CBAM methodology, the calculation for aluminium includes direct emissions but excludes indirect emissions from electricity consumption, although such emissions are covered in the methodology for certain other sectors, including cement and fertilisers.

Mr Boafo said the distinction was important because a lower electricity-related carbon footprint did not automatically translate into a lower carbon cost under every international regulatory framework.

“Electricity is commonly the largest component of an aluminium producer’s carbon footprint, yet the current CBAM treatment of aluminium does not differentiate imports on the basis of electricity-related indirect emissions.

“That does not erase the commercial value of hydropower. It means Ghana must demonstrate that value through verified carbon data, reliable power economics, buyer commitments and financing terms rather than assume that the border mechanism will recognise it automatically,” he said.

He added that the government should ensure that environmental and sustainability claims made about VALCO are supported by measurable information that investors, lenders and prospective buyers can independently assess.

ESG reporting and investment decisions

Mr Boafo also highlighted inconsistencies in Environmental, Social and Governance ratings, noting that different rating agencies may arrive at varying assessments because of differences in their methodologies and the weighting assigned to specific indicators.

He cited research examined in his review which found a highest correlation of 0.61 among the ESG rating agencies assessed, suggesting that their assessments were positively related but not entirely consistent.

He said the differences reinforced the need for project-specific sustainability reporting that provides investors with access to underlying performance data rather than relying exclusively on composite ESG scores.

His review also identified greenwashing as a continuing concern in sustainable finance, emphasising the importance of reliable disclosure and verifiable environmental claims.

Evidence needed for VALCO's expansion

For Ghana's aluminium ambitions, Mr Boafo believes the immediate priority should be to assemble a comprehensive evidence base that connects sustainability performance to the smelter's commercial prospects.

He proposed that this should cover traceable electricity sources, verified carbon emissions, production efficiency, environmental performance, workforce outcomes and the impact of operations on surrounding communities.

“For VALCO, the immediate implication is practical. Ghana should build an investable evidence pack around the variables that make the project distinctive: traceable power sources, verified electricity-related emissions, production efficiency, environmental performance, workforce effects and community outcomes.

“That evidence will not replace an investor’s analysis. It will ensure the analysis is built on Ghana’s actual conditions rather than on regional assumptions,” he said.

He further argued that sustainability information should be connected to operating costs, production reliability, buyer requirements and financing assumptions to help investors assess the commercial value of the smelter's potential advantages.

Mr Boafo's recommendations draw on his more than a decade of experience in corporate finance, including mergers and acquisitions advisory and business valuation, with experience supporting transactions across West Africa and the United States.

While his research does not specifically assess VALCO or its proposed investment arrangements, he believes its findings provide a basis for examining the evidence required to finance sustainable industrial development in Ghana.

He said the country's ambition should be to ensure that the modernisation of VALCO is supported not only by the necessary capital and technology but also by independently verifiable evidence of its long-term economic, environmental and social value.

Sources

1. Boafo, J. A., Maclean, E. O., Danzerl, N. O. P., & Amoafo-Danquah, K. P. (2025). Sustainable banking and ESG integration: A systematic review of green finance practices in global banking systems. Interdisciplinary Journal of Management Sciences, 2(1), a07. Published 28 July 2025. Table 1 and sections 3.2 and 3.3 report the dataset metrics and country distribution. The discussion sets out the methodological limitations and research recommendations. Full research article (PDF) | DOI: 10.38140/ijms-2025.vol2.1.07

2. Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation. GIADEC secures strategic investors for the modernization of VALCO and construction of alumina refinery. January 2026. Reports investor selection, the production target of at least 200,000 tonnes a year by the end of 2028, and the five evaluation pillars. GIADEC investor-selection announcement

3. Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation. Government inaugurates negotiations team for VALCO modernisation. 21 August 2026. Describes the team’s mandate to negotiate definitive terms and the smelter’s historical connection to the Akosombo power project. GIADEC negotiations announcement

4. LME Insight. How carbon costs have evolved to reshape aluminium pricing. 22 May 2026. Reports the industry estimate of 60 to 80 percent for electricity-related indirect emissions, depending on the power source. The estimate is not specific to VALCO. LME Insight article

5. European Commission. Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Confirms that the definitive regime applies from 1 January 2026. European Commission CBAM overview

6. Regulation (EU) 2023/956, Article 7(1) and Annex II, as amended. Provides the legal basis for taking only direct emissions into account for the listed aluminium goods. Consolidated regulation, 20 October 2025

Ghana News.title: JUSAG says strike continues despite progress in talks with Judicial Service management
Ghana News.content:
The entrance to the Accra High Court was locked to prevent people from entering.

The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has maintained its strike despite what it describes as progress in discussions with the Chief Justice and management of the Judicial Service over its outstanding demands.

The association says it will only consider ending the industrial action after receiving a revised and improved approval from the government that addresses its concerns.

In a statement signed by its General Secretary, Abdulai Yakubu, JUSAG said its leadership and that of the Senior Staff Association of the Judicial Service of Ghana (SSAJUG) held a meeting with the Chief Justice and management following the declaration of the strike.

According to the association, the meeting was productive, with management expressing commitment to working with the government to address the outstanding demands.

JUSAG also disclosed that it had sighted a revised letter from the Ministry of Finance concerning the payment of allowances.

It said management had further agreed to present the outstanding issues to the Office of the President for expedited resolution.

While commending the Chief Justice and management for their interventions, the association said it would await the outcome of the discussions before its National Executive Council (NEC) takes a decision on the next steps.

However, it stressed that the latest developments had not resulted in the suspension of the strike.

“We wish to inform staff and the public that THE STRIKE IS STILL ON,” the statement emphasised.

JUSAG added that it would communicate any change in the status of the industrial action after receiving a revised and improved government approval that satisfies its demands.

Government approves arrears payment

The latest developments follow a November 2 letter from the Ministry of Finance approving payment of ten months' salary and allowance arrears for Judicial Service staff and members of the Lower Court Bench.

The approved arrears are to be paid in two instalments, with the first covering January to May 2026, scheduled for November, and the second covering June to October 2026, expected in December.

The approval was communicated in a letter signed by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, directing the Controller and Accountant-General to give effect to the payment arrangement.

Meanwhile, the strike has disrupted activities at several court premises across the country, including the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Accra Circuit Court and some District Court offices, with security personnel restricting access.

Despite the disruption, the Office of the Judicial Secretary has announced that the Supreme Court will convene for its normal court business on Tuesday, November 3, following a directive by the Chief Justice.

Ghana News.title: Welfare Hub wins MoMo fintech bootcamp and hackathon in Kumasi
Ghana News.content:
Three teachers from the Ashanti Region have emerged as zonal champions in the MoMo Fintech Lab Hackathon after developing a digital platform to automate welfare contributions and payments for workers’ associations.

The team, known as Team Kasa, comprising Mohammed Salifu, Kamila Hassan and Mukhtar Al-Farouk, secured the Middle Belt zonal title with its prototype, Welfare Hub.

The innovation aims to eliminate the challenges of manually collecting membership dues and distributing welfare funds, while promoting safer and more efficient digital financial transactions.

Organised by MoMo Fintech, the bootcamp and hackathon provided participants with an opportunity to identify challenges within the digital financial ecosystem and develop practical solutions to address them.

The initiative comes amidst the rapid growth of cybercrimes in digital financial sector, emphasizing the importance of the cyber protection for mobile money users and financial transactions.

During the programme, participating teams worked on innovative ideas aimed at addressing challenges within the mobile financial services sector, with a focus on developing solutions that promote safer, more reliable and accessible digital financial transactions.

Chief legal, regulatory affairs and reputation management officer at MobileMoney Fintech Limited, Papa Asai, stressed on the need for innovation, collaboration and technological advancement in addressing emerging threats within the digital financial space.

Papa Asai highlighted the importance of equipping young people with the technical knowledge and problem-solving skills to respond to evolving digital security challenges.

He encouraged participants to move beyond identifying problems to developing solutions capable of making a meaningful impact on society.

After rigorous stages of the competition, Welfare Hub, led by Mohammed Salifu alongside Kamilu Alhassan and Farouk Muftahu Mohammed, emerged the overall winner.

Susu Vault, represented by Jeffrey Owusu Peprah and Godfred Owusu, secured the first runner-up position, while EaziPay, developed by Fosu Boateng Klinsman, Wedam Atigidiwe Prosper and Boahen Felix, finished in the third position.

The three teams emerged from seven finalist projects selected to showcase their ideas and solutions during the competition.

The other finalist teams were Merchant ShiftBook, Athena Techne, QUEBE and FAMEK Campus.

The bootcamp and hackathon form part of efforts to encourage young innovators to apply technology and creative thinking in addressing real-world challenges.

By bringing together young talents to develop solutions to emerging digital financial threats, the programme highlighted the potential of innovation in strengthening confidence and security within Ghana's growing digital financial ecosystem.

Ghana News.title: Energy Commission Renewable Energy Challenge: Government urged to fund TVET students to develop renewable energy prototypes
Ghana News.content:
There are heightened calls for the government to prioritise funding for students in the technical and vocational education and training sector to develop more innovative prototypes and contribute to sustainable energy solutions in Ghana.

The appeal was made during the seventh edition of the Energy Commission Renewable Energy Challenge held in the Ashanti Region.

Technical students from various senior high schools in the northern and southern part of the country showcased innovative prototypes designed to address the country’s renewable energy needs.

Head of Public Affairs at the Energy Commission and coordinator of the Renewable Energy Senior High School Challenge, George Sarpong, said inadequate funding remained a major obstacle hindering the development of students’ projects.

He called on the government and other stakeholders to provide financial support for research, prototypes development and scaling up of students’ innovations.

“Usually, the challenge has to do with funding because it is a huge project and a huge competition that brings senior high schools onto one platform to develop renewable energy solutions. The students have to raise money to conduct research and build prototypes, so we need support,” he said.

Mr. Sarpong disclosed that participating schools spend approximately GH¢35,000 to develop its prototype, underscoring the financial demands of the competition and the need for sustained investment.

At the zonal level, Ahantaman Girls’ Senior High School emerged winner of the southern zone, while Dabokpa Senior High Technical School won the northern zone competition.

The students appealed to the relevant ministries and authorities to support and scale up their innovations to make them accessible to communities, particularly rural farmers.

“We are calling on the various ministries to support and scale up our projects. With adequate funding, these innovations can be extended to farmers in rural areas, especially considering that agriculture employs more people than the government sector,” they said.

Professor Francis Kermanson of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), who was a judge for the competition, commended the students for their creativity and innovation.

He noted that their works demonstrated Ghana’s potential to advance renewable energy solutions.

However, he stressed the need to address funding challenges facing technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions to enable students to develop more sophisticated prototypes.

“The challenges facing TVET schools need to be addressed to help them develop even better prototypes. I am very impressed with what I have seen so far from the technical schools,” he said.

The grand finale of the Energy Commission Renewable Energy Challenge is expected to take place in Accra, where the zonal winners will compete for the national title.

Ghana News.title: Rent Control orders UGEL, private hostel operators to refund excess rent by November 17
Ghana News.content:
The Rent Control Department (RCD) has directed the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL) and all private hostel operators across the country to suspend rent increases that have not undergone the required legal assessment and refund excess rent paid by affected tenants by November 17, 2026.

The directive, issued on November 2, 2026, requires affected operators to immediately restore previous rental rates and stop collecting increased rents until the applicable assessment process has been completed and statutory requirements satisfied.

The Department said the decision followed a petition from the University of Ghana Students’ Representative Council (UGSRC), seeking a review of proposed residential fees by UGEL.

Following the petition, the Rent Control Department requested clarification from UGEL.

After considering the matter, the Department extended the directive to all private hostel owners and operators nationwide.

The RCD maintained that private hostel accommodation falling within the scope of Ghana’s rent laws is subject to its regulatory oversight, stressing that describing premises as student accommodation or a private hostel does not automatically exempt operators from complying with rent legislation.

Under the directive, operators are required to maintain previous rental rates until the necessary assessment and statutory procedures for implementing revised rents have been completed.

The Department has also ordered operators to refund the difference between the previous rental rate and the increased amount actually paid by affected tenants.

The refund exercise is expected to run from November 3 to November 17, 2026, with operators required to identify affected tenants, calculate excess payments and provide documentary evidence of refunds for verification.

However, the Department clarified that refunds will cover only the difference resulting from the increased rental rates and will not include original rent payable under previous arrangements or separate legitimate charges unrelated to the increases.

The RCD has also warned hostel operators against intimidating, threatening, harassing or victimising tenants who question rent increases, seek refunds or report suspected violations.

It further cautioned against using threats of eviction, denial of accommodation or other unlawful means to compel tenants to accept unassessed increases or abandon complaints.

The Department said it would conduct inspections, examine tenancy and payment records, verify refunds and investigate complaints as part of its monitoring and enforcement measures.

It cited provisions of the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220), including sections 25(1)(b), 25(1)(i), 26(1) and 27(1), warning that operators found to have contravened the law could face the prescribed legal consequences.

The directive applies not only to UGEL and University of Ghana-affiliated accommodation facilities but also to all private hostel owners and operators nationwide whose accommodation falls within the scope of applicable rent laws.

The Acting Rent Commissioner, Frederick Opoku, signed the directive, which was issued by Sylvia Kenou, Head of the Corporate Affairs and Communications Unit of the Rent Control Department.

The Department has urged all affected operators to comply immediately, warning that failure to suspend unassessed rent increases and refund excess payments by November 17 could attract enforcement action in accordance with the law

Ghana News.title: Art Africa Gallery spotlights women’s struggles, breast cancer awareness through ‘She Carries the Market’ exhibition
Ghana News.content:
Art Africa Gallery has held the fourth edition of its Colour Cure exhibition, using art to spotlight the responsibilities women bear in society and raise awareness about breast cancer.

The exhibition, themed She Carries the Market, features works by seven female artists – Abena Oyiwaa, Betty Acquah, Vicki Adoe, Fauziya Fliege, Serene Kalme, Nyornuwofia and Charity Derby Akeiti – as well as documentary photographer Ask Photos. The works explore the often-overlooked labour, resilience and experiences of women.

Speaking on behalf of the gallery, Partner Manager and co-curator, Henry Kwaku Duah, said the initiative was established by Ghana’s Ambassador to South Korea, Kojo Choi, to amplify women’s stories, support female artists and promote breast cancer awareness.

He said this year’s theme draws inspiration from Makola Market, where women traders and kayayei carry heavy physical loads while shouldering responsibilities that extend beyond their livelihoods.

“Sometimes, we see women only from the outside and fail to recognise what they carry within. From the market to the home and the workplace, women bear responsibilities that deserve greater appreciation,” he said.

Mr Duah said the theme was intended to resonate with all women, including those balancing formal employment with childcare and household duties.

He urged the public to visit the gallery and purchase artworks, noting that a portion of sales would support breast cancer awareness through Sonotech Medical Centre.

He said the exhibition also benefited from partnerships with Samsung, PaySwitch Company Limited, Data Bloom Africa and other organisations, which he hoped would help build a lasting community around art and breast cancer advocacy.

Co-curator Sarah Emefa King, known as Sasa, said the exhibition was personal, having witnessed breast cancer affect members of her family and participated as an artist in Colour Cure two years ago.

She praised the eight exhibitors for bringing distinct perspectives to the theme, from the raw realities documented by Ask Photos to the expressive paintings of established artists Betty Acquah and Vicki Adoe, alongside emerging voices.

“Each artist brings something different. Photography captures the realities around us, while painting allows us to imagine possibilities beyond hardship. Together, these works show that women cannot be confined to one image or expectation,” she said.

Documentary photographer Ask Photos said her participation was a way of contributing to breast cancer advocacy, stressing that the disease could affect anyone.

“I feel people sometimes believe sickness will never touch them. But cancer could absolutely affect me, too. By contributing a percentage of my art sales, I can support the work being done in breast cancer awareness,” she said.

Veteran artist Betty Acquah, exhibiting at Colour Cure for the fourth time, said her three works reflected women’s strength and determination.

Her piece Balancing Act draws on the agility and resilience of kayayei who carry heavy loads, sometimes without using their hands to steady them.

“I wish I could give more towards breast cancer awareness. For now, we are contributing a percentage of sales, and I hope we can do more in the future,” she said.

For first-time exhibitor Abena Oyiwaa, a self-taught artist who has painted for five years, the inspiration lies in the invisible labour and social pressures women endure.

Her work explores the tension between society’s expectations around education, marriage and motherhood and women’s personal aspirations.

“I want to show the beautiful chaos of being a woman, especially an African woman, and what we go through beyond our appearance and what people see,” she said.

The exhibition brought together the CEO of PaySwitch Company Limited, Mr Aaron Demenu; the Ambassador of Japan to Ghana; the spouses of the Turkish and Danish ambassadors to Ghana; and other artists.

The exhibition opened to the public on October 24 and is scheduled to run for one month, through November 23, 2026.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.
