World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Threatens to Leave Kenya for U.S. If Opposition Loses 2027 Election
World.content:
Nairobi — Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has suggested that he could move permanently to the United States with his family should the Opposition fail to unseat President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua, who leads the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), linked his possible departure to the political direction of the Mt Kenya region, warning that a divided electorate could undermine the Opposition's prospects of taking power.

Speaking during a Sunday night interview with a vernacular television station, the former Deputy President maintained that the Opposition had sufficient political support to defeat Ruto but cautioned that internal rivalries could hand the incumbent an advantage.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He expressed optimism about the Opposition's chances, arguing that victory would be achievable if its leaders resisted attempts to fragment their political support.

"I am convinced that the Opposition will win, if it does not allow itself to be divided," he said.

However, Gachagua appeared to place part of his political future in the hands of Mt Kenya voters, urging them to resist competing political interests and rally behind one presidential candidate.

He warned that he would have no reason to continue living in Kenya if the region ignored his calls for political unity and allowed its support to be split among rival camps.

"If our people allow themselves to be divided, I will just board a plane and go to the US. I have a home there," he said.

Gachagua further indicated that he could make the decision before the 2027 polls if he became convinced that political leaders from the region were misleading voters and frustrating efforts to build a united political front.

"If I see that our people have been misled and divided through their own leaders, because I will be woke, I will not be here in Kenya," he added.

The DCP leader maintained that he had done his part in attempting to bring together Mt Kenya's political leadership and would not accept blame should the region fail to heed his appeals.

He reiterated that he had the option of relocating to America alongside his family, insisting that he had already established a home there.

"I have tried to unite the region, so no one will ask me any question. No one will ask me the reason for fleeing. I will just go to America with my people because I have a home there," he said.

The remarks come weeks after Gachagua returned to Kenya from an extended visit to the United States, where he reportedly met Kenyans living abroad and spent time at his American residence.

He departed Kenya on August 26 and made a low-key return on October 20, following nearly two months away.

Close 

His latest comments also come against the backdrop of growing political manoeuvring within Mt Kenya as leaders position themselves ahead of the 2027 elections.

The region, which commands a significant share of the national electorate, is expected to play a decisive role in determining the outcome of the presidential contest.

Gachagua has been seeking to consolidate his influence in the region and secure its backing for a common Opposition candidate as political parties work towards building an alternative coalition to challenge Ruto.

World.title: Liberia: Civil Servants Rank As Liberia's Third-Biggest Taxpayer
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberia's third-biggest taxpayer this year is its own payroll office.

The Civil Service Agency is credited with US$41.1 million from January through October on the Liberia Revenue Authority's list of top revenue contributors. Only two mining companies paid more. The government's own wage bill outranks Orange Liberia, every bank, every fuel importer and every private business in the country.

The figure almost certainly reflects income tax withheld from public employees' pay and handed to the LRA. That is how a payroll office ends up on a list of taxpayers. Money the government pays its workers comes back to it as tax. The revenue is real, and it counts toward the record collections the government has celebrated this year.

A record built on a few pillars



Collections have risen fast. The LRA said it collected about US$818 million in 2025, beating its target of US$804.6 million and up from US$699 million in 2024. For 2026, it set a target of US$1.176 billion. Collections passed US$1 billion by mid-September.

The LRA's year-to-date figures through Oct. 31 show where much of that money comes from. The 10 biggest contributors paid US$570.7 million. ArcelorMittal Liberia accounted for US$276 million and Bea Mountain Mining Company for US$125 million, together 70% of the top 10.

ArcelorMittal's total is inflated by a single transaction. In March, the company paid a one-time US$200 million fee to extend its mining rights to 2050 and reserve capacity on the Tokadeh-Buchanan railway, a payment the International Monetary Fund has confirmed. Strip out that fee and ArcelorMittal's contribution this year falls to about US$76 million. The fee also explains the company's uneven monthly payments: it paid just US$2.7 million in October, a fraction of its average.

Without the one-time fee, the top 10 paid about US$370.7 million. Even on that basis, the two miners account for more than half. Bea Mountain has grown into one of the state's most important payers. Its US$125 million in 10 months is more than three times the US$37.6 million the Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative recorded from the gold miner for all of 2023, though the two sources count payments differently. In October alone, Bea Mountain paid US$16.6 million, more than any other contributor and six times ArcelorMittal's payment for the month.

The payroll, the pump and the bottle

Once the miners and the government's own payroll are set aside, much of the rest of the list is also less than it appears.

Fuel importers form the next largest block. Aminata & Sons paid US$21.8 million, Conex Petroleum Services US$16.3 million and West Oil Investment Liberia US$12.3 million, together more than US$50 million. Most of what fuel importers pay is import duty and petroleum petroleumtax, built into the price at the pump. The companies write the checks. Drivers, commercial transport operators, generator users and, through them, nearly every household bear the cost. The same is likely true of much of the US$14 million paid by Monrovia Breweries, which is largely excise on beer and drinks.

On the adjusted figures, the two miners, the government's payroll, the fuel importers and the brewery account for about US$306.5 million of the US$370.7 million paid by the top 10. That leaves about US$64 million, roughly 17%, from the remaining three:

Orange Liberia, US$35.7 million

APM Terminals Liberia, US$16.6 million

The LISCR Trust Company, which administers Liberia's shipping registry, US$12 million

What emerges is a revenue base resting on commodity exports, consumption taxes and the government's own wage bill. Comparatively little comes from profitable private Liberian businesses paying tax on what they earn.

The names that are missing

The absences are as telling as the names on the list.

Lonestar Cell MTN, Orange's main competitor in mobile telephony, does not appear among the top 10, which means it paid less than the US$12 million that marks the cutoff. No bank appears. Neither does Firestone Liberia. The rubber company paid US$11.6 million in 2023, according to the LEITI's most recent report, making it the third-largest extractive payer that year, but it does not reach the top 10 this year. Nor does any palm oil concession or other agricultural company.

The list does not say why. Lower profits, tax holidays and incentives in concession agreements, losses carried forward and arrears could each explain part of it. But the gaps show how narrow the taxpaying base remains outside two mines, and how little the sectors that employ most Liberians, agriculture and small trade, contribute directly to the treasury.

The IMF said tax revenue rose to 15.9% of gross domestic product in 2025, from 14.5% in 2024. It has pointed to a planned value-added tax in 2027 and mining tax reforms as critical to sustaining the gains. A World Bank review of Liberia's public finances put the country's tax compliance gap at about 3% of GDP, money owed under existing laws that goes uncollected.

New money, old tensions

The October figures also show where some newer money is coming from, and the questions that come with it.

APM Terminals paid US$2.6 million in October, well above its monthly average of US$1.66 million this year. That came the same month Gbarpolu County Sen. Amara M. Konneh asked the Senate to summon the port operator and others over container delays and what he called "a multiplicity of opaque transaction costs and fees" passed on to consumers.

Close 

October's top 10 also includes a new name, "LTMI Collection," with US$1.4 million. That appears to be revenue collected through Liberia Traffic Management Inc., the private operator that took over vehicle registration and driver licensing from the Ministry of Transport on March 1. That followed a February directive from Boakai activating a 25-year concession first signed in 2018. The concession has been challenged in both houses of the Legislature.

What it means

The LRA is collecting more, its systems are expanding, and some sources, Bea Mountain above all, are growing quickly. But the figures suggest the record year rests on a few pillars, and each carries a risk.

Mining revenue depends on world gold and iron ore prices and on operations at two companies. A drop in either, or a stoppage at either mine, would hit the treasury directly. ArcelorMittal's US$200 million fee was a one-time payment, and the government cannot count on it again to fund recurring spending. Revenue from fuel and drink falls hardest on ordinary households. And the tax withheld from civil servants' pay grows only as fast as the government's own wage bill, which the same revenue must pay for.

World.title: South Africa: Rigging Claims, Xenophobia Raise Fears of Polling Station Tensions
World.content:
Cape Town — Days before South Africans vote in the local government elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026, social media is carrying unverified claims of election rigging alongside posts that blame foreign nationals. This has raised concerns about the potential for online hostility to spill into real-world tensions.

The Centre for Analytics and Behavioural Change (CABC), through its High-Risk Events Monitoring programme, logged 79 potentially harmful posts between 22 and 29 October. This included allegations of electoral fraud, hate speech and calls that could incite violence.

One post urged people to gather at voting stations to stop foreign nationals from voting. Of the 79 posts, 51 were tagged as misinformation or disinformation, 33 as hate speech and 12 as incitement to violence. The categories overlap, so a single post can fall into more than one. The posts attracted approximately 546,600 views, 29,600 likes, 4,100 shares and 1,350 comments across platforms.

According to CABC, the wider conversation was much larger.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Over the eight days to 29 October, the CABC recorded more than 15,310 mentions of the elections from 6,426 unique authors, with volumes rising steadily from 25 October.

Illegal immigration was the leading topic.

The organisation found that conversations about illegal immigration were largely driven by frustration with government immigration policies and perceptions among some users that protests against immigration were being silenced. Elements of collective blame directed at foreign nationals were also identified. Users were angry about the government's immigration policy and what they saw as an attempt to silence protests on the issue.

The monitoring also reported on the mobilization of foreign nationals to campaign for political parties, with concerns that immigration related grievances could fuel tensions around the electoral process.

Most of the South African conversations were critical of the ruling political parties, with users expressing concern over the ongoing struggles facing citizens. Other posts criticised governing parties or focused on the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) and its preparations.

Election-related discussions increased steadily from 25 October, with a spike of approximately 1,000 additional mentions on 26 October.

The quietest day was 24 October, with 1,253 mentions, which the CABC said coincided with Economic Freedom Fighters ( EFF) leader Julius Malema's campaigning in Mpumalanga, where he put "unemployment and poor service delivery at the centre of his party's election campaign."

The highest volume of mentions was recorded on 27 October, reaching 2,615. According to the CABC, this increase was driven partly by debates between the African National Congress (ANC) and the Democratic Alliance (DA) over housing delivery in Cape Town.

The ANC's mayoral candidate argued that the party had a stronger housing delivery record, claiming it had "delivered more housing in that period than the DA has in 20 years".

According to CABC, the log records approximately 546,600 views, 29,600 likes, 4,100 shares and 1,350 comments across entries with available metrics.

Three narratives driving online hostility

The CABC identified three recurring narratives in the online conversation: allegations of election rigging, xenophobic claims linking foreign nationals to electoral manipulation, and calls that could translate online hostility into confrontation at polling stations.

The first centres on distrust in the IEC and the credibility of the electoral process.

Several users cast doubt on the IEC and the credibility of results before voting took place. One post claimed the ANC had already voted on behalf of citizens and offered what it presented as proof of ANC–IEC collusion. The CABC logged 95,500 views for it. Another user suggested that a delay in announcing results would allow them to be doctored. Other posts alleged the IEC was compromised or asked whether an ANC or DA victory could occur without rigging.

The CABC said these posts show how suspicion of election administration is being expressed "as specific, but unverified, allegations". It stressed that criticism or distrust alone is not necessarily misinformation.

"Distrusting an institution is not misinformation. Posting specific accusations with nothing behind them is," said CABC. "Claims that the count is rigged hand people a ready-made explanation for any result they dislike. When those claims are tied to foreign nationals, they can send people to a polling station looking for someone to blame."

CABC warned that unsubstantiated rigging allegations could undermine confidence in election results, particularly when used to explain outcomes that political supporters or voters may dislike.

The second narrative links foreign nationals to alleged electoral manipulation and political advantage.

One user claimed the ANC was replacing South Africans with foreign nationals, using a derogatory term for migrants. Another alleged that Home Affairs was issuing identity documents to foreign nationals in Cape Town, a post with 35,000 logged views. A third claimed migrants would be used to dilute South Africans' votes and rig elections.

The CABC said the common thread is "an unsubstantiated suggestion that immigration and documentation are tools for manipulating the electorate". It warned that this framing risks confusing immigration status with eligibility to vote and reinforcing hostility towards migrant communities.

Close 

The third narrative raised concerns about the possibility of online allegations translating into confrontation at voting stations.

Some posts went beyond claims of unfairness to calls for direct action. One user urged South Africans to gather at voting stations on 4 November to prevent foreign nationals from voting for the ANC and the EFF, a post with 3,366 logged views. Another warned that foreign nationals were allegedly being mobilised to campaign for a political party.

The CABC said these examples "do not establish organised intimidation or impending violence". However, they illustrate how unverified claims about migrant participation might be translated into confrontational activity near polling stations. Lawful observation and political mobilisation, it said, must be distinguished from threats, discriminatory targeting and interference with voters.

In its conclusion, the organisation warned that allegations of electoral fraud and xenophobic narratives could reinforce one another.

"The clearest risk is not proof of widespread manipulation, but the possibility that unverified claims weaken confidence in electoral processes and encourage hostility towards perceived foreign voters," reported the CABC.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 2, 2026
World.content:
Sudan's El Fasher Remains a Ghost Town One Year After RSF Takeover

One year after the capture of El Fasher, North Darfur, by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the city remains largely deserted, with survivors and aid workers reporting widespread destruction, fear, and ongoing human rights abuses. Thousands of residents are still missing, and others are believed to be detained in overcrowded prisons where torture, disease and inhumane conditions have been reported. 40,000 to 60,000 people are estimated to have returned or visited the city. Many are still reluctant to return because of the trauma, the insecurity, and the fear that new arrivals have taken their homes. International investigators have documented mass killings and sexual violence during the siege. The UN estimates that around 6,000 people were killed. However, researchers believe the actual death toll could be significantly higher.

HRW Accuses Zambian Forces of Abductions, Torture and Crackdown on Critics



Human Rights Watch has accused Zambian security forces of forcibly disappearing, arbitrarily detaining and abusing opposition members, journalists, lawyers and government critics following the August 2026 general elections. The organisation documented 14 apparent cases of enforced disappearances, 61 cases of alleged abuse in custody and 71 cases of potentially politically motivated arrests or prolonged detention without charge. Several detainees have reportedly faced beatings, torture, restricted access to lawyers and medical care, while opposition figures, including leader Brian Mundubile, have been charged with treason. Human Rights Watch has called on President Hakainde Hichilema's government to end the crackdown, release those arbitrarily detained and investigate alleged abuses, including the controversial killing of former government minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a security raid.

Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed Sends Cabinet Ministers for Military Training

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put cabinet ministers and senior government officials through military training. He said that military discipline can help strengthen leadership and advance national development. Images shared on social media show ministers, including Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba, participating in exercises at the Hurso military training centre. Abiy said that military institutions can teach discipline, patriotism, teamwork and accountability, helping create leaders capable of achieving the country's development ambitions. The unusual initiative comes as Ethiopia faces ongoing conflicts in Tigray, Amhara and Oromia, as well as heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

Gauteng Shuts 20 Liquor Outlets in GBV Crackdown

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi said that the province has shut down 20 liquor outlets following more than 7,300 inspections as part of efforts to tackle gender-based violence and protect women and children. The province plans to deploy 1,022 response teams across 122 high-risk areas and recruit an additional 56 social workers to support victims and survivors. Authorities are also strengthening specialised sexual offences courts, victim-friendly facilities, shelters and security measures, while municipalities work to address crime hotspots. However, Lesufi acknowledged that progress remains slow, with only 21 of the 67 government instructions to combat violence against women and children completed. 38 remain underway and eight have yet to begin.

DR Congo Hunger Crisis to Worsen, With 30 Million at Risk

More than 28.8 million people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are expected to face acute food insecurity through December, according to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) assessment. The crisis is being driven by ongoing conflict and displacement in the east, rising food and fuel prices, disease outbreaks, including the expanding Ebola epidemic, and climate-related shocks. North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri remain the worst-affected provinces, with more than 10 million people experiencing high levels of food insecurity. The situation is expected to worsen between January and June 2027 when the number of people facing acute hunger could reach 30.3 million, including 4.2 million in emergency conditions.

Close 

Malawi's President Says He Remained in Control During South Africa Stay

Malawi President Peter Mutharika has assured citizens that he remained in full control of government during his three-week private leave in South Africa, maintaining regular contact with ministers, government officials and his party. Mutharika dismissed concerns about his absence. He said that the country remained under control and that any challenges were largely political. His return comes as Malawi faces foreign currency shortages, a fuel crisis and frequent power cuts. His absence also sparked speculation about his health on social media, although he did not directly address the rumours. He called for national unity and urged Malawians to work together for the country's progress.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe's Connor Grist is Swimming Towards a Bigger Dream
World.content:
For Connor Grist, the idea of representing Zimbabwe at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games began with a conversation in a car with his then-coach.

Two years later, the 17-year-old is preparing to compete on one of the biggest stages of his young career, guided by a simple belief: the work you put in is what you get out.

Grist will represent Zimbabwe in the 400-metre freestyle, his main event, and the 200-metre freestyle at the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, from October 31 to November 13.

His goal took shape when he first started swimming in 2024. His coach at the time spoke about the prospect of travelling to the Youth Olympic Games, planting an idea that gradually became a personal ambition.



"When we made it, I was so happy," Grist said, recalling the moment he saw the qualifying time on the scoreboard at a competition in South Africa.

"I knew what I had to do to get the time, or to get the right amount of points to make the team. When I looked up at the board, and I saw that time, I was so happy."

For a teenager used to the competing demands of school and sport, a place on the national team is the result of setting a goal and working consistently towards it.

Grist's route to swimming was shaped partly by discovering what did not suit him. At Peterhouse, his first school, he played rugby and water polo, but found the physicality of rugby and the environment surrounding water polo less appealing.

Swimming offered something different: a sport in which his progress depended largely on his own commitment.

"I chose swimming because when I was playing other sports, I found out that I wasn't the best at those sports, but also you're relying a lot on other people," he said.

"Whatever happens in swimming, at the end of the day, whatever you put in is what you're going to get out. It's not up to anyone else but yourself."

That sense of personal responsibility has become central to his approach, particularly as he prepares for an international competition while in the middle of his International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE) exams.

Training takes up between two and four hours a day, in addition to gym sessions. Yet Grist insists that serious sport and academic work can coexist, provided he manages his time and concentrates on the areas where he needs to catch up.

Rather than treating school and swimming as competing priorities, he has learnt to work around both.

His coach, Lindsy Tudor-Cole, head coach at Spartan Swimming Club and responsible for Zimbabwe's team preparations for Dakar, describes him as an athlete who understands the demands of improvement.

"Connor is a really coachable kid. He is an extremely hard worker. He's super disciplined," she said. "Whatever he's told, he does it 100 per cent."

Tudor-Cole said preparations had been particularly demanding because the athletes were balancing two major milestones: their examinations and the biggest competition of their swimming careers so far. She praised Grist for handling the pressure, despite difficult days during the build-up.

For Grist, support has extended beyond his coach. His school has congratulated him and accommodated changes to some of his sporting commitments, while his parents have backed his ambition since he first told them he wanted to reach Dakar.

He also draws inspiration from swimmer Kyle Lee, whom he met at last year's World Aquatics Championships for open-water swimming. Lee's combination of sporting excellence and kindness towards other athletes has shaped Grist's understanding of the person he wants to become.

"He's definitely an inspiration for me to be the best I can, but also be a great person at the same time."

Dakar will bring Grist face to face with competitors from countries where swimming can take precedence over other school sporting commitments. Tudor-Cole acknowledges that Zimbabwe's athletes face stiff competition, but believes the experience will help them understand the international standards they must work towards.

Close 

Her message to young Zimbabweans watching is straightforward: believe in themselves, remain consistent and commit to the work.

Grist shares that long-term outlook. He is not travelling to Dakar with a promise of medals or a fixed expectation of where he should finish. Instead, he wants to swim his races to the best of his ability and use the experience as a foundation for what comes next.

"My goal in my life is to be the best I possibly can, regardless of what that ranks me in the world," he said.

For now, the teenager who once heard about the Youth Olympic Games on a car journey is focused on the next race. The bigger dream remains firmly in sight.

"I hope to go as far as I can in swimming," he said. "I want to be the top guy in the sport one day."

World.title: Senegal: Côte d'Ivoire's Bosson Greccy Hillary Dreams of Making Athletics History
World.content:
Bosson Greccy Hillary, Ivorian 100-metre sprinter, posing for a photo in the stands of the FÃ©lix HouphouÃ«t-Boigny (FHB) Stadium in Abidjan, on October 20, 2026.

A school physical education test set Bosson Greccy Hillary on a path to the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Now the 17-year-old Ivorian sprinter is preparing to compete in the 100 metres, with a dream of one day writing her name in the history of athletics.

Between training sessions, the demands of university and the pressure of competition, she is moving forward with determination, supported by those around her and driven by a passion she discovered almost by chance.

“I discovered athletics in ninth grade during physical education tests. My teacher told me, ‘You are, you are fast, you have an athlete’s build, so you can do it.’ That is how I got into it. And I am quite motivated. What motivates me is that, at the beginning, things were a little complicated, difficult, but I tell myself that I absolutely want to put my name in the history of athletics worldwide,” she says.

Her journey has been built step by step. After making her debut in youth championships, Hillary joined a training group before moving to the athletics training centre at the National Institute of Youth and Sports (INJS). She has also participated in the School Games in Algeria, as well as national championships and other competitions that have helped her gain experience.



For Hillary, the event carries an immense dream: winning a gold medal.

“I really want to win an Olympic medal, that is to say, the gold medal. I want Côte d’Ivoire to have its first Youth Olympic medal. And I also want to make a name for myself, as I always say, to put my name in the book of athletics.”

Her ambition is supported by a family bond that plays a central role in her journey. Before every race, her father’s encouragement reassures her, particularly when the pressure builds.

“Throughout my career, my father has always been there. He is the one who supports me the most. He tends to tell me, ‘Go ahead, you can do it. Hard work is the only thing that pays off.’ He talks to me before every race, which has helped me become who I am today.”

The young sprinter’s development does not take place solely on the track. Having earned her baccalaureate, she is now in her first year at university. Balancing classes, training and everyday life requires careful organisation.

“To balance training, my studies and my daily life, I organise myself and try to manage my time well. I give my best during training while remaining serious about my studies. It is not always easy, but sometimes sacrifices have to be made,” she explains.

For her coach, Audrey Guetty, this dual commitment is an important part of Hillary’s development. At the training centre, continuing her education is a priority, just as much as improving her athletic performance.

Close 

“This year, she is in her first year at university, to show that, despite sport, she was able to obtain her baccalaureate. So, sport and studies are possible together, and she is doing very well,” Guetty says.

On the sporting front, managing stress remains a challenge. Guetty says Hillary tends to talk a lot when she is nervous, a reaction that can be misunderstood by those who do not know her well.

“The main challenge she must overcome is her stress. If you see her with her friends, you will see her talking a lot and pacing around. Some people will say, ‘This girl doesn’t know where she is going.’ But in reality, when she is stressed, all she does is talk. Stress is important in sport, but the good kind of stress, not the bad stress.”

The coaching team is also working on her start, a technical aspect that required adjustments. According to Guetty, recent training sessions have shown clear improvement. The immediate goal is to help Hillary beat her personal record of 12.41 seconds, with guidance and exercises tailored to her needs.

For Guetty, the Youth Olympic Games should be a stepping stone. Taking part could open up opportunities for Hillary to compete at the World Championships, on the Diamond League circuit and, eventually, at the senior Olympic Games.

In Dakar, Hillary will carry her ambitions, her father’s support and the work of her coaching team. At 17, she knows that the road to the top requires patience and sacrifice. Her dream is already taking shape: to improve, break her personal record and one day write her name in the history of athletics.

World.title: Matt Rhule draws the line after fan verbally attacks his 13-year-old daughter following latest Nebraska loss
World.content:
Matt Rhule knows the coaching world will test your ability to keep moving forward during difficult times. But when someone involves your family, a line has been crossed — one that is difficult to explain to those who did not 

We see it far too often. That is no excuse for fans who target the families of college football coaches. The social media backlash, trash talk at school and verbal shots from fans who believe they are entitled to voice their opinions because they paid for a ticket — the list goes on.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

FLORIDA STATE FIRES MIKE NORVELL AFTER FAN REVOLT, CLEMSON LOSS SPARKS DECISION TO PAY MASSIVE BUYOUT

While Matt Rhule is fair game for criticism when Nebraska loses or fails to perform on the field, targeting his family is completely unacceptable. The Cornhuskers head coach has every right to call out the individuals who verbally attacked his daughter.

Speaking Monday after Nebraska suffered another fourth-quarter collapse — this time blowing a lead to Washington after the Huskies scored 14 points in just 45 seconds — Rhule said he can handle the criticism.

But targeting his family is an entirely different matter.

"A guy walked up to my 13-year-old daughter and was like, ‘F-you and F your dad.’ I’m not going to keep coaching if it means my kids grow up screwed up," Rhule told reporters "I said to my daughter, ‘If daddy’s gotta retire, if I have retire because I don’t want you guys growing up in that environment …"

CAM WARD'S SISTER SAYS HER FAMILY HAS BEEN TARGET OF 'THREATS, HARASSMENT' BY FANS ANGRY ABOUT BROTHER'S PLAY

Verbal attacks come with the job, but Matt Rhule's children didn’t 

No, Matt Rhule is not quitting or walking away from the Nebraska football program. But, you could tell by watching his news conference that the Cornhuskers head coach is also feeling the heat when it comes to where the program currently stands.

Obviously, we live in a cynical society where folks feel as though if someone makes millions of dollars to coach a game that they are subject to the criticism. Sure, I don't disagree with that, as long as that doesn’t include the threat of physical attack or someone going off the deep end.

GOOD LUCK, SEC: AUBURN AWOKE A MONSTER IN ATHENS, AND FLORIDA PAYS THE PRICE IN GEORGIA’S COCKTAIL BEATDOWN

There is a reason we are 'fans', which is short for fanatic.

On the other hand, when the verbal attacks start making their way from the head coach to a family member, that's when the plot is officially lost.

"I’m not leaving. I’m not quitting. I’m fighting for those people," Matt Rhule explained. "For the people who are listening to the game while they’re on a combine [harvester]. We are going to fight for those people. But please don’t ever question how hard these kids are working or how hard these coaches are working or how hard I’m working."

And yes, it can get a little chaotic for coaches across different sports.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Schools will provide extra security when needed

Having spoken to plenty of coaches around multiple sports over the years, you would be surprised at just how far some of this can go.

There are schools that will assign security to family members on game days, put a police officer outside a coach's home when a season goes in a negative direction or even have the need to keep family members away from attending games altogether.

While this shouldn’t be the case, unfortunately, we live in a social media society that brings out the worst in some fans who decide to take things way too far, over a game.

If you think losing doesn’t drive these coaches crazy because they are making a large amount of money in the process, you aren’t understanding the personal side to their lives.

It's not that serious folks, and a 13-year-old doesn’t deserve to catch heat for something their father decided to do for a living.

World.title: Lions say 'preliminary indications are positive' for linebacker Jack Campbell after neck injury
World.content:
There is some good news for Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell, per the team, but details of his condition and whether he has motion in his extremities remain scarce following Monday's latest update.

The Lions on Monday announced "preliminary indications are positive" for Campbell's condition.

But "out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time."

PACKERS WR CHRISTIAN WATSON GETS CHECKED AT HOSPITAL AFTER SCARY INJURY, SOMEHOW RETURNS TO LAMBEAU FIELD

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

And while this is somewhat uplifting and paints a picture that the player's medical situation is trending in a good direction, it leaves a lot unclear.

Specifically, no one has said whether Campbell has regained full or any mobility since he was removed from the Ford Field turf on Sunday on an immobility stretcher and cart.

This was the third update on Campbell's status the Lions have delivered since the end of their game against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday.

The first update said Campbell was being transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury. The second update announced he would remain hospitalized overnight for "continued evaluation and monitoring."

Neither of those updates relieved concerns about whether Campbell had movement in his extremities, either. And that is usually the first thing NFL teams want to say when violent collisions happen and players leave the field immobilized.

That message, if it is to come at all, will have to continue to wait, perhaps out of caution that what is finally reported remains true.

Uncertainty was very much a worry to anyone who saw the play that led to Campbell's problem.

Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson caught a pass in the middle of the field and was soon sandwiched by two Lions' defenders, including Campbell. The problem is Campbell arrived at the contact while falling to his knees and appeared to have his head slanted upward, so he made contact with his facemask rather than his shoulders and arms.

World.title: Pentagon's top spies tasked with 'no-fail' mission as Hegseth puts foreign midterm meddling in crosshairs
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Ever since the 2016 presidential election that first got President Donald Trump elected and the ensuing Russiagate scandal, there has been increased scrutiny on foreign meddling in U.S. elections and threats to the American voting system.

Now, 10 years later, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is directing his entire intelligence and spy forces on ensuring foreign adversaries do not interfere in Tuesday's midterms.

The Pentagon chief has ordered America's military intelligence and cyber agencies to mobilize against foreign threats to the 2026 elections by directing his department's sprawling intelligence apparatus to make election security a priority in what he calls a "no-fail mission."

The September directive reaches beyond U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency, instructing the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise — including agencies responsible for military and geospatial intelligence — to "mobilize every authorized asset, capability, and partnership" against foreign election threats.

HOW TO WATCH CRITICAL 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RACES IN TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME AND FL

The order puts some of the military's most sophisticated intelligence capabilities behind a mission that has grown considerably since Russia's interference in the 2016 presidential election. But with Americans preparing to vote, the extent to which Hegseth's directive has changed the Pentagon's existing election-security operations remains unclear.

The Department of War declined to provide Fox News Digital with additional details about how the order is being implemented. Cyber Command separately declined an interview request about its election-security efforts.

In practice, the directive can mean military intelligence agencies are tasked with identifying foreign hackers or influence operations overseas, warning civilian agencies about threats headed toward U.S. targets and, when authorized, Cyber Command taking action against the foreign actors or infrastructure behind them.

The military's role largely stops at the U.S. border: state and local officials run elections, while agencies including the FBI and Department of Homeland Security handle the domestic side.

The Pentagon's election security mission is not new. Cyber Command and NSA have spent years tracking and disrupting foreign threats around American elections, including operations targeting Russian actors during previous election cycles.

The effort began taking its current shape ahead of the 2018 midterms, when the agencies formed a "Russia Small Group" focused on foreign interference. It later evolved into a joint Election Security Group, combining NSA's intelligence-gathering capabilities with Cyber Command's ability to conduct operations against foreign cyber threats.

By 2022, then-Cyber Command and NSA chief Gen. Paul Nakasone was describing election security as an "enduring, no-fail mission" — language echoed by Hegseth four years later.

"Rest assured, we were doing operations well before the midterms began, and we were doing operations likely on the day of the midterms," Nakasone said after the 2022 election, describing the military's role as "understanding your foreign adversaries and operating outside the United States."

The agencies again established an Election Security Group for the 2024 presidential election, but whether that structure was recreated for this year's midterms has been less clear.

Gen. Joshua Rudd, the current head of Cyber Command and NSA, told lawmakers in April that foreign interference was "reasonable to expect based on what we've seen in the past" and said his command was "postured and ready to support as required or tasked." He said at the time that he was unsure whether the Election Security Group had been reconvened.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

Five months later, Hegseth issued his department-wide directive, addressed not only to Cyber Command and NSA but also to the directors of the Defense Intelligence Agency and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The order instructs military intelligence agencies to collect and analyze intelligence on foreign election threats while directing Cyber Command to use its existing authorities and capabilities to counter potential foreign cyber activity in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

It does not publicly grant new authorities or establish a new election-security organization, instead reinforcing a mission the military has increasingly treated as an enduring responsibility.

U.S. intelligence officials, meanwhile, say they have seen no evidence that a foreign adversary has attempted to interfere with voting machines, physical election infrastructure or the counting of votes ahead of Tuesday's midterms.

Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, said last week that intelligence officials continue to see nothing contradicting that assessment, but urged Americans to remain "on high alert" for foreign disinformation, particularly as artificial intelligence makes such campaigns easier to spread.

But officials continue to track foreign influence efforts from Russia, China and Iran, with Russia remaining the most active foreign influence threat, CNN reported Sunday.

U.S. elections are attractive targets for foreign adversaries because the stakes extend far beyond who wins office: influencing American voters or undermining confidence in the process can shape U.S. policy, weaken public support for policies they oppose and deepen divisions without ever touching a voting machine.

Lawmakers briefed on classified intelligence last month said Russia was using disinformation to target candidates and undermine confidence in the election, while China's influence efforts were more narrowly focused on candidates viewed as hostile to Beijing.

The Pentagon's role focuses on threats originating overseas, while state and local officials administer elections and civilian federal agencies lead domestic election-security efforts.

World.title: Poland's constitutional crisis deepens as Prime Minister Tusk faces accusations of power grab
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Friday’s late-night confrontation at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, which drew riot police and protesters and prompted President Karol Nawrocki to turn his plane around and return to Warsaw, has reignited a bitter debate over whether Prime Minister Donald Tusk is restoring the rule of law or overstepping constitutional limits.

The dispute erupted after the tribunal announced the suspension of its president, Bogdan Święczkowski, a move that supporters of Tusk’s government described as necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics denounced it as an unconstitutional power grab.

Marcin Przydacz, the head of the International Policy Bureau in Nawrocki’s office, took to European TV Monday morning denouncing Tusk’s actions, saying, "Even lawyers who are close to the Tusk government say that there's absolutely no legal basis for such behavior."

POLISH PRESIDENT TURNS PLANE AROUND AFTER 'COUP' AT NATION’S TOP COURT

The dispute is also triggering diplomatic fallout, with at least three Polish ambassadors resigning in protest. Przydacz, a former parliament member of the now-opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, says Poland’s permanent representative to the U.N. since 2021, Krzysztof Szczerski, resigned Monday, which followed the resignations over the weekend of the ambassadors to China and Romania.

"This crisis didn’t begin on Friday," said Simone Rodan‑Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "Poland has been living with a deeply compromised Constitutional Tribunal for more than a decade."

Rodan-Benzaquen said the confrontation cannot be understood in isolation. Parliament has continued appointing judges under Poland's constitution, but several of those appointments have been blocked from taking office amid a years-long standoff between the government, the presidency and the tribunal itself.

"This isn't simply a case of Tusk deciding to pack a functioning, independent court ahead of an election," Rodan-Benzaquen tells Fox News Digital. "There is a genuine institutional crisis that predates his government, and a legitimate question of how to resolve it."

That underlying conflict exploded into public view Friday after Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska suspended Święczkowski and his deputy, triggering protests outside the tribunal and prompting Nawrocki to abandon a trip to Senegal. Police detained three people after some demonstrators clashed with officers outside the court complex.

HUNGARY AND POLAND DEFEND TOUGH MIGRATION POLICIES AS FRANCE REELS FROM VIOLENT UNREST

Rodan-Benzaquen cautioned that concerns about Friday's actions are not limited to supporters of the opposition, saying they "raise serious questions about the legality and proportionality of the methods being used."

Critics of the government have described Friday's events as an unprecedented assault on Poland's constitutional order. "My former boss, Margaret Thatcher, would have been absolutely appalled by what we're witnessing in Poland," Nile Gardner, director of the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at the Heritage Foundation told Fox News Digital. "This is clearly a crisis for Poland and an attempted coup by Donald Tusk."

"This has all the hallmarks of a Soviet-style coup operation," added Gardner, who said Tusk waited until Nawrocki was traveling out of the country, accusing the prime minister of undermining the tribunal and further destabilizing Poland ahead of next year's election. "It's the sort of thing you'd expect actually from a third world dictator."

Others reject the coup characterization. Boštjan Udovič, chair of international relations at the University of Ljubljana, says the dispute centers on the government's attempt to restore judicial arrangements that critics of the previous PiS government say were inconsistent with both Poland's constitution and European legal standards.

"Tusk wants to restore the situation as required by the constitution and the international institutions," Udovič said. "I think that he hoped the transition would be easier."

Tusk defended his government's actions as part of an effort to restore the rule of law, accusing both the president and the tribunal of improperly blocking judges elected by parliament from taking office. "The solution to the conflict is simple," he said on Monday. "The president recognizes the judges legally elected by [parliament], because that is what the Constitution stipulates." He accused Nawrocki of "choosing forceful confrontation, which could cost Poland very dearly. A democratic state under the rule of law cannot yield to violence."

POLAND ARRESTS RUSSIAN ALLEGEDLY HIRED TO KILL UKRAINIAN-AMERICAN WHO WAS 'INCONVENIENT TO THE PUTIN REGIME'

"Restoring the rule of law is essential," Rodan-Benzaquen says, warning against viewing the dispute purely through a partisan lens. "But the legitimacy of that restoration depends not only on its objectives, but also on the legality of the means used to achieve it."

The divide in Poland has increasingly been reflected abroad, with European institutions and political leaders offering sharply different interpretations of the crisis.

The European Commission has largely backed the Polish parliament's authority to appoint judges. European Commissioner Michael McGrath said selecting new judges lies within the powers of Poland's parliament.

French opposition leader Marine Le Pen, meanwhile, accused Brussels of applying a double standard. "One cannot claim to defend democracy and the rule of law while remaining silent when the constitutional balance of a member state is gravely threatened," she posted on X. "The proliferation of such strong-arm tactics within the European Union itself is beginning to raise serious questions."

"America is on Poland’s side," U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose posted to X, urging restraint. "Our concern is for the stability, security, and democratic future of a country we are proud to call our friend and ally… Poland has come too far and accomplished too much to let political differences, no matter how strongly felt, put any of that at risk."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For Rodan-Benzaquen, the larger issue extends far beyond the events of Friday night. "One side claims to be defending constitutional order against the abuses of the other, while the institutions that should arbitrate the dispute have themselves become the object of the dispute," she said.

With parliamentary elections in Poland only a year away, the battle over who gets to define the rule of law may prove more consequential than the confrontation that unfolded this weekend.

Calling Tusk’s tactics "straight out of the Putin playbook," Gardner warns Poland is in "an incredibly dangerous situation right now, and the blame is squarely at the door of Donald Tusk and his government."

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

World.title: Pro wrestler Vinny Pacifico cast in ‘I Dream of Pizza,’ adding to résumé: ‘Who would say no to this?’
World.content:
Professional wrestling is a hard sport to find a decent work-life balance around, especially if you want to become a top star in the industry. Adding film and TV endeavors to the mix creates an entirely different kind of chaotic travel schedule that few people can really balance well.

For independent pro wrestler Vinny Pacifico, finding that balance in life has been paramount. The competitor from Staten Island, New York, has been able to make a name for himself in the ring while making waves on the silver screen. Directed by Matt Provenzano, "I Dream of Pizza" takes a look at a pizza-making prodigy leaving Italy for New York City to start his own pizza shop. The only issue – it’s been taken over by an Italian crime family. Antoinette Crowe-Legacy, Michael Leavy, Giorgio Cantarini and Vic Dibitetto are among those appearing in the film.

Pacifico told OutKick Dropkick the skills that have made him solid in the ring have also helped with his acting career as well. When Pacifico was presented with "I Dream of Pizza," he said there was no way he could turn it down.

"When they came to me about it, it was described as like a ‘Goodfellas’ and ‘Ratatouille,’ and I said, ‘Wait a minute. Are you kidding me? Who would say no to this?’ I love ‘Ratatouille.’ I'm a huge fan of that. … I love ‘Ratatouille,’ like that's a great freaking movie. So, once I heard that, I was all in, and that was it, you know, we kind of just made an agreement. I said let's do it. This is something that I'm really excited about. I'm Italian myself and it's finally my first ever Italian film."

"It's about a kid who wants to have an Italian restaurant, and it kind of gets taken over by mobsters. Great story. It's a positive fun story, a lot of twists and turns to it. The cast that I mentioned isn't the full cast," he added. "There's a few more surprises getting ready to be announced soon, but I think this is gonna be really, really fun. I'm really excited about this. It's filming in New York, and I believe some of it's being filmed in Italy."

Pacifico said he felt "blessed" to be able to have the opportunities to film and continue to work in pro wrestling.

He’s been back and forth between Coastal Championship Wrestling in Florida and Hollywood Wrestling for the most part. But even as his Q score in Tinseltown increases, Pacifico said he planned on continuing his work in the ring for as long as he can.

"Until I can't do it anymore," he told OutKick Dropkick when asked if he saw a finish line for his pro wrestling career given his emergence in the film industry. "I don't wanna stop. I wanna do both until … I want to do both forever. I don't want to stop either of them and I never will stop either of them. I believe that I will find a way to keep my body healthy enough to continue wrestling no matter what. Again, everyone says that, right? Everyone says, ‘Oh, I wanna wrestle ‘til I can't anymore,’ but I'm gonna, I'm going to make sure that I keep my body healthy, that I do physical therapy all the time, that I make sure my body is up to speed where it needs to be to continue wrestling well into my 60s and 70s if I can. That's what I want."

Pacifico understood what that means – keeping his body in tip-top shape no matter what he’s doing, where he’s traveling or what other obstacle is in his way.

"I wanna be able to do it. It's not, like I said, it's not likely. It’s a very hard-on-your-body industry. The flights, the bumping, the weapons, it's very hard on your body. But there is no end date in mind at all. I love doing both. I really, genuinely enjoy doing both, and it's been so much fun. But like I said though, I am going to, I have been, and I'm going to be very strict on my body and how I can keep it safe and keep it healthy.

"Everywhere, every wrestler should be doing that because this is your job. As a wrestler, your body needs to be at its best form. You gotta take care of it, massages, acupuncture, you know, whatever your body needs to continue moving in a way that keeps you in the ring safe, keeps your opponent safe, and keeps your body going. And the flights. I had a month where I flew coast to coast like eight times. Flights do damage to your body, you know, sitting crammed in a seat. It's not easy. Taking care of yourself on flights, stretching before your flight, taking vitamins. These are things that I feel for me, I've been doing, and it's been helping me out a lot."

World.title: Lindsay Clancy in court as defense seeks to block retrial in murder case
World.content:
A judge on Monday ruled that he will determine later this month whether Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three children in 2023, will face a retrial on three murder counts.

The defense and prosecution argued several proposed motions, including the defense’s motion to drop charges against Clancy, on Monday. At the end of the nearly three-hour hearing, the judge scheduled a status hearing for Nov. 16, at which he will decide on the motions.

Clancy’s defense team argued that she can’t be retried on double jeopardy grounds, meaning a defendant cannot be prosecuted twice for the same crime, in a bid to have the charges dismissed.

In court, defense attorney Martin Weinberg argued that the prosecution must prove it met the manifest necessity standard to warrant a mistrial and, in turn, a retrial.

Lindsay Clancy appears in Plymouth Superior Court on Sept. 29, 2026. Greg Derr / USA Today Network via Reuters

But Weinberg said the defense team believes there first should have been a voir dire, or questioning, of the holdout juror “which could have established further that the reasons were personal, rather than simply because of the internal chemistry of jury deliberations.”

That questioning, Weinberg argued, could have led to the juror being discharged, allowing deliberations to continue with another juror, “and that’s the viable alternative that we claim countered the manifest necessity that the rule requires for double jeopardy,” he said in court.

In response, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said the court must determine whether manifest necessity was met based on what happened in court and what the court knew at the time, not on information revealed in the media after the trial.

“Your decision to declare it in this trial should be assessed based on what happened here in this courtroom,” Sprague told the judge. “In cases where a mistrial had already been declared, it is clear from the record that this juror did not refuse to deliberate; he refused to agree.”

In a motion Thursday, the prosecution asked the judge to reject Clancy’s motion to dismiss charges against her, arguing they have a right to seek justice for her three slain children, even though the first trial ended in a mistrial in September.

A retrial date will set a retrial date for Nov. 16 if the judge does not dismiss Clancy’s charges. In court on Monday, he suggested it could start in March.

Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, indicated in the last week of the trial that he was ready to start a retrial as soon as possible. Days after the judge declared a mistrial in the state case, he also asked President Donald Trump to pardon his client. Presidents can pardon only federal offenses.

At Monday’s hearing, the defense also argued for reduced charges as an alternative to dropping charges altogether, which could pave the way for a bench trial instead of a second jury trial.

In addition to the motion to dismiss or reduce charges, the defense sought to preserve juror records and to investigate the lone holdout juror, whom other jurors have said was the sole roadblock to a unanimous decision.

Prosecutors, meanwhile, filed a motion Monday that bars lawyers and law enforcement involved in the case from speaking to the media.

Clancy is accused of strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old — with exercise bands on the evening of Jan. 24, 2023, before throwing herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed and in a wheelchair.

During her trial, Reddington argued that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis and was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations when she carried out the killings.

Prosecutors, however, have said she was aware of her actions and planned the murders ahead of time. She was not actually in psychosis when she killed the children, they said.

It remains unclear whether both sides will argue the same fact patterns if there is a retrial.

The jury deadlocked three times, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial, despite Reddington’s best efforts to attempt a last-minute emergency stay. Supreme Judicial Court Associate Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt later denied it.

The foreperson reported one holdout, who they said was not following the law of “beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Jurors have since spoken out, with several pointing to one juror they said would not uphold the reasonable-doubt standard and was the only one of 12 jurors who wanted to convict Clancy. They said he would not engage in discussions and failed to provide evidence to support his reasoning.

The lone juror, Michael P. Desronvil, has since said he has felt harassed since the end of the trial and insisted he “didn’t have any doubts.”

The trial captivated the nation as online sleuths peddled conspiracy theories that Clancy was not the one who killed the children. Rather, that her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, carried out the murders and framed her for it.

In a statement following the first trial, Patrick Clancy’s lawyers slammed true-crime creators pushing the theories and called them a “campaign of misinformation” that was “publishing what they know to be outright falsehoods that Patrick was somehow involved in the death of his young children and other vile claims.”

The lawyers added that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally” and that “law enforcement has been notified.”

Patrick Clancy testified for the prosecution in the first trial, detailing the horrors he found at his home when he returned from running errands the night of the murders. He has also filed a civil suit against Clancy’s doctors, alleging that misdiagnoses and several prescription medications worsened her condition.

Reddington told NBC News that Clancy rejects those conspiracy theories about her ex-husband.

“She knows, and it’s readily apparent that Patrick has been set upon and his life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve. Period. Full stop,” Reddington said in September.

He added that after the trial, Clancy “was not very good” and remained “suicidal.”

“She’s strong. She has incredible family support,” he said of his client. “But she is suicidal. I mean, she’s on 24/7, one-on-one suicide watch. I worry about her every day.”

World.title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
World.content:
The messages, which began around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time (3:45 p.m. ET), warned residents not to go outside because of radiation hazard, chemical threat and street fights.

Another message professed, in Russian, that all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert. “Don’t worry,” it added. “Oreshnik is in action,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable hypersonic missile.

That message referenced a Telegram channel called Hitcorecorp. Major pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash said it spoke with the group and that it took responsibility for the hack. NBC News could not verify who the group is and whether it was responsible for the alerts.

Shortly after the alerts went out late Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said the country’s “Air Alert” app had likely been “compromised by the enemy,” confirming there was no “radiation threat” and urging calm.

In separate statements, the app’s creators said “unauthorized third parties interfered with the operation of the app,” forcing them to temporarily suspend its operations. It later called the incident a “cyberattack,” saying it was gradually restoring the service. “The team is carrying out additional measures to protect the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future,” one of the statements said.

Ukrainian media reported that users across the country received the alert, and authorities in the western Lviv region reported that some of the public warning sirens and loudspeaker systems broadcast a “radiation hazard” signal.

“I was outside with my dog when the first alert came,” said Olena Yermakova, 32, a researcher in Kyiv.

She picked up her dog and ran inside, she said, before checking the news to see what was happening.

Because the message was in Russian, “I thought it was a hack by the Russians,” she said. “But the seconds before that were absolutely terrifying. I started running through a checklist in my head of what to do during a nuclear threat and whether I had all the supplies at home, and my hands started shaking.”

00:44 Russian drone strikes in Ukraine kill two teenage girls 00:00 00:00

Still, many other Ukrainians did not appear unduly alarmed or panicked by the alerts. In fact, many shared memes online, poking fun at what they saw as a blatant fake, and the fact the warning was issued in Russian. “No one was particularly surprised,” one user wrote on X. “They might as well have thrown in a dinosaur attack, too.”

The state emergency service of Ukraine said Monday the national alert system was operating normally, and an NBC News producer in Kyiv did not experience any further issues with the “Air Alert” app.

Meanwhile, Russia’s emergencies ministry also said early Monday that its mobile application has suffered a “massive cyberattack,” resulting in what it said was “dissemination of fake information to the public.” The public alert system was restored and was operating normally, it said shortly after. It emphasized that the app was only “an additional, supplementary information service.”

Screenshots shared by Russian media and some regional authorities suggested the alert, issued in Russian, warned of “nuclear warheads” launched at Russia. As with the Ukrainian alert, the wording was casual and did not appear official.

Russian authorities did not say who was to blame for the alleged cyberattack, only saying “malicious actors” were behind it.

It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.

It came just hours after a temporary ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow came to an end in the occupied southern Ukrainian region of Kherson.

The truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, held without violations from either side for six days, allowing the evacuation of hundreds of residents from the frontline town of Oleshky, which had been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe.

World.title: Supermarkets across Europe hit by new fridge cyberattacks
World.content:
The Ahold Delhaize supermarket chain in the Netherlands told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of an “IT incident” affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of its stores. “Our teams are working hard to fully assess the situation,” the company said in an email.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked. The Carrefour supermarket chain in the country said a “cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact,” affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores.

Sweden’s grocery retailer chain ICA told NBC News its systems were not affected, but that it had been informed of “an incident at a small number of stores that use an external supplier and have their connectivity outside ICA’s central network.”

The incident has affected the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems, the company said in an email. “ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the incident,” it said.

The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It said it was working to discard the affected items.

Privately held grocery retail group Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.

In Ireland, food wholesaler Musgrave said that a cyber incident had affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.

“Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue and we took immediate action,” it said in a statement. “Our investigation is ongoing.” The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News.

In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said that one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and also turned up the temperature to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, public broadcaster ERR reported.

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

Sweden’s national cybersecurity center — which said it could not speculate on who was behind the attacks — is working on several incidents affecting grocery stores across the country, the head of the center, John Billow, said on Monday.

“We have in recent weeks... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” the cybersecurity center’s Billow said.

World.title: Democrats in key battlegrounds throw Joe Biden under the bus on the border
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue.

Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country.

“I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan.

He’s not alone.

In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

“I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.”

Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired his critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year.

Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024.

Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings.

Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38%, polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term.

“The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night.

Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.”

In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.”

Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border.

In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.”

She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.”

Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement.

“I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad. “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.”

Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.”

Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz.

Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum, he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people.

“We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.”

“So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.”

World.title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
World.content:
Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange.

“It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia.

Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions.

Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade.

01:54 Indonesia wildfires spark wave of protests 00:00 00:00

The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution.

On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster.

“We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.”

The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces.

The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning.

“We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.

Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem.

In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea.
