After tomorrow's elections, Trump may choose to bomb Iran again — an option he has discussed with Israel. The U.S.' partners in the Gulf are on edge and bracing for potential conflict. Qatar has been actively leading negotiations with Iran over the past 72 hours to prevent further fighting.



🎧 Qatar has been tight-lipped about the negotiations, but Iran says there's a two-day plan to stop attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks with the U.S., depending on the U.S. response. Trump said that the U.S. has neutralized key components of Iran's military but has a couple of targets left, according to NPR's Aya Batrawy. Gulf states worry that further attacks will destabilize the region and disrupt global energy supplies.

The Supreme Court will hear arguments tomorrow in a case between the Catholic Church and Colorado's taxpayer-funded pre-K programs. The case questions whether religious schools can refuse admission to children of gay and trans parents, which would violate a state law against discrimination. For decades, the Supreme Court upheld the separation of church and state. But in the past 10 years, the court's conservative majority has increasingly shifted focus to the First Amendment's protection of religious freedom. This shift complicates Colorado's inclusive pre-K initiative aimed at ensuring that virtually all 4-year-olds in the state get a pre-K education. To meet its goal, the state included religious schools in its program, as long as they comply with state laws prohibiting discrimination on the basis of race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Sponsor Message

Your turn

toggle caption i Getty Images

"Your Turn" is a special series from NPR's Allison Aubrey, exploring how to navigate your way through midlife.

Burnout can be a challenge during midlife. As work and home obligations take up more of your focus, burnout can slowly sap your sense of joy and wonder in everyday life. Psychiatrist Judith Joseph says there's a term for this: anhedonia. It's the inability or reduced capacity to experience pleasure from things that are normally enjoyable. Joseph says it can accompany what she calls "high-functioning depression," and she describes it as depression's "silent sister." Here's what the research shows about high-functioning depression:

➡️ Research published in the journal Cureus confirmed the hypothesis that people with high-functioning depression have increased levels of anhedonia and trauma. Parents and caregivers had the highest high-functioning depression scores.

➡️ High-functioning depression is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5. People who keep functioning may not recognize their symptoms or seek treatment until they're burned out.

➡️ Joseph has developed an anhedonia quiz. While it's not a diagnostic tool, it can be helpful to take stock of the obstacles preventing you from living a more joyful life.

➡️ Joseph also developed a framework to combat anhedonia, called the Five V's: Validation, Venting, Values, Vision and Vitals.

Want to know more? Read more about the Five V's, 

Behind the story

by Tamara Keith , senior political correspondent

toggle caption i Photo by Erik S. Lesser/AFP via Getty Images

At this stage in the midterms, all that's left is the voting and the waiting. On election night, I'll be in Studio 31 at NPR headquarters with browser tabs full of spreadsheets, watching the results roll in and sharing context with NPR listeners.

One of those spreadsheets lists all the congressional districts that have been redrawn since 2024 as part of a mid-decade redistricting push by President Trump. Facing down the historical precedent that the president's party usually loses seats in the midterms, the president pressured Republican-led states to create more sure-thing GOP districts.

Sponsor Message

But headed into voting, the results in two-thirds of those districts are very much up in the air. In some cases, Democrats are favored. These are places Trump would have won by 10 points just two years ago.

Last month, I saw that the president had a campaign rally scheduled in Greenville, N.C. But national Republicans essentially stopped running ads for Michael Whatley — Trump's handpicked nominee — and diverted resources to states with more competitive races. So, why was the president holding another rally? I reached out to a few sources in the state.

What I learned is that the real reason for the president's trip was almost certainly to help the Republican candidate in eastern North Carolina's first congressional district. It is now one of the most hotly contested and expensive House races in the country, despite new district lines that should have made it an easy Republican pick-up.

Two days of driving through this very large district, one Trump rally, two bags of gummy candy and a lot of coffee later, I was back in the office digging into my spreadsheet of congressional districts. NC-01 isn't an isolated case. A majority of districts redrawn to be a firewall for a Republican majority have turned out to be far more competitive than expected.

So, Tuesday night (and beyond), I'll be filling in the wins and losses to see how this gambit turned out. In the meantime, read more from me about how Trump is spending his final days on the campaign trail. And, you can listen to everything you need to know about the midterms on Up First: The Sunday Story.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., 53, has been hospitalized after experiencing a stroke. His office reports that he is expected to make a full recovery. Hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The FBI concluded that North Korea carried out the attack. Oil companies reported huge profits in the quarter that just ended. Together, ExxonMobil, Shell and Chevron earned more than $36 billion as the war in Iran drives up gas prices.

World.title: Two economists studied California's billionaire tax. They reached wildly different conclusions
World.content:
Two economists studied California's billionaire tax. They reached wildly different conclusions

toggle caption i PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

In 1978, California voters approved Proposition 13, a historic tax revolt that became an opening salvo in the Reagan revolution and its national movement to slash taxes. Now, Californians are voting on Proposition 40, which could prove to be just as revolutionary — but in the opposite direction: it would create America's first-ever wealth tax targeted at billionaires.

As Election Day approaches, economists have been duking it out over this proposed wealth tax. It could provide a sort of nerdy preview of a coming national fight over taxing the superrich. Will this wealth tax help rein in runaway inequality and fill the state's coffers — or will it convince billionaires to fire up their private jets and set up residence in mansions outside the state? Some megabillionaires have already fled California since the tax was proposed.

Sponsor Message

On one side of this debate is economist Gabriel Zucman, a leading advocate for taxing the superrich who splits his time between UC Berkeley and the Paris School of Economics. Zucman helped design the national wealth tax proposals of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders when they were running for president (which I covered back then in the Planet Money newsletter and podcast ). He is the author of a new book with a blunt title: We Need To Tax Billionaires . Naturally, he supports California's wealth tax, and he co-authored an influential analysis estimating it could raise about $100 billion in revenue.

"If California says, 'We can tax billionaires. We can tax the wealthiest, most powerful people in the world,' it will be the beginning of not only a broader U.S.-wide movement, ultimately paving the way for a federal wealth tax — but I think it will be the beginning of an international movement," Zucman tells Planet Money.

On the other side of the debate is Stanford economist and Hoover Institution senior fellow Joshua Rauh. His analysis, co-authored with Benjamin Jaros, comes to a wildly different conclusion: the tax could lead to an exodus of billionaires out of California, damaging the state's economy and blowing a hole in the income tax revenue the state already collects from billionaires.

Sponsor Message

" It would not raise $100 billion for the state," Rauh argues. Instead, he estimates, this tax could actually end up draining California's state coffers. " We calculate that Proposition 40 would cost the state of California $39 billion."

It's a classic Berkeley-Stanford rivalry, but the stakes are much higher than a football game. California voters are deciding whether to pursue a historic wealth tax experiment, which could influence tax policy around the nation, even the world. Indeed, the superrich, fearing that this wealth tax could spark a widespread movement, have poured a staggering $333 million into a group trying to defeat this proposition, according to a recent report in The New York Times.

A golden opportunity in the Golden State?

The wealth tax Prop 40 proposes is pretty straightforward: a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, with some assets exempted. It would apply retroactively to any billionaire who was a resident of California on January 1, 2026. The money would be earmarked mostly for the health care of low-income Californians, to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.

A wealth tax is sort of like a property tax, except it extends beyond real estate and taxes a whole range of assets: stocks, superyachts, Basquiat paintings, dinosaur skeletons, Mercedes G Wagons, samurai swords, basically everything a rich person owns. Of course, figuring out what all a billionaire's stuff is worth — especially assets that rarely change hands — can get complicated. Do you value a Picasso or a yacht by the price originally paid, what it might sell for today, by how much they've insured it for? And so on. That said, most of the wealth held by California billionaires is in publicly traded stocks, whose value is easy to determine.

Zucman, together with Jasper Boll and Emmanuel Saez, released an analysis of the California billionaire class and this proposed wealth tax.

Sponsor Message

"California billionaires' wealth has reached $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, as large as all the annual income reported on income tax returns of all Californians," they wrote. They found that California billionaire wealth had exploded by 144% between 2023 and 2025, thanks largely to the AI boom. "Over the longer run, the real wealth of California's billionaire class — the top 0.001% richest households — has been multiplied by 25 from 1982 to 2026, while average real family income in California has only doubled."

Zucman says a crucial problem with the existing tax system in California, America, and beyond is that the superrich have been seeing their wealth snowball bigger and bigger while paying relatively little in income taxes. Billionaires can structure their finances to generate little or no taxable income, making the income tax rate "totally irrelevant," he argues. Zucman believes a wealth tax will help address this, thereby helping to fight rising inequality, counteract the political power of "the oligarchs," and raise much-needed funds for everyone else.

Zucman, Boll, and Saez estimated that the state wealth tax proposed by Prop 40 could raise "about $100 billion, with comparatively minor impacts on income tax revenue." They arrive at that figure by taking 5% of their $2.3 trillion estimate of billionaire wealth, then reducing the projected revenue by 10% to account for avoidance, evasion, and the possibility that some billionaires ended their California residency before January 1, 2026.

Rauh argues that this 10% reduction to account for billionaires avoiding the tax is too optimistic.

Why past wealth taxes have been "abject failures"

As we've previously reported in the Planet Money newsletter , wealth taxes have been tried before around the world and they have had a dismal track record. Even Zucman, a wealth tax champion, writes in his new book that past wealth taxes "by and large, have been abject failures."

Zucman and his coterie of other (typically French) economists have spent a lot of time studying why past wealth taxes failed and have sought to design new ones that address those failures.

Sponsor Message

One crucial problem was that wealth taxes tended to have loopholes that allowed the rich to shelter their assets, making these taxes a leaky bucket. For example, before France scrapped its wealth tax back in 2018 , it exempted qualifying business assets, including shares in companies their owners ran. That, Zucman says, was a big loophole that drastically reduced the amount of revenue it raised.

Another crucial problem — which is at the center of the debate on this California wealth tax proposal — is that some superrich people move to avoid the tax. France became a cautionary tale, with critics often pointing to estimates that tens of thousands of millionaires left while its wealth tax was in place. However, how much of that exodus was caused by the wealth tax remains disputed.

Zucman acknowledges that the flight of rich people has been an issue with past wealth taxes, but he also argues that this problem has been overblown. He, for example, pointed to a recent working paper about Norway, which has had a wealth tax since 1892 . It found that recent increases to this existing wealth tax, alongside other tax increases on the rich, drove at most 100 rich people to leave. But, it found, those departures didn't do much to dent the resulting gains in wealth-tax revenue. That said, Norway is a nation, not a state, and moving to another country is a bigger deal than, say, moving from California to Nevada.

To avoid the failures of past wealth taxes, Prop 40's designers have tried to plug potential leaks. Unlike France's old wealth tax, it would tax business holdings, including shares in companies that billionaires run. And by making it a one-time, retroactive tax tied to where billionaires lived on January 1, 2026, they hope to prevent billionaires from escaping the bill by simply moving away.

Sponsor Message

However, whether these provisions will actually work is at the heart of the debate.

Are Prop 40 supporters just California Dreamin'?

Rauh recently released a competing analysis with a provocative conclusion: instead of raising $100 billion, as Zucman and the measure's supporters claim, this wealth tax could ultimately cost the state billions.

First, Rauh argues, at least seven famous billionaires had already left California before the January 1, 2026, residency cutoff, putting their fortunes beyond the tax's reach. Those billionaires are Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, Steven Spielberg, Travis Kalanick, and David Sacks.

Those departures alone, Rauh says, reduced the potential revenue from this wealth tax by "around $30 billion."

Zucman, however, disputes that those fortunes are beyond California's reach. He says the legal experts he trusts believe it's unlikely that any of these billionaires successfully ended their California tax residency before the cutoff. Ending your residency, he argues, takes more than a last-minute move across state lines. Prop 40 was designed with this in mind. It was announced in late October 2025 , giving billionaires only about two months to establish residency elsewhere before January 1, 2026. Talk about a New Year's Day hangover.

Take Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Sure, he's moved just across the border to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe — and meanwhile spent more than a hundred million dollars trying to defeat Prop 40. But, Zucman says, he still frequently commutes to work in Silicon Valley. A quick change of address, he argues, doesn't necessarily mean you've left California behind for tax purposes. Rauh counters that Brin, backed by what we can only assume are the best accountants and lawyers, has likely succeeded in establishing Nevada residency. He stands by his assumption that Brin and the others are beyond the tax's reach.

Like much of the debate over how much this tax will ultimately raise, this dispute has as much to do with the law as it does economics.

Sponsor Message

Which leads us to the second reason Rauh believes this proposed wealth tax will raise much less money than its supporters hope: the courts. Billionaires, armed with the best lawyers money can buy, will mount a slew of constitutional challenges to this tax. And given this wealth tax's novelty — and the Supreme Court's conservative majority — there's a real risk that at least part of Prop 40 could be struck down.

For example, Prop 40's controversial retroactive provision. It would tax some billionaires based on where they used to live. Rauh argues that could violate the Constitution's due process protections, although the Supreme Court has upheld other retroactive taxes in the past. The tax also reaches beyond California's borders, targeting wealth held around the world, which could create legal issues. Rauh also raises legal concerns about how the tax would value privately held companies. He says that venture capital deals can put a price on a company that overstates what it's actually worth. Taxing an owner's share of that inflated value, he argues, could create constitutional problems.

The architects of Prop 40 designed the law with legal challenges in mind, and it has all sorts of fallback provisions meant to keep the tax working if the courts strike down any part of it. But how much revenue would survive those legal battles? This is another big disagreement between Rauh and Zucman.

Rauh and Jaros estimate a big range of possible outcomes. But their central estimate, which has generated plenty of headlines, cuts the remaining projected revenue in half to account for legal uncertainty. That is a strong assumption — not a certainty about how the courts will rule — and Zucman disputes it.

After accounting for billionaire departures and the anticipated legal challenges, Rauh and Jaros estimate the wealth tax would bring in only "around $30 billion."

Sponsor Message

But that's not the end of their gloomy estimate. Because Rauh and Jaros expect even more billionaires to flee the state if Prop 40 passes, taking their existing income tax payments with them.

Zucman questions that prediction: if moving won't necessarily get billionaires out of paying this retroactive, one-time tax, why would they leave? They're already on the hook, and this isn't an annual tax.

Rauh's answer: because they will rationally fear that this won't be the last wealth tax that California passes. The sense that California is becoming a hostile environment for the superrich could drive departures even if another wealth tax never materializes, he argues. After all, Zucman and many other supporters of Prop 40 see this one-time tax as only the beginning. Zucman advocates for an annual wealth tax in his book, and he told us, yeah, he doesn't really want this to be a one-time tax.

The way Rauh sees it, Prop 40 trades a stream of income-tax revenue in the future for a more immediate payout of wealth-tax revenue today. His calculation assumes those income tax losses continue indefinitely. All of which is how he and Jaros arrive at their shocking conclusion: "On net, the state loses $39 billion in expectation because of this tax," Rauh argues.

Zucman objects that their calculation factors in future income tax losses from billionaires fleeing feared wealth taxes — but none of the revenue those hypothetical wealth taxes would bring in.

"That's absurdly one-sided," Zucman says. "You can't just count the loss and not the gain."

Zucman also argues that the income tax losses from departing billionaires would be smaller than Rauh predicts. Using public financial disclosures, his team estimates that some of the richest billionaires — including Larry Page and Sergey Brin — pay relatively little in income taxes.

Rauh defends their calculation, arguing it follows standard procedures for scoring tax proposals. "It would be absurd to count revenue from not yet proposed taxes," he says. He also argues that the public financial disclosures Zucman and his team focus on give an incomplete picture of how much billionaires pay in income taxes.

Sponsor Message

The pull Of Silicon Valley

How much income tax revenue California could lose depends not just on what billionaires currently pay, but also on how many leave if Prop 40 passes. And the state has a powerful magnet that could keep them there: its thriving tech ecosystem.

For years, conservatives have been painting California as a progressive basket case, predicting that Democratic mismanagement would plunge its economy down the tubes and send rich people fleeing. Yet the state has become the epicenter of the AI boom. In 2025, Bay Area companies attracted three-quarters of all U.S. AI funding — and more than half the worldwide total — according to the Bay Area Council Economic Institute.

Economists refer to this industrial clustering as "agglomeration." Companies, workers, and investors in the same industry benefit from being near one another. It's like a gigantic magnet for economic activity. Zucman suggests these agglomeration effects are so strong that billionaires will still want to live and work in California even if there is a wealth tax.

Zucman points to Mark Zuckerberg as an example. Rather than simply leaving California, Zuckerberg reportedly struck a deal with Meta's board that would let him pay the tax without sacrificing control of his company. Essentially, the deal would let him sell nonvoting shares to cover his potential wealth tax bill while holding on to enough voting shares to keep control of the company. In return, he agreed to stay in California for eight years, subject to conditions, including Meta remaining headquartered there.

Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, told Bloomberg in January that he was "perfectly fine" with paying the wealth tax envisioned by Prop 40. Under it, he would be on the hook for something like $8 billion. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Huang said. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."

Sponsor Message

Rauh, however, doubts that California's tech ecosystem has enough gravity to keep billionaires there if the tax passes. "Agglomeration effects are fragile," he argues. A wealth tax could saddle startup founders with big tax bills based on their companies' valuations, even before they've cashed out. Prop 40 includes provisions that would allow qualifying taxpayers with illiquid wealth to defer payments, but Rauh argues those protections are inadequate.

" You have to understand that the entire startup ecosystem of California is threatened by taxes like this," Rauh argues. He predicts that "investors will pull out of California if the wealth tax is passed."

Zucman hears echoes of an earlier fight in all these warnings about taxing wealth: the fight over taxing income back in the early 20th century. Back then, he says, critics argued that an income tax would drive people away and hurt the economy.

He points to Wisconsin's adoption of a progressive income tax in 1911 as a crucial turning point. Two years later, America adopted the federal income tax we know today. Zucman hopes California can play a similar role for taxing wealth.

"I have little doubt that it will work very well for the state of California," he says. "And then very quickly you'll see other states doing the same."

Ultimately, Zucman hopes this movement will lead to a federal wealth tax. He acknowledges that billionaires are less likely to move to avoid a national wealth tax than a state one.

Rauh also expects less flight under a national wealth tax. But he argues that such a tax would still discourage investment and threaten the U.S. economy.

California voters are now being deluged with ads and glossy mailers in what has proven to be one of the most expensive ballot fights in the state's history. If wealth tax supporters have their way, the rest of America could face a similar choice in the near future. For now, it's up to Californians to decide whether this wealth tax is a golden opportunity or a costly mistake.

World.title: When it comes to election pressure, this year's Georgia or Michigan could be anywhere
World.content:
When it comes to election pressure, this year's Georgia or Michigan could be anywhere

toggle caption i Scott Olson/Getty Images

There's one big difference, Tina Barton says, between running an election in a battleground state and a non-battleground.

It's what happens when there are mistakes.

"If a human error happens, it's easily explained in the press and it's not a story," Barton says. "You have a human error in a battleground state and all of a sudden it can become a massive conspiracy."

Barton would know.

In 2020, she oversaw elections as city clerk of Rochester Hills, Mich. On election night, her office mistakenly sent an unofficial absentee vote file twice because the first one didn't initially appear to send.

Sponsor Message

Such mistakes happen every election cycle in a national process run by tens of thousands of human beings. A machine isn't plugged in. A poll worker sleeps through their alarm clock and doesn't open a precinct on time. Someone gets handed the wrong ballot.

In Barton's case, the issue didn't impact actual votes, and it was corrected in the tally the following day.

But it changed her life regardless.

The chairwoman of the Republican National Committee accused her office of improperly giving votes to Democrats, and Barton received a rush of death threats, including a voicemail saying she deserved a "throat to the knife" because she had "frauded out America of a real election."

More than half a decade later, for better or worse, election officials in swing states like Michigan, Georgia and Arizona are more used to that level of pressure and scrutiny.

In this year's midterms, however, because the races that will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate are spread around the country, local officials in places like Iowa, Alaska, New York and Kansas may find themselves in the national spotlight for the first time.

Chris McGinn is executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials. In an interview with NPR earlier this year, he noted that Texas has been a reliable Republican state for the better part of 50 years, which has meant fewer competitive elections and less pressure on voting officials in federal election cycles.

A huge part of McGinn's job has been preparing clerks for the possibility that could change this year, considering the U.S. Senate race there could decide the balance of power in that chamber. The Republican nominee for that seat sought to help President Trump overturn his 2020 election loss.

Sponsor Message

"We're still in a state of not thinking it can happen to us — 'That happens in other places,'" McGinn said. "One of the things that I jokingly but realistically preach to our members is we don't want to be Florida in 2000."

On a whole, the threat environment for voting officials seems calmer than it did in the period following 2020.

Wendy Link — the supervisor of elections for Palm Beach County, Fla., a county that includes part of a toss-up congressional district this year — says her office still regularly gets "love letters," as she calls them, but she's not as worried for own safety as she has been at different points in the job.

"We get emails saying, you know, 'We're going to send our army to arrest you, you'll be spending your time in Guantanamo Bay,'" Link told NPR. "So do I love reading some of the emails? No. Do I think some of them are clearly intended to intimidate me? Yes. But am I reaching out and asking for a security detail? No."

But Barton, the former Michigan clerk, worries it could all escalate again if the midterms are close. She's now vice president of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, which helps local officials game-plan and prepare for different worst case scenarios.

"It can happen whether you're a red state or a blue state. Controversy can find you," Barton said. "All it takes is some ballot equipment going down, a problem with ballots jamming, a website going down."

Researchers who study election misinformation say most false narratives usually emerge from real events like those Barton mentioned, which are then seized on by influencers or politicians to falsely imply they're happening intentionally or at a wider scale than they actually are.

This year CSSE doubled the number of trainings the organization led when compared to 2024 — a sign of new concerns around the Trump administration's actions in elections but also an expanded understanding of what it means to be in a battleground state.

Sponsor Message

When Barton talks to officials in competitive districts, her message is simple.

"I've told them all, you better be on your game," Barton said.

World.title: How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?
World.content:
How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?

toggle caption i mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images

How you brush your teeth — and what you use to do it — matters.

Recently, dentist Dr. Jin-Ho Phark says he's noticed patients asking about fluoride-free toothpaste options. Phark is an associate professor of clinical dentistry at the Herman Ostrow School of Dentistry of University of Southern California.

"There's a lot of interest from the patients," Phark says. "I hear that also regularly from students."

One product that patients are asking about in particular is a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite. Many patients, Phark says, may have seen the products on social media, "being pushed by influencers and other people quite intensively."

Sponsor Message

The traditional fluoride toothpaste became common in the late 1950s, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, when Procter & Gamble Co. released Crest nationally. Over the next few decades, oral care products with fluoride as their active ingredient became widely available around the world. These products help protect the outer layer of teeth from cavity-causing bacteria.

And dental health is important because it's related to so many systems in your body, from your heart to digestion.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

"There are these connections made between your oral health, and the bugs that you have in your mouth, and systemic health and even the composition of your gut microbiome," says Dr. Livia Tenuta, a dentist who specializes in preventing tooth decay and associate professor at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry.

The claim

The promise of hydroxyapatite? Many of the things you care about when it comes to toothpaste: cavity protection, whitening, enamel-strengthening. But without fluoride.

Health experts widely agree that fluoride — a naturally occurring mineral — is beneficial to health. But curiosity is growing about fluoride-free options.

"There is an increasing number of people who are refusing fluoride totally, or hesitant to take it, especially for their children," says Bennett Amaechi, a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio.

Sponsor Message

That hesitancy stems from a history of skepticism about fluoride. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has blamed the fluoridation of water for a number of health problems, including arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer, IQ loss, neurodevelopmental disorders and thyroid disease.

Low levels of fluoride are generally considered safe and key to preventing cavities. Amaechi says there's no concrete evidence about potential harms of fluoride when it comes to children's IQ. And research that has found associations between fluoride and IQ has looked at very high levels of fluoride — over twice what's recommended in the U.S. water supply. The CDC previously named the addition of fluoride to public drinking water one of the top 10 great public health achievements of the 20th century, alongside vaccinations and family planning. They also say fluoride in water reduces cavities by 25%.

Still, Kennedy's criticism of fluoride seems to have made its way to toothpaste — and opened up space for products that use hydroxyapatite instead.

So what is hydroxyapatite?

The hype around hydroxyapatite is, in part, due to its similarity to tooth enamel. There's also some research that suggests hydroxyapatite can help with tooth sensitivity.

Tooth enamel is mostly made of calcium and phosphate. Those minerals form the outer layer of your teeth, which protects the internal layers of tissues, nerves and blood vessels, from damage.

Your enamel is stronger than your bones, but still susceptible to damage over time from things like sugary foods and dental plaque. Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars, and produce acids that eat away at the outer layer of your teeth. Tenuta says over time, that process sets the stage for tooth decay, often referred to as caries, or eventually cavities (a hole in a tooth that comes from this decay).

She says fluoride toothpaste helps protect teeth by "remineralizing" them with calcium and phosphate.

Sponsor Message

"When [fluoride is] available in our saliva, in the dental plaque that we were not very perfect in brushing, that fluoride that is left over after brushing with the fluoride toothpaste will actually bring minerals back to the tooth," Tenuta says.

Fluoride works with those minerals to form a new compound that protects teeth. It acts like a shield for your enamel. But you need to brush with fluoride toothpaste consistently. Dentists recommend twice daily to keep those minerals around in our mouths.

Hydroxyapatite is thought to work in a slightly different way. These products seem to get into tiny crevices in the tooth enamel.

Many hydroxyapatite products use a form called nano-hydroxyapatite, which has smaller particles that, in theory, can more easily penetrate pores in enamel, though research data is limited.

The evidence

Amaechi, who studies hydroxyapatite use, says fluoride is extensively researched, especially in long-term studies. But he says early research on hydroxyapatite is positive.

"When it comes to remineralization and preventing caries manifestation, it is as effective as fluoride," Amaechi says.

Amaechi was an author on a 2021 study in the journal Scientific Reports, that followed 177 children for almost one year, and compared hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste. The researchers tracked tooth decay in each group, and found that both groups had similar outcomes. That study included funding from Dr. Wolff Group, a German company that owns two brands that make hydroxyapatite toothpastes.

That company contributed funding to another study, published two years later in the journal Frontiers in Public Health. Researchers found similar results after tracking 171 adults, comparing tooth decay in participants using a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to those using a fluoride toothpaste for 18 months. Both groups showed similar outcomes, suggesting that hydroxyapatite worked as well as fluoride in the study. However, the participants in the study were mostly healthy young adults without any severe oral health problems.

Sponsor Message

Tenuta says she'd want to see more long-term studies, especially in people with high risk of tooth decay.

"There are very few studies and they recruited participants of low caries risk," she says.

One shorter-term study in 2019, published in the Journal of Investigative and Clinical Dentistry, did compare a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste in 133 people who were at higher risk of caries. After a little over five months, the researchers found both toothpastes performed similarly.

The bottom line

Hydroxyapatite toothpastes tend to be more expensive than fluoride ones — some over a dollar more expensive per ounce.

For patients who are open to both options, "I will advise them to use fluoride because fluoride has more evidence supporting its efficacy," Amaechi says.

Tenuta agrees.

"I would recommend as a best option to stick to a fluoride toothpaste because that's what we have a lot of evidence behind," she says.

The American Dental Association, a professional group for dentists, said in an email to NPR they acknowledge more people are using products with forms of hydroxyapatite and that some evidence suggests those products can contribute to remineralization.

However, research on the ingredient is new, "and evidence regarding its clinical effectiveness remains limited and ambiguous, especially regarding clinical indications," wrote ADA Consumer Advisor spokesperson Dr. Ada Cooper.

Instead, the ADA recommends you brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste, floss daily and regularly visit a dentist.

World.title: Can the Carney government's second budget help put Canada on a path to net zero?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the spring of 2024, nine months before he formally entered politics, Mark Carney made a couple of public appearances to discuss the state of the Canadian economy and the possible paths forward.

And on at least one specific area of policy Carney suggested he would do things differently than Justin Trudeau.

"Personally, would I swap one battery plant for a million, million-five heat pumps?" Carney asked himself rhetorically during a Q&A in Toronto, referring to a series of deals the Trudeau government signed to attract battery manufacturing facilities to Canada. "Yeah, I would. Because that would deliver — let's deliver stuff for people."

The government, he said, needed to "make choices that deliver for people today as part of a larger change."

Earlier this month, Carney acted on something like that idea, announcing a $2-billion heat pump rebate program that the federal government projects could benefit approximately 820,000 households.

The Carney government hardly invented the idea of helping Canadians retrofit their homes or install heat pumps — the Trudeau government had its own initiatives, including a specific program for households that used oil to heat their homes. But the new program did add something to a Carney climate agenda that has so far been defined by the Trudeau-era policies he has subtracted.

Nonetheless, the Canadian Climate Institute greeted the announcement as a "modest" boost toward greater electrification.

"It's modest in terms of the level of ambition that this government is showing on other public policy files. It's modest in terms of the amount of money that this government is spending on other public policy files. And it's modest in terms of the time frame and the number of homes impacted," says Rick Smith, president of the climate institute.

"I hesitate to use this overused expression, but it's a good first step."

That more needs to be done is fairly indisputable.

Analysis published by the Canadian Climate Institute last month confirmed that Canada is not on track to meet its greenhouse gas emissions target for 2030. The Trudeau government set a goal of reducing emissions by 40 per cent below 2005 levels, but the institute estimates emissions might only fall by 21 per cent.

WATCH | More about Thursday's budget: Carney's second federal budget set to be revealed Thursday | Duration closed caption 2:14 A senior government source tells CBC News that Prime Minister Mark Carney's second budget is expected to include new affordability measures, business tax incentives as well as new investments in infrastructure, defence, culture and more.

That Canada would not achieve its target for 2030 was tacitly acknowledged by the prime minister in June when he said the changes made by his government would mean that "our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government's plan."

The Carney government remains committed to aiming for net-zero emissions by 2050, but the institute's projections still show what it calls a "cavernous gap" between Canada's current track and the mid-century goal.

Could this week's federal budget go some way toward filling that gap?

What will the budget mean for climate policy?

Pre-budget submissions from climate-focused groups — the Green Budget Coalition, New Economy Canada, Clean Energy Canada, Efficiency Canada and the Pembina Institute — offered a number of proposals for boosting clean electricity and supporting home and building retrofits. Such initiatives would seem to be in line with where the Carney government would like to focus.

Carney has said Canadians' affordability concerns are weighing on climate policy and he has put clean electricity at the centre of his agenda moving forward.

"The path to net-zero is electrification," the prime minister said earlier this year, announcing the government's new electricity strategy.

That strategy embraced the goal of doubling Canada's electricity grid by 2050. But getting to that goal without overly burdening ratepayers might require significant amounts of federal funding. Carney himself has spoken of "using the government balance sheet" in a way that "spreads out the cost over a long period."

WATCH | Are Canada's climate plans cooked? Are Canada’s climate plans cooked? | Duration 2:46 Parliament is back in session and there’s a lot going on: a trade war, talk of Alberta separation, and international alliances being redrawn. Prime Minister Mark Carney has been clear: he doesn’t think the old climate plan he inherited from the Trudeau government holds up to Canada’s new reality. So, where does climate fit in what Carney calls the next “world order?” For more on this topic, listen to the What on Earth? podcast: https://app.magellan.ai/listen_links/eahTaM

To that end, the climate institute has proposed a new federal fund to help provincial utilities manage the cost of expansion. Tyler Meredith, a former policy adviser in the Trudeau government, has proposed a new federal transfer of $5.4 billion per year contingent on legislated conditions (similar to the way the federal government provides provinces with funding for health care).

"First and foremost [to doubling electricity and getting Canada on track to net-zero] is helping provinces finance the electricity build out and the interconnections that are needed," says Merran Smith of New Economy Canada, a coalition of business and labour organizations.

"I'm not sure they're going to have exactly what the answer is [in the budget], but I'll be looking for progress on identifying how the federal government thinks it can work collaboratively with [provincial utilities]."

That the government chose to put a picture of electricity transmission lines on the cover of the budget might bode well for such hopes. But obviously the details within the budget will matter more than the nice photo on the front.

The future politics of climate policy

In an op-ed published earlier this fall, Rick Smith argued that Carney could now be measured against his own climate commitments, including the target of net-zero by 2050.

The prime minister has, for instance, set ambitious goals for electric-vehicle adoption. Recent changes to vehicle regulations were met with disappointment from climate groups, but the government also promised a new national charging infrastructure strategy.

The Carney government has also talked about improving industrial carbon-pricing systems and perhaps linking provincial carbon markets — a federal-provincial working group is scheduled to offer recommendations on the latter next summer.

"To the extent that the current government has a climate change plan, it is a series of specific commitments that the prime minister has made that the federal government has yet to put the legs under," Smith says.

WATCH | UBC professor says federal climate policies weakened: UBC professor says federal climate policies have been weakened significantly | Duration closed caption 1:32 Following the announced Canada-Europe LNG agreement, UBC professor and energy policy expert Kathryn Harrison spoke to BC Today host Michelle Eliot. She said the Carney government is prioritizing fossil fuel development and public views of affordability over the measures needed to achieve Canada's climate goals.

The Carney government's approach to climate policy so far is no doubt downstream from the political reality of this particular moment.

When the Environics Institute surveyed Canadians in 2019, 24 per cent said climate change was the most important issue facing the country. When Environics asked again this year , just three per cent said the same, putting climate change far behind concerns about Donald Trump and the cost of living.

The Carney government also faces only limited pressure within the House of Commons to take action to reduce emissions — the Conservatives are primarily focused on opposing existing federal climate policies.

But as Abacus Data laid out earlier this year, the fact that Canadians are prioritizing other issues right now does not mean Canadians aren't worried about climate change. As of this spring, 80 per cent of Canadians said they were at least moderately concerned about climate change.

Abacus also detected a certain amount of uncertainty about the direction and effectiveness of the Carney government's approach to climate policy. And such doubts have at least the potential to become a problem in the future.

"The Carney government's challenge … is to ensure that if climate becomes a bigger issue, Canadians believe it has a credible plan to respond," Abacus Data's researchers wrote.

This week's budget is another opportunity to fill both the political credibility and the practical emissions gaps.

World.title: 20-year-old co-pilot among 9 victims in Florida plane crash, mother says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Parts of a business jet appear to have broken off before the aircraft crashed in South Florida and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board, a federal investigator said on Monday.

Video recorded by passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Greenacres, about 11 kilometres southwest of West Palm Beach.

Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

"Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire," Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. "I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody, like how it happened today."

National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas Chapman said during a news conference Monday that the aircraft appeared to start breaking up before it made impact and that he expects parts of the plane will be found far away.

"We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact," Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."

WATCH | Officials provide timeline for fatal crash: Florida jet crash | NTSB member provides initial timeline | Duration closed caption 1:58 Thomas Chapman, a member of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, provided an initial timeline for the Bahamas-bound flight that crashed in Florida over the weekend, killing all nine onboard.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel G. Flores said at the news conference that the county "doesn't have a clue" when residents living around the crash site will be able to return home.

There were around 77 mobile homes in the area and residents of those homes have been evacuated to a shelter, Flores said.

"Our concern right now is clearing the scene so that our residents can get back to normal," Flores said. "We don't really have a timeline as to when they are going to be able to comb through all the evidence and do everything they need to do, and that leaves our community looking for answers."

The Bahamas-bound jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas. Airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office declined to discuss the death investigation, saying it is still in its early stages.

Mother identifies co-pilot

Camila Corteleti told the New York Post and New York Times on Monday that her daughter, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, was the co-pilot on the jet.

Filgueiras earned her licence in 2023 when she was a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School, according to local news reports at the time.

Her pilot's licence showed she had the rating to fly the jet, but not to be in command of the flight.

WATCH | Investigators probing cause of 'cataclysmic' plane crash: Mayday call captures final moments before Florida jet crash | Duration 1:31 All nine people on board a private Learjet 60 bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, are dead after the plane nosedived into a South Florida neighbourhood in the afternoon on Nov. 1. The jet erupted into a giant fireball when it crashed into a busy roadway in Palm Beach County, narrowly missing the entrance to a mobile home park. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration says it’s now looking to recover the jet’s black box and confirm the cause of the crash.

Her father, Allan Filgueiras, told The Associated Press he wasn't prepared to speak about the crash.

Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter asked for sympathy for the crash victims.

"Please keep them in your thoughts and prayers," she said.

Jet lost altitude at alarming rate

On Sunday, the jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, and airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on board.

The plane was heading east at about 35,000 feet when the pilot started to report problems.

The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (210 metres), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. Rain pounded the region on Sunday.

"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers.

The situation rapidly deteriorated.

First responders attend the scene of a deadly plane crash in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sunday. The crash, which killed nine people, is being investigated by federal officials. (Mark Elias/The Associated Press)

The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (610 metres), then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.

"We're descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.

"We are in an overspeed condition, descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground."

The plane banked sharply to the right before crashing and exploding.

"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."

World.title: Trump administration ramps up midterm battles, asks Supreme Court to intervene in California case
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections threatening Republican control of Capitol Hill, CBC’s Ellen Mauro breaks down how a shifting balance of power could challenge President Donald Trump’s agenda — and the key tools he can use to counter Democratic opposition.

What happens to Trump if the Democrats crush the midterms

U.S. President Donald Trump's Justice Department has shown a willingness to intervene directly in Tuesday's midterm elections before polls have closed, breaking with decades of practice meant to avoid the appearance that its law enforcement powers are being used in a partisan manner.

In California, the Justice Department seeks to set aside mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters it alleges are likely non-U.S. citizens ineligible to vote. The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from those voters.

It is one of two cases which underscore the department's willingness to intervene in election ​disputes before votes are counted. The cases have raised concerns among Democrats that, after polls close Tuesday, there will be an effort to sow doubt about the midterms, as Trump did with baseless claims of fraud following his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, culminating in the Jan. 6, 2021 riot at the Capitol.

Voters enter the C. Blythe Andrews Jr. Public Library to cast their ballots on the final day of early voting for midterm elections in Tampa, Fla., on Sunday. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)

Outside groups aligned with Trump filed more than 60 lawsuits challenging his 2020 defeat, all of which ⁠were unsuccessful.

"The right-wing fringe outside groups are not going to have to do that this year because the [Justice Department] is clearly standing ready and willing to do it," said Elisabeth Frost, a voting rights lawyer with Elias Law Group, which frequently represents Democrats in court.

The House and Senate, which Republicans currently control by slim margins, could change hands if Democrats manage to pick up a net four seats in each chamber. All 435 House seats are up for election in the midterms, while only about one-third of the Senate's 100 seats are.

California, with 52 House of Representatives seats, can take weeks to count ballots and some of Tuesday's midterm races could be subjected to recounts and court challenges.

"Those within the recount or contest margin of error — the candidates, outside groups and the administration — will fight those tooth and nail," said Victoria Bassetti, senior adviser at States United Democracy Center, a non-profit group focused on protecting free, fair and secure elections.

LISTEN | The CBC's Jonathan Montpetit on what Trump might protest: Day 6 9:26 How will Trump’s voter fraud claims affect the midterms? For months, U.S. President Donald Trump has made claims about rampant voting fraud and helped steer election deniers into positions of power over the midterm elections. Evidence suggests voter fraud is rare, but Jonathan Montpetit, a senior investigative journalist with the CBC, says there are signs Trump has been successful in sowing doubt about the vote.

Data analysts question government's list

The U.S. Constitution ​assigns the responsibility of administering elections to states, though the federal government has some oversight to protect against discriminatory and other illegal practices at the state and local level.

In the California case, U.S. District Judge David Carter slammed the administration's efforts in denying its request on Oct. 28.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," he said.

WATCH | Breaking down the possible midterm scenarios: What would a U.S. midterms win look like for Democrats and Republicans? | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 6:05 The highly anticipated U.S. midterm elections are just days away with the Democrats seeking net gains of four seats in the Senate and three in the House to flip power in Congress from U.S. President Donald Trump's Republicans. Politics professor Chris Galdieri explains what a good night would look like for both parties.

The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals also refused on Friday to block the ballots.

California has said that the state's safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust. As well, because the list originated from the Department of Homeland Security, state officials and immigrant rights groups fear it is being used as a pretext for contentious deportation efforts.

Multiple studies and state audits show that ineligible voting, including by non-citizens, is rare. When it occurs, it is disparate and not, to date, part of an organized effort that could sway a particular race.

An outside analysis of the list compiled by the Department of Justice has raised troubling questions. More than four in 10 names flagged as possible non-citizen voters in California by the Trump administration cannot be found on the state's voter rolls, said two data analysis members of UCLA's Voting Rights Project, who filed a lawsuit challenging it, along with the Los Angeles-based Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA).

The research found that 8,880 of the names, representing 42 per cent of the entire list, do not correspond to anyone in California's current voter file.

"The expert analysis further makes clear that the mandated voter list endangers a significant number of eligible California voters," said the filing, which was cosigned by Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor and an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government's list.

Alaska setback for Trump administration

The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach ​toward how states run elections. The Justice Department has told ⁠election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.

It has lost a series of lawsuits seeking to obtain voter rolls, including sensitive personal information, from dozens of states.

WATCH | Alaska Supreme Court ruled that both Dan Sullivans can be on ballot: Trump slams Democrats for Alaska's double Dan Sullivan drama | Duration closed caption 2:01 U.S. President Donald Trump is demanding an investigation after reports surfaced that Democratic staffers were told to 'find as many people named Dan Sullivan as you can" in an apparent effort to stack Alaska's midterm ballot with people sharing the name of incumbent Republican Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan.

The Trump administration has also vowed to appeal a ruling in Alaska.

Alaska has become a particularly intense legal battleground after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan to challenge Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

The Justice Department lawsuit, which Trump said he directed the department to file, asked a court to halt certification and order an investigation if the margin suggested voter confusion could have affected the outcome.

U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason, in Anchorage, dismissed the case on Sunday, finding ​Alaska could not conduct such a probe while preserving the secrecy of ballots.

The lawsuit marks a rare federal intervention in the voting process and signalled a willingness by the administration to contest the election results in court.

Separate from the election result, the Justice Department has vowed to investigate whether any laws were broken in the effort that saw the politically inexperienced Dan Sullivan qualify for the ballot.

The administration already sought to restrict voting by mail for this year's midterms — a mode of casting ​ballots used more often by Democratic-leaning voters — but the Supreme Court in September rebuffed that effort.

According to an NBC News tracker, more than 24 million mail-in ballots have been cast so far, as of Monday.

World.title: Charges laid in homicide of missing 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police say an 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy who was reported missing last year was the victim of a homicide.

Now, charges have been laid in connection to his death, B.C.'s Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT) said in a news release Monday.

Branko Bijelic, 51, of Burnaby has been charged with second-degree murder and indignity to human remains.

Sarah Bijelic, 46, of Burnaby has been charged with one count of manslaughter.

IHIT said Burnaby RCMP received a request to check Kai Pavlovic's well-being on Sept. 26, 2025. Police were unable to find him "despite significant efforts," and the case was escalated to the serious crimes unit, and then to IHIT.

The investigation ultimately led to the discovery of Pavlovic's remains, according to the release. Police did not say when or where his remains were found.

"We recognize the concern this investigation has caused within the community, and our thoughts are with Kai’s loved ones and those affected by this tragedy," Sgt. Freda Fong said in IHIT's release. "We thank the public for their assistance and for coming forward with information."

In October last year, police said they believed Pavlovic was with a "caretaker" but shared few other details. They had asked the caretaker to come forward and confirm he was safe.

Police launched a province-wide billboard campaign to find Pavlovic last year.

World.title: Ministry alleges thousands of OSAP applications came from single IP address
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At two career colleges now under the Ontario government's microscope, more than half of the thousands of student financial aid applications last year came from a single IP address, officials allege in documents filed in court.

The government has also received more than 200 tips about that network of schools, including allegations that certain recruiters were submitting students' Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) applications at those schools, which is not allowed, and completing their coursework, those same documents show.

The Academy of Learning did not provide comment on the new court filings in response to a request from The Canadian Press, but has previously denied allegations of wrongdoing. They say the schools have implemented a long list of corrective actions, including cutting ties with some recruiters and bolstering admissions practices. The ministry's allegations have not been proven in court.

The newly filed allegations against the schools come as Premier Doug Ford's government is under increasing fire for its handling of OSAP. Critics say alleged misuse of the system was allowed to fester under lax oversight, then when it was brought to light Ford left innocent students paying the price.

WATCH | Province extends OSAP freeze to 2027: Ontario extends OSAP freeze for private colleges into the new year | Duration closed caption 2:29 Ontario has announced its pause on OSAP payments to any students enrolled in private post-secondary institutions will remain in effect until at least the new year. CBC’s Lorenda Reddekopp spoke to students who are left in limbo.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn says his government acted on tips and conducted in-depth inspections that ultimately led to barring the schools from OSAP eligibility and launching a broader probe.

Quinn earlier this year drastically reduced the amount of OSAP grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of "sustainability" as the program was facing rising costs.

Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial OSAP grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year.

The Academy of Learning operates as franchises but the three schools barred from OSAP share a parent company, Opulence Education Group. Its campuses in Toronto on Bay Street and in North York, and one in Brampton East, accounted for one-fifth of that spending.

The three schools were among six that in May the province made ineligible for OSAP, citing an "inability to reliably determine bona fide studies," a decision the schools are challenging in court. As part of that case, the province issued a final decision in August and added that to the court record in October.

"The ministry is not satisfied that the institutions have adequate processes in place to ensure that its records and processes can be relied on for the proper administration and disbursement of OSAP funding to eligible students," the decision says.

Ministry officials who last year inspected the campuses at issue looked at a sampling of student accounts and found evidence of shared IP address activity across students referred by the same recruiter, the government alleges.

Shared IP addresses do not mean misconduct: school group

In completing its final decision to deny the schools OSAP eligibility this year, the ministry appears to have taken a closer look at IP address activity.

There were 6,001 OSAP applications from students at the Brampton East campus for the 2025-26 year and 3,136 of them — 52 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. There were five more IP addresses responsible for 100 or more applications, they allege.

At the North York campus, 3,460 out of 6,070 OSAP applications for that year — 57 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Two other IP addresses were responsible for another 255 applications, they allege.

The Bay campus saw 6,966 OSAP applications that year, with 1,736 — 25 per cent — coming from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Five other IP addresses submitted 100 or more applications, they allege.

The Academy of Learning argued in an earlier letter to the ministry that shared IP addresses may be due to multiple people living at the same address, but the ministry is calling that into question.

"While patterns of shared IP addresses among students attending the same physical school campus space accessing their student accounts may be expected, patterns of shared IP address activity among the institution's asynchronous learners referred to the institution by the same recruiter is significant and renders the institution's proposed explanation unlikely in this case," the ministry wrote in the court filing.

In its letter to the province to rebut any nefarious assumptions about students' logins, the Academy of Learning also wrote, "the presence of the same IP address among different users does not, by itself, establish misconduct, misrepresentation, or unauthorized activity."

Quinn has tasked KPMG with an audit of OSAP payments to career colleges and in October referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, while pausing such payments to all private post-secondary institutions. It is not known if the referral contains specific allegations relating to the Academy of Learning.

It comes after warnings from Career Colleges Ontario, the federal government, and hundreds of tips and complaints about possible misuse of the OSAP system.

Ministry received over 200 tips about school group

The new ministry court filings reveal that since Jan. 1, 2024, it has received more than 220 tips, complaints, referrals and investigations relating to the three Academy of Learning campuses, with the volume and consistency of the concerns "significant," the government alleges.

"The ministry received related third-party complaints and tips alleging that certain recruiters were acting on behalf of students, including in submitting OSAP applications, in uploading supporting documentation on students' OSAP accounts, and in completing coursework on behalf of students, and that recruiters were using OSAP funding as a recruitment or marketing tool," the ministry wrote.

The schools have since cut off ties with some recruiters, they have said.

Academy of Learning did not directly respond to a request for comment by The Canadian Press on the allegation that recruiters were completing students' coursework, but has noted in a corrective action plan last year that it added enhanced IP tracking to identify possible third-party access and added two-factor authentication "to safeguard against third-party completion of assignments."

WATCH | Ontario Liberals request audit into OSAP spending: Liberals demand audit into private college OSAP spending | Duration closed caption 2:24 The Ontario Liberals are asking the auditor general to investigate OSAP spending at private career colleges. The request comes after a sharp increase in financial aid spending at a small number of schools. CBC's Lorenda Reddekopp breaks down what we know.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said given all the information that is now public about what the government knew or should have known about the skyrocketing OSAP usage at some career colleges, it is shocking they did not act with more urgency.

"I think the more details that we learn through these court proceedings, the clearer it is that the minister was completely incompetent at doing his job," she said. "It is stunning that these five-alarm fires were being ignored by the government."

Liberal critic Tyler Watt also said the new revelations reflect poorly on Quinn.

"Minister Nolan Quinn keeps insisting he's taken this scandal seriously, but every new revelation raises more questions about what his ministry knew, when they knew it, and why they failed to act," he wrote in a statement.

Quinn's office said when serious concerns are identified, they do not hesitate to cut an institution off from OSAP entirely, as was done with the Academy of Learning locations in this court case.

"Any misuse of OSAP is unacceptable," Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement. "We have zero tolerance for bad actors who threaten the integrity of our post-secondary system."

Quinn has indicated he will introduce further legislation this fall to enhance accountability in the system.

World.title: Nathan Fielder lookalike contest coming to Toronto this month
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A roomful of Nathan Fielders will take over Toronto's Paradise Theatre this month as part of a lookalike competition for the Canadian comedian, actor and filmmaker.

The roughly hour-long contest will take place at the multi-arts venue on Tuesday, Nov. 17, beginning at 8 p.m. ET.

Organizers say competitors may be asked to deliver mock business pitches or take part in "Nathan-inspired karaoke," including tracks by Evanescence and Lana Del Rey — a fitting nod to a viral video posted to YouTube 12 years ago, in which Fielder sings Del Rey’s breakthrough hit, Born To Die.

Toronto comedians Andrew Phung, known for Kim's Convenience and Run the Burbs, and Hannah Spear, a Second City alumna and actor, are set to co-host and judge.

The poster for the Nathan Fielder lookalike competition, which will take place on Nov. 17 in Toronto. (Mubi, Bad Dog Theatre Company)

Contestants will compete for gold, silver and bronze, though the prizes have not yet been announced. The event is sponsored by streaming service Mubi, which, along with Bad Dog Theatre Company, is providing the prizes. The evening will end with a screening of the first episode of The Curse, the series Fielder co-created with Benny Safdie.

Entry is free for both contestants and spectators, but the theatre's capacity is limited. People can sign up through the QR code on event posters or the RSVP link shared by the Instagram accounts of Mubi Canada and Bad Dog Theatre Company. An RSVP does not guarantee admission; organizers say entry will be first come, first served.

Organizers reported more than 100 people signed up as of Oct. 30.

The Toronto event follows a New York City contest held Oct. 25 in Washington Square Park, where Nathan Fielder lookalikes competed alongside Elizabeth Holmes impersonators. The contest was inspired by You Can See Everything, the hit documentary about Holmes co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

Organized by comedian Maddy West and a friend, it drew dozens of people, with more than 200 responding to the event's registration form. Social media posts from the day showed contestants in Fielder-inspired outfits and Holmes's signature black turtlenecks and blonde hair. Joe Sivick won the Fielder category, and actor and comedian Nicole Travolta won the Holmes category.

The Nathan Fielder lookalike craze also crossed the Pacific, with a competition held in Sydney on Nov. 1.

A poster shared by X user Levi Fishman also advertises a Nathan Fielder lookalike contest at Lafayette Park in San Francisco on Nov. 7. The poster says: "Winner literally gets crowned the most Nathan of Fielder (crown and bragging rights)."

The format has a precedent beyond Fielder. A Timothée Chalamet lookalike contest in New York in 2024 drew a large crowd and made headlines when Chalamet himself briefly appeared.

Similar contests followed in other cities, including competitions for actors Paul Mescal in Dublin, and Jeremy Allen White in Chicago, and singer Harry Styles in London.

The gatherings often start with a simple flyer or social post and turn into a public spectacle, with contestants dressing the part and spectators sharing photos and videos on social media. The Toronto contest is taking that familiar format indoors, with a deliberately Fielder-esque twist: rather than relying on resemblance alone, contestants will have to perform.

World.title: Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' after posting homeless Halloween costume
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Martha Stewart has issued a second apology after she shared a photo of herself in a Halloween costume widely criticized as mocking people experiencing homelessness.

The multi-millionaire, known for building a massive food and lifestyle empire, posted a photo of herself on Instagram over the weekend with a dirt-streaked face and ripped clothes, holding a sign that read, "I AM HUNGRY. HELP ME!!"

The post was swiftly deleted, but not before internet users had grabbed screenshots of the costume, sharing it widely on social media, where it stirred up disbelief and fury.

"The level of out of touch is stellar," one Reddit user wrote .

"Rich people never cease to amaze me with their callousness," another chimed in .

Many called it a real-life "let them eat cake," moment, referencing the infamous myth that queen consort of France, Marie Antoinette, said this when told the peasants had no bread to eat.

The controversy comes amid a worsening cost-of-living crisis in the U.S. — a recent survey found that 47 per cent of Americans reported financial problems from rising prices, up from 30 per cent in 2025, according to PBS.

This image, shared in a carousel to Stewart's personal Instagram account, @marthastewart48, was quickly deleted after it began to spark furious backlash. (Instagram/Martha Stewart)

As the backlash grew, Stewart issued a statement Sunday on her Instagram.

"It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up," she wrote. "My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."

It was her second apology, after her first attempts at addressing the wave of anger went poorly.

Earlier on Sunday, after entertainment outlet JustJared made a post about the criticism, the 85-year-old Stewart had left a comment, claiming that she had only wanted to raise awareness about homelessness.

"My costume was designed to bring the homeless and the hungry to everyone's mind and boy it certainly did!!! But not in the correct way, because I did not explain it and I am so sorry I care and I support causes who care. Do all of you???" she wrote.

Stewart, shown here preparing a breakfast frittata in a 2020 file photo, was the first U.S. self-made female billionaire, earning that title in 2000. Her current net worth is around $400 million US. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

Her critics weren't buying it. Some replies pointed out that the costume was offensive regardless of intent, and others noted Stewart hadn't mentioned awareness at all in her original post — which had used the caption to plug candles she had for sale on home-shopping network QVC instead.

Actress Indya Moore, known for the TV series Pose, was one of those calling out Stewart's actions.

"Halloween is caricature: monsters, villains, idols. People do not dress up as groups who are in crisis," she wrote in an Instagram story. "If you were serious about poverty, you'd use your platform to back policies that tax the rich, put free food in front of people who are hungry and homeless, and provide free health care and education."

Moore shared a list of charity organizations, suggesting Stewart consider supporting them with her vast wealth of resources.

"I really feel like the culture around wealth and making money is so deeply interwoven with shaming people who are poor, who are struggling financially and economically, and it's so disturbing," she said in a followup video.

Stewart, who has an estimated net worth of $400 million US, lives primarily at her 150-acre estate in Katonah, New York, known as Cantitoe Corners or Bedford Farm. Purchased in 2000 for $15.6 million, according to People magazine , it is one of several properties Stewart owns.

Stewart arrives for the launch of 2023's Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue in New York City on May 18, 2023. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters)

There are around 145,500 people experiencing homelessness in New York state, according to the state's latest figures. More than 30 per cent of them are children, double the rate of the rest of the U.S.

In Canada, around 65,000 people experience homelessness on a given night across 75 Canadian communities, according to a 2025 report .

Stewart's second apology has left many still skeptical. Negative comments have hit her brand's official Instagram, as well.

Under one post plugging a new recipe, one user wrote, "No martha … you can't maple cake your way out of this."

World.title: N.S. minor hockey player accused of sex assault pleads guilty to three charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.
