It can grow as tall as 1 meter, and its buds can reach 5 centimeters in diameter. This extremely versatile plant easily adapts to its surroundings, flourishing in temperate oak forests or in a tropical rainforest’s humidity.

Cempasúchil production in Mexico is primarily focused on the flower’s ceremonial purposes. In late October and the first days of November, the country is covered in an orange blanket of cempasúchil as people across Mexico invoke the spirits of their loved ones during Day of the Dead festivities.

Even centuries after the tradition began, cempasúchil flowers still brighten Mexicans’ altars, lighting the way back home for the souls of the departed so that, for just one night a year, we can see our loved ones again.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: South Africa Special Votes Start With Delays
World.content:
Central Johannesburg seen from above (archive photo) photo. Central Johannesburg seen from a high tower, with the city centre streets below.

South Africa's local elections began on Monday with a rocky start, as late ballot papers delayed voting at several Cape Town stations. The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), the independent body that runs the country's elections, estimated that about 780,000 special votes were cast on day one.

Special voting is for people who cannot reach a station on election day, and the main vote follows on Wednesday, 4 November 2026. Follow the count in our South Africa local elections live hub.

Key Facts

About 780,000 special votes were cast on Monday, 2 November, which IEC chief electoral officer Sy Mamabolo called a conservative estimate. Delays: Several Cape Town stations opened late and stayed open until 6 p.m. local time (11 a.m. ET).

Several Cape Town stations opened late and stayed open until 6 p.m. local time (11 a.m. ET). Scale: About 2.6 million voters are approved for special votes on 2 and 3 November, and 127,000 officials work at about 23,000 stations.

About 2.6 million voters are approved for special votes on 2 and 3 November, and 127,000 officials work at about 23,000 stations. Next: Special voting ends Tuesday, 3 November, and election day is Wednesday, 4 November.

Special voting ends Tuesday, 3 November, and election day is Wednesday, 4 November. Prediction markets: Polymarket, a trading platform, gives Helen Zille, the Democratic Alliance's Johannesburg candidate, about 56% to be next mayor (2:22 p.m. ET, 2 November).

Special Voting Opens With Delays

Special voting is for registered voters who cannot reach a voting station on election day because of infirmity, disability or absence. About 2.6 million voters are approved to vote on Monday and Tuesday, with the rest visited at home.

Several Cape Town stations opened late because ballot papers had not finished being distributed, Mamabolo told a briefing. Those stations stayed open until 6 p.m. local time (11 a.m. ET), an hour past the official 5 p.m. close (10 a.m. ET).

Mamabolo apologised and said the delay was "not a political machination" but a consequence of a pressurised process to produce the ballot paper. A station in Matjhabeng, a municipality in the Free State province, was reported closed until 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET), and he said the IEC verifies provincial reports before releasing them.

Why the Ballots Were Late

The Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court on constitutional matters, ruled in favour of the African National Congress (ANC), the party that has long dominated national politics. The ruling added 181 ANC candidates who had been excluded because their lists were not fully formalised by the 28 August deadline.

Candidates from 32 other parties in similar circumstances were also added, and an extra 6.6 million ballots had to be printed. Distribution of the reprinted papers was still under way as special voting began.

Rain, Heat and the Road to Wednesday

Mamabolo promised a smoother second day, and noted that with "127,000 people, as well as 23,000 voting stations, aberrations are going to arise." Rain affected access in the Eastern Cape, and heat caused problems in Limpopo, North West and parts of Mpumalanga.

A booth-positioning issue was reported at Rivonia Village Hall in Johannesburg. Masego Sheburi, the IEC's deputy chief electoral officer for electoral operations, said booths should be placed in an "ATM position", so officials can observe the process without seeing how individuals mark their ballots.

Voters who were approved for a home visit are covered by the IEC's special-vote arrangements for 2 and 3 November. Check the IEC's own channels if a visit was missed.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where users trade on outcomes, lists Helen Zille at about 56% to become Johannesburg's next mayor. Zille is the Democratic Alliance's mayoral candidate and a former Western Cape premier.

Herman Mashaba, a former Johannesburg mayor who now leads the party ActionSA, trades at 7.4%. The Rev. Frank Chikane, a church leader widely reported as the ANC's frontrunner, trades at 6.3%.

About US$137,000 has been traded on the market, with prices read at 2:22 p.m. ET on 2 November. These are bets, not polls, and Johannesburg's mayor is chosen by the city council after the vote, so coalition deals will matter.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What the Polls Said

Ipsos, a research firm, published a poll on 30 October that put the ANC at 30% nationally and 27% in Johannesburg, with the Democratic Alliance (DA) at 30% in the city. The DA is the ANC's main rival in Johannesburg.

MarkData, another research firm, surveyed Johannesburg from 10 August to 14 September and found the DA on 35% and the ANC on 21.8%. The two Johannesburg results differ, and they were fielded at different times with different methods.

What It Means for US Readers

South Africa is seven hours ahead of US Eastern time after US clocks changed on 1 November. Election day on Wednesday, 4 November runs from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time, which is midnight to 2 p.m. ET.

The IEC has not confirmed when the first results will appear. We will update the live hub as it releases them.

What Is Not Known

The 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. voting hours come from our earlier coverage and were not re-verified at the IEC for this article. The exact time the first results will be announced is also unconfirmed.

Sources differ on the total number of ballot papers reprinted, so we do not give one. Whether every special voter will be reached at home is also not yet clear.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many special votes were cast on Monday?

The IEC estimated about 780,000 on 2 November. Chief electoral officer Sy Mamabolo called that a conservative estimate.

When is election day?

It is Wednesday, 4 November 2026. Special voting for approved voters runs on Monday, 2 November, and Tuesday, 3 November.

Who runs South Africa's elections?

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), an independent body, runs them. Sy Mamabolo is its chief electoral officer.

World.title: Mexico’s Mixquic Cemetery Lights Up Tonight
World.content:
Candles on the graves of San Andrés Mixquic's cemetery, seen from the roof of the San Andrés Apóstol church, pictured on 2 November 2009. Photo: Thelmadatter / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Mexico City ends its Day of the Dead season tonight with a sea of candles, as families light the graves of their dead at the San Andrés Mixquic cemetery in the borough of Tláhuac. The ceremony, called the Alumbrada, begins at 8 p.m. local time (9 p.m. Eastern Time, ET) on Monday, 2 November 2026.

It closes the Mixquic programme that began on 29 October, and we follow the wider festival in our Day of the Dead live hub. Mexico City is on Central Standard Time (UTC−6), which is six hours behind London and one hour behind New York after US clocks went back on 1 November.

Mixquic Lights Its Cemetery Tonight

The Alumbrada, which means "the lighting", takes place in the Mixquic cemetery in south-eastern Mexico City. Graves there are decorated with marigolds, votive candles and offerings, and families gather around them through the night.

The official programme ran from 29 October to 2 November. It began with tomb cleaning on 29 October and continued on 31 October with the "Rodada del Mictlán", a bike ride. Pre-Hispanic ball-game exhibitions run from 31 October through 2 November.

The programme ends with vigils on 1 and 2 November. The start time of 8 p.m. comes from the official programme, and we did not reach the Tláhuac borough's own page to confirm it.

Day of the Dead altars in the Zócalo, Mexico City (archive photo)

Why the Zócalo Catrina Is Still Drawing Crowds

Alfredo Arista, an adjudicator for Guinness World Records, validated the giant Catrina at 33.41 metres (about 110 feet) on 29 October 2026. A Catrina is the elegant skeleton lady that has become a symbol of the holiday, and this one stands in the Zócalo, Mexico City's main square.

The figure is the centrepiece of the Monumental Offering, a public altar dedicated to the engraver José Guadalupe Posada, whose satirical skeleton print Calavera Garbancera inspired the Catrina. It stays on view through Monday, 2 November, and no closing time has been published.

It has fibreglass bones, a steel frame, internal LED lighting and a 27-metre dress embroidered in the Tenango style, a Mexican hand-embroidery tradition, with marigolds and hummingbirds. The Taller de Arte Xibalbá, an art workshop led by director Carlos Báez, built it.

More than 100 people took part, among them artists, engineers, architects, blacksmiths and painters. The square also holds marigold fields and an exhibition called "Ajolotes en el corazón".

What It Means for US Readers

The Alumbrada starts at 9 p.m. ET on Monday, 2 November. We did not verify any livestream or US broadcast of the ceremony.

Mexico City authorities and the city Culture Secretariat are the sources to watch for official figures. Local time is six hours behind London and one hour behind New York.

What Is Not Known

No official attendance or incident figures for 1 and 2 November have been published yet. The Catrina's closing time on 2 November has not been stated.

No poll or prediction market applies to this topic. We will report the figures here once city authorities release them.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Mixquic Alumbrada?

It is set for Monday, 2 November 2026, from 8 p.m. in Mexico City, which is 9 p.m. ET. The time comes from the official programme.

Where does the Alumbrada take place?

It takes place at the San Andrés Mixquic cemetery in Tláhuac, a borough of Mexico City. Families light candles on the graves of their dead.

How tall is the record Catrina in the Zócalo?

Guinness World Records validated it at 33.41 metres, about 110 feet, on 29 October 2026. It stays on view through Monday, 2 November.

Growers in Mexico’s avocado belt burned up to 52 tonnes of export fruit after weevil larvae turned up. The state confirmed the pest, but no export ban, loss estimate or restart date for held shipments has been published.

Mexican avocado growers burned up to 52 tonnes of export fruit in Peribán, western Michoacán, after weevil larvae were found. Alejandro Méndez, Michoacán’s environment secretary, confirmed the pest on Sunday, 1 November, and said suspect lots stayed off the market.

Mexico is the main source of US avocados, so a pest in the Michoacán belt matters to American buyers. Senasica, Mexico’s national agri-food health agency, took part in the destruction and backed it.

What Growers Destroyed and Where

Up to 52 tonnes (about 115,000 pounds) were destroyed, a maximum that could change as inspections continue. The fruit was burned and buried in pits under pest-control protocols.

The fruit came from Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit, three other western avocado states, and was meant for the US market. It was destroyed in Peribán, with Senasica staff and a state plant-health board present.

Dates differ between accounts: two place the burning on Thursday, 29 October, while later ones say the weekend. A growers’ union says the pest was only suspected, with no official diagnosis.

Why Shipments Are Under Scrutiny

Under the US federal rule for Mexican Hass avocados, fruit may enter only from approved orchards in municipalities inspected for named pests. The 2011 text of the rule names several seed weevils and a seed moth.

As written, a detection means the affected orchard loses certification until US and Mexican plant-health agencies agree the fix worked. The rule relies on fruit cuts at packing houses and at US ports of entry.

Mexican accounts say shipments bound for export were held, and no number has been given. APHIS, the US Department of Agriculture’s plant-health inspection service, has published no statement on the case.

A Growers’ Stoppage Is Also Straining Supply

Separately, small Michoacán growers stopped cutting fruit on Friday, 23 October, to demand better prices. The union wants about 40 pesos a kilo (about US$2.13 at 18.8 pesos per US$), against about 15 pesos (about US$0.80) now.

APEAM, the association of Michoacán avocado exporters and packers, met growers and state officials on 27 October without a deal. It warned that the actions put the export program at risk, and no restart date is known.

What It Means for US Readers

Mexico, led by Michoacán, is the main source of US avocados, so a long stoppage can tighten shelves. Shoppers and restaurants should watch for price moves, though no official export suspension over the pest has been cited.

The wider concern is a pest spread or a lasting export hold, and neither has been reported. The 52 tonnes are small beside US demand, which runs into tens of millions of kilograms a week.

Related reports: US Restarts Avocado Checks In Michoacán After Security Deal and Mexico Deploys 1,557 Personnel to Secure Michoacán Avocado Trade. More is on the Mexico hub, with guides to who runs the economy and who holds power.

The capital is covered on the Mexico City page. Readers heading to Michoacán should check US State Department travel advice first.

What Is Not Known

Senasica has not published which weevil species was found, and no US agency has commented. The 52-tonne figure is a stated maximum, and no loss estimate has been issued.

It is unknown how many shipments were held, or whether any left Mexico. The exact date of the burning is also unclear, with accounts split between 29 October and the weekend.

The claim that the pest halted exports is not confirmed. Shipments were held, but no official export suspension was cited and no date for held shipments to resume is known.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many avocados were destroyed in Mexico?

Up to 52 tonnes (about 115,000 pounds), a maximum that could change as inspections continue. Growers burned and buried the fruit under pest-control protocols.

Which pest was found in the avocados?

Larvae of an avocado seed weevil, a beetle whose grubs bore into the fruit’s pit. Michoacán’s environment secretary confirmed it, but the species has not been named.

Has Mexico stopped avocado exports to the US?

No official export suspension over the pest has been cited. Some shipments were held, and a separate growers’ harvest stoppage since 23 October has strained supply.

Is the growers’ harvest stoppage still on?

As of 31 October, cutting remained suspended and no restart date was known. Growers want higher farm prices, and talks with exporters had produced no deal.

Who is Senasica?

Senasica is Mexico’s national agri-food health agency. Its staff took part in the destruction, but it has issued no statement of its own.

Sources: Alejandro Méndez, Michoacán state environment secretary, statement of 1 November 2026; Senasica and Mexico Agriculture Ministry (no statement on this case located as of 2 November 2026); US federal rule 7 CFR 319.56-30, Mexican Hass avocado import program (govinfo edition of 2011; the current text was not reachable); USDA APHIS (no statement on this case located). Exchange rate: about 18.8 pesos per US$ (2 November 2026).

World.title: Bolivia Drought Hits 114,000 Families
World.content:
BOLIVIA · CLIMATE

Key Facts Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

What is happening Drought has hit 63 Bolivian municipalities since 1 June, and the government warns of floods, frost and fires.

Why it matters The rainy season starts in November, with drought in the highlands and valleys and flood risk elsewhere.

The numbers 114,048 families are hit, with 60,106 hectares of crops and 75,013 head of livestock lost.

Who is who Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano coordinates the response; the civil defense vice ministry counts the families.

What to watch Whether the Bolivian government releases new money, and US weather agency NOAA’s next update on Thursday, 12 November.

Prediction markets Polymarket gives El Niño a 73.5% chance of peaking at 2.5 or above on its warming index (2 November, 2:05 p.m. ET).

What it means for you US travellers should check the State Department advisory for Bolivia, because floods can close roads from November.

Bolivia’s defense ministry counts 114,048 families hit by drought in 63 municipalities since 1 June. The government fears floods and frost next as El Niño strengthens.

Drought has hit 63 Bolivian municipalities in six of the nine departments since 1 June, the Ministry of Defense says. The figures run to 29 October and count 114,048 families, 60,106 hectares of lost crops and 75,013 lost animals.

President Rodrigo Paz declared a national emergency on Saturday, 31 October, as El Niño, a warming of Pacific waters, builds. The defense minister says the decree lets each ministry act within its own remit.

What the Defense Ministry Counts

The ministry registers 114,048 families: 78,217 classed as affected and 35,831 as damnificadas, meaning direct losses. The earlier figure of 78,217 families, given at the decree announcement, is therefore only the affected group.

Oruro, on the high plateau bordering Chile, has the most families with direct losses, 17,554. La Paz follows with 6,679 and Chuquisaca with 4,678.

The ministry says 167,511 hectares of farmland are affected, and 60,106 of them are lost. It also counts 1,486 affected communities and 75,013 head of livestock lost.

What the Emergency Changes

Decree 5759 declares a national emergency over drought and the risks linked to El Niño in 2026 and 2027. Paz signed it after CONARADE, the national disaster-risk council, recommended it on Friday, 30 October.

Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano says the declaration does not mean the emergency is solved, but a step toward a faster, coordinated response. Each ministry acts within its remit, especially on water, health, farming, roads and the environment.

The decree sets no specific amount of new money, and the defense minister says financing mechanisms are still being worked out. Funds for affected towns depend on local emergency declarations under Law 602, the national disaster law.

Civil defense is the disaster-response arm of the Ministry of Defense, and it coordinates the effort. Regional and local governments, the armed forces and international cooperation agencies are asked to join in.

What Forecasters Expect

NOAA, the US weather and climate agency, issued an El Niño Advisory on 8 October. It says a strong to very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027, with odds above 83%.

NOAA puts the chance of a historic event at 83% for October to December. It defines that as a three-month index of 2.5 degrees Celsius or more.

Justiniano stresses these are warnings that allow prevention, not certainties that every event will happen. The Altiplano, valleys and the Chaco plain face drought, while other zones could see heavy rain, floods and river overflows.

Frost, hail and forest fires are also listed risks, and the rainy season starts in November. Rain, flood and frost warnings differ by region across the country.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a US prediction market, gives 73.5% odds that El Niño’s peak reaches 2.5 or above (2 November, 2:05 p.m. ET). That is on RONI, the Relative Oceanic Niño Index, a three-month gauge of Pacific warming used by NOAA.

About US$162,100 has been traded across the event’s five price bands, and the 2.25 to 2.5 band sits at 22%. These are bets, not polls, and they gauge how strong El Niño may get, not what Bolivia will do.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

The decree names no foreign donor and no amount of new money. It is not known whether lenders or aid agencies will fund the response.

NOAA’s forecast of a strong to very strong El Niño matters beyond Bolivia, because the event shifts weather patterns across the Americas. US travellers should check the State Department’s Bolivia advisory, as floods can disrupt roads during the rainy season.

Related reports: Bolivia Declares El Niño Emergency Oct 31 and Peru Growth May Fall to 2% If El Nino Lasts. More is on the Bolivia hub, with guides to who runs the economy and who holds power.

The country’s largest city is covered in Santa Cruz de la Sierra Explained. Its department is one of those named in the drought count.

What Is Not Known

No total budget for the emergency has been announced, and financing procedures are still being completed. Which foreign lenders or donors will pay is also unknown.

The president spoke of 63 communities in drought, whereas the ministry data count 63 municipalities in six departments. This article uses the ministry’s figure.

No loss estimate in US$ has been announced, and nothing is known yet on effects for food prices or exports. How long the emergency lasts is also unknown.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many families has Bolivia’s drought hit?

The Ministry of Defense counts 114,048 families in 63 municipalities from 1 June to 29 October. Of these, 78,217 are classed as affected and 35,831 as having suffered direct losses.

What did Bolivia declare on 31 October?

President Rodrigo Paz signed Decree 5759, a national emergency for drought and El Niño risks in 2026 and 2027. It lets ministries, regions and town halls direct money and staff to affected areas.

Which regions are worst hit by the drought?

Oruro has the most families with direct losses, 17,554, followed by La Paz with 6,679 and Chuquisaca with 4,678. The ministry counts six departments in all.

Could floods follow the drought in Bolivia?

Officials warn parts of Bolivia could see heavy rain, floods and river overflows in the rainy season, from November to March. The defense minister calls these warnings, not certainties.

How much new money has Bolivia set aside for the drought?

The decree sets no specific amount of new money, and the defense minister says financing mechanisms are still being worked out. No total budget has been announced.

How strong is this El Niño?

NOAA says a strong to very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027, with odds above 83%. Its next update is due on Thursday, 12 November.

Sources: Ministry of Defense of Bolivia and the Vice Ministry of Civil Defense, drought impact data for 1 June to 29 October 2026 and statements of 30 to 31 October 2026; Presidency of Bolivia, Supreme Decree 5759, National Emergency Situation for drought and El Niño 2026-2027 (Gaceta Oficial, 31 October 2026), and CONARADE Resolution 014/2026 (30 October 2026); NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO Diagnostic Discussion (8 October 2026); Polymarket market data on the 2026-27 El Niño peak RONI (2 November 2026, 1:29 p.m. ET); US State Department travel advisory for Bolivia.

World.title: Chile Leader Tours Europe Amid Minister Row
World.content:
CHILE · POLITICS

Key Facts Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

What is happening Chile’s President Kast is touring Europe as opponents prepare to impeach Justice Minister Fernando Rabat.

Why it matters Chile is the world’s largest copper producer; the row tests whether Kast can keep his cabinet together.

The numbers A minister needs a majority of deputies present, then 26 of 50 senators, to be removed.

Who is who The PDG, or Party of the People, is a populist party with about 14 deputies.

What to watch Whether the opposition files the impeachment, expected in early November, and how the PDG votes.

What it means for you No direct change for travellers; a weaker cabinet could slow mining, tax and security bills.

Chile’s President Kast set off on a European tour as his justice minister faces an impeachment push. A small party, the PDG, may decide whether it succeeds.

Chile’s President José Antonio Kast, a conservative who took office in March, left for Europe on Sunday, 1 November. He was due in Madrid on Monday, 2 November, while opposition deputies prepare to impeach his justice minister.

The minister, Fernando Rabat, faces a planned impeachment over decrees that cut prison sentences for people convicted of sexual crimes against minors. Rabat denies wrongdoing, and Kast has kept him in office.

Where Kast Is Going

After Madrid, Kast is due in Rome on Tuesday, 3 November. Pope Leo XIV, head of the Catholic Church, is due to receive him at the Vatican on Wednesday, 4 November.

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, is also expected to meet him during the Italian stop. The exact day of that meeting has not been confirmed.

Kast also attends the Ibero-American Summit, a meeting of Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking leaders, in Madrid on 4 and 5 November. He is due back in Chile on Friday, 6 November.

What Rabat and the Government Say

Rabat said on 29 October that he heard no argument in the Chamber of Deputies that justified an impeachment. He says he acted within the Constitution and the law, and that his conscience is clear.

Asked whether he would resign, Rabat thanked Kast for his confidence. He calls the push a political move and has not said he will quit.

Gonzalo Arenas, a senior official for government communications, said on radio on 30 October that the mood was difficult. He said not all governing legislators were aligned yet.

Hotuiti Teao, an independent deputy close to the governing UDI party, said on 27 October he would vote for the impeachment. The UDI is a conservative party in Kast’s coalition.

Why the PDG Holds the Key

An impeachment of a minister needs a majority of the deputies present in the 155-seat Chamber. The Senate then needs 26 of its 50 members to remove him.

The PDG, or Party of the People, is a populist party with about 14 deputies. Franco Parisi, its secretary general, founded it, and both sides are courting its votes.

Juan Marcelo Valenzuela, the PDG caucus leader, said on 29 October that views inside the bench are divided. He called the sentence cuts a political error but said Rabat’s future is for Kast to decide.

Parisi demanded on 27 October that Kast remove Rabat. Pamela Jiles, a PDG deputy, has instead offered to help save him.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the row matters less for copper output than for the reform agenda. A president who loses a minister may find it harder to pass mining, tax and security bills.

No change to entry rules or travel advice has been announced. The dispute is a domestic fight over sentencing decrees.

Rio Times readers can find the mechanics in Chile Opposition Seeks to Impeach Minister. The exit of Luis Silva, the deputy justice minister, is covered in Chile Replaces Deputy Justice Minister Silva.

More is on the Kast approval report and the Chile hub. The Santiago city page covers the capital.

What Is Not Known

As of the latest reports found, the impeachment has not been filed. The opposition says it expects to file in the first week of November.

The Chamber’s website could not be opened, so signature counts are unverified. Seat counts for the opposition differ between sources, so none is given here.

How the PDG will vote, and whether Rabat will resign first, is unknown. Rabat’s own statements on Monday, 2 November, could not be confirmed.

The Presidency’s website could not be opened, so the tour dates rest on several consistent local reports. Who acts as head of government while Kast is away is not stated.

Whether the decrees broke the law is the opposition’s claim, and no court ruling was found. Rabat says he followed the law and is presumed innocent of any wrongdoing.

What Comes Next

The next step is the filing in the Chamber of Deputies, then a committee and a floor vote. An impeachment is a political process, not a criminal trial.

Filing does not remove Rabat, and Kast can still keep him in office. Only a Senate vote of 26 of 50 members would do that.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Chile’s justice minister facing impeachment?

Opposition lawmakers say Fernando Rabat’s ministry approved decrees that cut sentences for people convicted of sexual crimes against minors. Rabat says he followed the law.

Is Kast really in Europe during the crisis?

Yes, Kast left Chile on 1 November for Spain, Italy and the Vatican. He attends the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid on 4 and 5 November and is due home on 6 November.

What is the PDG and why does it matter?

The PDG, or Party of the People, is a populist party with about 14 deputies. Its votes could decide whether the impeachment passes the Chamber.

Could Rabat be removed?

Only if a majority of deputies present and then 26 of 50 senators vote for it. Kast could also ask him to resign.

Sources: Constitution of Chile, articles 52 and 53, Library of the National Congress; Holy See, Vatican City (papal audience calendar); Chamber of Deputies of Chile and Presidency of Chile (websites could not be opened); statements by Rabat, Arenas, Teao, Valenzuela and Parisi, 27 to 30 October 2026 (all accessed 2 November 2026).

World.title: UN Details Russian Ties Near Chad Border
World.content:
CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts What is happening UN documents describe Russian instructors beside the Central African army, as Chad disputes a Saturday border raid.

Why it matters Russian forces, rebels and spillover from Sudan’s war meet in Vakaga, a region on the Chad border.

The numbers UN: over 1,900 fighters disarmed since July 2025; over 17,000 civilians displaced by a 30 June attack.

Who is who Faustin-Archange Touadéra is the Central African president; Wagner, a Russian private army, first deployed there in 2018.

What to watch Whether Chad answers the Central African government’s 22 October statement, and how the UN Security Council handles the peacekeeping mandate renewal.

What it means for you State Department: do not travel; US sanctions on Wagner bar US firms from dealing with it.

UN reports show Russian instructors working with the Central African army near the Chad border. Chad and Bangui still disagree about a raid on 10 October.

A UN experts’ report describes Russian instructors fighting beside the Central African army, whose north-east operations now touch the Chad border. Chad says a Saturday 10 October raid crossed its border, while the Central African government says it did not.

For US readers it matters because Washington sanctions Wagner, a Russian private army, and tells citizens not to travel to the country. The Central African Republic is a landlocked state north of Congo, run from Bangui, its capital.

What the United Nations Has Documented

A UN Panel of Experts, which monitors sanctions on the country, published report S/2026/481 on 10 June 2026. It says state-allied forces are the army, Russian instructors, local militias and armed actors called “Wagner Noirs”.

Interviewees told the experts the term refers to former fighters, disarmed and demobilised, who now work alongside Russian instructors. The experts said unclear command and control raises concerns about accountability and civilian protection.

The experts logged joint army and Russian operations in the north-east, including a patrol near Birao that presumed rebels ambushed. Birao is the main town of Vakaga, the region where Chad, Sudan and the Central African Republic meet.

What the UN Mission Told the Security Council

Valentine Rugwabiza, who leads the UN peacekeeping mission, told the Security Council on Tuesday 20 October that the three-border area remains tense. She said national forces are running operations in Vakaga against feared cross-border attacks by armed groups.

She said more than 1,900 combatants have disarmed since July 2025. Armed groups attacked Am-Dafock, a town on the Sudan border, on 30 June and displaced more than 17,000 civilians.

Her statement does not mention the 10 October raid or Chad’s protest. The Council is preparing to renew the mission’s mandate, and she asked it to keep adequate force levels.

What the Two Governments Say

The Central African defence ministry said on Saturday 10 October that its army and Russian allies ran preventive operations against foreign mercenaries. Bangui says the operation took place in Vakaga.

Chad’s foreign minister, Ahmed Kogri, summoned the Central African ambassador on Sunday 11 October. He said an armed incursion in the Tissi border area on Saturday seriously wounded several soldiers and civilians.

The Central African Presidency said on Thursday 22 October that the attack took place only on Central African soil. Neither government has made public evidence that outsiders can check.

Dimitri Sytyi, a presidential adviser who directs the Russian House cultural centre in Bangui, spoke on Tuesday 20 October. He said drone readings, maps and a statement from rebel leader Noureddine Adam keep the operations inside the country.

Who the Russian Forces Are

Wagner is a Russian private military company that, according to the US Treasury, first deployed to the country in January 2018. On Thursday 26 January 2023 the Treasury said Wagner personnel engaged in serious crimes there and in Mali, including mass executions.

Central African officials say “Russian allies”, and the UN experts say “Russian instructors”. The statements cited here do not name the Russian unit that took part on 10 October.

Related Rio Times reports are Central African Republic Denies Chad Rift and Wagner Near Chad Border, Report Says 25 Oct. More is on the Central African Republic hub and in Central African Republic Neighbours, Borders and Trade.

What It Means for You

The US State Department, Washington’s foreign ministry, tells Americans not to travel there, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping. It says the US government has limited ability to provide emergency services to citizens.

Aid workers and business travellers should treat Vakaga and the borders with Chad and Sudan as unsafe. US sanctions on Wagner mean American firms must avoid dealings with it.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the 10 October raid crossed into Chad, since each side gives a different account. No independent investigation has been published.

No full casualty count exists, and the evidence each side cites is not public. The UN experts’ report dates from June, four months before the raid.

What Comes Next

Watch for a Chadian reply to the 22 October statement and for any joint border security plan. The UN Security Council is preparing to renew the peacekeeping mandate.

None of this means fighting has resumed. Official statements from Bangui, N’Djamena, Chad’s capital, or the UN would settle the open questions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened on the Central African Republic border with Chad?

On Saturday 10 October, the Central African army and Russian allies ran an operation in Vakaga. Chad says it crossed the border and wounded soldiers and civilians, while Bangui says it did not.

What do the United Nations say about Russian forces there?

UN sanctions experts describe Russian instructors working alongside the Central African army and local militias in the north-east. Their report dates from 10 June, four months before the raid.

Who is Wagner?

Wagner is a Russian private military company that first deployed in the country in January 2018, according to the US Treasury. The Treasury sanctioned it in 2023 and accused its personnel of serious crimes there.

Is it safe for Americans to travel to the Central African Republic?

The State Department tells Americans not to travel there, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping. The US government has limited ability to provide emergency services to citizens there.

Sources: UN peacekeeping mission in the Central African Republic, statement to the Security Council, 20 October 2026; UN Panel of Experts, report S/2026/481, 10 June 2026; US Treasury, Wagner designation, 26 January 2023; US State Department, Central African Republic travel advisory (all accessed 2 November 2026).

World.title: 3 Rockets From Ethiopia Land in Kenyan Town
World.content:
KENYA · SECURITY

Key Facts What is happening Police say three rocket-propelled grenades from Ethiopia landed in Moyale, Kenya, and were found on Sunday, 1 November; army experts detonated them.

Why it matters The grenades fell on a town now sheltering tens of thousands of people who fled fighting between Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional forces on the other side of the border.

The numbers Three grenades, no injuries here, about 50,000 arrivals from Ethiopia, a figure the UN calls fluid; the UN seeks US$8.9 million.

Who is who Moyale police and a bomb team from Kenya’s army secured the scene; police have not said who fired. UNHCR is the UN refugee agency.

What to watch Whether police name who fired, whether more rounds land in Kenya, and whether shelters near the border move farther inland.

What it means for you US travellers should avoid Moyale and the Ethiopia border area; Nairobi and the main safari areas are far to the south, but check the US State Department’s advisories.

Three rocket-propelled grenades from Ethiopia landed in the Kenyan border town of Moyale and were destroyed without injury. The incident adds to a crisis that has pushed tens of thousands of people into northern Kenya.

Three rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs, shoulder-fired rocket weapons) from Ethiopia landed in the Kenyan border town of Moyale, police said. They were found on Sunday, 1 November, and army experts destroyed them without injury.

What Police Say Happened

Police said residents reported unexploded material near Sessi Primary School in Moyale on Sunday. Officers found one grenade at the school and two more at the Meteorological Department offices.

A bomb disposal team from the Kenya Defence Forces, Kenya’s army, joined police to secure and remove the devices. They detonated all three safely.

Police reported no injuries from this incident. They have not said who fired the grenades.

A Border Town Split in Two

Moyale is a twin town in Kenya’s Marsabit County that sits directly on the border with Ethiopia. Armed clashes erupted on the Ethiopian side on Thursday, 22 October, and civilians have crossed since.

The clashes involve forces and groups from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regions, two of its federal states. UN agencies say clashes continue daily and heavy weapons have been reported.

UN agencies say stray fire from across the border has already injured Kenyan civilians in Moyale. Kenya’s army is securing the border, they add.

Tens of Thousands Have Crossed Into Kenya

UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, says significant cross-border movements have been recorded since 22 October. Local authorities estimate about 50,000 people have entered Kenya, and the agency calls the figure fluid.

Most arrivals are women and children, UNHCR says. They are sheltering with host families, in public buildings and in open spaces.

UNHCR says food is the most urgent need, followed by safe water, shelter, sanitation and health care. Relief supplies have reached nearly 12,000 people, and safer sites away from the border are sought.

The United Nations is appealing for US$8.9 million for the most critical life-saving needs over the next three months. UNHCR, UNICEF (the UN children’s agency), IOM (the UN migration agency) and the World Food Programme support the response.

What It Means for You

Americans should avoid Moyale and the Kenya-Ethiopia border area while grenades and stray bullets are landing in town. Check the US State Department’s current Kenya and Ethiopia travel advisories and carry medical evacuation insurance.

Moyale lies far from Nairobi, Mombasa and the main safari areas. Aid donors face a growing appeal in a country where annual inflation reached 7.3% in October, the statistics office said.

Related Rio Times reports include 50,000 Flee Moyale Clashes Into Kenya and Kenya’s October inflation. Background is in the Moyale fighting explainer, the border displacement report and the Kenya hub.

What Is Not Known

Police have not said who fired the grenades, from which side of the Ethiopian fighting, or whether they were aimed at Moyale. No verified death toll from the fighting has been published.

Local reports also mention one grenade overnight on 31 October near the same school. Only one source carries it, so it is unconfirmed whether it is part of the three found on 1 November.

Local reports say exam candidates at some Moyale schools were moved after stray bullets. The education ministry had issued no Moyale statement, and no Ethiopian statement on the grenades was found.

What Comes Next

Watch for a fuller police statement, any arrests or attribution, and whether bomb disposal teams find more unexploded rounds. A funding response to the US$8.9 million UN appeal will show how quickly shelters can move away from the border.

The discovery does not mean Kenya is a party to the fighting, and no Kenyan official has said so. It shows that the war across the border is now landing on Kenyan soil.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Moyale, Kenya?

Police say three rocket-propelled grenades from Ethiopia landed in Moyale and were found on 1 November. Army experts detonated them safely, and no one was hurt.

Who fired the rockets at Moyale?

Police have not said. Forces and groups from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regions are fighting across the border, but no authority has blamed either side.

How many people have fled into Kenya?

Local authorities estimate about 50,000 people have crossed since 22 October. UNHCR says the figure is still changing as registration continues.

Is it safe for Americans to visit Moyale?

Avoid Moyale and the Ethiopia border while grenades and stray bullets are landing in town. Check current State Department advisories for Kenya and Ethiopia.

Sources: National Police Service, Kenya; Ministry of Interior and National Administration, Kenya; UNHCR, Moyale Emergency Inter-agency SitRep #4 (30 October 2026); Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (all accessed 2 November 2026).

World.title: Argentina Airport Strike Set for 6 November
World.content:
ARGENTINA · AVIATION

Key Facts — Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 61.2 points (October 2026 edition).

— What is happening A state workers’ union has announced a stoppage at 27 Argentine airports on Friday, 6 November. Only medical, humanitarian, organ-transport and official flights are guaranteed.

— Why it matters The date falls two days before Pope Leo XIV arrives on Sunday, 8 November, so delays could reach pilgrims, officials and travellers connecting through Buenos Aires.

— The numbers The action covers 27 airports, including Ezeiza, the main international hub, and Aeroparque, the city airport. The union says under 10% of about ARS 220 billion (US$143 million) in yearly airport fees returns to operations and pay.

— Who is who ATE is Argentina’s main state workers’ union, led by Rodolfo Aguiar. ANAC is Argentina’s civil aviation authority, whose staff it represents, and President Javier Milei’s government is the employer.

— What to watch Whether the government orders minimum service levels, as it did in September, and whether the union keeps the 6 November action in place.

— What it means for you US travellers booked through Buenos Aires on Friday, 6 November should check flight status with their airline and follow the State Department’s Argentina advisory.

ATE, Argentina’s state workers’ union, plans a stoppage at 27 airports on Friday, 6 November. No cancellations are confirmed and no official response was found.

Argentina’s main state workers’ union, ATE, announced on Monday, 2 November, a stoppage at 27 airports on Friday, 6 November. Delays and cancellations are possible, including at Ezeiza, Buenos Aires’ main international airport, and Aeroparque, its domestic airport.

The date matters to visitors because Pope Leo XIV arrives on Sunday, 8 November, for a visit to 11 November. No flight has been cancelled so far, and the scope of any disruption is not yet known.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 61.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Union Announced

ATE calls its action a retención de tareas, a work stoppage in which staff stop their normal duties. The union says only health, humanitarian, organ-transport and official flights would be guaranteed.

At Ezeiza and Aeroparque, ATE adds a paro a la japonesa, a strict-checks protest covering aircraft, ramp gear, works and runways. Such checks can slow operations without a full walkout.

ATE says the reason is airport safety, not pay alone. It lists missing fire extinguishers and protective gear, ambulances in poor condition and a lack of medical supplies.

The union has sent a complaint to the national Labour Secretariat, headed by Julio Cordero. It asks for full hygiene and safety inspections at the airports named.

Why the Date Matters

Pope Leo XIV is due in Argentina from Sunday, 8 November, to Wednesday, 11 November, between stops in Uruguay and Peru. The government has made Monday, 9 November, a national holiday.

The programme includes a flight to Córdoba on Tuesday, 10 November, and a farewell at the international airport on Wednesday, 11 November. Large crowds are expected to travel between provinces.

ATE leader Rodolfo Aguiar says the protest targets the government, not passengers. He also says the union gave legal notice of the action in advance.

What Happened the Last Time

ATE planned a similar action at 27 airports on Thursday, 3 September, and Friday, 4 September, in two daily windows. The government ordered 75% of operations kept running, and ATE rejected the order.

On the morning of 3 September, ATE postponed the first window but kept the afternoon action. How many flights were delayed that week is not confirmed here.

What It Means for You

US travellers with flights through Buenos Aires on Friday, 6 November, should check status with their airline before leaving for the airport. Passengers heading to the papal events should allow extra time.

The announcement names no other day. The US State Department’s Argentina travel advisory is the official US guide for the trip.

Related Rio Times reports include Argentina Airport Operator Pledges US$1.5 Billion and Argentina Raises Domestic Airport Fee to US$9. The Pope Leo visit schedule and the Córdoba guide cover the trip.

More is on the Argentina hub and the Argentina power structure guide. The Buenos Aires city page covers the capital.

What Is Not Known

No statement from the aviation regulator, ORSNA, the national airport regulator, or any airline on the 6 November action was found. No government order on minimum service levels was found either.

The hours of the stoppage and the number of flights at risk are not stated. The union’s fee and safety-equipment claims are its own and were not independently checked.

Sources differ on which airport receives the Pope on 8 November, so that detail is left out. The programme of the visit is still described as subject to change.

What Comes Next

The stoppage is set for Friday, 6 November, and the Pope arrives on Sunday, 8 November. A government order on minimum services, as in September, would be the next sign to watch.

The announcement does not mean the airports will close or that the papal visit is in doubt. It means delays are possible on one day.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there an airport strike in Argentina on 6 November?

ATE, a state workers’ union, has announced a stoppage at 27 airports for Friday, 6 November. The government has not been found responding.

Will flights be cancelled on 6 November?

The union warns of delays and cancellations, including at Ezeiza and Aeroparque. No cancellation is confirmed, and the union has not stated the hours of the action.

Does the strike affect the Pope’s visit?

The stoppage falls two days before the Pope arrives on 8 November. No official statement links it to the visit programme.

What should US travellers do?

Check flight status with the airline and allow extra time on Friday, 6 November. The US State Department publishes the official Argentina travel advisory.

Sources: ATE, the state workers’ union: announcement of airport action on 6 November; Argentine Labour Secretariat; US State Department travel advisories (all accessed 2 November 2026).

World.title: Gota a Gota Extortion Cases Keep Climbing in Costa Rica, OIJ Data Show
World.content:
Extortion complaints linked to informal gota a gota loans in Costa Rica reached a record 935 in 2025, more than double the 427 filed in 2022, according to data from the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). The trend has not eased this year. The OIJ’s criminal analysis unit recorded 840 complaints from January through Oct. 15, 2026, leaving 95 cases short of last year’s total with two and a half months still to go.

Michael Soto, the OIJ’s interim director, described gota a gota lending as a well-established criminal phenomenon. He also said that people file few complaints, which means the official figures likely understate the scale of the problem. The loans are typically offered without paperwork, guarantors or credit checks, often to people who need cash quickly for medical costs, utility bills or food. Lenders collect payments every day and charge interest that borrowers frequently cannot pay down, turning a small loan into a debt with no clear end.

When payments fall short, collectors turn to intimidation, according to the OIJ. Victims have reported threats at their homes, harassing phone calls and, in some cases, physical attacks. Authorities say the groups also pursue relatives when a borrower cannot pay. Investigators link the organized groups behind the loans to drug trafficking and money laundering. In October, a national team defender was among four people detained in a gota a gota extortion investigation, a case that remains at the investigative stage.

Authorities have also identified a newer variant known as chorro a chorro. It involves loans of millions of colones to borrowers with higher incomes, rather than to people facing an emergency. The yearly figures show the sharpest jump between 2022 and 2023, when complaints rose from 427 to 864. They dipped slightly to 857 in 2024 before reaching the 2025 high.

Across the five years, complaints have been highest in August, September and October, and lowest in December and February. Authorities urge anyone being pressured by an informal lender not to give in to threats and to report the case to the OIJ as soon as possible. Knowing the warning signs of a gota a gota loan can help people avoid the trap before it starts.

World.title: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
World.content:
Nearly 2,000 Chinese businesses have been established in Nicaragua during the first two years of the free trade agreement with China, according to the president of the Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua. Shujin Huang made the statement to official media outlets after an event marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen.

He said the association continues to promote additional investment from China, describing Nicaragua as a safe country with a competitive market. The free trade agreement between the two countries entered into force on January 1, 2024. The Banco Central de Nicaragua reported that net foreign direct investment from China reached 29.3 million dollars in 2025.

That figure represented 1.9 percent of the 1,502.5 million dollars in total net foreign direct investment recorded by the country that year. In 2024, any Chinese flows were not reported separately and would have been included in aggregate categories if present at all. Huang said the businesses operate mainly in commerce, with some also active in free-zone maquilas. The relatively low official investment total relative to the number of establishments indicates that most are small-scale operations.

The Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua was founded in May 2024 and was officially registered as a legal organization under Ministerial Agreement 24-2024-OSFL, allowing it to operate in its own name under Nicaraguan law. Its founding event included participation by Chinese Ambassador Chen Xi and Nicaraguan officials including National Assembly President Gustavo Porras, Foreign Minister Denis Moncada and Presidential Adviser Laureano Ortega Murillo.

As part of the commercial expansion, construction of a Chinatown complex advances in Managua near the Rotonda Universitaria. The project, also known as Plaza China or Plaza 101, involves a two-story structure of approximately 8,000 square meters with an investment of about 3 million dollars. It is planned to house around 100 businesses operated by Chinese, other Asian and Nicaraguan owners.

The site currently holds roughly 30 businesses. Administrators have described the work as being in an intermediate phase, including installation of a stone arch more than six meters high carved in a dragon style and brought from China. The complex is intended to concentrate commercial activity, gastronomy and cultural offerings. Huang cited the existing Plaza China as an example of growing Chinese capital presence, noting that more than ten foreign-investment businesses already operate there.

Nicaragua and China restored diplomatic relations in December 2021 after Managua broke ties with Taiwan. The free trade agreement was signed on August 31, 2023. Official Nicaraguan statements have presented the pact and related initiatives as measures to expand trade and investment opportunities. The association’s stated goals include supporting Chinese investors and promoting the policy of one China.

As of now, the association continues to encourage further arrivals of Chinese capital. Construction on the Managua Chinatown project remains under way, with officials and association representatives describing it as a visible marker of the commercial presence that has developed since the trade agreement took effect. The Banco Central de Nicaragua has not published a full country-by-country breakdown beyond the 2025 net total that places China at 29.3 million dollars.

World.title: Costa Rica Uses Smartphones to Create 3D Maps of Pacific Coral Reefs
World.content:
A Costa Rican conservation organization is using ordinary smartphones to create detailed three-dimensional maps of coral reefs along the country’s Pacific coast, giving researchers a new way to track the health of underwater ecosystems threatened by rising ocean temperatures and climate change.

The project, led by the nonprofit Raising Coral, is taking place in Golfo Dulce and around Caño Island Biological Reserve, two important marine habitats near the Osa Peninsula in southern Costa Rica. Instead of relying entirely on expensive underwater cameras and specialized equipment, researchers are using Samsung Galaxy smartphones to photograph sections of the reef. The images are then processed into detailed 3D models that allow scientists to examine coral growth, identify damage and measure changes over time.

The technique, known as underwater photogrammetry, involves taking numerous overlapping photographs of the same area from different angles. Computer software combines the images into a three-dimensional reconstruction, essentially creating a digital copy of the reef. These digital models give researchers a much clearer picture of what is happening beneath the surface than traditional visual inspections alone.

Marine biologist María Laura Sandoval, who manages Raising Coral’s South Pacific restoration program, explained that the technology allows conservation teams to examine entire sections of reef rather than relying exclusively on what a diver can observe during a limited period underwater.

The system also makes it possible to return to the same location months later and compare new images with earlier models, helping researchers determine whether corals are growing, declining or recovering. The project uses Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra phones equipped with a special underwater photography feature called Ocean Mode. The technology helps improve image quality and color accuracy beneath the surface.

Once collected, the photographs are sent to researchers at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California San Diego, where specialized software transforms them into 3D models. The effort is part of a collaboration involving Raising Coral, Samsung, the marine conservation organization SeaTrees and Scripps.

Tracking the Effects of El Niño

The project comes at an important time for Costa Rica’s Pacific reefs, which have faced repeated pressure from unusually warm ocean temperatures. During the 2023–2024 El Niño event, high sea temperatures caused widespread coral bleaching and losses around the Osa Peninsula.

Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel the tiny algae living inside their tissues. These algae provide much of the coral’s food and color, so their disappearance leaves the coral looking pale or completely white. Bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but prolonged exposure to unusually warm water can prevent recovery and eventually kill it.

Researchers began using the smartphone mapping system in December 2025, initially surveying reefs approximately every four months. Since July 2026, however, the team has increased its monitoring to once a month to better observe possible changes associated with El Niño conditions.

The more frequent measurements should help scientists identify changes in coral cover and growth before they become apparent through less detailed monitoring. According to Sandoval, the technology has already helped produce information for a technical assessment supporting coral restoration around Caño Island. The surveyed areas showed coral coverage ranging from approximately 18% to 40%.

Those figures provide a snapshot of conditions in the areas studied, rather than evidence that the reefs have already recovered.

Restoring Costa Rica’s Reefs

Raising Coral has worked on reef restoration in Costa Rica since 2016, beginning in Golfo Dulce before expanding into other coastal areas. The organization grows coral fragments in underwater nurseries and later transfers them onto damaged reefs, where they can continue developing.

Some corals are attached to specially designed metal structures that hold them above the ocean floor, helping protect them from sediment while creating additional habitat for fish and other marine animals. The current restoration partnership aims to grow and transplant approximately 1,000 corals annually between 2026 and 2029, for a total of 4,000 corals across Golfo Dulce and Caño Island.

But planting corals is only part of the challenge. Conservationists must also determine whether transplanted colonies survive, continue growing and eventually help restore the surrounding ecosystem. That is where the 3D mapping technology becomes especially useful. By comparing models captured at different times, researchers can measure changes in individual coral colonies, examine the structure of the reef and monitor the return of marine life.

The information can also help conservation organizations demonstrate whether restoration efforts are producing measurable results.

Making Marine Conservation More Accessible

One of the project’s biggest advantages is its potential to make underwater research more affordable for smaller conservation organizations. Traditionally, creating detailed 3D maps of coral reefs required costly camera systems and specialized training. The use of smartphones could make the process easier for conservation teams with limited budgets.

Local residents are also participating in the project through Raising Coral’s community training program, which prepares people to work as coral gardeners and assist with restoration and monitoring. The approach creates opportunities for coastal communities to become directly involved in protecting the marine ecosystems that support fishing, tourism and other local activities.

Similar smartphone-assisted reef restoration and monitoring work is also taking place in Fiji, the Galápagos Islands and Indonesia. For Costa Rica, the technology could eventually provide a more practical way to monitor marine habitats beyond the current project sites, although its effectiveness on a larger scale still needs to be demonstrated.

Why Healthy Reefs Matter to Costa Rica

Coral reefs support a wide variety of marine life, including fish, sea turtles, sharks and countless smaller organisms. Around Caño Island, reefs provide habitat for numerous fish species and contribute to the area’s reputation as one of Costa Rica’s better-known snorkeling and diving destinations.

Golfo Dulce also supports important marine ecosystems, although its reefs face additional challenges from sediment carried into the water by rivers and runoff from surrounding land. When reefs deteriorate, the effects can extend beyond the corals themselves, reducing habitat for fish and potentially affecting the coastal communities that depend on healthy marine environments.

Restoration efforts cannot eliminate the broader threats posed by warming oceans, pollution and changing ocean conditions. However, better monitoring can help researchers understand which corals are surviving and where conservation work may be most effective. The new technology also makes the underwater world easier to understand for people who may never have the opportunity to see these reefs in person.

Instead of relying solely on scientific measurements, conservationists can use detailed 3D images to show communities, visitors and potential supporters how a reef is changing. Since Costa Rica has built much of its international reputation around protecting nature, the project offers another tool for understanding what is happening beneath the Pacific Ocean and determining whether efforts to restore its coral reefs are succeeding.

World.title: Alejandro Tabilo Falls to Rafael Jódar Again in Paris Masters Opener
World.content:
Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo suffered another disappointing defeat against Rafael Jódar on Monday, losing 6-2, 6-3 in the opening round of the Paris Masters as the Spanish teenager continued his remarkable rise in men’s professional tennis. Jódar, seeded ninth at the season’s final ATP Masters 1000 tournament, needed just one hour and 16 minutes to eliminate the Chilean on the indoor hard courts of Paris La Défense Arena.

The result marked Jódar’s fourth consecutive victory over Tabilo and his second against the Chilean in less than a week. The two players had met on October 27 at the Swiss Indoors in Basel, where Jódar won 6-4, 6-2. Their quick rematch in Paris offered Tabilo an opportunity to reverse that result, but the Spaniard once again proved too difficult to overcome.

Tabilo, ranked No. 30 in the world, entered the match hoping to end a difficult stretch of results on the European indoor circuit. Instead, he managed just five games against an opponent who has become one of his toughest matchups this season. Jódar, 20, arrived in Paris ranked No. 11 and was competing in his first tournament since entering the world’s top 10 in the latest rankings.

The Spaniard has enjoyed an extraordinary 2026 campaign, establishing himself among the leading young players on the ATP Tour and reaching the Shanghai Masters final in October. His success has also put him in contention for a place at the ATP Finals in Turin, where the season’s leading singles players compete for the year-end championship.

Monday’s victory keeps those hopes alive while adding another difficult result to Tabilo’s recent record. The two players have now met five times in 2026, with Jódar holding a commanding 4-1 advantage. Their first meeting came in March at Indian Wells, where Tabilo recorded a convincing 6-1, 6-2 victory.

At the time, the Chilean appeared to have the upper hand in the matchup. But the balance shifted dramatically during the North American hard-court season. Jódar defeated Tabilo in three sets in the Washington semifinals in August, recovering from losing the opening set to win 6-7(8), 6-4, 6-4.

They met again later that month at the Cincinnati Open, where the Spaniard delivered an even more convincing performance, winning 6-2, 6-1. The pattern continued in Basel last week and again in Paris on Monday. For Tabilo, the defeat extends a frustrating period in which strong performances earlier in the season have given way to repeated early tournament exits.

The Chilean reached the final of the Rio Open in February, losing to Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry after a competitive three-set match. He also made the fourth round of the French Open and reached the semifinals of the Washington ATP 500 tournament during the summer.

Those results demonstrated his ability to compete at a high level on both clay and hard courts. However, his results have become less consistent during the final months of the season. After reaching the second round in Tokyo, where he defeated American Tommy Paul before losing to Denis Shapovalov, Tabilo exited the Shanghai Masters against Spain’s Pablo Carreño Busta.

He then suffered successive first-round defeats to Jódar in Basel and Paris. The latest result highlights the challenge Tabilo faces against the tour’s emerging generation, particularly opponents who can maintain pressure throughout a match and prevent him from establishing his preferred rhythm.

Tabilo, a left-handed player who reached a career-high ranking of No. 19, has demonstrated that he can defeat leading opponents when his serve and aggressive groundstrokes are working effectively. But his recent meetings with Jódar have exposed the difficulty of reproducing that level consistently against a player whose confidence has grown throughout the season.

For Jódar, the victory represents another step toward the ATP Finals and a continuation of his breakthrough year. For Tabilo, Paris ends almost as quickly as Basel did, leaving the Chilean with another early exit and questions about how to regain his best form heading into the 2027 season.

His immediate challenge will be turning the positive results from earlier in 2026 into more consistent performances against the world’s leading players.

World.title: Costa Rica Reopens Cambronero Highway After Nearly Two-Months
World.content:
Costa Rica has reopened the Cambronero section of Route 1, restoring an important highway connection between the Central Valley and the Pacific coast after nearly two months of closure caused by damage to a temporary bridge. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) confirmed that traffic resumed on Sunday at approximately 5:30 p.m., following repairs to the modular bridge at kilometer 71 of the Inter-American Highway between San Ramón and Esparza.

The reopening comes as welcome news for drivers, freight companies and travelers who have been forced to use alternative routes since September 7, when a tractor-trailer struck the bridge and caused extensive damage to its metal structure. The accident forced authorities to close the crossing while engineers assessed the damage and determined how to repair the bridge safely.

The closure disrupted one of Costa Rica’s main road connections between the Central Valley and the northwestern Pacific region, sending additional traffic onto Route 27 and other roads. According to MOPT, the repairs cost approximately ₡380 million and involved a complicated process of removing damaged components, reinforcing the bridge and reinstalling it.

Before workers could replace the affected sections, they had to construct a temporary support structure capable of holding the bridge’s weight. Crews then removed portions of the bridge deck, moved sections of the metal framework and replaced damaged pieces before returning the structure to its original position.

The work also included reinforcing the bridge and making additional improvements intended to increase safety for motorists. MOPT and the National Road Council (Conavi) said the repairs allowed them to reopen the route earlier than initially expected. Although vehicles can once again travel through Cambronero, authorities emphasized that the repairs are temporary and do not resolve the underlying instability affecting the hillside.

The modular bridge provides a single-lane crossing while the government prepares a permanent solution to restore the original two lanes. Drivers should continue using caution when approaching the bridge, following posted traffic controls and allowing additional time for possible delays.

Some additional work will continue in the area, although authorities have indicated that these activities should not require another prolonged closure. The government is moving forward with a larger project intended to stabilize the hillside and restore the highway to its original configuration.

MOPT and Conavi have received eight bids from companies interested in carrying out the permanent work. Officials expect to evaluate those proposals during the remainder of 2026, with construction potentially beginning during the second quarter of 2027. The project would address the ground instability that originally made the modular bridge necessary and eventually allow the temporary structure to be removed.

However, the timeline will depend on the government completing the contracting process and selecting a company to perform the work. Public Works Minister Efraím Zeledón has also discussed the possibility of eventually adding a third lane in the area, although that idea remains under evaluation and is not part of an approved construction plan.

Cambronero has experienced repeated problems with landslides and unstable terrain over the years, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall. The mountainous section of the Inter-American Highway has steep slopes and difficult geological conditions, making repairs and maintenance especially challenging.

The reopening should provide relief for motorists traveling between San José, San Ramón, Esparza and destinations farther along the Pacific coast. During the closure, drivers were directed toward alternative routes, including Route 27 between San José and Caldera and Route 3 through the Monte del Aguacate.

Those detours increased travel distances and created additional expenses for businesses transporting goods between the Central Valley and northwestern Costa Rica. The disruption was particularly significant for trucks and commercial vehicles, which faced additional fuel costs, tolls and longer journeys.

Tourists driving between San José and destinations in Puntarenas and Guanacaste also had fewer options for reaching the Pacific coast. With Cambronero reopened, drivers once again have access to the Route 1 connection, although the temporary bridge means the crossing has not returned to normal two-lane operations.

For now, the government is asking motorists to drive carefully through the area and respect traffic controls while work continues. The immediate road connection has been restored, but the larger challenge of permanently stabilizing this vulnerable section of Costa Rica’s Inter-American Highway remains unresolved.

World.title: US Midterm Vote Won’t Necessarily Lift Costa Rica’s 12.5% Tariff
World.content:
Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States could reshape the political climate around the 12.5% tariff Washington applies to many Costa Rican goods. But two international relations analysts say a change in control of Congress would not, by itself, bring that duty down. Voters on November 3 will choose all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 33 of the 100 Senate seats. Republicans currently control both chambers.

Analyst Carlos Murillo said the tariff is among the most sensitive issues for Costa Rica in the vote. He warned that President Donald Trump could rely on other legal instruments to keep his trade policy in place even if Congress or the courts push back, so a new majority would not automatically reverse measures that affect the country. What could change, Murillo said, is the political context in which those measures are applied.

The tariff took effect on July 24. It stems from investigations the Office of the US Trade Representative opened in March under Section 301 of US trade law into some 60 economies, over what Washington called insufficient efforts to block imports of goods made with forced labor. Costa Rica landed at the top of a range of 10% to 12.5%.

Coffee, pineapple, bananas, orange juice, plant cuttings, fruit and vegetable seeds, and certain refined sugars remain excluded, according to the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex). Trade Minister Indiana Trejos said at the time that Costa Rica respects labor rights and rules-based trade, and that her ministry would keep working with exporters and Washington to improve market access.

Nuria Marín, also an international relations analyst, described the midterms as a referendum on Trump’s presidency. She said Democrats have strong chances of retaking the House, while the Senate is harder to call. She put the president’s approval at around 30%, down from a peak of about 50% in March 2025, and said that level of support is not normal in the United States. Marín linked the slide to rising prices driven by tariffs and higher energy costs, which she said have squeezed household budgets for the same voters who backed Trump’s promise to fix the economy.

A Congress with more Democrats could tighten oversight of the president, particularly on trade, she said. But she cautioned that many decisions rest with the executive branch, so lawmakers would not be able to block everything. That limit extends to two other areas that matter to Costa Rica. In the analyst Marín’s view, a change in legislative control would not necessarily alter US migration policy or anti-drug cooperation directly, because both fall largely under the executive, where Trump retains broad powers.

Security ties between the two countries have been a recurring focus. US Ambassador Melinda Hildebrand met with representatives of the Supreme Court, the Public Ministry and the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) on September 30 and reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to fighting drug trafficking.

Murillo said Costa Rica has taken on significant commitments with the United States on policing, military and organized crime matters, which raises the stakes of any shift in US foreign policy or regional security priorities. He also pointed to fuel. Gasoline and diesel prices are a decisive issue for US voters because they hit family spending directly, he said. In Costa Rica, he added, local fuel prices are trending upward but have not yet fully reflected international increases because of the country’s price-setting system.

Murillo said the loss of a Republican majority could also sharpen confrontation between Trump and his opponents in Congress. Both analysts suggested that the policies with the most direct effect on Costa Rica, from the tariff to migration rules and security cooperation, will continue to be shaped largely by the White House rather than Capitol Hill, whatever the result on Tuesday.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Pesticide Problem and the Beauty of Backyard Gardening
World.content:
Isn’t it ironic that Costa Rica, our country famed throughout the world for its amazing flora and fauna, is also at or near the top worldwide for pesticide and herbicide use per unit of farmland? Ironic, and disgusting. And infuriating. Infuriating because this land is blessedly fertile. One can quite literally throw a few seeds into the ground and with a bit of care, watch plants come to life naturally. Home gardens flourish throughout the nation, and while all are not 100 percent organic, chemical use is typically minimal.

Of course, it is not the backyard planting responsible for the unwanted ranking. The main culprit is big agro. Multinational companies convert huge swaths of land into monoculture farms. Banana and pineapple plantations apply massive amounts of chemicals with names like mancozeb, glyphosate and ethoprophos in order to kill fungi, weeds, and anything else that might endanger the profitable yield of the valuable export crops.

I once spent a year in a small town in the southern zone of Costa Rica that was located in the heart of Del Monte’s pineapple plantations. The village was surrounded by a vast desert of pineapples. Almost everyone in the area worked for the company. Pay was minimal, but there were other benefits such as a free clinic for the laborers, a necessity due to the harsh labor-intensive work, that required long hours in the hot sun, and regular exposure to the variety of unhealthy chemicals used to ensure a steady supply of pineapples to sell worldwide.

There is an interesting parallel between this type of agriculture and the mega-resorts beginning to spring up in Costa Rica. Both are sources of steady employment for locals. Both are owned and operated primarily by outsiders. Both pay lip service to the environment. Mega resort developers will chop down trees, fill in mangroves, handle sewage and waste haphazardly, and either pay whatever fines come their way, or pay the right officials to look the other way.

Everywhere I have lived in Costa Rica, we have done our own small personal gardening. I live on a 700 square meter lot in a barrio of San Isidro de el General, about one mile uphill from downtown.
