World.title: Watch: Unseen images of drone sinking Greek tanker off Bulgarian coast
World.content:
Euronews has obtained images of the Liberian-flagged vessel targeted by sea drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast on 28 October.

 

The incident marked the fifth drone attack recorded in the NATO country’s exclusive economic zone last month.

The Greek-managed Contship Jet tanker was travelling from Israel’s port of Haifa to Constanța in Romania when it was struck by three maritime drones.

All 18 crew members - 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians - were rescued by Bulgarian naval and border police vessels and taken to the port city of Varna for medical checks.

Image of Greek-managed Contship Jet tanker which was impacted by sea drones, 28 October 2026 Euronews

Bulgaria's Military District Prosecutor's Office announced it had opened a preliminary investigation into the attack the next day. Russia is suspected of being behind a recent wave of attacks targeting commercial vessels in the Black Sea.

Some of the containers on board were carrying lithium-ion batteries, flammable liquids, gases and other hazardous materials, the maritime.bg site reported. Navy teams reported no signs of pollution after taking samples from several locations in Bulgarian territorial waters.

Image of Greek-managed Contship Jet tanker which was impacted by sea drones, 28 October 2026 Euronews

The incident came as defence ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey met in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, to discuss security in the Black Sea region.

In a statement after the talks, the three NATO countries strongly condemned the strikes on vessels in the Black Sea and called for an “immediate cessation of attacks that threaten commercial ships, maritime infrastructure and the safety of maritime activities.”

They also agreed on stronger intelligence sharing, early warning capabilities and coordination in the region.

Sea drone which struck Greek-managed Contship Jet tanker, 28 October 2026 Euronews

A recent wave of such incidents off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria has led some alliance members to wonder if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to test their support for Ukraine as it continues to fight against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country's parliament earlier this month that “the logic points in that direction … The problem is that we cannot prove it.”

The crew aboard the tanker were rescued by Bulgarian naval and border police vessels, 28 October 2026 Euronews

In response to the attacks, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on 15 October in a post on X that the alliance had "strengthened" its "posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities."

World.title: Ebola kills over 5,300 in fastest-growing outbreak on record
World.content:
Africa's latest Ebola outbreak has killed nearly 5,400 people, the vast majority of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), according to the continent's top health agency.

 

Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) told the AFP on Monday that the outbreak, which has spread to other countries on the continent, has killed 5,376 people – 5,372 in the DRC and two each in Kenya and Uganda.

The outbreak, which began in the DRC in May, has infected more than 10,000 people, with an over 50% fatality rate, according to the country’s latest data from 31 October, making it the fastest-growing and most widespread Ebola epidemic on record.

Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 cases, almost all involving people who had travelled from the DRC, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

In October, Kenya recorded nine infections, marking the first time the country had reported an Ebola case.

That same month, Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, reported an Ebola case involving a 42-year-old Swiss woman whose husband works at his country’s embassy in Abuja. The couple had travelled to Uganda before returning home.

The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment. The virus is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and causes haemorrhagic fever.

In recent weeks, clinical trials of the Ervebo vaccine, which has proved effective against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, have begun.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to block 20,000 California midterm ballots
World.content:
The Trump administration has appealed to the Supreme Court over claims that a list of more than 20,000 ballots in California include non-US citizens. Multiple courts and independent analysis have rejected the claims.

On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump is making a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.

The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, claims to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls. In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations.

A district court judge rejected the DoJ request, warning that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.

"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," wrote Los Angeles District Judge David Carter in rejecting the Trump administration's initial lawsuit in October.

Battle for US midterm elections heats up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In bringing its case to the Supreme Court on Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.

Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.

It is unclear if the Supreme Court will respond in time for a ruling to have an effect on tomorrow's election.

Analysis shows thousands of eligible voters on ballot blacklist

The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.

Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).

A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.

Trump's fixation on voter fraud

Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.

For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own ​constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.

The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.

California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.

Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.

World.title: France: Petition to ban TV channel gets 500,000 signatures
World.content:
Support for the petition has surged since last month's shooting of a Black man by a reported avid viewer of CNews. Critics say the channel, often compared to Fox News, is a platform for anti-immigrant sentiments.

A petition urging the French government to ban a television news channel known for its hard line on immigration and crime has accrued more than 500,000 signatures amid accusations that its sensationalist coverage contributed to the racist killing of a Black man.

The petition to shut down CNews was launched in June, but support spiked after a Frenchman of Congolese origin was killed in a racially motivated attack in the Paris suburbs on October 23.

A 39-year-old man has been charged with murder and attempted murder over the incident in the commuter towns of Trappes and La Verriere west of Paris in which he said he was "targeting individuals who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African," a prosecutor has said.

France: What is CNews?

French media have reported that the suspect was an avid consumer of CNews, which has been described as a French version of Fox News and criticized for giving too much airtime to anti-immigrant rhetoric.

The petition to "remove CNews from French broadcasting" argues that the channel, which is owned ​by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bollore, is not an ​information channel but a"propaganda machine."

Critics have claimed that CNews' broadcasting increasingly mimics lines taken by ​Le Pen's far-right National Rally (RN), which is leading in polls ahead of next year's presidential election.

Le Pen has promised to privatize public broadcasting in France, a policy from which CNews would stand to benefit.

At a rally in the northern Paris suburb of Aubervilliers last week, protesters held up posters reading slogans such as "CNews kills."

During nationwide cost-of-living protests on October 17, protesters threw projectiles and broke windows at the channel's Paris headquarters.

Meanwhile, two Green lawmakers have urged France's lower house of parliament to withdraw accreditation for CNews to protect "democracy" from "racist hatred."

Earlier this year, France expelled Russian news pundit Xenia Fedorova, who had been accused of peddling Kremlin propaganda on CNews.

Le Pen launches presidential campaign amid unrest in France To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CNews refuses to comment on 'political petition'

The channel has also been accused of broadcasting racist comments about Bally Bagayoko, a Frenchman of Malian descent who is the mayor of Paris' largest suburb, Saint-Denis, and who has gained prominence for his role in defending students in his constituency against police violence during recent protests.

CNews, which has previously denied allegations it promotes far-right views and racist tropes, saying it defends freedom of expression, told the French AFP news agency it would not comment on a "political petition."

At its launch in 2017, CNews had just a 1% market share but last year became France's most-watched free-to-air news channel.

Under National Assembly rules, a ⁠public ​debate can be organized in parliament ​if a petition attracts at least 500,000 signatures.

However, a parliamentary commission must ​ first review the petition and decide whether a debate can take place.

World.title: What might Trump have planned for Iran following the midterm election?
World.content:
While the US midterms could open a window for diplomacy with Iran, they could also unleash a new military escalation. DW spoke with analysts to identify eight factors that could tip the balance toward war or peace.

The US Republican Party is entering the midterm elections with Donald Trump's administration seemingly unable to either win or diplomatically resolve the Iran war. If the Republicans lose control of the US Congress, the administration will have to navigate an entirely different political landscape for the rest of Trump's second term, but the course of the war is not decided just in Washington — or in Tehran.

Seeking to identify key factors that could tip the balance towards war or peace in Iran, DW spoke with Omid Memarian of DAWN, a Washington-based think tank focused on reforming the US's Middle East policy; the Finland-based political scientist Leila Morovati; and Babak Rezaeedaryakenari, a professor of international relations at Leiden University in the Netherlands.

1. US midterms: Is Trump set for more scrutiny?

A Democratic victory would push Trump to focus more on domestic issues and would likely expose the financial costs of the war in the US Congress, Memarian told DW. However, Trump could continue limited strikes on Iran without formally declaring war.

Memarian said Trump would seek a way out that "saves face" after Tuesday's election.

With Trump, Memarian said, Iran is engaged in a "big gamble with someone who does not behave like a conventional politician." This increases the risk of renewed attacks.

How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rezaeedaryakenari made a similar point: "The president has broad authority and freedom of action, especially in foreign policy and the conduct of military operations. A Republican defeat, even with increased pressure from Congress, doesn't necessarily stop new attacks."

2. Deadlock in Israel puts pressure on Netanyahu

Israel's October 27 election ended in deadlock. Neither the coalition around incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, nor the camp supporting former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot managed to secure an outright majority.

Memarian said the political uncertainty could push Netanyahu to act on major decisions while he still wields power — making the transition period the "most fragile and dangerous" for renewed escalation.

No clear winner emerges in Israel's election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A change of government in Israel would not fundamentally alter Israel's Iran policy, Memarian said. Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, "may be more deferential to America" and coordinate more closely with Washington. But ties with Trump are personal, and Eisenkot "certainly won't be like Netanyahu, who could sell any plan or scenario to Trump."

Rezaeedaryakenari said Israel's security concerns about Iran "are not limited to Netanyahu himself." A new government could change the timing of a confrontation and coordination with Washington, but the security establishment and ruling coalition would also shape the risk of an attack, he said.

3. Nuclear impasse: 'The ladder of tension'

Iran's nuclear program remains the biggest open issue between the governments, with the US rejecting the Iranian narrative that the program is meant only for civilian use.

But the two sides are also at odds on how the talks themselves should be set up, Memarian said.

"The US wants negotiations to start not only with a focus on Iran's nuclear program, but with concessions right at the outset," he said.

Iran seeks the lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen assets before nuclear talks begin. If the sides don't move closer, Memarian warns, the odds of a renewed war rise.

Until the sides agree on an agenda, Memarian said, they are likely to keep "climbing the ladder of tension."

Morovati, a Finland-based political analyst, said the nuclear program was "the crux" of the standoff. Iran's government sees it as a survival guarantee and bargaining chip, she said. In turn, Washington fears that a nuclear Iran would upend its security calculations and long-term strategy for the Middle East and beyond, which is why it insists on putting the issue on the table first.

4. Strait of Hormuz: Is Iran's leverage also a risk factor?

Before the United States and Israel launched the war in late February, about 20% of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has since drastically cut on the energy exports through the naval chokepoint, using at as leverage on US and Israel.

But, Memarian said, Iran's restrictions in the strait won't trigger escalation on their own.

Should US officials decide that a broader attack is needed to change Iran's calculations, any incident could serve as a pretext, Memarian said. If Washington considers the risks too high, it may opt for an economic blockade while keeping negotiations on the table. In that scenario, "even occasional tensions in the Strait of Hormuz won't pull America into war," according to the US-based analyst.

5. The Houthis in Yemen: Iran's allies, not subordinates

The Houthi rebels in Yemen have also been targeting energy exports on the Red Sea — including attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure. But Memarian notes the Yemeni rebels' roots and struggle are "entirely domestic and organic" despite their ideological closeness to Tehran.

Memarian said the Houthis made "pragmatic calculations" and their actions did not necessarily translate into an escalation between Iran and the United States.

Still, the United States could use the rebels' action as a pretext to strike Iran again.

More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rezaeedaryakenari offered a slightly different assessment. Houthi attacks on shipping and on countries in the region, he says, "can both widen the war and accelerate coalition-building against the Islamic Republic." Countries that don't want war with Tehran "may turn to closer military cooperation to protect their trade and security." That doesn't necessarily mean entering the war directly, he adds, "but it could narrow the Islamic Republic's room for maneuver."

6. Regional mediators: Four countries with a lot at stake

With direct talks between the governments of Iran and the United States stalled, the world turned its attention to Qatar, Oman, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. While each nation plays a different role in the crisis, they all have a direct stake in ending the war.

"They are close to the US, but also want to maintain ties with Iran and build regional alliances to prevent future conflicts," Memarian said.

Morovati said the failure of the United States to support its Arab allies during the war could eventually push them to reconsider their policies and turn to the US's rivals.

7. What will Trump administration do after the election?

During the campaign, Trump said he expected a deal with Iran soon after the midterm elections. Meanwhile, the Reuters news agency cited three senior Iranian officials and an additional source as saying that Tehran has deliberately prolonged talks to weaken Trump politically.

Memarian said Iran's leaders believed that a Republican defeat would increase pressure on Trump to end the war. But Trump will remain the key foreign policy decision-maker, and congressional pressure is unlikely to play a deciding role.

He said the present moment offers the "best opportunity" to end the standoff before Trump leaves office in January 2029.

"Iran's leaders need to think about their endgame," Memarian said, warning that Trump could launch a massive attack, inflict serious damage and then declare victory.

Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rezaeedaryakenari said "escalatory factors" would have the upper hand in the coming months — and the likelihood of a military escalation is high.

Iran's government can only avert a new round of war with a fundamental policy shift and concessions that the country's leaders would consider close to surrender. However, he said, such a retreat would also threaten the regime's survival by weakening its ideological justification and eroding support.

8. Economic toll: Warring parties not at breaking point

High oil prices, shipping risks and economic strain are putting pressure on all sides as the war enters its ninth month. Could that push Tehran, Washington and regional capitals toward compromise?

"The economy is the Achilles' heel of every party to this war," Morovati said, "and that holds even for countries beyond the region."

Energy prices as a source of pressure on the US government, Morovati said.

"We've seen that energy supply and the expectations of the American public have been influential," Morovati said, "and this is one of the problems the Trump administration faces."

At the same time, Morovati said, Arab countries do not act as a united bloc toward Tehran.

"If they come under severe security and economic pressure, they may take joint action, but so far that hasn't happened in practice," Morovati said.

What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Memarian also sees the economic costs as an incentive for a deal. But he also claims that each side believes that inflicting more pain on the other will strengthen its hand in future talks.

"That can easily turn this into a war of attrition, and in recent months that has been the approach," Memarian said. Neither side has yet reached the point where it sees compromise as unavoidable.

World.title: Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia
World.content:
Ice hockey's ruling body is deciding how to respond to a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport that allows Russia back into international competition. Germany hasn't ruled out pulling out as a tournament host.

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, announced shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for this Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," said Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities. We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions."

Franz Reindl, 71, was elected president of the IIHF in early October Image: ActionPictures/IMAGO

The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.

Canada to 'maintain restrictions' on Russian athletes

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."

Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he said in a statement.

German hosts mull 'possible consequences for Worlds

Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim next May.

"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.

"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly."

Frank Lutz is expected to meet with government officials in Berlin this week Image: Adrian Goldberg/BEAUTIFUL SPORTS/picture alliance

The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.

Many disappointed, Russia delighted

Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

The International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.

Russian reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

The Russian Olympic Committee team won silver at their last tournament, the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing Image: Maxim Thore/Bildbyran/IMAGO

No return to business as usual

A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations appears to be a possibility.

Latvia is prohibited by law from competing against Russian teams. Finland has said individual players would be free to opt-out of tournaments that include Russia, while Swedish Ice Hockey Association chairman Anders Larsson, who is a member of the IIHF Council, told Swedish news agency TT that "a boycott is not on the table."

However, at the same time he also noted that "our position is that Russia cannot participate in international championships in the current situation."

Further-reaching implications?

There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.

Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all."

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

World.title: European supermarkets targeted in second reported cyberattack
World.content:
Supermarkets across Europe have been targeted in cyberattacks once again. Three weeks after a defrosting attack in France, supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden reported freezer malfunctions.

Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden reported anomalies in their freezer systems on Monday in an apparent cyberattack similar to one in France three weeks ago in which unidentified malign actors were accused of having hijacked refrigeration systems — setting them to defrost and spoiling fresh and frozen foods.

In Monday's incident, Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop said "a limited number" of shops had been hit, with ICA spokeswoman Helena Johansson saying the company is "looking into what has happened and the scale of it."

"Fridges and freezers have either stopped working entirely or have been partially impaired," Coop spokesman Carlos Cancino told the French AFP news agency. He noted that six of roughly 800 Coop stores in Sweden had been impacted, adding, "I haven't received any information that this is a cyberattack."

Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize on Monday said an overnight "IT incident" had hit freezers in several of its stores in Belgium and Luxembourg.

In Ireland, public broadcasterer RTE reported that 13 supermarkets had been impacted.

Chains Carrefour, Intermarche and Spar were targeted as well, with Carrefour's Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen saying, "It's a cyberattack… There's no other reason."

Belgium's prosecutor's office opened a criminal investigation into the attack, the Reuters news agency quoted a spokesperson as saying.

'A deliberate attempt to disrupt European food supplies'

European Commissioner ‌for Agriculture and ‌Food ​Christophe Hansen on Monday called the attacks "a deliberate attempt to disrupt Europe's food supplies," stating that ⁠while "food ​security is ​not currently ​at risk, ‌the food waste ​and ⁠impact on businesses ⁠are ​real."

"These incidents ‌show ​that cyberattacks can disrupt services, affect ​businesses and directly affect ⁠citizens’ ​daily lives" added ​a Commission ​spokesperson.

Though no one has claimed responsibility, authorities are convinced that problems with freezer cooling and defrosting systems at European supermarkets are the result of remote cyberattacks Image: Marie Mannes/REUTERS

How are hackers getting into supermarket refrigeration systems?

As on October 12, Monday's disruption prompted the discarding of spoiled products and again raised concerns about food security.

The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjobo in southern Sweden said temperatures in their systems were remotely dialed up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).

Monday's outages in Sweden mirrored a similar situation in early October that saw dozens of supermarkets targeted in France Image: Fredrik Sandberg/TT NEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

Sweden's National Cybersecurity Center boss John Billow told the Reuters news agency on Monday that his department is investigating.

"We have in recent weeks... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed ⁠operational technology devices in Sweden that ​we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch," he added.

That "exposed operational technology" includes everything from refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras, alarm networks and an expanding ‌range ​of devices that were once largely mechanical but are now often monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals as they seek to exploit security vulnerabilities.

World.title: LA communities kick out Big Oil
World.content:
After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Oil infrastructure is running just a stone's throw away from homes in LA neighborhoods Image: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

Why residents campaigned to end city oil drilling

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

How LA is plugging hidden oil wells To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

Previous attempts to ban oil production

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

Some oil wells are hidden in plain sight, such as this building hiding an active oil-drilling operation Image: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

Who will foot the bill for the cleanup?

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup." For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

World.title: Germany's chancellor called for Korean unity. Does Seoul want that?
World.content:
Germany, like Korea, was once divided by rival political systems and by one of the world's most fortified borders. Chancellor Merz called for a reunified Korea during his recent visit — but the prospect seems faint.

The story of South and North Korea — two nations that share history, language and much of their cultural heritage — sounds familiar to Germans.

Their own country spent decades divided by opposing regimes until geopolitical winds shifted and allowed East and West Germany to reunite peacefully in 1991.

Just two years later, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl visited the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on the Korean Peninsula and expressed hope that South and North Korea would also be reunited by the end of the decade.

That never materialized. Some 35 years since Germany achieved its dream of reunification, Seoul and Pyongyang are still bitterly divided by political systems, economy, and their geopolitical alliances.

German chancellor and president tour Asia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Overlooking the DMZ, which separates the two Koreas, on Friday Chancellor Friedrich Merz could only repeat the hopes stated by Kohl in 1993.

"We Germans know how painful the division of a country is," Merz stated in a message shared on social media. "We also know that whoever stands firm in their values and has the courage for dialogue can tear down walls."

"We wish the people in Korea unity in freedom," Merz said.

To analysts following the day-to-day inter-Korean politics, this sounds like a distant dream.

Young Koreans ask 'why bother' with reunification

As the Koreas continue to eye each other warily across the DMZ, their dramatic differences in wealth and political freedom are clearly on display.

But the biggest single issue might be that neither side appears to want reunification.

"The feeling has changed in the last couple of decades," Choo Jae-woo, a professor of foreign policy at Kyung Hee University, told DW. "Younger South Koreans just see the North as another country that happens to be next to us, is poor and threatening, and they have no sentimental attachment to it, like older generations do."

"More and more people are asking why they should bother about reunification," he said.

Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A study by Seoul National University's Institute for Peace and Unification Studies in September indicated that 39.1% of South Koreans believed reunification was impossible, the highest proportion since the survey was started some two decades ago.

Many were concerned about the vast amounts of money that it would take to build the North's infrastructure, including roads, hospitals, schools and all other requirements for a modern functioning society.

Officially, South Korea's government has not abandoned reunification as a national objective. Its constitution still calls for peaceful union based on freedom and democracy, but Choo points out recent governments are promoting the idea far less frequently than in the past.

North Korea's clear signal against unity

North Korea has not been nearly so reticent about where it stands on the matter.

"In December 2023, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced that the constitution was being changed and that peaceful reunification was no longer possible," Choo said. "Instead, South Korea would be seen as a hostile rival and that he no longer had any intention of bringing the two together."

The revised North Korean constitution was approved in March 2026 and Kim's regime has moved aggressively to scrub all references to reconciliation and national unity.

"I do not think the North can make it any clearer that it has no intention of getting any closer to South Korea," said Mason Richey, a professor of politics and international relations at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul. He added that analysts, officials and ordinary Koreans in the South "roll their eyes" when the issue of Korean reunification crops up.

Beyond the lack of desire on both sides, there are a number of additional challenges that would need to be overcome, he said.

North Korea's regime wishes to protect its own power and prestige, which would inevitably be under threat if a democratic system were introduced for a unified nation.

Bridging the enormous gap in economic development would be a huge undertaking that would put immense pressure on the South, Richey said, even if outside assistance were forthcoming. And while a united Germany has been able to bring its regions to relatively comparable levels, it is worth noting that East Germany in 1990 was still substantially more developed than North Korea is today.

Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

United Korea would pose major issues for US and China

Professor Choo said reunification would not just be a domestic issue. The two nations have divided strategic and security loyalties, with the South allied to the US and the North tied to China and increasingly, Russia.

Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Those superpowers would not want to give up their ally for reunification as it would be a major strategic issue for them, as well," Choo said. "The US would not want a united Korea that leaned towards China, and Beijing would resist reunification if it meant the US could have its military on the Chinese border in what is presently North Korea. That's just impossible for either side to imagine."

Ultimately, he said, the present status quo on the peninsula may be an imperfect solution, but it is the best way of preserving regional stability. A decade into the future, however, the economic, social and security situations may have radically altered — "and that is why we can never say never."

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Global pedestrian Karl Bushby returns home to UK after 28-year trek
World.content:
Karl Bushby, a British man who traveled 50,000 km without transport over the past 28 years, has come home. Starting in Chile, he crossed the Americas, Russia and parts of Central Asia and Europe — almost all on foot.

British adventurer Karl Bushby, 57, arrived back his hometown in England on Monday after crossing four continents on foot.

He was met by a cheering crowd of about 500 people in the northeastern city of Hull at the end of his 50,000-kilometer (31,000-mile) journey, which began in the far south of South America in 1998.

"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team, Earth. That's what it took to get me back," Bushby told the crowd.

On his trip, he obeyed two rules: to avoid all forms of motorized transport to advance; and not to return until he had finished what he had set out to do.

A very final leg of his journey was to take him to north Hull, where he was to reunite with his mother, Angela, his 36-year-old son, Adam, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

Bushby was welcomed by a large crowd in his hometown of Hull Image: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

What did Bushby experience on his epic journey?

Bushby, a former paratrooper, began his adventure in Chile aged 29 after a marriage breakup that saw his wife return to Northern Ireland with their son.

During the trip, he crossed an iced-over Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia with French explorer Dimitri Kieffer in 2006 — nearly losing his life in the process — and, returning to Britain early last month, he swam the English Channel from northern France to Dover over four days.

He interrupted, or was forced to pause, his journey several times, including when he was refused a visa by Russia, which caused a journey originally planned to take 12 years to last more than double that time.

He also spent some jail time in Panama for entering the country without a visa.

The COVID-19 pandemic also caused delays, and he spent some time living at a base in Mexico.

But he always resumed the trek at the exact spot where he had left off.

Bushby transported the necessaries largely on a handcart Image: Paul Ellis/AFP

The famous German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled "Walk of Life."

In an interview with the AFP news agency from northern France in September, Bushby expressed apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.

"I've got to try and get established in the grown-up world again," he said.

World.title: Feijóo se reivindica como gestor tras el accidente de Urda: “España no se arregla con frivolidad ni tampoco con bravuconadas”
World.content:
Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha reivindicado este lunes ante la plana mayor del PP “la gestión, el rigor y la experiencia” frente a la “frivolidad y las bravuconadas”. Con ese mensaje, el líder del PP busca ponerse en valor como candidato a la presidencia del Gobierno frente a los cabeza de lista del PSOE y de Vox, Pedro Sánchez y Santiago Abascal, y capitalizar electoralmente el fuerte impacto de la tragedia ferroviaria de Urda en la sociedad española. El jefe de los populares, que ha reunido este lunes festivo al Comité Ejecutivo Nacional en la sede del partido, ha defendido también que debería ser el presidente del Gobierno, y no el ministro de Transportes, quien “diera la cara” este martes ante la Diputación Permanente por la catástrofe. “Si de mí dependiese”, ha expresado Feijóo ante los suyos, “os garantizo que el que daría mañana la cara no sería el ministro, sería el presidente, porque el ministro ya habría cesado”. Feijóo ha subido el tono y ha tildado de “infame”, “cruel y ”ruin” la actitud de Óscar Puente.

La dirección del PP ha guardado un minuto de silencio por las víctimas de la catástrofe ferroviaria y ha estallado también en un largo aplauso cuando Feijóo ha recordado en su discurso a la exministra de Trabajo Fátima Báñez, fallecida en el accidente, que fue una dirigente muy querida en las filas populares. Muchos barones y cuadros del PP que llegaban a Génova reconocían la dificultad de retomar la actividad política con normalidad. “Ahí vamos, entre la tristeza y volver a empezar”, admitía un presidente autonómico a las puertas de la sede del PP.

En ese contexto, el discurso del líder del PP se ha centrado en reivindicarse como un gestor para tomar las riendas del país tras la conmoción por el segundo accidente mortal en la alta velocidad en un año, frente a Sánchez y Abascal. “La frivolidad no arregla los problemas, tampoco las bravuconadas”, ha reflexionado Feijóo en referencia velada a uno y otro. “Para resolverlos hace falta rigor, criterio y capacidad de gestión. No me cansaré de repetirlo. Por eso vuelvo a reiterar, reivindico la gestión, el rigor y la experiencia y por eso reivindico la seriedad. Amigos, la seriedad no es un defecto, la seriedad es una forma de respeto y los españoles de una vez por todas merecen respeto”.

Feijóo ha insistido en ese mensaje, con el que busca también cortocircuitar el posible repunte de Vox, que ya ha crecido antes en otras crisis graves. “España no necesita al frente de sus instituciones a un influencer, sino a alguien que sepa gobernar, y con toda humildad digo: yo sí sé hacerlo”, ha remarcado. Los populares han decidido redirigir la campaña hacia la gestión tratando de reforzar el perfil presidenciable del líder y buscando conjurar en ese terreno el riesgo de otro avance de la extrema derecha por una reacción emocional de la sociedad española ante el desastre ferroviario.

Con esa estrategia, el PP cree también que puede captar a votantes descontentos del PSOE, como Génova sostiene que está ocurriendo ya, según sus trackings internos, en los que está aumentando la transferencia procedente de los socialistas al PP. Pero los populares mantienen, a su vez, una fuga con Vox, que intentan frenar también girando el marco de la conversación hacia la gestión de lo público y endureciendo el tono. “En la gestión es donde no nos adelanta ni Abascal ni Sánchez”, afirman fuentes de Génova. La sensación entre los barones del PP es que Vox crecerá porque capitaliza el enfado pero que “se va a poner en valor el perfil de gestión cuando la gente ve que está en peligro la seguridad”, opina uno de ellos en privado. Los presidentes autonómicos populares ven en todo caso las elecciones sentenciadas. “Esto el PSOE no lo levanta, es imposible que le den la vuelta”, reflexionaba uno de ellos a las puertas de Génova.

Feijóo se presenta como un gestor, pero también eleva el tono para competir con Vox, y este lunes ha calificado de “infame, cruel y ruin” la actitud del ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, al haber señalado las órdenes equivocadas que dio el operario del centro de control de Atocha a los trenes siniestrados. “Ya no es que no sean buenos gestores, es que dudo que sean buena gente”, ha afirmado Feijóo. “El miércoles los equipos de rescate estaban en el terreno, siguen todavía. Y mientras ellos buscaban la vida, el Gobierno buscaba otra cosa. Buscaba cómo quitarse la responsabilidad de encima. Y buscaba a quién endosarle esa responsabilidad”, ha cargado. “Resulta que nueve meses después de Adamuz las familias siguen sin saber qué ocurrió en aquel momento. Nueve meses para no explicar nada. Pero aquí, aquí no. Aquí tardan horas en encontrar un culpable. Como si todo un sistema ferroviario se redujera a un trabajador”, ha incidido sobre ese operario de Atocha que dio la orden al AVE de reanudar la marcha a velocidad normal, cuando el protocolo decía que solo debería hacerlo a un máximo de 40 kilómetros por hora. “Todo nuestro apoyo a los maquinistas, a los controladores y a los empleados de Adif y de Renfe”, ha subrayado.

“Fijaos, cuando comparecen, ¿de quién hablan? ¡De sí mismos!“, ha criticado Feijóo. ”El ministro habló del calvario que le espera. Encima en campaña electoral dijo. No, señor ministro: el calvario no lo está sufriendo usted. El calvario es de las familias que esperan un cuerpo. El calvario es de quienes no volverán a ver a sus seres queridos. El calvario es de los heridos. El calvario es de todo un pueblo”.

El PP defiende que el ministro de Transportes ya debería haber sido cesado y Feijóo ha acusado al PSOE de esperar a hacerlo a lo que digan las encuestas. “Decidir si cesas a un ministro por lo que te digan las encuestas te da el nivel moral de esta gente, que es ninguno”, ha cuestionado el líder del PP. Antes, en una entrevista en Telecinco, había acusado al Gobierno de “hacer una auditoría demoscópica” sobre Puente y no sobre las vías de tren y de interesarle “más el relato que las víctimas”. Y ha culpado al Ejecutivo, en su lugar, del accidente de Urda tras “ocho años de negligencia continuada” en el mantenimiento de las infraestructuras.

Una vez recuperada la actividad orgánica tras la tragedia ferroviaria, el PP retomará los actos electorales el próximo sábado en Valladolid, la tierra de la que procede el ministro de Transportes, para tratar de desgastar a Pedro Sánchez si mantiene en el cargo a Óscar Puente. “El número uno en las listas del PSOE en toda España va a ser Puente y así lo haremos saber”, advierten en Génova a sus rivales. Feijóo se lanza a la carrera electoral tras el accidente sin mítines hasta el próximo fin de semana, pero con una intensa exposición en los medios de comunicación esta semana, en la que protagonizará actos informativos mañana y tarde tratando de capitalizar la crisis que le ha estallado al Gobierno cuando falta menos de un mes para las elecciones generales del 29-N.

World.title: Iryo defiende la fiabilidad de sus trenes, incluido el siniestrado, en la línea Madrid-Sevilla
World.content:
Una de las operadoras ferroviarias envuelta en el grave accidente de Urda (Toledo), Iryo, ha salido esta mañana a atajar cualquier duda sobre la fiabilidad de sus trenes cuando circulan por la línea Madrid-Sevilla. “Iryo utiliza exactamente las mismas herramientas que el resto de trenes de última generación que operan en las vías españolas, a excepción del S100 de Renfe (la serie más antigua). Todos ellos tienen instalado el [sistema de seguridad] ERTMS y tanto los sistemas LZB como ASFA se integran como un subsistema del mismo. Esto permite hacer las transiciones de ETCS a LZB o ASFA automáticamente para garantizar seguridad y agilidad operativa”.

El tren 6076 que el miércoles partió a las 7.54 de la estación madrileña Puerta de Atocha con destino Sevilla, quedó paralizado en el kilómetro 118, en puertas de la estación de Urda, tras la caída del sistema de señalización LZB que se había producido a las 8.30. Su maquinista comunicó al centro de control del gestor de la infraestructura Adif en la propia Atocha la circunstancia de tren parado a las 8.41 y a las 8.48. También trasladó al centro de control que le era imposible reiniciar el sistema LZB y, con ello, la marcha. La respuesta del operario de Adif al mando de esa crisis fue que arrancara cuando pudiera y avanzara a velocidad normal. Hacia su posición avanzaba un AVE de Renfe al que se había ordenado también marcha normal (a un máximo de 200 kilómetros por hora al no contar con LZB) al amparo del sistema de balizas laterales BSL y del propio sistema de seguridad ASFA. El fatal alcance por detrás al Iryo se produjo a las 8.53. La unidad de Renfe recorrió 25 kilómetros, según el ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, “de forma inexplicable” (ocupaba el mismo cantón o segmento de vía entre señales que el Iryo) y sin que mediara orden alguna de frenado.

“Desde su inicio de operaciones, Iryo ha aumentado un 10% su inversión en el mantenimiento de toda su flota”, afirma este lunes la compañía. Además de quedar probada la imposibilidad de reiniciar el LZB por parte del tren de Iryo, según los audios de las comunicaciones entre la maquinista y el operario de Adif, el consejero delegado de la operadora, Fabrizio Favara, ya señaló como excesivo el tiempo de reinicio del LZB para sus trenes en una comparecencia el pasado 5 de octubre en el Senado, en el marco de la comisión que investiga los accidentes de Adamuz (Córdoba) y Gelida (Barcelona).

Fuentes cercanas a Iryo explican que el reinicio del sistema de seguridad embarcado en los trenes, nativo para el sistema ERTMS y adaptado al LZB para poder circular en la línea Madrid-Sevilla, se lleva entre tres o cuatro minutos. Con el segundo intento fallido de reanudación de la marcha por parte del tren parado en Urda esa mañana de miércoles, el protocolo de Iryo ordena a la maquinista contactar con el equipo de mantenimiento de la propia operadora. La conductora llamó a la empresa mientras hablaba también con el centro de control de Adif.

El impacto letal del AVE se produjo mientras se llevaban a cabo estas gestiones en cabina del tren Iryo, y con un equipo técnico de Adif tratando de levantar el sistema LZB desde las 8.35 en la estación de Urda. Tampoco tuvieron éxito en esa misión antes de la tragedia.

En su comparecencia en rueda de prensa del pasado viernes, Óscar Puente desligó al tren de Iryo que bloqueaba la vía de la causa del siniestro, el segundo con víctimas mortales en la línea Madrid-Sevilla en diez meses. Sin embargo, apuntó que la operadora ferroviaria podía haberse visto desincentivada de invertir en mejorar la interconexión con el LZB de las vías por ser este último un sistema de retirada. Desde 2021 se ha trabajado en la implantación del más moderno ERTMS, sistema de señalización que comenzará a vigilar la circulación en la línea a Andalucía en el inicio de 2027.

World.title: La receta europea frente a las “incertidumbres” de un mundo hostil
World.content:
Foto de familia previa al inicio de las intervenciones en el WIP 2026. De izquierda a derecha: Vanessa Hernández, directora general de Prensa y Operaciones de Prisa; José Manuel Salazar-Xirianachs, secretario ejecutivo de la Comisión para América Latina y el Caribe (CEPAL); Pilar Gil, consejera delgada de Prisa; Raquel Gil, 5ª Teniente Alcalde de Barcelona; Jaume Collboni, alcalde de Barcelona; Jaume Duch Guillot, consejero de Unión Europea y Acción Exterior de la Generalitat de Cataluña; Josep Rull, presidente del Parlamento de Cataluña; Eva Menor, consejera de Igualdad y Feminismo de la Generalitat; Salvador Illa, presidente de Cataluña; Maria Eugènia Gay Rosell, Teniente Alcalde de Barcelona y diputada de Presidencia; Joseph Oughourlian, presidente del grupo Prisa; Francisco de la Torre, alcalde de Málaga; Arancha González Laya, presidenta del WIP; Jaume Serra, director general de radio y negocio audiovisual de Prisa Media; Fernando Carrillo, vicepresidente primero del consejo de Prisa.

El foro World In Progress (WIP) propone “esperanza” ante las amenazas que se ciernen sobre la UE y aboga por una mayor conexión con América Latina

Las amenazas que se ciernen sobre las democracias occidentales, y en particular sobre Europa, son conocidas. La enfermedad ha sido diagnosticada. Y no va a desaparecer de la noche a la mañana. Por eso, más que lamerse las heridas ante un presente cargado de incertidumbres —de la inteligencia artificial a la deriva totalitaria, del desmembramiento del viejo orden mundial al auge de la polarización y del odio—, tal vez valga la pena pasar a la acción. Ofrecer “confianza” a los ciudadanos frente al desasosiego imperante y “esperanza” ante quienes tratan de certificar la muerte del proyecto comunitario. Aunque el optimismo nazca más de la voluntad que del análisis de los hechos, hay que salir a jugar la partida de ajedrez para no ser, como Stefan Zweig, espectadores de una decadencia largamente anunciada.

Esos dos conceptos (esperanza y confianza como reverso del miedo) y la idea de dar la batalla y mirar adelante han sido el hilo de Ariadna del foro World In Progress (WIP) que, organizado por PRISA, el grupo de editor de EL PAÍS, ha celebrado este lunes la primera de sus dos jornadas en Barcelona. Líderes políticos, institucionales y empresariales, así como intelectuales y académicos, han debatido en torno a los retos de un mundo abiertamente hostil, sobre todo para los valores fundacionales de Europa, que, convertida en “laboratorio” de un choque de fuerzas que empujan en direcciones opuestas, vive una “encrucijada”, como ha señalado Arancha González Laya, presidenta de un foro donde han estado muy presentes las víctimas del accidente ferroviario de Urda (Toledo). WIP ha acogido también dos encuentros de alto nivel con aforo más reducido, uno con el exministro de Hacienda de Chile Andrés Velasco y otro con el presidente de LaLiga, Javier Tebas.

Las sombras que acechan no se han negado; al contrario, se han delineado con precisión, como para ayudar a buscar, también, puntos de luz. El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha recordado al gran pensador europeo, Zweig, que vio cómo “un mundo desaparecía ante sus ojos”. No sería deseable, ha afirmado Sánchez, que asistiéramos ahora al fin del modelo de democracia liberal y valores humanos que representa la UE. Y, aunque todo parece ir mal (o nada parece ir demasiado bien), hay que seguir porque “ningún destino está escrito, depende de las decisiones que tomemos”. Con las elecciones del 29-N a la vuelta de la esquina, y el superciclo electoral europeo (Francia, Italia, Polonia) en el horizonte, el presidente ha alertado sobre las “fuerzas que buscan debilitar Europa y socavar su unidad” cuando lo que se necesita es “fortalecerla”.

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, este lunes en el foro World in Progress, en Barcelona. GIANLUCA BATTISTA

La guerra ha vuelto al escenario europeo (Ucrania). La rivalidad entre Estados Unidos y China es cada vez más acerada. Y el orden internacional se inclina a la ley de la selva (Gaza, Irán), mientras el papel de Naciones Unidas declina sin pausa. Rebeca Grynspan, candidata a secretaria general de la ONU y actual responsable de Comercio y Desarrollo, ha admitido que la institución se ha vuelto “reacia al riesgo” y que “necesita reformas” para ser más relevante en su papel a favor de la paz. “Es más necesaria que nunca. Se han desdibujado las lecciones del pasado y estamos en una encrucijada”.

A Europa, ante ese panorama, no le queda otra que ser “más fuerte, más autónoma y estar más unida”, aunque sin renunciar a sus señas de identidad. Y ese robustecimiento pasa, también, por las armas, como ha dicho de forma más clara el ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, partidario de avanzar hacia “un auténtico ejército europeo” capaz de “disuadir” a otras potencias, como Rusia, de las tentaciones imperialistas que despliega cada vez con menos rubor. Para ese fin es esencial alcanzar la “autonomía estratégica” (también en inteligencia artificial), como ha dicho el presidente de Indra, Ángel Simón, que ha vinculado la defensa con el bienestar de unos ciudadanos que expresan un descontento larvado con latigazos súbitos de violencia, como se ha visto en las calles de Milán, París o Barcelona: “No habrá mantequilla si no construimos cañones”.

Ángel Simón, presidente de Indra, interviene este lunes en el foro World In Progress de Barcelona. GIANLUCA BATTISTA

Aunque el eco de los cañones (las acciones de guerra híbrida de Vladimir Putin) empieza a escucharse, los ciudadanos europeos parecen por ahora más preocupados por la mantequilla. La carestía de la vida, la crisis de los servicios públicos y, sobre todo, la dificultad para acceder a una vivienda (requisito para cualquier proyecto de vida) están en la raíz del desasosiego. Y por eso el futuro de las democracias, objeto central de preocupación del WIP, pasa necesariamente por la “cohesión social”, por un “proyecto compartido que transforme la incertidumbre y confianza y esperanza”, ha dicho el alcalde de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni. En un “tiempo de incertidumbres” y ante un mundo “en refundación global”, los gobiernos deben proporcionar “seguridad”, ha agregado el presidente de la Generalitat, Salvador Illa, que ha alertado sobre las “falsas promesas” que ofrecen “todas las formas de totalitarismo”, como también atestiguó Zweig en El Mundo de ayer, un libro con pasajes que parecen hablar sorprendentemente del hoy.

El WIP ha transitado por la amenaza de la extrema derecha, la erosión de la diplomacia a manos del “poder duro” y el uso de la economía (Ormuz) como arma de guerra. Esas (no) reglas del juego perjudican a Europa... y a América Latina, socio de presente y de futuro ante una administración de Donald Trump abiertamente hostil al proyecto de la UE. El acuerdo de comercio con Mercosur ha sido un paso de gigante. Pero no hay por qué parar ahí, han coincidido voces a uno y otro lado del Atlántico. El ex alto representante de la UE para asuntos exteriores, Josep Borrell, ha dicho que crear un área de libre comercio entre las dos regiones lanzaría “un poderosísimo mensaje político”, y ha animado a América Latina a avanzar en su propia integración.
