Las democracias tienen también sus urgencias, y por eso la ralentización del crecimiento económico, los retos que plantea la inmigración o las próximas convocatorias electorales han ocupado parte del debate. La contienda se libra primero en España, y después en Francia e Italia, que parecen protagonizar un cambio de papeles (la inestabilidad ha cruzado los Alpes), un signo más de los tiempos. Édouard Philippe, ex primer ministro y candidato al Elíseo la próxima primavera, ha advertido de que una victoria de la ultra Marine Le Pen socavaría la “confianza” de los socios. Matteo Renzi, también ex jefe de gobierno en su país, ha pedido recuperar el espíritu de los padres fundadores de la UE: “Dieron el mensaje de que Europa era el lugar de la esperanza. Hoy hay que devolver esa vitalidad y entusiasmo al proyecto europeo”.

World.title: Arcadi España: “Hablemos de los impuestos que se pagan, pero también de los servicios que se reciben”
World.content:
El de los impuestos puede ser un debate pasional y hasta apasionado, pero Arcadi España, ministro de Hacienda del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, pide que sea también un debate “racional”. “Cuando hablemos de impuestos hablemos de todo, de lo que damos, pero también de lo que recibimos con los servicios públicos”, ha pedido el ministro en una conversación con el director adjunto de EL PAÍS, Miguel Jiménez, en el marco de la primera jornada de la tercera edición del World in Progress (WIP), el foro internacional organizado por el grupo PRISA en Barcelona. La petición del ministro no es baladí, porque llega a las puertas de una campaña electoral en la que el Partido Popular ya ha lanzado promesas de grandes rebajas de impuestos. “Si esta es su propuesta fiscal, tendrían que decir cómo van a recortar los gastos”, ha avisado España, quien avanza que el programa del PSOE en materia fiscal se basará en “garantizar la suficiencia del Estado del Bienestar, dar facilidades a las empresas y hacerlo desde un punto de vista racional”.

La conversación ha versado en un momento sobre qué significan los impuestos en una sociedad. Jean-Baptiste Colbert, ministro de Finanzas con el rey Luis XIV de Francia, decía que era el arte de desplumar a un ganso obteniendo la mayor cantidad de plumas con el mínimo de graznidos. El ministro prefiere otra cita, del jurista estadounidense Oliver Wendell Holmes: “Los impuestos es el precio que pagamos por la civilización”.

19:41 Europa y el reto de volver a crecer, con Arcadi España en el WIP 2026 Arcadi España García, ministro de Hacienda de España, junto a Miguel Jiménez, director adjunto de EL PAÍS, en el foro World in Progress de Barcelona. Foto: ALBERT GARCIA | Vídeo: EPV

“Cualquiera que crea mínimamente en un Estado de Bienestar tiene que aceptar que haya impuestos, porque de alguna manera se tienen que pagar las nóminas de policías y profesores”, ha recordado España, quien ha pedido que se hable siempre tanto de los impuestos que se pagan como de los servicios que se reciben. “Tenemos que tener un debate apasionado, pero racional. Otra cosa es hablar de la gestión de los recursos y de la progresividad”, ha dicho, añadiendo que en anteriores ocasiones la derecha ha prometido rebajas fiscales en la campaña y ha terminado subiendo los impuestos una vez en el Gobierno. El ministro también ha explicado que España tiene una presión fiscal menor que la de países como Alemania, Francia o Italia.

Pero parte del descontento viene de la percepción de que los recursos no se usan siempre de la forma más eficiente, y de que aunque la economía crezca, el progreso no termina de llegar al bolsillo de los ciudadanos. La apuesta del ministro para afrontar las dificultades es “más Europa”. “Tenemos un mercado único de más de 400 millones de ciudadanos que deberíamos armonizar más para que sea una potencia. Y la Comisión Europea debería proveer de bienes públicos europeos en materia de seguridad o defensa, y para ello se necesita un presupuesto común a la altura de las necesidades”, ha expresado España, quien ha admitido, sin embargo, que existe “un cierto cansancio de Europa” por el exceso de burocracia y por los ataques eurófobos de la ola de extrema derecha global.

El ministro defiende que haya figuras impositivas europeas armonizadas, a la vez que se lucha contra el fraude y se intenta que los grandes patrimonios tributen ahí donde les toca. “Vivimos un momento en que la desigualdad, que es intrínseca al capitalismo no regulado, ha llevado a que la brecha sea gigantesca. Es tal el poder de determinadas personas que supera a la capacidad de control de un estado”, ha expresado, insistiendo en la necesidad de “trabajar por una tributación básica mínima a nivel global”.

World.title: Josep Borrell: “Los minerales críticos pueden ser la base para la integración de América Latina”
World.content:
Expertos piden en el WIP fortalecer la institucionalidad de los países y sembrar consensos frente a la polarización para que la región no caiga en un nuevo ciclo de extractivismo

Hablar de consensos hoy en América Latina y el Caribe parece una auténtica quimera. Poco tienen en común las agendas de las dos mayores democracias de la región —el Brasil de Lula y el México de Claudia Sheinbaum—, con la Argentina de Javier Milei, el Chile de José Antonio Kast, la Colombia de Abelardo de la Espriella o El Salvador de Nayib Bukele. Pero aunque pensar en acuerdos políticos parece más lejano que nunca, la integración es un elemento fundamental para que el subcontinente pueda tener una voz propia en la economía global, transforme sus riquezas en oportunidades y no caiga en un nuevo ciclo de extractivismo de sus recursos. Esta es la principal conclusión a la que llegaron los participantes de la mesa América Latina y Europa en una economía global fragmentada durante el foro World in Progress Barcelona (WIP), organizado por el Grupo Prisa (editor de EL PAÍS).

“América Latina tiene que integrarse más. Es un imperativo más categórico. La falta de una estrategia explícita la debilita”, ha asegurado el ex alto representante de la Unión Europea para Asuntos Exteriores y Política de Seguridad Josep Borrell, quien ha dicho que la falta de una estrategia de integración hace que la región “juegue bajo las reglas de los demás” y puede hacerla caer en un nuevo ciclo de extractivismo, ya que el 70% de sus recursos minerales —fundamentales para la transición energética— salen en bruto, sin ser refinados. “Igual que nosotros [la UE] lanzamos nuestra integración sobre el carbón y el acero, ellos pueden lanzar su integración sobre las bases de sus riquezas: los minerales críticos de los que dependemos todos: el agua, los alimentos y las energías renovables”, ha insistido. “La integración política vendrá después”.

48:29 América Latina y Europa ante una economía global fragmentada, en el WIP 2026 Josep Borrell, José Manuel Salazar-Xirinachs, y Victor do Prado, del CEBRI, durante la conversación moderada por Núria Vilanova, presidenta del Consejo Empresarial Alianza por Iberoamérica (CEAPI). Foto: Gianluca Battista | Vídeo: EPV

Además, Borrell, quien desde su rol como representante de Exteriores europeo forjó un acercamiento con América Latina, ha dicho que Europa también puede hacer más para fomentar el desarrollo de la región. En ese sentido, ha recordado que solo un 9% de las exportaciones latinoamericanas y caribeñas tienen como destino países europeos. Y ha planteado eximir de aranceles a “todo producto producido en cualquier país latinoamericano” y crear una “gran área de libre comercio” común.

Con más de 660 millones de habitantes, América Latina y el Caribe tiene algunos activos fundamentales, como cerca del 40% de la biodiversidad mundial, grandes reservas de agua y alimentos —que exporta a nivel global—, además de algunos de los minerales clave para la transición energética. Pero la economía de la región crece a un ritmo lento del 2% y mantiene lastres como un “enorme problema de desigualdad” y la “falta de instituciones que conducen a una violencia incontrolable”, ha asegurado Borrell.

“El papel de las instituciones fuertes es fundamental. Las capacidades institucionales son las que permiten mover las agujas”, ha coincidido en este sentido el secretario ejecutivo de la Comisión Económica para América Latina y el Caribe (CEPAL), José Manuel Salazar-Xirinachs. En una región que, como ha reconocido el costarricense, está “caracterizada por la polarización entre países y dentro de los países” y que está a la sombra de Estados Unidos, pero también cortejada por China, con quien tiene fuertes lazos comerciales, su organismo ha publicado recientemente el informe Rupturas y oportunidades: propuestas para que América Latina y el Caribe prospere en la nueva era geopolítica.

En él propone “evitar alineamientos rígidos para abrir al máximo los espacios”. Además, reconoce que la nueva realidad ha creado espacios para diversificar alianzas, algo que, a juicio de Salazar-Xirinachs, puede favorecer a los intereses de América Latina. “Cuando pensemos en política exterior, distingamos el tema de valores con el tema de seguridad y el tema económico”, ha pedido.

El secretario ejecutivo de la CEPAL también ha defendido la necesidad de fomentar la gobernanza y crear estrategias claras que vayan por encima de los ciclos electorales. “Nada ocurre en cuatro años de un gobierno o incluso un sexenio”, ha dicho y ha puesto como ejemplo los casos de República Dominicana o de su país, Costa Rica, donde, pese a los cambios de gobierno, “se mantiene la institucionalidad y continúan las estrategias”.

El acuerdo entre la Unión Europea y Mercosur, que entró en vigor en abril de este año después de casi tres décadas de negociaciones lastradas y abre un mercado de 700 millones de habitantes, también ha sido motivo de conversación en la mesa. El exdiplomático brasileño Víctor do Prado, quien es experto en comercio internacional y miembro del Consejo Consultivo Internacional y Senior Fellow en el Centro Brasileño de Relaciones Internacionales (CEBRI) ha asegurado que el tratado ya tiene consecuencias positivas sobre el comercio entre los dos bloques, pero que en su país hay frustración por las barreras con las que se están encontrando los sectores del acero y la carne para exportar sus productos.

Y pese a que Josep Borrell ha reconocido que “apenas se ha llegado a un acuerdo, se han empezado a poner barreras bajo la alfombra” por ambas partes, ha aprovechado para proponer que se amplíen esas alianzas a toda la región. “¿Por qué no avanzamos un escalón más en este proceso de integración y aceptamos que todos los insumos, todo producto producido en cualquier país latinoamericano, sea considerado producto libre de aranceles cuando entra en Europa?”, ha dicho el exrepresentante europeo. En ese sentido, ha reconocido que, pese a que esa área de comercio común plantearía problemas sectoriales, “daría un poderosísimo mensaje político”.

World.title: Almudena Cid, una prótesis de cadera a los 43 y el debate sobre la jubilación de los deportistas: “Que nuestro esfuerzo aparezca reflejado en la vida laboral”
World.content:
En los años 70 y 80, tiempos en los que solo los deportistas amateurs podían competir en los Juegos Olímpicos, en España y otros países occidentales se clamaba contra el “amateurismo marrón” del bloque soviético: deportistas que cobraban un salario como funcionarios del Estado, habitualmente como oficiales del ejército y se entregaban profesionalmente al deporte. Un convenio similar es el que, pasadas las décadas, vienen a reclamar ahora los deportistas olímpicos españoles en aquellos deportes –atletismo, remo, piragüismo, gimnasia…-- en los que es imposible una relación profesional con sus clubes pese a que dedican un horario laboral completo a entrenamientos y formación, y son el orgullo nacional cuando brillan con himno y bandera en las grandes competiciones internacionales. Y no miran de refilón a un Telón de Acero ya inexistente, sino a un país tan cercano como Italia, en el que el Estado se ocupa de enrolarlos en el ejército y la policía para que tengan consideración de profesionales, coticen a la seguridad social la decena de años o así y tengan, como cualquier asalariado o autónomo, derecho a una pensión contributiva satisfactoria cuando se jubilen. Un derecho del que no gozan muchos, y lo reclaman.

La exgimnasta Almudena Cid, de 46 años, olímpica en cuatro Juegos Olímpicos, hasta 2008, es quizás la persona que más ha luchado porque los exdeportistas alcancen una jubilación justa pese a que a lo largo de su carrera muchos no cotizaron o lo hicieron de forma insuficiente. Y el domingo pasado, en el programa Salvados, de La Sexta, habló con claridad. “Que tu historial de vida y ese esfuerzo aparezca reflejado de alguna forma en tu vida laboral y que no te lo recuerden solo las lesiones”, reclamó Cid, que recordó que muchos deportistas de élite llegan al final de sus carreras con secuelas físicas, dificultades económicas y sin una protección suficiente de cara a la jubilación. Cid participó en el programa junto a exdeportistas como Fernando Romay y Lola Fernández Ochoa, con quienes defendió una “jubilación justa” para quienes dedicaron buena parte de su vida a representar a España. Romay, que comenzó a jugar en el Madrid y con la selección a finales de los años 70, cuando los deportistas no estaban incluidos en la seguridad social, explicó que, pese a poder retirarse, no tendría derecho al 100% de la pensión que le correspondería, mientras otros exdeportistas relataron que necesitarán seguir trabajando durante años para completar los periodos de cotización exigidos.

Solo en 1980 se incluyó a los futbolistas en la seguridad social, y al resto de deportistas profesionales, ciclistas, balonmanistas y baloncestistas, y solo hombres, a lo largo de la década, hasta 1991. Atendiendo a sus reclamaciones, el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez aprobó en septiembre un real decreto por el que todos aquellos que demuestren que tuvieron una relación profesional con un club y equipo a partir de 1980 hasta 2003, excluyendo a los futbolistas, que gozan de otro régimen, tendrán derecho a que, utilizando los fondos del Consejo Superior de Deportes (CSD), el Gobierno cotice lo que ellos no hicieron y aumenten los años de cotización en su vida laboral. Y a los deportistas internacionales que no puedan ser considerados profesionales e incluidos en el fichero DAN (deportistas de alto nivel) que coticen como autónomos, LaLiga de Fútbol Profesional les abona la cotización después de haber llegado a un convenio con el CSD y el COE hace cuatro años. Esto incluye a prácticamente todos los olímpicos que, pese a percibir becas, ayudas del Estado y premios que pueden generar unos ingresos anuales sustanciosos, no pueden firmar con ninguna empresa ni organismo contratos profesionales. Las leyes laborales excluyen la posibilidad de que con las federaciones puedan establecer relación profesional, y los clubes no tienen capacidad económica para ello, pese a que algunos de atletismo, como el Valencia hace algunos años, lo intentaron aprovechando subvenciones oficiales que luego desaparecieron.

Quedan fuera de la protección aquellos que a partir de 2003 prefirieron no darse de alta como autónomos para asegurar su cotización. La propia Cid recordó que el problema va más allá de las generaciones anteriores. Según explicó Lola Fernández Ochoa, muchos deportistas continúan desempeñando su actividad en una situación que describió como la de “falsos autónomos”, ya que compiten bajo la tutela de las federaciones, pero sin que exista una relación laboral que garantice plenamente sus derechos sociales.

La exgimnasta enmarcó esta lucha dentro de un movimiento surgido en los últimos años y respaldado por exolímpicos, sindicatos y especialistas en derecho deportivo. Aunque los deportistas reconocen algunos avances normativos recientes, consideran que siguen siendo insuficientes para resolver el problema de fondo: que quienes dedicaron su juventud a competir por España no lleguen a la jubilación con pensiones precarias o carreras laborales incompletas.

En palabras de Cid, el objetivo es que el esfuerzo realizado durante décadas no quede reflejado únicamente en las lesiones o en las medallas guardadas en un cajón, sino también en los derechos sociales de quienes construyeron una carrera deportiva de élite. Además de la cuestión económica, los participantes del programa pusieron el foco en las secuelas físicas y emocionales de la retirada. Cid, que fue intervenida de una cadera y lleva una prótesis desde los 43 años, denunció la falta de seguimiento que reciben muchos deportistas una vez terminan su carrera. “El deporte de élite te deja secuelas y patologías de por vida”, afirmó.

El asunto ya fue abordado en un acto en el Congreso de los Diputados en octubre de 2024, cuando distintos medallistas y deportistas de élite expusieron una paradoja: haber dedicado décadas a competir al máximo nivel sin generar derechos suficientes para una futura pensión. Entonces denunciaban que las medallas olímpicas y los éxitos internacionales no computaban en una vida laboral marcada por las becas deportivas, la ausencia de contratos y regímenes de cotización insuficientes.

World.title: Al menos 24 muertos por un bombardeo ruso contra una escuela en Ucrania
World.content:
Zelenski acusa al Kremlin de lanzar una decena de bombas contra un centro utilizado para distribuir ayuda humanitaria en la región de Zaporiyia

Al menos 24 personas han muerto en un bombardeo de Rusia en la región de Zaporiyia, en el sureste de Ucrania, según ha denunciado este lunes el presidente Volodímir Zelenski. El mandatario ha señalado que las fuerzas rusas han lanzado los ataques contra una escuela en la localidad de Komishuvaja, que se utilizaba para la distribución de ayuda humanitaria.

“Tras el primer ataque aéreo, se produjo un segundo ataque con nueve bombas más, que impactaron directamente en el refugio donde se encontraba la gente”, ha denunciado Zelenski a través de Telegram. El líder ucranio ha afirmado que las fuerzas rusas sabían que la escuela en Komishuvaja era un centro clave para el reparto de ayuda humanitaria y altamente concurrido por la población local. “Esta es una prueba más de que Rusia no desea ningún tipo de desescalada ni una justicia real”, ha lamentado el mandatario.

Zelenski había informado en un primer momento de 18 fallecidos y cinco heridos, pero el número de víctimas se ha elevado tras una actualización del Servicio de Emergencias de Ucrania. Según ha explicado en su cuenta de Telegram el responsable de la Administración Militar Regional de Zaporiyia, Mijailo Semikin, un gran número de personas estaban “desaparecidas” después del ataque.

Rescatistas ucranios buscan cuerpos tras un bombardeo ruso en una escuela en Komishuvaja, este lunes. Handout (via REUTERS)

El Gobierno ucranio ha anunciado un despliegue para avanzar en las operaciones de rescate y en la búsqueda de personas. “Las operaciones de búsqueda y rescate siguen en marcha en el lugar de los hechos. La lucha por salvar cada vida continúa”, ha dicho Semikin.

Kiev acusa a Moscú de recrudecer los ataques contra civiles en las últimas semanas, en medio de las tensiones entre Zelenski y la Administración de Donald Trump, que se ha alineado con el Gobierno de Vladímir Putin tras sellar un acuerdo para la compra de diésel. “Rusia cuenta con seguir matando. Se necesita una respuesta a esto, una respuesta del mundo. Fuerte y dura. Una respuesta a Rusia. Y apoyo para Ucrania. Hay que proteger la vida. ¡Gracias a todos los que ayudan!“, ha comentado Zelenski.

World.title: Council of State strongly criticises Heinen’s income tax reform
World.content:
The Council of State has delivered a withering verdict on finance minister Eelco Heinen’s plans for a capital gains tax system, saying the proposal had been drawn up too hastily and without proper consideration.

The administrative court said the deadline of 2028 for implementing the law was unrealistic because it would not give the tax office, banks and other institutions time to adapt their systems.

The report from the Council of State, which acts as the government’s constitutional advisor, is the latest setback for the cabinet as it tries to steer its budget for next year through parliament.

Heinen had hoped to speed up the reform of the income tax system to prevent the government losing more money from the current Box 3 mechanism, which the Council of State struck out in 2021 when it ruled that it unfairly discriminated against some savers.

Coalition and opposition parties are divided on how to reform Box 3, the section of the tax return form which calculates the tax due on assets savings based on an estimated rate of return.

D66, CDA and the left-wing opposition parties wanted to formalise this by taxing investors on their actual gains, but Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, and opposition groups such as JA21 favour a capital gains tax instead.

€10 billion shortfall

The latter option would create an estimated €10 billion shortfall in the immediate term because assets will not be taxed until they are sold.

The existing mechanism is costing the state €3.5 billion a year in lost revenue because savers can reduce their tax bill if they show their actual returns were lower than the estimated figure, but do not have to pay more if it is higher.

The Council of State criticised the minister’s decision to use a “novelle”, a device that allows legislation to be amended after it has been passed by the Lower House but is still wating to be approved by the senate.

Heinen said that would allow capital gains taxes to be levied on real estate and startup business in 2028 as a stepping-stone towards introducing the tax on all assets from 2030.

But the Council of State said the plans were too complicated, would only affect around 10% of all asset wealth and would have to be enacted at “very high speed”. It would be better to change the entire system in one go in 2030, the report said.

World.title: Drought may be cracking Groningen’s medieval churches
World.content:
Medieval churches in Groningen may be cracking because of drought as well as earthquakes, according to a study reported by broadcaster NOS.

Researchers from water and soil research institute Deltares and the Hanze University of Applied Sciences looked at how drought affects the wierden, man-made dwelling mounds, under churches in Oostum and Den Ham, northwest of the city of Groningen.

The study was commissioned by the province and the Old Groningen Churches Foundation (Stichting Oude Groninger Kerken).

The research began after new damage appeared in the church at Oostum in 2018, two years after suspected earthquake damage there had been repaired. There have been no major quakes in the area since, but the damage appears to be getting worse.

The nave of the Oostum church has stood for 800 years. “It’s not a given that this church will still be here in another 800 years,” researcher Floris Boogaard told NOS, “because it is ageing very fast now.”

Boogaard said lab tests showed the church stands on clay that swells when wet and shrinks during drought, while peat in the ground oxidises and compacts as groundwater levels fall.

He said increased traffic, changes to the surroundings and earthquakes all contribute to cracking, but that drought is the only one of those factors to have changed significantly in recent years, while the cracks have become much worse.

“The climate is changing,” he said. “Dry periods are significantly longer: in 2018 it was dry for two months, and that really does have an effect.” This year also had exceptionally long dry spells and droughts.

The two-year study is still underway, and the researchers say longer-term research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn. They warn that other historic buildings face the same problem.

Possible solutions are still being examined, but the researchers say the churches need stable water levels around them. At Oostum, pits could be dug around the church to collect rainwater, which would then slowly seep into the ground.

World.title: Banning the infinite scroll: Pro MP files bill on addictive apps
World.content:
Social media platforms, games and dating apps should be banned from using designs like the infinite scroll that keep users online and push them into spending money, according to a bill being submitted to parliament on Monday by Pro MP Barbara Kathmann.

Kathmann told broadcaster NOS her bill would class manipulative features in the design of online platforms as “unfair commercial practices”, which are already illegal under Dutch consumer law. She says the current rules are geared to physical products, but online platforms have become “the new high street or marketplace”.

“If a doll is unsafe, we take it off the market,” she said. “If social media platforms are unsafe, they have to go back to the drawing board and be adapted.”

The proposal also covers chatbots. Kathmann said these products contain tricks “that make us addicted and tempt us into spending money, so that a handful of tech billionaires earn a fortune”.

She would prefer the issue to be tackled at EU level, but that would take too long, and hopes a Dutch law will prompt Brussels to act. She is working with MPs in Germany, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Italy and Portugal who want similar legislation.

Last year, a Dutch court ordered Meta to let Instagram and Facebook users in the Netherlands set a chronological, non-algorithmic feed as their default, in a case brought by digital rights group Bits of Freedom. The appeals court upheld the order in March.

World.title: Two men arrested after dinghy with 36 people rescued in Zeeland
World.content:
Border police have arrested two Sudanese men on suspicion of human trafficking after a rubber dinghy containing 38 people was brought ashore on the Dutch coast.

Rescue services were called out to a “suspicious situation” off Zeeuws-Vlaanderen, which borders Belgium, on Saturday morning. They found the boat adrift without a motor near the harbour of Cadzand.

Police said they found jerrycans full of fuel on board, suggesting the motor may have been lost at sea. A spokesman said the rescue operation was carried out to “save people from a distressing situation”.

Media reports said the boat contained 36 migrants, but the Marechaussee, the Dutch border police force, said their identities were under investigation.

One person on board claimed asylum and six were minors. All those on board were taken to the asylum reception centre in Ter Apel, Groningen, later in the day after being checked over by ambulance staff and questioned as witnesses.

Refugee charities said the episode underlined the need to create safe migration routes in Europe. Small boat crossings from the Netherlands are rare, but thousands of people try to reach the UK by sea from France and Belgium every year.

Sofie Croonenberg, an adviser on forced migration at Stichting Vluchteling, told AD.nl: “Human traffickers play a role in this, but the solution lies in expanding safe ways to request asylum in Europe.”

World.title: Prosecutors raise reward for arrest of “Bolle Jos” to €2m
World.content:
Dutch prosecutors have raised the reward for the capture of the convicted drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers, nicknamed “Bolle Jos” or “Chubby Jos”, to €2 million.

The tenfold increase is an attempt to raise the pressure on the 35-year-old, who is believed to be hiding out in Sierra Leone, where Dutch authorities say he is in a relationship with the daughter of president Julius Maada Bio.

Leijdekkers is the most wanted fugitive on Europol’s list of top criminals after Dutch and Belgian courts sentenced him to a total of 103 years in prison in absentia. The reward is the largest of its kind ever offered by the Netherlands.

Two years ago was found guilty in Rotterdam of transporting nearly seven tonnes of cocaine in six shipments, an armed robbery in Finland and ordering an assassination. He has denied all involvement in drug trafficking through his lawyers.

The prosecution service said information leading to his arrest would be handled in strict confidence and not shared with other police forces or the authorities in the west African country.

Dutch justice minister David van Weel said last month that the European Union had withheld €18 million in budget aid to Sierra Leone because of its continued refusal to hand over Leijdekkers.

But the country’s leaders said the payments had been delayed because of “procedural issues” and had nothing to do with the row over Leijdekkers’ extradition.

Earlier Sierra Leone said the Dutch pressure in the case was “scandalous” and accused Van Weel of engaging in “neo-colonialism”.

Chief minister David Moinina Sengeh said: “Hand on heart, our security intelligence does not know where Leijdekkers is. If they know, show the pictures.”

World.title: No sign of deal on budget ahead of crucial week in parliament
World.content:
Budget talks between the coalition and opposition parties at the weekend have failed to produce an agreement, meaning the plans will go before parliament this week without majority support.

The coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD had hoped to strike a deal with the opposition before the plans are debated this week, but were unable to find a breakthrough despite speaking to three different combinations.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said at his weekly press conference last Friday that he still wanted to come up with an agreement that balanced the demands of left- and right-wing parties, while the opposition groups have repeatedly urged him to pick a side.

Jetten appeared to be close to securing the support of the left-wing parties Pro and Volt in September after agreeing to abandon €6 billion of welfare spending cuts. But the cabinet is unprepared to meet the two parties’ other demands to raise wealth taxes to make up the shortfall.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said after meeting Jetten and other coalition leaders in the Catshuis, the prime minister’s official residence, that “there is no political will to work with us”.

“That’s because the cabinet has chosen to give more money to those with the largest fortunes,” Klaver added.

Abortion and surrogacy

Pro and Volt are the only combination that can offer the three coalition parties the votes they need for a majority in both houses of parliament. Jetten also held a video conference with the leaders of three right-wing parties – the farmers’ party BBB, JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

The parties have drawn up a laundry list of issues where they want the cabinet to make concessions or block legislation, including reforms to facilitate late-term abortions and surrogacy, which the Bible-belt SGP opposes.

The farmers want agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen to scrap his plans to reduce nitrogen pollution by putting up low-emission zones around protected nature areas and offering buyouts to livestock farmers, but none of the coalition parties are prepared to go back to the drawing board.

The three parties said in a statement that they saw “opportunities to talk further”, but there were no signs of a significant shift in their direction. Jetten said on Friday that it was “not sensible” to make the budget vote dependent on non-financial issues.

A third potential route to a majority in the lower house, via the minor parties ChristenUnie and 50Plus, along with the far-right splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower, also seemed doomed after ChristenUnie leader Mirjam Bikker came away from talks saying the process was “not going well”.

“We’re doing things we should have sorted out in August,” Bikker said. “And that’s frustrating”.

Jetten warned at his press conference that opposition parties were jeopardising vital measures to ease the cost of living, such as an extension to the discount on fuel duty, if they voted down next year’s budget.

MPs are due to debate the budget measures on Wednesday, with the votes due to take place on November 12.

World.title: Hackers tamper with fridges at 17 Dutch firms as attacks spread
World.content:
Hackers tampered with fridges at at least 17 businesses in the Netherlands overnight, Danish manufacturer Danfoss has told broadcaster NOS, as similar attacks hit supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden, including dozens of branches of Albert Heijn’s sister chain Delhaize.

A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that the Dutch systems targeted were used by businesses including butchers and small neighbourhood shops, but would not name them. None of the Dutch victims is a large supermarket, he said. Albert Heijn also told NOS none of its branches was affected.

One of the businesses impacted was a frozen food storage site. “The systems there are normally set to -20°, but last night we found they were at -10°,” the spokesperson said. “We were able to step in quickly.”

Danfoss advised Dutch customers on October 13 to disconnect the systems from the internet. Those hit overnight were not on a secure network and still used a default password, the spokesperson said.

A Delhaize spokesperson confirmed the hack on Monday morning, newspaper HLN reported, and said shops in both Flanders and Wallonia had been hit. Delhaize, which is calling it an “IT incident”, told NOS that some branches in Luxembourg had also been affected and that it had immediately disconnected its refrigeration systems from the internet.

Carrefour told Flemish broadcaster VRT that 15 of its 700 Belgian stores had been hit. Colruyt said five independently run Spar stores had similar problems, and butcher chain De Laet & Van Haver also reported a sudden rise in temperatures.

RTL Info reported temperatures rising to around 15°, mainly in freezers. Store managers got a text message from Delhaize at around 4am warning them of the problem, and some stores brought in refrigerated lorries to save their stock.

In Belgium, equipment from another manufacturer, Copeland, was also attacked, NOS reported.

In Sweden, supermarket group Ica said a “limited number” of its stores had been affected overnight, and Coop told news agency TT that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their refrigeration. One Ica store in southern Sweden said on social media that its fridges and freezers had been set to 50°.

French attack

Last month, on the night of October 11, hackers raised the temperature of refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, including Intermarché, E.Leclerc and Coopérative U stores, to 50°, destroying fresh and frozen food.

The stores used equipment from Danfoss, which told news agency AFP that most of the affected systems were outdated and no longer received security updates.

Delhaize and Albert Heijn are both owned by Zaandam-based Ahold Delhaize, which reported a cyberattack to Dutch police in October after shutting down several IT systems. Delhaize told NOS it was investigating whether that attack was linked to Monday’s hack.

World.title: Stroopwafel wars: supermarkets slash prices to 34 cents a pack
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch supermarkets are locked in a price war over stroopwafels, with discount chain Dirk now selling a pack of 12 for 34 cents, Het Parool reports.

That works out at just over 2.8 cents a biscuit, which makes it one of the few food items actually getting cheaper.

Meanwhile, tourists are paying around €13 for a single stroopwafel in central Amsterdam.

In mid-October a pack of Bakker Joop stroopwafels cost 42 cents at Jumbo and 38 cents at Dirk. Albert Heijn was charging 42 cents for a pack of its own brand.

All three have since cut further. Jumbo and Albert Heijn are now at 36 cents, although Albert Heijn’s packs hold only 10 biscuits. That leaves its customers paying the most per waffle, at 3.6 cents each.

Retail expert Paul Moers told the paper that the supermarkets make nothing on the deals, they are so-called “lost leaders” that bring people into the shops, who then inevitably buy other things.

The holdout

Not every chain has joined in. Frisian supermarket Poiesz still charges €1.15 for the same Bakker Joop pack, which earned Moers’ “respect”.

He expects the prices could drop by a few more cents, since the chains are already making heavy losses. Eventually, he said, “the joke will wear off” and the supermarkets will move on to another product.

In Gouda, the stroopwafel’s home town, bakers are unbothered. “It’s comparing apples and oranges,” said Mike van den Berg of Berg’s Bakery and Van Vliet Siroopwafels. “As a baker you have to believe in your product.”

Moers had a final word on the bargain biscuits. They contain no butter, he said, which “says something about how blandening of Dutch taste”.

World.title: Poland launches operation along Russian border in response to reports of planned sabotage
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń. “Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.” “We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services. RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups. In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”. That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region. A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential. Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK. However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”. The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”. List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026 Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train. In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations. World.title: First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year. Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries. The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology. The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males. The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added. “I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.” Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas. With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps. The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees. “Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.” The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers. Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022 The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out. The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites. World.title: Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis. However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters. On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw. At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors. The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her. Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”. Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”. Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”. ⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94 — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026 The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal. Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence. At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker. The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners. Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki. Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”. On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki. @PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute. Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026 Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted. On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”. Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki. “One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki. One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool. Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw. Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego. Policja nie chce go przepuścić! Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3 — Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026 The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening. On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered. The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence. However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK. “I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.” Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026 Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański. He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”. That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties. She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio. Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995. 🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia” – sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026 While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added. Wszystkie osoby uczestniczące w… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) October 30, 2026 The court’s spokeswoman, Weronika Ścibor, told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “seven people elected as [TK] judges this year” had been escorted into the building by officers from the State Protection Service (SOP), a body responsible for protecting state officials. SOP is subordinate to the interior minister. She said they had entered the grounds of the court through a gate that leads from the prime minister’s chancellery, rather than the main entrance from the street where protesters are gathered. Korwin-Piotrowska also confirmed to TVP that she was one of seven judges who were inside the TK on Friday evening. Rzeczniczka Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Weronika Ścibor komentuje sytuację w TK. Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026 The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński declared outside the court that “as of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism”. Kaczyński called on Nawrocki to return to Poland from his state visit to Senegal and defend the court. The president himself quickly confirmed that he had done so, with flight trackers showing his plane turning around in midair and heading back to Poland. Meanwhile, Zbigniew Kapiński, the chief justice of the Supreme Court – a separate entity from the Constitutional Tribunal – told Kanał Zero that he was “appalled” by what was happening, which was “undoubtedly a coup d’état”. World.title: Poland approves first fast-track renewable energy zones
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity. The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures. The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years. Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆 ❓Czym jest OPRO? ✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich… — Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026 Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly. Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days. The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels. Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”. The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly. Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects. EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late. Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU. However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". We cannot do what we do without your support. The Left, a junior partner in Poland’s ruling coalition, has proposed a bill to abolish the Church Fund, which provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy. It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund. However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted. 📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️ Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️ ✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026 The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings. It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty. Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half. For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.” At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found. In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025 An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained. Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law. “I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”. Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge. In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled. Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed. Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners. A long-term decline in trust in the Catholic church in Poland has accelerated over the last year, with only 35% of Poles now saying they trust the church. Meanwhile, the armed forces now enjoy record-high trust of 94% https://t.co/ErCBE4HwWR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 17, 2025 Religious communities also criticised the proposal for not having been discussed with them in advance. In a press statement sent to PAP, the Polish Episcopal Conference (KEP), the main organ of the Catholic church in Poland, said any solution should comply with the country’s agreement with the Vatican, as well as the constitutional principle that relations between the state and religious communities be regulated by mutual agreement. Bishop Jerzy Samiec, head of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland, the country’s biggest Protestant body, pointed to the significant costs churches face in maintaining their properties, including care homes and other facilities. The Catholic Church, Poland’s dominant religious institution, has seen a long-term decline in public trust, with only 35% of Poles saying they trusted it in 2025. That has coincided with a series of crises in recent years, in particular over revelations of child sexual abuse by members of the clergy and negligence in dealing with them by the church hierarchy. A variety of surveys, including from the church itself, show that religious attendance and identification have been declining in Poland in recent years. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition leader sparks controversy with speech on potential EU exit talks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, has sparked controversy by appearing to suggest that Poland and some other allied European Union member states could launch the process of leaving the EU if they fail in efforts to reform it. His remarks were condemned by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and other figures from the pro-EU ruling coalition, who have long accused Kaczyński and his national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party of seeking “Polexit” from the EU. However, Kaczyński responded by accusing Tusk of misrepresenting his words, insisting that he wants Poland to reform the EU rather than leave it. Kaczyński pomylił Krynicę z Kremlem. pic.twitter.com/tX0G04krze — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) October 29, 2026 The comments in question came in an hour-long speech by Kaczyński at the Krynica Forum, an annual conference bringing together leaders from politics, business and civil society, which he used to outline his vision for sweeping reforms of the EU. Repeating his longstanding criticism of Brussels, Kaczyński warned that there had been a “consistent drive to transform the EU into a centralised state” with too much power over national governments. He also called the European Parliament in its current form a “parody”. But soon, said Kaczyński, “a window of opportunity” for reform may appear because “completely different governments could emerge” in Poland, France and Spain, all of which will hold elections within the year. PiS has previously enjoyed close relations with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party in France and the nationalist Vox party of Santiago Abascal in Spain. The EU is preparing a "German plan" that would "annihilate the Polish state", said Kaczyński as Poland marks Independence Day. He warned that the incoming opposition government will "strive to implement this plan" and called on Poles to "fight" against it https://t.co/QDbxmiaazJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2023 Kaczyński suggested that Poland, if led by PiS, could work with other like-minded EU governments to push for reform of the bloc by influencing public opinion, identifying breaches of EU treaties, creating a blocking minority in the European Council, and trying to change the EU’s treaties. However, the PiS leader then warned that, “if [those] approaches fail to yield results, the states that want change could conclude a new treaty with the elements we are seeking, but with a delayed entry into force”. Kaczyński then noted that the EU treaties “include provisions specifying the terms under which a state may withdraw from the EU. This all begins with negotiations. And simply begin these negotiations”. “It is a tough approach, a risky one, but the situation is so dire that it is worth employing such a method if all others fail to yield results,” he added. The remarks immediately prompted condemnation from figures in Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused Kaczyński of effectively calling for Polexit – something they have long claimed he wants, even though PiS has not explicitly called for it before. “Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the terms of its withdrawal from the EU,” wrote Tusk himself on X. “This is, among other things, what the current struggle in Poland is about – a tough struggle. I do not intend to lose it.” “So they do want Polexit after all,” wrote foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Customs borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania…An end to subsidies for farmers and investments…And they swore on their lives that they’d never do that.” In a video published later on Thursday, Tusk declared that next year’s parliamentary elections would help decide “whether Poland remains in the European Union or leaves it”. Jarosław Kaczyński ogłosił właśnie, że Polska powinna zacząć rokowania o warunkach wyjścia z Unii Europejskiej. O taką między innymi stawkę toczy się dziś w Polsce walka. Twarda walka. Nie zamierzam jej przegrać, nawet jeśli nie wszyscy zagrają ze mną. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 29, 2026 Kaczyński responded by saying that “Tusk is lying as usual”. He emphasised that he believes “the EU is needed but it requires thorough reform” so that it “benefits not the elites, but ordinary citizens”. PiS deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek said on Thursday that his party was “considering all scenarios, including the possibility that the EU will kill itself”. However, he added that the priority remained reforming the bloc and “PiS has no plans to leave the EU”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). When PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it regularly clashed with Brussels over a variety of issues, including judicial reform, trade, climate policy, and migration. Since Tusk, a former president of the European Council, took power in 2023, his government has greatly improved relations with Brussels. Tusk jak zwykle kłamie. Najwyraźniej wychodzi z założenia, że dzień bez kłamstwa jest dniem straconym… Unia Europejska jest potrzebna, ale wymaga gruntownej reformy. Kryzys i zapaść w jej obecnym kształcie to efekt rządów Merkel i jednego z jej pomocników, Tuska. Nie ma co się… — Jarosław Kaczyński (@OficjalnyJK) October 29, 2026 Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU funding since joining the bloc in 2004. A study published earlier this year found that the country’s economy is 42% larger than it would have been had Poland not been part of the EU. Opinion polls consistently show a large majority of Poles in favour of remaining part of the EU. However, recent years have seen an uptick in support for Polexit, as well as for anti-EU far-right parties. PiS has increasingly found itself competing against such parties for votes. Regular polling by state research agency CBOS shows that, while opposition to EU membership fell to a record low of 5% in 2022, it has subsequently risen, standing at 14% in the most recent survey.
