World.title: Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority. Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse. However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed. Pierwszy taki wyrok w Polsce. Biskup skazany za zwlekanie z powiadomieniem prokuratury o pedofilach w sutannach Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026 The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law. In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine. In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year. Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison. Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021. In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims. Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN. A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers. It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information. On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good. In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance. In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”. The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up. The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”. In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy. World.title: Prague Music Week Brings Czech and International Music Names to Prague
World.content:
From November 4 to 6, Výstaviště Praha will become a hub for musicians, industry professionals, and fans interested in everything happening both on and off the stage.

The fourth edition of Prague Music Week—themed “Women Shaping the Industry”—will feature keynote interviews with Aneta Langerová and Jana Kirschner, as well as discussions with local artists such as Lenny, Jiří Burian, Eva Saija Burešová, Klára Vytisková, and Ventolin.



A newly confirmed guest is singer Ben Cristovao, who will join a panel addressing the surge of AI-generated music.

International guests include renowned PR expert Fiona Bloom, Sziget Festival Operations Director Ádám Kiss, diversity, equity, and inclusion specialist Brechje Merckx, and representatives from Spotify.

Will also join: Finnish music industry professional Maija Talvisto; Christine Osazuwa—founder of Measure of Music and an expert in music data and analytics; Vasja Veber, co-founder of the leading analytics platform Viberate; Kristina Janušauskaitė, Executive Director of the IFPI European Office.

The event will offer practical workshops, speed-meeting sessions, opportunities to receive feedback on one’s own work, a technology expo, industry awards, informal gatherings, and space for forging new collaborations.

Tickets for the festival portion of the program are available for purchase via the GoOut and NFCtron networks.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Music Week (@praguemusicweek)

Conference tickets can be obtained via a voluntary contribution through the NFCtron platform. More information is available at www.praguemusicweek.cz.

Prague Music Week will feature an Expo spanning 2,000 m², showcasing companies and products that are driving the music industry forward.

Throughout the day, attendees can combine conference sessions with exploring new innovations, participating in hands-on activities, and connecting with exhibitors.

The Expo will also include an “Experience Lab,” where visitors can try out new skills and discover the technologies used in producing music events.

World.title: German Rock Legends Scorpions to Play Prague’s O2 Arena in 2027
World.content:
One of the most successful hard rock bands of all time will perform on June 9, 2027, at Prague’s O2 arena.

Fans can look forward to an evening filled with unforgettable hits, iconic guitar riffs, and the electrifying energy that has defined the Scorpions for over six decades.

Led by charismatic frontman Klaus Meine, the band will revisit tracks that have left an indelible mark on the history of rock music, including “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” “Still Loving You,” and the timeless ballad “Wind of Change.”



In 2027, the Scorpions will embark on another extensive world tour titled “Love, Peace & Rock’n’Roll,” following up on their successful “60th Anniversary – Coming Home” anniversary concerts.

The schedule includes approximately thirty performances across three continents—ranging from European festivals and arena shows (including stops in their native Germany) to dates in North and Latin America.

The Scorpions rank among the most significant and influential rock bands in music history. Formed in 1965 in Hanover, Germany, the group has built a global reputation over the course of an extraordinary career, thanks to their unmistakable sound, high-energy live shows, and an ability to connect with audiences across generations. They have sold over 100 million records and performed countless times on the world’s biggest stages.

Their major breakthrough arrived in the 1980s with the albums Blackout and Love at First Sting, which catapulted the band into the global rock elite. It was during this period that hits such as “No One Like You,” “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” and “Big City Nights” emerged—songs that remain an essential part of their live repertoire to this day.

The Scorpions also gained fame for their emotive ballads, most notably “Still Loving You” and “Send Me an Angel.”

A truly special place in their discography is held by the song “Wind of Change,” which became a symbol of the political and social changes at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.

Inspired by the atmosphere at the end of the Cold War, the song remains one of the most famous rock ballads of all time.

World.title: Sherlock Holmes Exhibition Lets Visitors Play Detective in Prague
World.content:
Visitors can test historical investigative techniques, examine crime scenes and follow clues at a new interactive Sherlock Holmes exhibition in central Prague.

The exhibition, located on the third floor of the Bílá labuť department store, covers more than 2,000 square metres and features over 200 exhibits.

Rather than simply moving between display cases, visitors take on the role of an investigator and work through a series of tasks inspired by the methods used by detectives more than a century ago.



Each visitor receives a detective’s notebook to record observations and clues. The notebook guides them through the exhibition as they investigate evidence, solve puzzles and gradually build their own picture of the case.

One section focuses on the history of criminal investigation around the turn of the 20th century. It includes authentic objects loaned by the Police Museum, ranging from historical fingerprinting equipment and tools used by safecrackers to more disturbing evidence connected with violent crimes.

The exhibition also explores the development of forensic science. Visitors can make footprint impressions, examine insects found at a crime scene, send messages by telegraph and learn how investigators studied bullets and other evidence. Several interactive stations test whether visitors can identify clues and apply the techniques used by detectives of the period.

The literary side of the exhibition looks at the life and work of Arthur Conan Doyle. Visitors can see early editions of the Sherlock Holmes stories and learn more about the author behind one of literature’s most enduring fictional detectives.

A reconstruction of Holmes’s famous Baker Street apartment is among the main attractions. The exhibition then moves into a series of crime scenes where visitors search for evidence and attempt to connect the clues. Some puzzles draw on well-known Sherlock Holmes stories, while others require close attention to details hidden throughout the exhibition.

Period newspapers are also part of the investigation, and visitors are encouraged to look carefully: a coded message may be concealed within the reports.

The final section examines Sherlock Holmes’s lasting influence on popular culture, including books, comics, films and television adaptations. Vintage Sherlock Holmes comic books are also on display.

A scavenger hunt for younger visitors has been added for the current school year, with children asked to find objects hidden throughout the exhibition. The format also works well for school groups, which can divide into smaller teams and compare their discoveries.

Visitors are allowed to take photographs without flash. A full visit typically takes between 90 minutes and two hours, and booking a timed entry is recommended.

Opening hours: Daily from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Duration: The exhibition is scheduled to run at least until January 10, 2027.

Admission: Adult tickets start at 380 CZK, while family tickets start at 980 CZK.

World.title: Czech Billionaire Strnad Offers €30 Billion for Ray-Ban Family’s Firm
World.content:
Czech billionaire Michal Strnad has offered €30 billion to acquire Delfin, the investment vehicle of Italy’s Del ​Vecchio family and the key shareholder in eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica.

News of the offer, which was first reported by Italian newspaper Il Domani, comes amid growing tensions within Delfin, whose investment portfolio includes also large holdings in Italy’s ​financial sector.

Il Domani published a copy of a letter dated October 20 ​outlining the offer.



“I am looking for long-term investment opportunities in companies ⁠operating in, or investing in, businesses positioned at the top of their value chain,” ​Strnad said in the letter said, according to the newspaper.

Delfin “perfectly fits my investment approach and ​strategy,” the letter added.

Jan Osuch, a spokesperson for AKIPIA, which oversees some of Strnad’s investment activities outside the defence sector, said the group did not comment “on market speculation or potential business negotiations.”

Strnad earlier ​this year bought a 14% stake in Italian tyre maker Pirelli, opens new tab from China’s ​Sinochem.

Strnad, 34, heads the family’s defence company Czechoslovak Group (CSG) which listed in Amsterdam earlier this year.

Delfin shareholder Leonardo ‌Maria ⁠Del Vecchio, one of the six children of the late Ray-Ban billionaire Leonardo Del Vecchio, confirmed he had been recently informed of an offer for the company received from a foreign investor.

“The work of a lifetime by my father must remain part of ​Italy’s heritage”, he said in a ​statement.

The late Luxottica ⁠founder built his business empire from scratch having grown up in a Milan orphanage.

Delfin’s ownership is divided equally among Del Vecchio’s ​eight heirs: his six children, his widow Nicoletta Zampillo and her ​son from ⁠a previous marriage.

A sale would require a virtually unanimous decision from the heirs, who have become increasingly at odds with one another.

In addition to its stake in EssilorLuxottica, Luxembourg-based Delfin holds stakes in ⁠Italian ​insurer Generali and lenders Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) and ​UniCredit, for a combined current market value of €43 billion.

Delfin declined to comment. A representative for Strnad was not ​immediately available for comment.

World.title: Prague’s Only Christmas MINT Market to Take Place on November 28–29
World.content:
Don’t leave your Christmas shopping until the last minute this year.

On the weekend of 28–29 November, head to Hall 13 at Holešovice Market and discover original gifts directly from the people who made them.

MINT Market will bring together more than a hundred carefully selected brands from across the Czech Republic, offering a relaxed alternative to the pre-Christmas rush in shopping centres.



On Saturday from 10 am to 6 pm and Sunday from 10 am to 4 pm, visitors can look forward to independent fashion, designer jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations, original accessories and plenty of Christmas gift inspiration.

And, of course, there will be the relaxed and friendly atmosphere that has become an essential part of MINT Market. The event is suitable for all generations and admission is free.

The youngest MINT Market visitors and their families can enjoy the beautiful NOOK Family Lounge, featuring high-quality wooden toys, a creative play area, a quiet zone with books and space to relax, as well as facilities for babies and parents, including a changing table and a peaceful place for breastfeeding.

There will also be Christmas-themed creative workshops.

MINT Market has been active for sixteen years. During that time, it has become an important platform for small and emerging creators, often directly from Prague, who are given the opportunity to present their products to a wide audience.

Residents of Prague and the surrounding area thus have several opportunities each year to purchase quality products that are literally made by their neighbors – locally, sustainably, and with an emphasis on honest craftsmanship.

MINT Market is not just about shopping. Since 2010, the project has been run by a team of people who systematically support small and local brands and are the only ones bringing high-quality Czech design to more than twenty cities across the country.

What started as a small project has gradually grown into a community of more than 1,500 creatives and a platform that has hosted over 450 events and welcomed more than 1.3 million visitors.

World.title: Czech Government Proposes Voluntary TV and Radio Fees Without State Budget
World.content:
People in the Czech Republic could soon be allowed to decide whether they want to pay television and radio licence fees under a new funding model being prepared by the government.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the Finance Ministry is working on a system that would make contributions to Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) voluntary while ensuring the two public broadcasters receive a guaranteed level of funding.

The proposal is expected to be discussed by the coalition council on Monday.



For now, however, the existing system will remain in place. Although the government had initially hoped to introduce changes at the beginning of 2027, Babiš said the legislative timetable makes that unlikely.

Under parliamentary rules, the bill requires a 60-day review period before moving forward. That means its second reading would fall during the Christmas period, delaying further debate until at least January 2027.

The proposed changes have already sparked political and public opposition.

On October 24, the Chamber of Deputies approved in its first reading a proposal to abolish television and radio licence fees. The governing coalition, made up of ANO, SPD and the Motorists party, added the measure to its priority legislative agenda. The vote took place early in the morning after a lengthy parliamentary debate.

Opposition parties have warned that changing the funding system could expose public broadcasters to greater political pressure. Government representatives have rejected those concerns, saying the planned reform does not threaten democratic standards.

Babiš has said the final model must comply with European requirements concerning the independence of public media and predictable funding.

The issue has also prompted demonstrations. On October 25, thousands of people gathered in Prague’s Old Town Square for a protest organised by the Million Moments for Democracy movement.

Participants expressed concern that changes to the financing of Czech Television and Czech Radio could increase political influence over the broadcasters.

World.title: Prague Welcomes a Week of Polish Films and Culture
World.content:
Prague will host a week of Polish cinema and culture from November 9 to 15, as the 3Kino – Polish Film Festival Prague returns for its 13th edition.

The festival will screen 13 feature films representing contemporary Polish cinema, with a program that also includes theater, stand-up comedy, exhibitions, music and events for children.



This year’s festival opens with The Doll (Lalka), directed by Maciej Kawalski. Based on the classic novel by Bolesław Prus, the film is among the most expensive Polish productions ever made and takes audiences to 19th-century Warsaw.

The story explores love, ambition and social divisions, with Marcin Dorociński, one of Poland’s best-known contemporary actors, in a leading role.

Freedom will be the central theme of this year’s edition. The festival will explore the idea through historical events as well as everyday life, personal relationships and decisions that can alter a person’s future.

The program extends beyond the cinema. Visitors can attend theatrical performances, stand-up shows and exhibitions, while this year’s edition will also put a special focus on Poland’s Lower Silesia region.

Among the accompanying events is the opening of photographer Rafał Pawłowski’s exhibition Shadows of Sounds. Another exhibition will mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, featuring a selection of Polish film posters.

The festival aims to bring Polish culture to audiences across Prague, with screenings and accompanying events taking place at several venues throughout the city.

Ticket sales are now open, and the full program is available on the festival’s official website.

World.title: The intersection of sleek design and modern wellness brands
World.content:
Explore how modern consumer brands are elevating their aesthetic appeal by investing in highly customized and visually striking product hardware.

Discover how deliberate styling and tactile materials redefine daily customer routines.

You probably remember when health tools hid inside bathroom cabinets, kept out of sight because their clunky plastic shells felt purely clinical. Today, wellness tools serve as personal fashion statements that you proudly display on living room tables and office desks.

Modern customers want daily items that mirror their curated tastes and fit their personal spaces. When your brand treats hardware design as an artistic craft, you turn simple wellness routines into meaningful daily rituals.

Why Are Wellness Tools Becoming Lifestyle Statements?

Your customers no longer separate wellness routines from their broader aesthetic choices. They curate their living rooms, nightstands, and carry bags with items that express their taste. When you produce clean hardware with balanced silhouettes, you invite buyers to keep your products in plain view.

Visibility drives regular daily use. A handsome object sitting on a counter prompts natural engagement, while an awkward gadget gets shoved into a dark drawer. By focusing on intentional shapes, you build products that seamlessly merge into home decor.

Thoughtful design also influences how customers perceive product quality and long-term value. Smooth finishes, understated colors, and ergonomic details create a premium experience that extends beyond basic functionality. When wellness tools complement personal spaces and individual preferences, they become desirable everyday accessories rather than purely practical devices.

How Do Color and Material Guide Consumer Choices?

Color establishes an immediate emotional connection with your audience. Earthy neutrals, muted pastels, and soft cream tones communicate calm and relaxation before a buyer even reads your ingredient list. If you choose harsh neon finishes, you risk sending mixed signals about serenity and health.

Material choices reinforce that visual promise. When people lift a device made with weighted aluminum or a soft-touch matte shell, their hands register quality. Thoughtful finishes create an impression of quiet sophistication that plain plastic cannot deliver.

How Do You Align Product Hardware with Brand Identity?

Customers judge your company within seconds of unboxing a new device. When you source sleek empty disposable vape pens that match your signature visual tone, you give customers an experience that feels deliberate and luxurious. That visual harmony bridges the gap between everyday utility and curated luxury. Your audience notices when physical hardware matches the graphic polish of your outer box.

Mismatched components break customer trust. You lose credibility when premium outer cartons hold generic items that clash with your voice. Consistent colors, unified fonts, and matching tactile surfaces establish a unified identity from the moment the package arrives.

Why Does Outer Presentation Drive Buying Decisions?

Your retail box acts as an interactive introduction to your brand story. According to data shared by the Forbes Business Council, roughly 72% of shoppers say that package styling directly impacts their purchasing decisions. That finding confirms that visual presentation carries just as much weight as product features.

Shoppers form split-second opinions based on packaging textures, embossing, and typography. If your exterior box looks rushed, shoppers assume the interior hardware lacks care as well. Investing in bespoke packaging signals that you prioritize quality across every single detail.

What Steps Create a Seamless Product Experience?

Building an unforgettable product requires harmony between visual appeal and reliable mechanics. You need a structured approach that guides your production decisions from concept to final delivery.

Structuring Your Hardware Design Strategy

Synchronize print colors: Match your Pantone shades across cardboard packaging, printed guides, and physical device shells.

Following these benchmarks keeps your production tight and reliable. Your buyers receive hardware that looks cohesive, feels comfortable, and performs reliably during routine use.

How Does Responsible Material Selection Support Growth?

Modern consumers care deeply about how companies manage resources. Guidance from the Environmental Protection Agency highlights that analyzing how packaging components are manufactured and discarded shapes sound business investments. When you integrate thoughtful materials into your supply chain, you satisfy conscious shoppers while reducing unnecessary waste.

Sleek presentation does not require excess plastic or non-recyclable wraps. By choosing compact paper boxes and recyclable device housings, your brand displays environmental integrity. Customers respect businesses that balance elegant design with mindful stewardship.

Style and practical functionality walk hand in hand across the modern self-care market. When you treat your hardware as an extension of personal taste, you build genuine customer loyalty that outlasts fleeting market trends.

World.title: Budapest to trial its first biomethane-powered bus – try it for free! Here’s where it will run
World.content:
Budapest is set to trial its first bus powered by biomethane (Bio-CNG), a renewable fuel. The vehicle was unveiled in the Hungarian capital on Monday at a press conference held outside MOL’s headquarters. It will begin its trial operation on bus route 132E.

MOL aims to support greener public transport

MOL Group’s key strategic objective is to support the green transition and sustainable urban public transport through smart, practical solutions, said Ambrus Halász, the company’s head of corporate communications.

He added that the group’s fuel portfolio is continuously expanding with products designed to support energy security, competitiveness and the green transition at the same time.

“An important milestone for us was the launch of our first biomethane operation in Szarvas on 14 October. This means that, going forward, we will also be able to supply markets with Bio-CNG,” he said, welcoming the opportunity provided by Budapest’s public transport companies BKK and BKV to test the biomethane-powered bus in the capital.

The pilot project aims to demonstrate that sustainably produced energy in Hungary can also be used to meet the needs of Budapest’s public transport system. MOL hopes to supply an increasing proportion of this type of energy for public transport and other applications in the future, said Ádám Horváth, director of MOL Group’s New and Sustainable Businesses within its Downstream division.

International trends suggest that the fuel portfolio of the future will be much more diverse, requiring several different solutions.

Although fossil fuels are expected to remain the dominant energy sources for some time, there is a growing need for alternatives that offer genuinely more sustainable ways of meeting energy demands, he explained.

“We are working to make our portfolio increasingly green, and to process more and more alternative feedstocks alongside crude oil at our refinery,” Horváth said.

He added that the company is investing in green hydrogen projects not only in Hungary but also in Croatia, with plans to expand into Bratislava in the future. Building a significant biomethane presence within MOL Group is another new strategic priority.

Why is biomethane important for public transport?

One of the main drivers behind this strategy is EU regulation, including the Clean Vehicles Directive. Under the rules, more than half of the buses purchased and put into public transport service between 2026 and 2030 must comply with the directive’s clean vehicle requirements.

Alongside electric and hydrogen-powered vehicles, compressed natural gas (CNG) also qualifies under these requirements.

MOL Group currently feeds seven million cubic metres of biomethane into regional and national gas networks every year, Horváth said. Using existing infrastructure, energy produced in rural areas can therefore be transported to Budapest through the gas network.

Photo: MTI

The company also wants to demonstrate the environmental and economic advantages of biomethane in public transport and establish it as a viable alternative internationally.

When total life-cycle costs are taken into account, biomethane can be competitive with diesel. It also produces lower nitrogen oxide and particulate emissions.

Furthermore, biomethane-powered buses operate much more quietly than diesel vehicles while offering a similar driving range and competitive refuelling times.

If you missed it: Big shake-up for Budapest public transport: capital and suburbs to get one transport system

When and where can passengers try the new bus?

The Bio-CNG bus will operate on Budapest’s 132E route until 4 November, BKK CEO Ádám Bodor announced.

He pointed out that transport is still responsible for 30% of Budapest’s carbon dioxide emissions, with public transport accounting for 3% of the total.

Although most Budapest residents travel by metro, tram or trolleybus, around 1,100 of the capital’s 2,300 public transport vehicles are buses. Most of these run on diesel, making their replacement with electric models one of the biggest challenges facing the city.

Bodor stressed that while switching to electric vehicles is important, other technologies could also contribute to more sustainable transport.

In his view, around 300 buses will need to retain internal combustion engines in the long term to ensure security of supply in Budapest. Nevertheless, testing new technologies and the latest versions of existing ones is particularly important.

BKV currently operates 37 compressed natural gas (CNG) buses, although these will gradually need replacing as they age, he added.

Passengers can use the biomethane-powered bus free of charge, as it will operate as part of the regular timetable during the trial period.

World.title: Inside Hungary’s Versailles: An American producer discovers Esterházy Palace – VIDEO
World.content:
What connects one of Hungary’s most magnificent Baroque palaces, the legendary composer Joseph Haydn and the Hollywood music industry? American producer Ray Brown explores these unexpected connections in a new Magyar Minute video filmed at Esterházy Palace in Fertőd.

Often described as the Hungarian Versailles, Esterházy Palace is famous for its magnificent interiors, extraordinary gardens and rich musical heritage. But beyond the chandeliers and gilded halls lies a fascinating story of aristocratic ambition, wartime destruction and remarkable restoration.

In his latest video for Magyar Minute, American producer Ray Brown visits the palace alongside Alpár Kató, founder of Daily News Hungary, where they are welcomed by Csilla Sütő, managing director of the Eszterháza Center.

During the visit, Brown discovers the remarkable legacy of Prince Nikolaus Esterházy (Esterházy I. (Fényes) Miklós herceg), the palace’s connections to Joseph Haydn and the history behind the composer’s famous Farewell Symphony.

The visit also has a personal dimension. Brown, whose father Harold Brown was a founding member of the legendary American band WAR, reflects on the universal power of music and imagines the palace as a spectacular venue for international concerts and film productions.

The four-minute video also reveals lesser-known details of the palace’s turbulent twentieth-century history, including traces of its Soviet-era past.

Watch the video: Inside Hungary’s Versailles

From its magnificent halls to its nearly 8,000 rose bushes, Esterházy Palace offers plenty of surprises. Discover why this extraordinary destination deserves a place on every visitor’s Hungarian itinerary.

World.title: Son of former Hungarian central bank governor now searched by elite fugitive hunters
World.content:
Ádám Matolcsy, the son of former Hungarian National Bank (Magyar Nemzeti Bank, MNB) governor György Matolcsy, is now being sought by specialised police fugitive-hunting units amid an investigation into alleged economic fraud and corruption linked to the central bank’s foundations. An international and European arrest warrant has been issued for him and his associate, György Stofa.

An elite group is on the hunt for Matolcsy

Hungarian police have transferred the search for the two men to the National Bureau of Investigation (Nemzeti Nyomozóiroda, NNI), which operates within the Rapid Response Police. According to news outlet Telex, the case may have been assigned to the NNI’s targeted fugitive-hunting division, commonly known as the police’s bounty hunters.

This shows that locating and apprehending the suspects has become a priority for the authorities. Matolcsy and Stofa were initially placed on Hungary’s wanted list on 21 October. European and international arrest warrants followed on 27 October. Neither man has reportedly contacted the authorities, and their whereabouts remain unknown.

Specialised units tasked with tracking fugitives abroad

The NNI’s fugitive-hunting officers specialise in locating individuals who deliberately evade law enforcement, often by travelling abroad, obtaining false documents or attempting to establish new identities.

The unit has a record of high-profile arrests, including the capture of Mária Dobrai, better known as Broker Marcsi, in Belize in 2016. It has also helped bring notorious Hungarian fugitive András Lakatos, known as Kisbandi, back to the country.

The officers work closely with foreign law enforcement agencies to find the suspects involved in the central bank scandal, exchanging intelligence to identify and apprehend suspects who may be hiding overseas. According to Telex, several investigators may now be working on the Matolcsy and Stofa cases simultaneously.

Stay up-to-date: Leading Czech magazine portrays Viktor Orbán in handcuffs

Investigation focuses on central bank foundation assets

The investigation concerns alleged financial misconduct involving the MNB’s PADME foundation and the management of its assets. Prosecutors suspect that a controversial securities-lending arrangement involving companies connected to the foundation was designed to transfer control over its wealth to business interests linked to György Matolcsy and his son after the former governor’s departure from office.

György Matolcsy, who led the central bank from 2013 to 2025, was detained on 21 October alongside two associates, former company executive Mihály Valkó and lawyer Tamás Sándor. A court ordered their pre-trial detention for one month on 23 October, although the ruling was not final at the time of reporting, as the defendants appealed. The investigation remains ongoing, and the allegations against Ádám Matolcsy and György Stofa have not been proven in court.

World.title: Hungary to scrap lifetime benefits for former presidents who leave office early, Magyar announces
World.content:
Hungary is preparing to abolish lifetime benefits for former presidents who fail to complete their terms, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in Parliament on Monday. The government will also scrap a controversial fund that allows former heads of state to distribute tens of millions of forints to charities and foundations every year.

Speaking before the agenda at Monday’s parliamentary session, Magyar said the government would soon submit legislation to ensure that presidents who leave office before their mandate expires – for example, because of plagiarism or treason – can no longer receive taxpayer-funded benefits for the rest of their lives.

Former presidents could lose HUF 73 million charity budgets

The announcement also addresses a separate controversy surrounding the 2027 budget proposal. The draft budget, submitted on Friday evening, had allocated HUF 73 million per former president for public-benefit donations next year. Under the original proposal, Pál Schmitt, János Áder, Katalin Novák and Tamás Sulyok would each have been able to distribute the money freely among charities, civil organisations and foundations.

The proposal attracted attention after Telex first reported on the allocations. Magyar responded to the newspaper’s Facebook post over the weekend with a brief comment: “I wouldn’t think so. 1 January is still a long way off.”

He has now confirmed in Parliament that the allocations will be amended before the final vote on the budget. The separate funds available to former presidents for charitable donations will also be abolished.

Magyar described the measures as part of the government’s effort to eliminate what he called the remaining privileges of the previous political system.

Photo: MTI

If you missed it: Egyptian president visits Budapest: Railway deal struck, new economic partnerships on the table

Government presents 2027 budget as start of national rebuilding

In his parliamentary address, the prime minister also outlined the broader goals of next year’s budget.

Magyar described the 2027 budget as carefully planned, saying it would only promise what the government could realistically deliver. He called it the beginning of Hungary’s reconstruction and said the government would work to put the country’s finances in order.

He added that the aim was to ensure that Hungarians could once again decide their own future. The government also intends to restore recognition and respect for those who have kept the country running in recent years.

According to Magyar, the foundations are being laid for further measures in the coming years, when economic growth picks up and European Union funding arrives.

He described the 2027 budget as the first step in a longer process, adding that the government had taken that step and would continue the work together.

Magyar to meet German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin

The prime minister also announced several upcoming diplomatic engagements. Next week, he will travel to Berlin for an official meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Magyar said he would be accompanied by the foreign minister, as well as the ministers responsible for the economy and energy, defence and the interior. The Hungarian ministers will also hold talks with their German counterparts.

Next Wednesday, Magyar is scheduled to travel to Dublin, where he will meet the leaders of the other 26 EU member states.

Reflecting on Hungary’s recent foreign policy developments, the prime minister drew a comparison with the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, noting that the country’s freedom fighters were left alone against overwhelming forces 70 years ago.

He argued that Hungary is no longer isolated and now has friends and partners stretching from Prague and Warsaw to Belgrade and Washington.

World.title: Shein and Temu shoppers hit by new EU fee as cheap orders now cost more
World.content:
A new EUR 2 handling fee on goods ordered directly from outside the European Union came into force on 1 November, adding further pressure on shoppers using Chinese online platforms such as Shein and Temu.

EU introduces new fee affecting Shein and Temu orders

Combined with an existing EUR 3 customs charge, some low-value orders could now face additional costs of up to EUR 5 per product category. Consumers ordering inexpensive goods from outside the EU will have to navigate another change to the bloc’s customs rules.

This is due to the Union introducing a new handling fee aimed at covering the growing cost of processing and inspecting imported e-commerce shipments. The EUR 2 Union Handling Fee (UHF) applies to individual product categories rather than every parcel, meaning the final charge will depend on the contents of an order.

Not every parcel will cost EUR 5 more

The new measure follows the introduction of a temporary EUR 3 flat-rate customs duty on 1 July, which applies to consignments valued at EUR 150 or less. The distinction between the two charges is important. While the EUR 3 duty is limited to lower-value shipments, the new EUR 2 handling fee applies regardless of the value of goods sold and shipped directly to consumers from outside the EU.

For example, three identical T-shirts ordered from Shein or Temu may be classified as a single product category, resulting in a combined EUR 5 charge under the two measures. However, if a parcel contains three different product categories, the additional costs could reach EUR 15, writes HVG.

The charges will primarily be collected from platforms, sellers or, in certain circumstances, transport operators. Nevertheless, companies may pass some or all of the costs on to customers through higher prices or separate fees.

Brussels targets the growing e-commerce market

The European Commission says the growing number of low-value online shipments has placed increasing pressure on customs authorities, which must process, assess and inspect millions of parcels. The new fee is intended to help finance these operations while encouraging online marketplaces to take greater responsibility for the goods they sell.

The changes could particularly affect platforms such as Shein and Temu, whose business models have relied heavily on shipping inexpensive products directly from China to European consumers. According to figures cited in recent reports, approximately 5.8 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2025, representing a 26 per cent increase compared with the previous year.

The European Commission reportedly estimates that the new charges could generate nearly EUR 6 billion annually for the EU budget between 2028 and 2034.

World.title: Wizz Air flight makes emergency landing at Budapest Airport due to bomb threat
World.content:
A Wizz Air flight travelling from London to Sofia was forced to divert to Budapest Airport on Monday after receiving a reported bomb threat. Hungarian Gripen fighter jets escorted the aircraft, while emergency services and counter-terrorism units were deployed.

Wizz Air flight makes emergency landing at Budapest Airport

The Airbus A321neo turned back over Bosnia and Herzegovina and requested permission to land at Budapest’s Liszt Ferenc International Airport.

The aircraft landed safely at 12:08 local time on Runway 2, according to initial reports. Firefighters, police and counter-terrorism personnel were waiting at the airport, with the aircraft subsequently parked at stand B5. The incident prompted the temporary closure of Runway 2, with all arriving and departing flights redirected to the airport’s other runway, reports Tudásmorzsák.

Hungarian fighter jets scrambled

Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi confirmed that the Hungarian Defence Forces had responded to the incident after a bomb threat was reported on the London-Sofia service. According to the minister, NATO’s air defence alert system issued an ALPHA alert, prompting Hungarian Gripen fighter jets to take off within minutes.

The military aircraft escorted the passenger plane to Budapest, ensuring its safe landing before returning to their base in Kecskemét. The minister praised the Hungarian military’s readiness, emphasising its ability to respond immediately to threats to the country’s airspace. Following the aircraft’s arrival, responsibility for further measures was handed over to the police.

Authorities have yet to release further details about the alleged bomb threat, including whether any suspicious items were found on board or whether the threat was deemed credible. The incident remains under investigation.

World.title: Hungarian tourist’s unique wheelchair stolen at Málaga Airport
World.content:
A Hungarian woman has been left without her newly acquired, custom-made wheelchair after it was reportedly stolen by another passenger at Málaga Airport in Spain. Spanish police are investigating the incident, while the family is seeking compensation from Wizz Air.

Hungarian tourist’s unique wheelchair stolen at the airport

A Hungarian tourist has lost a wheelchair worth more than HUF 1 million (currently more than EUR 2,700) during a family trip to Spain, according to a report by RTL News.

Emese Lakatos, 30, travelled to Málaga with her family after winning travel vouchers at the Wizz Air Budapest Half Marathon, where she participated using a handbike, a specially adapted bicycle powered by the arms. The vouchers helped make the Spanish holiday possible.

However, the trip took an unexpected turn when the family discovered that Emese’s wheelchair had disappeared at the airport.

Five-year wait for a custom-made wheelchair

The stolen device was particularly valuable to Emese, not only because of its price but also because of the years she had spent waiting for it. According to RTL News, the Hungarian woman had waited more than five years to receive her new, specially tailored wheelchair, which was completed just two weeks before the family’s departure.

Emese was reportedly the only wheelchair user on the Budapest-Málaga flight, making the possibility of an accidental mix-up with another passenger’s equipment unlikely.

Her mother told RTL that a Spanish airport employee had witnessed someone sitting in the wheelchair and hurriedly leaving the airport accompanied by another person. The family said airport staff initially promised to contact them if the wheelchair was spotted again. However, the equipment has not been recovered.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Wizz Air responds as police investigate

The incident was reported to Spanish police, and the family also sought assistance from the Hungarian consulate. Wizz Air, meanwhile, stated that security camera footage showed the device being transported to the aircraft door. The airline believes it was subsequently taken by another passenger.

The family is seeking compensation from the airline, but no payment has reportedly been received so far. During their stay in Spain, Emese was able to get around with a temporary wheelchair provided by Málaga Airport. Nevertheless, the replacement does not offer the same functionality or comfort as her custom-made equipment, which was designed specifically for her needs.

Spanish police are continuing their investigation into the disappearance. The case has also raised concerns about the handling and security of mobility equipment at airports, particularly when passengers rely on specialised wheelchairs for their independence.

World.title: Halloween horror: nails found in sweets given to children in Hungary
World.content:
A terrifying discovery has shocked families in Gyömrő after nails and other suspicious objects were found hidden inside sweets collected by children during Halloween trick-or-treating. Police have launched an investigation into at least three reported cases.

Nails found in sweet treats given to children during Halloween

Halloween celebrations in the Liget Residential Park in Gyömrő, Pest County, have taken a disturbing turn after several families discovered dangerous objects hidden inside sweets collected by children during the annual trick-or-treating event.

According to an announcement published by the local municipality, a young girl received a sweet containing a nail on the evening of 31 October. Fortunately, she spotted the metal object before eating the treat, avoiding a potentially serious injury.

Nail hidden inside a milk caramel

The municipality said the sweet was particularly suspicious because it had been wrapped in chocolate packaging but actually contained a milk caramel with a sharp nail concealed inside. Officials said the circumstances suggested the act was deliberate. The town administration subsequently filed a police complaint against an unknown perpetrator and urged parents to carefully inspect all sweets collected by their children.

However, the incident may not have been an isolated case. Gyömrő Mayor Szabolcs Kisberk told Hungarian tabloid Blikk that further reports had emerged from the residential community. According to the mayor, at least three separate cases involving suspicious sweets had been identified, writes Blikk.

In addition to the nail hidden in the caramel, another sweet reportedly contained an object resembling a broken plastic screw. A foreign object was also discovered inside a coconut-flavoured sweet. The incidents have raised serious concerns among local families, as Halloween trick-or-treating has become an annual tradition in the residential park, home to several thousand people.

Police investigating suspected attempted grievous bodily harm

The Monor Police Department has launched a criminal investigation against an unknown suspect on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Police confirmed the investigation in response to media inquiries but declined to provide further details, citing the interests of the ongoing inquiry.

The municipality has urged parents to thoroughly examine all Halloween sweets collected by their children, paying particular attention to damaged, unusual or suspicious packaging.

Anyone discovering a potentially dangerous object in a sweet is advised to contact the Gyömrő municipal office and the police immediately. Authorities hope the reported incidents are limited to the local community, but the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Serbia Bank Owner Arrested Following Licence Revocation
World.content:
Alta Bank HQ in Belgrade. Photo: Wikimedia/Andrei Romanenko

The owner of Serbia’s Alta Bank, Davor Macura, was arrested on Monday, three days after the National Bank revoked the bank’s licence.

Macura was arrested on suspicion of abuse of office for withdrawing money from Alta Bank’s treasury and obtaining a financial gain of 45 billion dinars (nearly 385 million euros).

In addition to Macura, G.M., director of the Bank’s Treasury and Cash Management Department, and I.P., an employee responsible for treasury operations, were also arrested on the orders of the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime. They are suspected of assisting Macura in committing the alleged criminal offence.

The prosecution suspects that Macura exceeded the limits of his authority up until October 31. G.M. and I.P., who were responsible for the direct handling of assets held in Alta Bank’s treasury, allegedly provided Macura with “access cards or used their own cards and were physically present to enable unauthorised entry into the bank’s treasury”.

“During these unauthorised entries, D.M. [Macura] allegedly removed money from the vault, thereby obtaining an illicit financial gain amounting to approximately 45 billion dinars,” the prosecution said.

The National Bank of Serbia, NBS, revoked Alta Bank’s operating licence on October 31 citing a significant deterioration in its finances and concerns over its liquidity.

“The Executive Board noted that the revocation of the licence was preceded by supervisory measures aimed at ensuring that the bank increased its liquidity levels,” the NBS said, adding that the interests of the bank’s depositors had been put at risk.

Alta Bank expanded its operations during the Serbian Progressive Party’s time in power under former President Aleksandar Vucic. In 2025, for example, Serbia’s state-owned electricity company, Elektroprivreda Srbije, EPS, changed its payment arrangements, directing Belgrade residents to pay their electricity bills into Alta Bank accounts.

Shortly before calling parliamentary elections, former President Vucic launched a podcast on his YouTube channel with Alta Bank among its main sponsors, featuring s for it displayed in the studio.

Vucic’s list in the October 25 parliamentary elections lost power after 14 years of rule to the Student List, which has won an absolute majority.

North Macedonia Bank takes control of Alta subsidiary

Meanwhile, in neighbouring North Macedonia, the central bank has placed Alta Bank AD Bitola under temporary administration, taking control of its assets following the collapse of its majority shareholder, Alta Bank AD Belgrade, in Serbia.

The measure on Sunday was intended to protect the bank’s assets and depositors amid a sharp withdrawal of funds, North Macedonia’s Central Bank governor, Trajko Slaveski, told a press conference.

Slaveski said around 2 million euros had been withdrawn from the Bitola-based bank within days, prompting the intervention. He stressed that the North Macedonian bank remained liquid and had a sound loan portfolio. The Serbian bank’s exposure to its North Macedonia counterpart was relatively small, he added, at around 1 million euros, and did not threaten its liquidity.

Under the temporary administration, which can last up to three months, central bank-appointed administrators will assume management responsibilities, while the Serbian-majority shareholder will lose its voting rights. Customers will be meanwhile allowed to withdraw no more than 10,000 denars [around 160 euros] per week through payment cards issued by the bank.

The bank said its branches will temporarily stop serving customers from Monday until further notice. Slaveski also said potential buyers may acquire the Serbian shareholder’s stake in the bank as a potential long-term solution.

World.title: Romania and Moldova Seal First Joint Defence Procurement Deal
World.content:
Romania and Moldova signed a military cooperation agreement on Monday, paving the way for the latter to access the European Union’s Security Action for Europe SAFE programme to finance the purchase of military vehicles.

The agreement marks the first joint defence procurement arrangement between the two countries and represents another step towards strengthening their military cooperation, officials said.

“This is a major opportunity for both countries to strengthen their cooperation in the fields of economy and security … and also a good way to protect our territories and our citizens,” Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said.

He added that SAFE funding would allow both countries to modernise their defence capabilities while supporting the development of Europe’s defence-industrial base through joint procurement.

Although Moldova is not an EU member and its constitution enshrines a policy of neutrality, it can participate in the programme through a partnership with an EU member state, in this case Romania.

Under the agreement, Moldova may join an existing procurement framework between Romania and Italian manufacturer IDV, Iveco Defence Vehicles, allowing it to acquire 62 multipurpose IVECO military trucks.

The vehicles, which will be produced at an IVECO plant in Romania, are intended to replace ageing Soviet-era trucks still in service with Moldova’s armed forces.

Moldovan Defence Minister Anatolie Nosatii said the acquisition would improve the army’s logistical and operational capabilities, while helping align military standards and strengthen interoperability with Romania.

Officials also indicated that Bucharest and Chisinau could extend their cooperation under SAFE to include air-defence and anti-drone technologies.

Both countries face growing security challenges stemming from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moldova, which borders Ukraine and lies close to the war-affected Black Sea region, has become concerned about the risks posed by Russian military activity and hybrid operations.

Although constitutionally neutral, Moldova has stepped up efforts to modernise its armed forces and strengthen cooperation with Western partners. Romania, an EU and NATO member sharing a border with Moldova, has been one of its strongest supporters, providing political, economic and security assistance as Chisinau pursues closer integration with the European Union.

The SAFE programme, adopted by the EU in 2025, provides up to €150 billion in loans to member states for joint defence procurement. It is designed to accelerate military investment, strengthen Europe’s defence industry and reduce reliance on non-European suppliers.

The framework also allows eligible non-EU partner countries, including Moldova, to participate in certain joint procurement arrangements.

World.title: Poland’s Rule-of-Law Crisis Deepens as Rival Judges Claim Control of Top Court
World.content:
A decade-long dispute over who controls Poland’s highest court escalated over the weekend, when a group of judges sought to remove its leadership, police were deployed to the building, and President Karol Nawrocki cut short a foreign trip to intervene.

The next flashpoint is seen on Tuesday, November 3, when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – one of the five judges elected by the current parliamentary majority but prevented from taking up their duties by the country’s president – has called a general assembly of Constitutional Tribunal judges to approve the court’s proposed budget for 2027. With the existing leadership, led by the court’s president Bogdan Swieczkowski, continuing to dispute her authority, it remains unclear whether the meeting can proceed as planned.

The battle over the makeup of the Constitutional Tribunal, which has the power to overturn laws that violate Poland’s constitution and should act as an independent check on government and parliament, dates back to 2015, when both the outgoing centrist government and its right-wing successor made contested appointments to it. During Law and Justice’s (PiS) subsequent eight years in power, major reforms to the judiciary raised concerns over political interference and brought Poland into prolonged conflict with European institutions over the state of the rule of law in the country.

Reversing those reforms was among Donald Tusk’s central campaign promises before his coalition took office in 2023 and his pro-European government has made restoring the court’s independence an essential part of repairing the country’s democratic institutions. The Tusk-led government has since refused to recognise the Tribunal’s legitimacy in its current form, but attempts to change the system through legislation have been blocked by opposition-aligned presidents.

The immediate deadlock concerns five judges elected by the current parliament whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. These judges subsequently took their oaths without him, but the Tribunal’s leadership prevented them from hearing cases. In October, the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s constitutional advisory body, concluded that the president could not use his role in the appointment process to obstruct duly elected judges from taking office.

However, PiS and President Nawrocki accuse Tusk of using unlawful methods to replace the court’s leadership with judges sympathetic to his government.

The competing claims came to a head on Friday, when the five judges attempted to assert their authority over the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska announced the suspension of its president, Swieczkowski, and his deputy, and declared herself the court’s acting head. The existing leadership rejected the move, leaving the institution with rival claims to authority.

Separately, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek sought to have Swieczkowski and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski, stripped of judicial immunity, potentially paving the way for criminal charges over their alleged obstruction of the Tribunal’s work.

The announcement brought more protesters to the Tribunal’s grounds in Warsaw, where supporters of the opposition had already been demonstrating for weeks against attempts by the newly elected judges to take up their posts. Senior PiS politicians joined the crowd, while police increased their presence around the building.

Meanwhile, President Nawrocki cut short a state visit to Senegal, ordering his plane to turn around over Spain and return to Warsaw. He arrived at the Tribunal in the early hours of Saturday, challenged the authority of the judges seeking to take control, and helped the court’s deputy president enter the building.

“Last night, Poland’s constitutional order was violated, and a constitutional state institution was forcibly taken over,” Nawrocki said in a statement issued shortly after 05:00 on Saturday morning. He demanded that police withdraw from the premises and announced emergency consultations with parliamentary party leaders.

In a televised address on Saturday evening, Prime Minister Tusk defended the intervention, accusing PiS and the PiS-aligned presidents Andrzej Duda and his successor Nawrocki of perpetuating the crisis. “Nobody had any doubt that the Tribunal, in the form imposed by PiS, was not a real court,” he said, arguing that repeated attempts to resolve the dispute through legislation had been blocked.

Tusk compared the situation to a thief who steals an elderly woman’s handbag, then complains of violence when caught, while bystanders suggest dividing the stolen money between the thief and the victim. “On certain matters, there can be no compromise,” he said.

A constitutional reset to end an undignified row?

Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, a leading civil liberties organisation, questioned whether Friday’s intervention by the government would help restore the Tribunal’s authority, calling the escalation “extremely harmful”.

“The confrontations between judges and the President of the Republic of Poland outside the entrance to the Tribunal building undermine the dignity and authority of state institutions,” the organisation said in a statement.

The European Commission weighed in on Saturday, backing the Polish parliament’s authority to appoint Tribunal judges. Meanwhile, US Ambassador Tom Rose warned that crowds outside the court risked worsening an already volatile situation. “The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals out of control,” he wrote on X, while stressing that Washington did not intend to interfere in Poland’s domestic affairs.

With parliamentary elections scheduled for 2027, Tusk’s coalition faces pressure to deliver on its promise to restore judicial independence, while the opposition has made resistance to the government’s intervention a central issue. In August, Tusk announced that he was determined to ensure the newly elected judges could take up their posts at the Tribunal by September, even if the process was not particularly elegant. Speaking at the Campus Polska Przyszlosci event, he said he needed to be certain that “our judges will enter that building”.

On Saturday afternoon, Nawrocki held meetings with parliamentary party leaders to discuss possible solutions. Among the proposals put forward by parties as far apart as the left-wing Razem and the far-right Confederation was a constitutional reset of the Tribunal, involving the replacement of all its sitting judges with a new bench appointed through a cross-party agreement.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Election Winner Pledges Reset with Russia
World.content:
Bulgaria’s acting President, Iliana Iotova, cemented a five-year mandate after winning the runoff election on Sunday. Backed by the Progressive Bulgaria government and her former Bulgarian Socialist Party, BSP, Iotova won 57.6 per cent of votes cast against the pro-EU opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov, on 39.5 per cent. Turnout was low at 29.1 per cent, but higher than the all-time low of 22.98 per cent registered in the first round on October 25.

“People believed in our way of politics, which pledged dialogue, conversations, searching for decisions, coordination,” Iotova said on Sunday evening in a briefing that Prime Minister Rumen Radev also attended and where he answered most of the questions.

“Bulgarians chose the future instead of the past, they chose peace, stability, normalcy”, said Radev, both of them dodging questions on the low turnout.

Iotova built her campaign as “the President of peace”: she has pledged to offer a more balanced attitude towards Russia and be skeptical about further military aid to Ukraine. She has also called for Bulgaria to be less obedient to the EU.

“If you say yes to everything, which was Bulgaria’s case for decades, you are voiceless … but things have changed a lot, times have changed in the EU, too”, Iotova said in a TV debate with Andrey Gyurov.

In an interview on October 30 on YouTube with two pro-Russian commentators, she said: “I don’t see Russia as an enemy state … I hope Russia will take part in Europe’s future security architecture.”

During her campaign, Iotova was criticised, along with Prime Minister and Progressive Bulgaria leader Rumen Radev, for remaining elusive about drone attacks in the Black Sea, including in Bulgaria’s zone, and for a lack of preparedness.

Her Vice will be Kiril Valchev, Director of the Bulgarian News Agency, the country’s official newswire, his nomination raising questions about Bulgaria’s media freedom and political ties.

After her victory on Sunday, Iotova said all the criticism from the opposition had been a form of aggressive political attacking, adding: “But we didn’t allow ourselves this speech of hate.”

Iotova was born in 1964 in Sofia. She worked as a TV presenter and news editor at Bulgarian National Television in the 1990s. Her time there is remembered for a controversy from 1995, when, on air, she prioritized coverage of then-Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov doing a traditional dance, or horo, at a public event instead of covering the death of 14 soldiers during an accident – the case became colloquially known as “the blood horo”.

Iotova’s involvement with the Moscow-aligned Bulgarian Socialist Party started in 1997, first as a head of the party’s press office. She joined the party аs Bulgaria was going through an economic crisis and was pressured by mass protests aimed at Socialist-led cabinets.

Iotova became an MP in 2005, when the BSP clung to power through a coalition with the NDSV, the National Movement for Stability and Progress, the now faded party of former monarch Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha.

She became a Member of the European Parliament in 2007 and again in 2014.

In 2016, she resigned from the EP to become a Vice President when Rumen Radev won his first term.

She remained in position until January 2026 when, following months of speculation, Radev resigned from the Presidency to form his own party, Progressive Bulgaria, which won the April elections. This made Iotova acting President, while Radev became the first politician to have served both as President and Prime Minister.

World.title: Coal Plant Case Against Montenegro Still Open Despite Upgrade
World.content:
Montenegro still faces a possible finding of non-compliance with Energy Community rules over its ageing Pljevlja coal-fired power plant, despite a major environmental upgrade, Adam Cwetsch, head of the Decarbonisation and Governance Unit at the Energy Community Secretariat, has told BIRN.

Montenegro’s only coal-fired power station, Pljevlja Thermal Power Plant remains a major challenge to the country’s green transition. Commissioned in 1982, the plant exceeded its permitted limit of 20,000 operating hours in December 2020, triggering infringement proceedings under the Energy Community Treaty.

In an interview, Cwetsch said the case concerning the plant’s breach of its permitted operating hours remains open.

“Pljevlja power plant has already exceeded the limit that was given to the power plant, which was 20,000 working hours,” he told BIRN.

World.title: ‘Life on Hold’: Poland’s Immigrants Face Years Waiting for Residence Permits
World.content:
Permanent waiting mode

When millions of Ukrainians crossed into Poland after Russia’s full-scale invasion, the voivodeship offices were given breathing room. From April 2022, deadlines in certain residence proceedings were suspended, along with the usual legal consequences of administrative delays. That provision, now Article 100d of the special act on assistance to Ukrainian citizens, however, applies to foreigners of every nationality. Initially intended to expire at the end of 2022, it was introduced under the previous Law and Justice government and repeatedly extended under Donald Tusk’s coalition. It now runs until March 4, 2027.

It is precisely this provision that migrant rights campaigners are now challenging. They acknowledge the solution was indispensable in 2022, but argue that almost five years later it has become part of the problem.

“It was meant to be a temporary measure to help the system cope,” says Vladimir Medvedev, co-founder of Glos Migranta. “It should have been lifted two years ago, yet here we are in 2026, and nothing has changed. The system is still not working.”

Under ordinary administrative rules, foreigners can formally challenge delays. Article 100d, however, suspends the deadlines and restricts those remedies, allowing offices to argue that no deadline has technically been breached even after months or years of waiting.

In May 2025, the Supreme Administrative Court refused to apply the provision to the period after June 2024, finding it incompatible with the constitutional right to a fair hearing. The law nevertheless remains in force. In June 2026, the Interior Ministry acknowledged in a letter to Poland’s Ombudsman that courts would likely decline to apply it in similar cases, but maintained that administrative offices must continue enforcing it.

“The Ministry understands the problem and its causes, but in our view, it is not doing enough to resolve it,” Marcin Kusy, director of its Migrants’ Rights Team at the Ombudsman’s Office, tells BIRN.

Since April 2022, the office has received 1,161 complaints concerning the legalisation of residence, and lengthy proceedings are among the most common problems raised by migrants.

“Unfortunately, we’re not talking about months of waiting, but years,” Kusy says. “The uncertainty alone takes a toll on people’s sense of security.”

There are practical consequences, too. Banks often require foreigners to produce valid residence documents before granting access to services, while proof of a pending application may not be enough. For migrants running businesses, being unable to open a bank account can make it impossible to operate.

“I’ve heard of cases where people’s existing accounts were blocked simply because they didn’t receive their new residence permit in time,” Medvedev says. Some, he adds, have resorted to paying taxes and bills in cash at the post office.

International travel presents another obstacle. A pending residence application may allow someone to remain legally in Poland, but without a valid residence card or visa, leaving the country can mean being unable to return, stuck between countries.

World.title: Exhibition in Kosovo Capital Asks What Antifascism Means Today
World.content:
At the Reporting House Museum, the exhibition moves from the architecture of imprisonment to the ways journalism and personal testimony shape historical memory. The question of who holds the camera and who is seen through its lens is addressed.

It features a painting of a photograph of Albanian migrants arriving in Italy by ship during the exodus that followed the fall of communism in Albania in the early 1990s. The photograph captures an unusual reversal: an Albanian migrant, Armando Lulaj, photographed journalists as they photographed the arriving migrants. Those who were the subjects of the image turned the lens on the people documenting them.

The painting was commissioned by Lulaj, who asked artist Zef Shoshi from the Manifesto Collective to produce what Lulaj described as his “last socialist painting”.

It is displayed above a real human skull, bringing together migration, artistic memory and the physical traces of human life.

“I am glad we made this part of the museum, as the first documentation of the exodus in Albania we have in the museum,” said BIRN Kosovo executive director Jeta Xharra.

Also in Reporting House, ‘A Wall Divides Us’ presents dozens of letters exchanged by Kosovo Albanian activists Xheva Krasniqi-Lladrovci and Fehmi Lladrovci between 1985 and 1990, coinciding with Milosevic’s rise to power in Serbia, growing repression of Kosovo Albanians, and the twilight of federal Yugoslavia.

Lladrovci was imprisoned in the former Yugoslavia for his agitation for Albanian rights. He and Krasniqi-Lladrovci had been engaged for just over a month when he was imprisoned. Their communication continued throughout his detention.

Xharra said it was “rare to find this much passion and political energy within the same letters”, presented publicly for the first time in almost 40 years,

“It particularly impressed me how Xheva was teaching the elderly generation how to read and write [in order to write to their dissident sons in jail] and arguing for more education for young Kosovo Albanian girls who were abandoning school when Milosevic closed Kosovo public schools in 1990.”

Alongside letters, the exhibition includes the red outfit Krasniqi-Lladrovci wore when she got engaged, and the ammunition vest she was in when she was killed in 1998 alongside Lladrovci while fighting Serbian security forces.

From denial to remorse

World.title: New Rules are Coming for Road Users in Croatia
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – New rules are coming into force for road users across Croatia, with higher penalties and significant amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

The Ministry of the Interior has now released for public consultation a draft of amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act. Index reports that it will introduce significantly stricter penalties for dangerous behaviour in traffic, new parking rules and easier removal of vehicles by tow truck, as well as special registration plates for taxis and electric cars.

higher fines for those filming and posting dangerous driving

One of the key novelties concerns drivers who film their own dangerous driving in order to post it on social media, which the legislator now treats as a significantly more serious offence. While such behaviour was previously punished as ordinary mobile phone use while driving with a fixed fine of 130 euros, the new proposal introduces fines of 800 to as much as 2,000 euros for anyone who uses a mobile phone or other device while driving to record their own unlawful behaviour and then makes it publicly available. The explanatory notes state that such posts have additional social harm because they encourage others to imitate them and normalise dangerous driving patterns.

police no longer need to attend minor collisions

For the first time ever, the law defines the concept of a “minor traffic accident,” which means an accident involving only material damage that does not impair the technical soundness of essential parts of the car and allows it to be easily removed from the road. Under the new Article 182, police officers are no longer obliged to go to the scene of such an accident if the participants are able to exchange details with each other or complete the European Accident Statement. Drivers who nevertheless refuse to immediately move their cars off the carriageway and continue to block traffic while waiting for the police will be fined 200 euros, whereas the fine until now was 60 euros.

a total ban on parking on squares

The draft also introduces the concept of a restricted traffic zone into the law, together with significantly stricter rules for stopping and parking in city centres. The previous practice whereby drivers, especially delivery vehicles, parked in city squares and pedestrian zones while invoking the rule about leaving a 1.60-metre passage for pedestrians will no longer apply. Article 82 introduces an absolute ban on stopping and parking in squares, in cultural-historical complexes and on surfaces that local authorities have designated exclusively for pedestrians, regardless of how much free space remains. At the same time, the rules for the operation of the tow-truck service are also changing. A tow truck will be legally able to lift an improperly parked vehicle from the pavement if the free passage between the car and any obstacle is less than one metre. An obstacle is no longer considered only a building, but also bollards, waste bins, outdoor café terraces or any other physical obstacle on the sidewalk.

special registration plates for taxis and electric cars

The law also introduces the obligation to issue special registration plates for two categories of vehicles — taxis and electric-powered cars. While in the case of taxis this is about easier control and alignment with market rules, for electric cars the reason is directly linked to the safety of emergency services. Lithium-ion batteries in electric and hybrid vehicles, in the event of a collision and fire, generate extremely high temperatures, release toxic gases and require completely different firefighting tactics from classic petrol and diesel engines. Special plates will enable firefighters, already upon arrival at the scene of a traffic accident, to recognise electric propulsion and immediately apply the appropriate extinguishing and rescue procedure.
