World.title: 135 Years of the Zagreb Tram – From Horses to Modernity
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – 135 years is the time period during which the now iconic blue Zagreb tram has snaked through the capital city. From being pulled by horses to new vehicles, let’s look back at the history of what we now know as ZET.

Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that frequent trams have been circulating Zagreb’s streets for 135 years now. They have become the blue symbol of the city, living history on the rails, and transport without which Zagreb can hardly function, something Zagreb residents felt most clearly during the recent multi-day ZET workers’ strike, which caused days of traffic problems until a court declared it illegal and banned it.

horse-drawn trams named after vineyard pests…

The first tram circled Zagreb back in 1891. It was pulled by horses and was far from the technical modernity we know today. Zagreb’s trams were once yellow and ran on only a few lines through the very city centre. People affectionately called them “konjka” (horse-tram), but also mockingly “filoksera”, after the notorious wine louse (phylloxera) that was ravaging vineyards in those years, because the workers laying the tracks had dug up and torn apart half the city. Before the trams, passengers were transported around Zagreb by omnibuses that resembled stagecoaches from Western films. They ran from the city centre to the bathing spots on the Sava and from the railway station to a few hotels. As ZET explains, “the city fathers in Zagreb began discussing the need to introduce a horse-drawn tram as a means of transport” in 1885.

French engineer Raoul Pierre Alexandre Gautier proposed a contract for the introduction of tram traffic to the Zagreb City Magistrate on the 20th of June 1887. The city municipality accepted his offer and on the 26th of March 1889 issued him a permit to build a tram line on the ground of the city streets. The Association of Engineers and Technicians allowed the construction of a 76-centimetre-wide track, and the Tramway Company, a special private enterprise, began work. The first tram depot was built on the site of today’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum.

ilica, zagreb’s modern main artery, was dug up

zagreb.hr

The first lines were built from the corner of Ilica and Mandaličina Street to Maksimir, from the corner of Ilica and Frankopanska Street to the Sava Bridge, and from the corner of Ilica and today’s Republic of Austria Street to the Western Railway Station. Construction began in May 1891, and the trams started running a few months later. Historian Lelja Dobronić, in the article “Old Notes on the Zagreb Tram” published in the magazine Kaj, cites a document from the 17th of August 1891: “Since the long-awaited rails from England and the carriages from Graz (in Austria) have finally arrived, Upper Ilica has been being dug up since last Thursday, and from today Frankopanska Street as well, so that the rails can be laid. Certainly by this Sunday the rails will be laid through the whole of Ilica and Jelačić Square. Up to 500 workers are working a day.”

At the time when Zagreb’s trams were pulled by horses, there were ten closed and six open vehicles available, manufactured at the Weitzer factory in Graz. The average speed of the horse-drawn tram cars was 7.5 km/h. Zagreb’s horse-drawn tram also carried passengers in Velika Gorica, where the joint-stock company Horse Railway was founded back in 1907. They had a seven-kilometre line from the railway station, through the centre of Velika Gorica, to Novo Čiče. It was called “konjača.” After 1945 the horses were replaced by a small diesel locomotive.

electrification and expansion

The electric tram started in August 1910, but horse-drawn trams continued to operate for the following year. Zagreb’s trams changed colour in 1923. They became blue instead of yellow, while the vehicles were reconstructed. A new model, the M-24, manufactured in Zagreb and running on the right-hand track, also appeared on the streets. Summer open-air trams soon became available as well. During the time of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH), Zagreb’s trams ran with increasing difficulty because of bombing, and services were suspended in 1944. Traffic resumed after liberation, and in the autumn of 1945 tracks were built through Vodnikova and Mihanovićeva streets. From then on, the tram lines had numbers. In the following years lines were built towards Žitnjak as well as the Mihaljevac–Dolje line. A building for ZET workers was constructed in Puljska Street.

bull, czech and katica…

At the beginning of the 1950s, Zagreb’s residents also received the first domestically produced tram, built in the ZET workshop. It was prototype 101 with 95 passenger seats. This was followed by cooperation with the “Đuro Đaković” wagon factory from Slavonski Brod and the purchase of M-201 vehicles.

The last example of the M-201 tram, nicknamed “Đuro” or “Bik” (Bull), ran until June 2024 on line 9. Its predecessor, the M-24, ran from 1924 to 1977. Today it is used as the Christmas tram. In 1977 Czechoslovak trams from the ČKD-Tatra factory in Prague were purchased. The Czech T4 model trams, known as “Čeh” (Czech), ran for years on lines 4, 6 and 14. Years later the Tatra KT4YU trams, better known as “Katice,” also arrived. An important date in the history of the Zagreb tram was the 25th of November 1979, when the line along Držićeva Street, across the Bridge of Youth, to New Zagreb was opened. That was when the tram crossed the Sava. In 1980 a tram-bus terminal was built at Črnomerec on the site of a former brickworks. In November 1985 the tram also started running across the Adriatic Bridge towards New Zagreb. Further development of ZET includes the abolition of the conductor’s job in 1996 (conductors had been cancelling and selling tickets in the vehicles for 105 years) and the extension of tram routes to Dubec and Prečko.

and then came končar…

Over the last thirty years or so the old trams, Bulls, Czechs and Katicas, have been replaced by trams manufactured at Končar, Zagreb’s technological giant.

“In more than 30 years of operation on Zagreb’s tram network, Končar trams have covered more than 140 million kilometres, confirming their quality, reliability and indispensable role in the lives of Zagreb residents,” Končar told Index. The company had already begun manufacturing electric rectifier stations for ZET back in 1954. “After almost three decades of cooperation on energy infrastructure, ZET and Končar began joint development of tram vehicles. Production of the TMK 2100 series trams began in 1993, and the prototype was presented on the 5th of September 1994 and immediately put into regular service,” the company notes, also recalling the TMK 2200 trams. “From June 2010 a total of 140 TMK 2200 series trams and two shorter TMK 2200-K trams (which carry the designation TMK 2300 in ZET’s fleet) have been produced for Zagreb,” Končar says. The company later also manufactured shorter trams for the Latvian city of Liepāja.

zagreb’s blue trams

In order to fill gaps in the timetable until the delivery of new vehicles, ZET bought 11 used GT6M trams from Augsburg, Germany, at the end of 2023 and during 2024. This sparked lively public debate because of their age and the fact that the passenger areas are not air-conditioned. The newest Zagreb trams, the TMK 2300, have been in service since February 2025, and there will be forty of them. Through their rich history Zagreb’s trams have become the city’s blue symbol, a mark of the development of domestic technology, and an indicator of Zagreb’s expansion ever further from its historic centre. Zagreb is, along with Osijek, the only Croatian city with tram traffic. Trams once also ran in Pula (from 1904 to 1934), Dubrovnik (from 1910 to 1970), and Rijeka and Opatija.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Accuses EU of Wanting to be a Superstate
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – Croatian President Zoran Milanović has accused the EU of wanting to become a superstate, adding that Montenegro, with which Croatia has multiple open issues, is otherwise welcome to join.

President Zoran Milanović stated that Montenegro is welcome to become a full member of the European Union, while at the same time criticising the direction in which the EU is developing. Index reports that the president believes the EU is increasingly trying to become a superstate, whereas it should focus on free trade, freedom of movement and the harmonisation of rules among member states.

Milanović spoke at the 27th Lučindan Gatherings in Zagreb, a traditional meeting of the Montenegrin community in Croatia. The event was also attended by Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović, who is on a working visit to Croatia. The two presidents discussed relations between the two countries and Montenegro’s European future.

“montenegro is welcome to join”

“Montenegro is a candidate for membership of the European Union, it is moving towards the EU and let it come. As far as I am concerned, it is welcome,” Milanović said. Nevertheless, he repeated his criticisms of the European Union, which he believes is exceeding the powers and possibilities on which it was originally founded. In his view, the EU should stick to economic cooperation, free movement and the alignment of rules, rather than striving to create a superstate.

Milanović told Montenegrins that the greatest value they have is their state. He emphasised that Montenegro has realised its statehood and that its future success does not depend exclusively on membership of the European Union. “The greatest thing you have is your state. Montenegro has realised itself, and everything else consists of greater or lesser advances that do not stand in the way of Montenegro being successful, well-governed and relatively prosperous,” Milanović said. He wished Montenegro to continue on its own path and develop as a successful and well-governed state. He concluded his address with verses by the Montenegrin ruler and poet Petar II Petrović Njegoš.

trust between croatia and montenegro must be strengthened

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović assessed that Croatia and Montenegro are friendly countries and that Montenegro’s membership of the European Union is in the interest of both countries. He stressed that improving relations requires continuing political dialogue and resolving existing open issues.

“It is our shared responsibility to build good-neighbourly relations, foster open dialogue, overcome current challenges and strengthen mutual trust,” Milatović said. He emphasised that a common European future implies political and economic cooperation, mutual respect and a willingness to resolve disagreements. He thanked the Montenegrin community in Croatia for preserving national identity, culture and ties with the home country.

The Lučindan Gatherings are a traditional event dedicated to preserving Montenegrin cultural identity, tradition and ties with Montenegro. They bring together members of the Montenegrin national minority in Croatia as well as representatives of the cultural and public life of the two countries. According to the 2021 census, 3,127 members of the Montenegrin national minority live in Croatia, or 0.08 percent of the total population.

World.title: Before You Apply: The Legal Deadline Blocking Croatian Descendants
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – There is a somewhat unknown legal deadline blocking Croatian descendants from obtaining their Croatian and as such EU passport.

That issue relates to the exact reason your family left the former Yugoslavia, and why exactly this could throw a spanner in the works of your EU future. Let’s turn the clock back to October the 8th, 1991… If you’re exploring your eligibility for Croatian citizenship by descent, you have likely come across a specific date repeatedly, and that date is October the 8th, 1991. In the (often confusing) world of Croatian citizenship law, this is the ultimate historical line in the sand. Under the descent and emigrant pathways of the Croatian Citizenship Act, your ancestor must have left the territory of what is now the recognised territory of Croatia before this exact date to grant you a pathway to a Croatian and therefore EU passport of your own.

For many second- and third-generation descendants of those who left what was then Yugoslavia, this seems straightforward at first glance. They look at their family history, note that their parents or grandparents moved to the United States 1960s, 1970s, or 1980s, and check the box. However, many “DIY applicants” face rejections from the Croatian side of the fence because they fail to realise that the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) enforces strict, hidden caveats regarding why and how your ancestor left when they did. Simply proving your family departed before the clock struck 1991 is not quite enough. To secure your Croatian citizenship, you must prove the exact legal nature of their exit. That is where, quite understandably, many people become unstuck and their citizenship applications get shoved to the back of a shelf somewhere to gather dust.

what exactly does croatia deem to be an emigrant?

The Croatian side evaluates citizenship applications based on a highly specific legal definition of what they deem an emigrant to actually be. Under the law as it stands, an emigrant is someone who left the territory of Croatia with the clear, permanent intention of abandoning their domestic residence and resettling somewhere abroad. Because of this ultra-narrow definition that leaves very little wiggle room, there are two major legal traps that routinely catch DIY applicants by surprise.

the so-called internal migration problem

If your ancestor was born in Croatia but moved to another republic within former Yugoslavia, such as Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or Slovenia, and then moved across the pond to North America, Croatia’s authorities may not view them as a legal emigrant from Croatia because of that, regardless of the fact that they still ended up in the USA. If that person’s initial move was treated as an internal migration within the same federal state, the chain of continuity for Croatian descent can be heavily compromised or, as is often the case, simply rejected outright.

the curse of the Croatian gastarbajteri…

A Monument to Croatian Emigrants – Anglogermantranslations

During the 1970s and 1980s, hundreds of thousands of people left the former Yugoslavia to work abroad as temporary economic migrants, often referred to as gastarbajteri (guest workers). Many of these individuals retained their active residency rights, property registrations, and legal ties to Croatia and as such to Yugoslavia, fully intending to return after a few years. If MUP reviews your ancestor’s file and determines that their departure was legally categorised as a “temporary economic migration” rather than a permanent severance of domestic ties, your application under the emigrant track can be denied.

verifying permanence…

Commons/Bain News Service

When you submit your application to a Croatian consulate, the reviewing officers will thoroughly inspect your paperwork to determine the legal permanence of your ancestor’s departure. A simple plane ticket or family story will not suffice. To build an airtight case, you must present a synchronised paper trail that cross-references multiple things.

The first is what’s known as a foreign naturalisation timeline. This works to document precisely when your Croatian ancestor applied for and received citizenship in their new country, showing a definitive shift in legal allegiance. Then come the international arrival records. These are official historical maritime or flight manifests matching the timeline of their permanent resettlement. Last but not least comes the so-called letter of motivation. This might seem odd, but there should always be an explicit structure built up of your family’s narrative, framing their historical departure to meet the rigid legal thresholds expected by Croatia.

for croatia, the year 1991 represents a minefield in several ways…

Proving the legal nuances of a person’s departure that took place forty or fifty years ago is a massive bureaucratic challenge. It requires a deep understanding of historical (and of course needlessly complicated) Yugoslav exit laws, international naturalisation records, and precise legal phrasing in the Croatian language. This is exactly why the structured service provided by Croatian By Descent is an essential safeguard for diaspora families.

croatian by descent‘s experts understand the complexities of the former state

Rather than treating your citizenship application like a roll of the dice, their team conducts an exhaustive upfront document review. They analyse your family’s specific migration timeline, identify potential legal vulnerabilities in how your ancestors left Yugoslavia, and meticulously format your application package. By coordinating the procurement of records and managing the precise drafting of your legal motivation letter, they ensure that the Ministry views your family’s departure as a definitive, permanent emigration. They handle the heavy administrative legal lifting, protecting your application from common 1991 cutoff traps and turning your family history into a flawless submission package. World.title: Dinamo Sack Mario Kovačević After Shock Defeat to Rudeš
World.content:
Dinamo have sacked head coach Mario Kovačević following Saturday’s 1-0 defeat to newly promoted Rudeš in the 12th round of the SuperSport HNL. The Zagreb club, led by Zvonimir Boban, confirmed the decision on Sunday.

B team coach Jerko Leko will take charge on an interim basis, starting with Thursday’s Europa League trip to Sunderland and followed by the league match against Varaždin.

The defeat in Velika Gorica proved the final straw. Junior Fernandes scored the only goal for Rudeš, while Dion Drena Beljo had two goals ruled out, one for offside and one for handball. Dinamo also finished with ten men after substitute Iker Almena was sent off for an elbow to an opponent’s head.

Speaking after the match, the 51-year-old said he understood the supporters’ anger and would not hide behind anyone. “If people are angriest with me, I accept the blame,” he said. Asked whether he still justified Boban’s faith in him, Kovačević pointed to his record over 16 months: a rebuilt squad, a league and cup double, and a solid start to this season. He called the Rudeš result a major slip, said four points in Europe was less than Dinamo had wanted, and insisted the season could still be turned around.

Kovačević took over in June 2025 and led Dinamo in 73 matches, winning 48, drawing 11 and losing 14. Last season he delivered the double, winning the SuperSport HNL and the SuperSport Croatian Cup.

Born in Jablanica, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kovačević played for Varteks, Belišće, Slaven Belupo, Međimurje, Slovenian side Nafta, Nedelišće and Dinamo Tirana before retiring in 2008. He began coaching in 2014 with Međimurje, and went on to work with Varaždin’s youth and senior teams, Polet Sveti Martin na Muri, Podravina Ludbreg, Mladost Ždralovi and Slaven Belupo.

In November 2023, Varaždin announced that Kovačević had been diagnosed with lung cancer. He stayed on the bench until early December before stepping away for surgery, and in late March 2024, he confirmed that the cancer had receded.

World.title: Zagreb Will Remain Directly Connected to Madrid This Winter
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – Zagreb will remain directly connected to Madrid this winter as Croatia Airlines decides to keep the direct link between the two capital cities open outside of summer.

The Spanish capital is one of the largest cities in the EU, a paradise for lovers of food, football, history and the irresistible Mediterranean lifestyle. Madrid, with an average altitude of 650 metres, is the second-highest capital in Europe after Andorra. Lana Mindoljevic writes for Putni kofer that this metropolis is now also available to Croatian travellers over winter. Croatia Airlines is, for the first time, opting to continue running its seasonal route between the Croatian and Spanish capitals even after the end of the summer timetable.

FLIGHTS ARE ON MONDAYS, THURSDAYS AND SATURDAYS, WITH A BREAK DURING PART OF THE WINTER

Direct flights between Zagreb and Madrid will operate until the 16th of January 2027, and then again from the 15th to the 27th of March 2027. In both periods they are scheduled three times a week, on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays. The only period without flights will therefore be from the 17th of January to the 14th of March. For all three days the departure and arrival times are the same. Departure from Zagreb is at 8:25, and the return from Madrid at 12:10. The flight lasts between two hours and 45 minutes and two hours and 55 minutes.

Such a schedule allows, for example, departure on Thursday and return on Monday, with four overnight stays in Madrid. For a shorter break one can combine Saturday departure with return on Monday. The morning flight from Zagreb leaves a good part of the first day for getting to know the city, while on the last day one has to count on leaving for the airport during the morning.

madrid is an excellent winter city break from zagreb

Madrid is an excellent choice for travellers who like to combine art, architecture and good food. The winter months give a special rhythm to the visit: a colder morning can be spent in a museum, the sunny part of the day in a park, and the evening in one of the city taverns. Although we associate Spain with sun and a warm climate, in Madrid in winter you should not expect spring temperatures. A warm jacket and comfortable shoes are a mandatory part of the luggage.

For art lovers the main asset is the famous museum triangle. The ‘Golden Triangle of Art’ consists of three renowned Madrid museums: Museo del Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza, which are home to some of the world’s most valuable art collections. In the Prado one can see Velázquez’s “Las Meninas” (The Maids of Honour), Goya’s “Black Paintings” and Bosch’s “The Garden of Earthly Delights”. The Reina Sofía Museum holds Picasso’s “Guernica”, while Thyssen-Bornemisza offers an overview of European painting through different periods. Instead of trying to see everything in one day, choose the museum that interests you the most and leave it enough time.

THE ROYAL PALACE IN WHICH NOBODY ACTUALLY LIVES

A first visit to Madrid is hard to imagine without the Royal Palace, Plaza Mayor and Puerta del Sol. These places can be connected into a walk through the historic centre, with stops for coffee and exploring the surrounding streets. The Royal Palace is the official royal residence even though no one has lived in it since 1967. It has a huge courtyard and an incredible 3,418 rooms, and today it is used exclusively for state ceremonies. The building is open to the public, and for visitors to Madrid the changing of the guard, which takes place every Wednesday and Saturday, could also be interesting.

TWO FAMOUS SQUARES THAT SHOULD NOT BE MISSED

The famous Puerta del Sol square, translated as the Gate of the Sun or simply ‘Sol’, is an unmissable stop, and on it is the ‘centre of Spain’. Namely, on Sol, in front of the building of the Royal Post Office, there is the well-known plaque that marks ‘kilometre zero’ of all Spanish roads. In the centre of the square there is also a statue of King Charles III, but it is not the most popular statue on the square. It is overshadowed by the statue of a bear standing on its hind legs to feast on the fruits of the madroño tree, a sculpture that essentially symbolises the growth of the city.

Plaza Mayor, a gigantic square in the very heart of Madrid, has always been the centre of events. Kings were crowned there, but heads were also cut off. Today coffee is often drunk and time is enjoyed surrounded by beautiful buildings. This very square is also home to the traditional Christmas market, which has been held there since 1860. For a quieter part of the day there is El Retiro park, one of the favourite city green destinations. Together with the Paseo del Prado area it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage. It is nice to fit it into a day dedicated to museums: after a few hours in front of paintings a walk in the open air will be welcome.

Madrid is also discovered at the table. In the La Latina neighbourhood, especially around Cava Baja and Cava Alta streets, taverns and bars line up where you can try small bites and share several dishes. Croquettes, patatas bravas and potato tortilla are a good start to such a gastronomic tour. For a cold afternoon save a place for churros with thick hot chocolate, one of the recognisable Madrid sweet stops. If you stay in the city over Sunday, you can spend the morning at El Rastro, the famous flea market where clothes, records, antiques and various small items are browsed, and then continue for lunch in La Latina.

the city of football

Madrid is known as a city of football, and many visit it precisely to take a look at some of its famous stadiums. In the case of Real Madrid it is Estadio Santiago Bernabéu, which can hold 81 thousand people, and in the case of Atlético de Madrid Wanda Metropolitano. If you are a football lover, you can opt for one of the guided tours and look at the clubs’ memorabilia, jerseys and trophies in the museums on that topic.

IN DECEMBER MADRID PUTS ON ITS FESTIVE ATTIRE…

A trip in December brings an additional reason to come: illuminated streets, Christmas decorations and the traditional market on Plaza Mayor. A walk through the city then easily turns into an evening tour of festive scenes. For now it is known that Advent begins at the end of November and will last until the end of December, and besides the main location with more than 100 wooden stalls other locations in the city are also decorated.

World.title: Slovenia Wants a Hydropower Plant Next to the Border – Croatia Says No
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – Slovenia wants to construct a new hydropower plant next to the border with Croatia, but Croatia is, so far, totally against the plan.

Croatia currently completely opposes neighbouring Slovenia’s intention to build the Mokrice hydropower plant on the Sava River, which would be located about 450 metres from the Croatian border. Index reports that there is concern that the project could ecologically endanger the Sava as it enters into the territory of Croatia and call into question the supply of drinking water in that area, whose sources also supply Zagreb with water. HRT reports that energy expert Ivica Jakić and director of the Slovenian company HESS Boštjan Pišotek spoke about this topic.

potential problems for croatian drinking water

This is otherwise a hydropower plant that would be the last in a series of six facilities on the lower course of the Sava. Slovenian Minister for the Environment and Spatial Planning Polona Rifelj announced the relaunch of the procedure for deciding on the predominance of the public interest of energy production over nature conservation, reports N1 Slovenia. The Croatian Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition opposes the project due to the possible deterioration of the condition of surface and groundwater downstream of the dam.

The organisations Croatian Society for the Protection of Birds and Nature, CEE Bankwatch Network and Biom have also warned of the risks. According to their claims, existing Slovenian hydropower plants have already reduced the transport of sediments towards Croatia, which has contributed to the deepening of the Sava riverbed and the lowering of the groundwater level in the wider Zagreb area. The associations warn that the construction of HE Mokrice, downstream from the confluence of the Krka River with the Sava, could further worsen the situation and endanger the sources of drinking water for Zagreb. The Croatian ministry also states that the benefits of the project would remain on the Slovenian side, while Croatia would bear the negative consequences. Among the possible impacts, additional erosion of the riverbed, endangerment of fish habitats and protected areas of the Natura 2000 network are highlighted.

slovenia: the project is in line with all rules and regulations

HESS director Boštjan Pišotek said that this is a project that is being developed in accordance with European rules. “Croatia was informed about the procedure from the very beginning, about 15 years ago when the development of the Mokrice hydropower plant project began,” Pišotek said. He emphasised that cooperation with Croatia has several levels and that this resulted in Croatia giving a positive opinion on the placement of the Mokrice hydropower plant in the space. The Slovenian Ministry for the Environment and Spatial Planning earlier stated that Croatia can participate in cross-border consultations and put forward comments, but that it does not have a right of veto on the project. The decision on issuing the permit remains within the competence of the Slovenian authorities, while respecting international and European regulations.

croatia will link up its own system

Energy expert Ivica Jakić explained how the Croatian Multipurpose Hydraulic System Zaprešić would link up with the Slovenian hydropower plant. “The Mokrice hydropower plant must come from the Slovenian side to solve for the Slovenians the problem of soil deepening and the problem of deposits. It is a logical solution that Slovenia is looking for and wants to have,” Jakić said. He added that Croatia will link up with its own system. “It will solve the stabilisation of the water flow and the deepening of the soil. It will help us, but also Slovenia in further regulating the flow of the Sava River through the Croatian part,” Jakić concluded.

World.title: Function of Croatian Judiciary Facing Serious Problems Once Again
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – The very function of the Croatian judiciary is facing serious problems yet again due to some judges refusing to participate in proceedings if they’re recorded.

President of the Constitutional Court Frane Staničić stated that the Court will function with great difficulty due to the decision of some judges not to participate in sessions that are audio-recorded. Index reports that in an interview for RTL Danas he revealed that he is extremely sorry that individual judges, as he believes, have stopped providing protection to citizens within the judiciary system. These are judges Andrej Abramović, Sanja Bezbradica Jelavić and Lovorka Kušan, who oppose the way in which the audio recording of sessions was introduced. They claim that no appropriate decision of the Court was adopted and refuse to participate in sessions which, in their opinion, are being recorded unlawfully.

“we really tried hard to come to an agreement”

Staničić said that the judges during the past year invested great effort so that the Constitutional Court would function normally and protect the rights of citizens. As an example he cited decisions on politically sensitive laws, among which are the Act on Building Management and the Act on Local Taxes. He emphasised that the decisions on those laws were adopted by a large majority, with only one or two votes against. He added that the number of separate opinions has significantly decreased, which according to his interpretation shows that the judges sought to reach agreement. “Unfortunately, due to the refusal of certain colleagues to participate in the work of the constitutional court bodies because of the introduced audio recording, the system will function with great difficulty,” Staničić said.

When asked why he introduced recording without a decision of all the judges, Staničić confirmed that there was no formal decision of the Constitutional Court as a collegial body. He claims, however, that there was an informal agreement and that all judges were familiar with the procurement and installation of the equipment. “I warned the judges several times that we would buy the system, that we had procured it, installed it and that we were testing it. At the session on the 6th of October, which was also recorded, I said in front of everyone that from that day, in accordance with the agreement, the sessions are being recorded. No one reacted to that,” he explained. He also commented on the appearance of judge Andrej Abramović, who had been a guest on RTL the day before. Staničić believes that Abramović should have pointed out his disagreement before the conflict among the judges arose because of the recording.

the introduction of audio recording doesn’t require the permission of all judges

“He said in your programme that he practically knew that recording was taking place, or rather that recording would be introduced, but that I am neither his father nor mother, so he would not warn me that something is not good,” Staničić said. “I’d like to openly ask the public to judge – is it in accordance with the role of a Constitutional Court judge that if he considers that something is not good, he collegially warns the President of the Court that he considers that this should not be done, or that he remains silent and then on the basis of his unexpressed disagreement creates this problem that has now occurred?” he added.

Staničić claims that he did not need a special decision of all the judges to introduce audio recording because as President he has the authority to decide on the manner of establishing the minutes. As the main reason for introducing recording he cited earlier disagreements about the content of the minutes of the sessions.

“I introduced audio recording for a simple reason: we had a series of problems with establishing the authenticity of the minutes. It happened that colleagues claim that something stands in the minutes that should not stand and vice versa,” he explained. As a particularly problematic case he cited the events from May of this year, when the judges discussed the composition of the panels of the Constitutional Court. According to his words, it was precisely the judges who now oppose the recording who at that time contested the minutes.

“The judges who today contest the audio recording at that time contested the minutes that were signed by two minute-takers and whose accuracy was confirmed by five judges. In such circumstances there is no other way to ensure an authentic record that no one will be able to contest,” Staničić said.

should some sessions be completely open to the public?

The President of the Constitutional Court believes that audio recording should contribute to transparency and the possibility of verifying what was said at the sessions. He also announced that he wants to open a discussion on the possibility that part of the sessions of the Constitutional Court will in future be accessible to the public.

“I personally believe that the Court should be more open to the public in general. I can announce that I will initiate a serious discussion at the Constitutional Court on the Court becoming more open, that perhaps even part of the sessions will be public,” he stated. He emphasised that the main task of the Constitutional Court is the protection of citizens’ rights, but he believes that due to the current conflict that task has fallen into the background. He also rejected claims that the recordings of the sessions are his private documentation.

“This is official documentation created in official premises, with official equipment, and is stored on the official servers and information system of the Constitutional Court,” he said.

Staničić claims that every judge can access the recordings and listen to them. He rejected the claim of judge Abramović that access was denied to someone, but at the same time emphasised that a distinction must be made between the possibility of listening and obtaining one’s own copy of the recording. “I received a request for a copy of the recording. Here a distinction must be made between the possibility of listening, which is absolutely not disputed, and the question of copies. I replied only to the colleague who requested it that her request will be considered in terms of scope and possibilities. Therefore, such a request has by no means been rejected,” he stated.

no agreement has been reached at all

In order to resolve the dispute, Staničić proposed the establishment of a working group that would prepare rules on audio recording. It would include him, the Secretary General of the Constitutional Court and one of the judges who oppose the recording. “Unfortunately, I did not receive a positive answer because participation in the working group is conditioned on the cessation of audio recording. I have already explained that this is impossible, because it is the only way in which I can ensure authenticity,” he said.

Staničić stated that one of the three judges who opposed the recording nevertheless participated in a session, although she retained her opposition. He believes that the remaining two judges could have done the same so that the work of the Court would not be hindered. “Unfortunately, the other two judges did not want to follow that example. They could have retained their opposition, but we want to protect citizens. However, they chose the opposite – not to protect the rights of citizens, but to deepen the conflict, which is unnecessary,” he said.

a new session has been announced for november the 13th

The President of the Constitutional Court said that he has no mechanisms by which he could force the judges to participate in the work. Nevertheless, he hopes that everyone will accept the responsibility they have towards citizens and enable the continuation of regular work. He announced that he will schedule a new session as soon as the two judges who oppose the recording return from an official trip, which he expects to take place on or around the 13th of November. In the meantime the question remains open whether an agreement will be reached on the manner of recording the sessions.

Staničić also said that the Constitutional Court has received requests from GONG, the media and citizens for access to the audio recordings. He emphasised that this is sensitive documentation that may contain secret data and that he cannot make it public on his own. Due to the great public interest he announced that he will seek the consent of all constitutional judges for the publication of the recordings. If he obtains it, he is ready to publish them, and if someone opposes it, he announced that he will publicly say who was against.

“This is a very sensitive issue and secret data that I cannot just give out. However, given the extreme importance of the issue and the interest of the public, I will propose and seek a consensus of all judges that the recordings be given to the public. If a consensus is reached, I will give the recordings. If it is not reached, if even one judge is against, I will publicly announce which judges were against it,” Staničić concluded.

World.title: Circuit court upholds prosecutor's suspended prison sentence
World.content:
A court has upheld a prosecutor's conviction for falsifying and using a plea agreement consent form, leaving her suspended prison sentence in place.

The second-tier Tallinn Circuit Court agreed with summer's ruling on Prosecutor Eve Soostar, who had been charged with falsifying the documents – apparently to lighten her workload.

The circuit court upheld the first tier Harju County Court's June 14 ruling and dismissed an appeal filed by Soostar's defense lawyer, finding no grounds to grant it.

The county court found the prosecutor guilty of falsifying a consent form for plea agreement proceedings and using the falsified form, sentencing her to six months in prison in suspended sentence provided the defendant does not commit any other intentional criminal offense over a one-year probation period.

The court found it proven that Soostar removed the victim's consent form from the criminal case file — in which the victim had expressed opposition to plea deal proceedings — and replaced it with a form she had prepared herself, in which the victim appeared to agree to the use of a plea bargain. She then attached a digital signature confirmation sheet from the victim's original consent form, which gave the impression the victim had signed the replacement form.

According to the court, by adding the falsified consent form to the file and forwarding it to the court, Soostar also fulfilled the definition of the offense of using a falsified document. The court agreed with the Prosecutor's Office that the purpose was to obtain the right to resolve the case via simplified proceedings, carrying out her duties with a lighter workload than other types of proceedings would have entailed.

Soostar was also accused of having falsified and used a falsified civil claim, but had been acquitted of those charges in June. Under the provision she was charged with, falsifying a document is a punishable offense, but the court found a civil claim does not meet the definition of a document in the relevant understanding of current law.

The court did not identify any mitigating or aggravating circumstances, and also ordered Soostar to pay €1,419 procedural costs.

World.title: Setomaa kindergarten holds its own Olympics in Värska
World.content:
While older kids were off school for fall break last week, Setomaa kindergarteners gathered at Värska School for a day of Olympic-inspired sports and games.

For the second year in a row, kindergarten classes from across Setomaa Municipality came together for a morning of playful games and movement.

Organizers hope the event will help foster a love of sports — and perhaps even inspire some to compete in the actual Olympics one day.

"This year, we're focusing specifically on Olympic events," said Setomaa Kindergarten principal Sanna Saarestik.

Participants could try their hand at hurdles, high jump, and even horseback riding — with hobby horses — among other activities aimed at making sports fun.

"Throwing a ball doesn't have to be dull or serious," she added. "Why not throw them through the Olympic rings?"

The young athletes each had their favorites and challenges. Jasmin said the high jump was the hardest event "because the bar just kept going higher," while Kristofer found the obstacles challenging during the hobby-horse riding event.

Emilia, meanwhile, said she did well at ball-throwing. Asked which balls were easiest to throw, she replied, "The smallest ones."

More opportunities for movement

Saarestik said the teachers did a great job planning activities that kept children engaged while getting them moving and working different muscle groups.

With families not always having many opportunities to be physically active together, she said, the kindergarten can help fill that gap.

"Maybe we'll even include parents in the Olympics next year," Saarestik added.

World.title: Tallinn's ice skating rinks begin new season
World.content:
Ice skating season has begun in Tallinn after several municipal-run rinks opened their doors over the weekend, with more expected to do so in the coming weeks.

On Saturday (October 31), skating rinks in Mustamäe and Lasnamäe saw the first ice skaters of the winter season. The Old Town rink will open on November 14 and Nõmme's on November 21.

One of Tallinn's largest ice rinks, at the Pirita Sports Center, will open in late November or early December, depending on weather conditions.

"Although autumn is still underway, our ice maintenance teams have done a great job and the first skating rinks are ready to welcome everyone interested," said Deputy Mayor Monika Haukanõmm.

This year, young people and seniors will also be allocated free sessions.

Tallinn's ice rinks offer free skating sessions for schools from Monday to Friday between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Advance registration is required, and skates can be rented on site for a fee if necessary.

Tallinn's seniors can skate free of charge on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.

Tallinn's schoolteachers are offered free skating courses so that they can teach pupils to skate safely. There will be morning events for children on the weekends.

One hour of skating at the capital's ice rinks costs €7.20–11.40, while discounted tickets for children and seniors cost €4.90–9.20. Season passes are also available, providing unlimited access to all city-owned ice rinks.

Visitors can bring their own skates or rent them on site for prices starting at €5.

The skating season at the Old Town ice park will last until the end of March, while the other Tallinn ice rinks will remain open until mid-March.

More information is available on the Uisupark website.

World.title: Therapist: No skills needed to benefit from creative arts therapy
World.content:
Creative arts therapy can help people of all ages express emotions and memories beyond words, with no artistic skills required, Estonian therapist Epp Sussen says.

Sussen, a board member for the Estonian Society of Creative Arts Therapies (ELTÜ), said people are used to talking, but memories and experiences often involve colors, sounds and sensory impressions that can't easily be put into words.

She said visual art therapy, for example, can benefit people of all ages, from children to elderly adults, and help with everything from personal reflection and career decisions to depression or recovery from something.

"There are so many different possibilities and very few contraindications," she added.

Fellow creative arts therapist Katre Eesmaa said people are often reluctant to try therapy because they believe they can't draw, for example. However, no form of creative arts therapy requires participants to know how to draw, paint, dance or play a musical instrument.

Eesmaa said there is a simple exercise that can help take pressure off facing a blank sheet of paper. "You draw 30 to 40 dots all over the paper, then connect them with lines," she explained.

Working at an easel can also allow people to step back and view their work from a distance. With abstract images, they can even turn the paper upside down to see what shapes or patterns emerge.

Once someone finds a suitable shape or image, then they can start to color it.

Creative arts therapists Katre Eesmaa (middle) and Epp Sussen (right) demonstrating a common exercise on "Terevisioon." Source: ERR

No talking necessary either

Sussen emphasized that the picture doesn't have to look good.

"People often get hung up on having to make something beautiful, but what matters more is the process," she noted, adding that even simply the act of squeezing and splattering paint can sometimes help.

"Plenty of young folks don't want to talk in therapy; they'd rather sit quietly and work on their drawing," Sussen said. "Drawing and painting can help them let out some of the emotions they're holding inside."

She explained that creative arts therapy can help people tap into different inner resources. While talking engages the rational mind, letting go and trusting the creative process rather than getting stuck on seeking the "right" color, for example, can help people discover something new within themselves.

The ELTÜ board member also stressed that creative arts therapists in Estonia don't make diagnoses.

"If someone draws a completely black picture, we're not diagnosing them with depression," Sussen said. "They can tell us themselves what the color black there means to them."

World.title: Tallinn bench marks birthplace of iconic Estonian novel 'Truth and Justice'
World.content:
A commemorative bench by Tallinn Central Hospital now marks the place where Estonian author A. H. Tammsaare penned his classic "Truth and Justice," first published in 1926.

Tammsaare wrote the first volume of the five-part work while living in a small two-room apartment on Õuna tänav. To find the quiet he needed to work, he rented an attic room in a summer house at Kirikuaia 6, said Maarja Vaino, director of the Tallinn Literature Center.

"Unfortunately, the house was demolished in the 1950s, and it's now the site of a children's clinic," she said. "But it's truly wonderful to see such an important cultural site in the city now marked with a bench."

Credited with the idea is historian, author and politician Jaak Juske, who said places vital to Estonia's cultural history deserve recognition, "especially when the surrounding cityscape has changed beyond recognition."

The birthplace of "Truth and Justice," one of the country's most foundational literary works, he added, is a perfect example.

Still relevant

Mayor Peeter Raudsepp said the century-old novel's themes of justice, mutual understanding, love and the absence thereof still remain relevant today.

He expressed hope that the bench would offer people a place to pause and reflect, "and maybe even inspire them to revisit Tammsaare's work."

World.title: Võro-language Minecraft, Zumba and film marathon on tap for language week
World.content:
Starting Monday, Võro Language Week will celebrate the regional Southeastern Estonian language with events from a Minecraft session to a Zumba class — all in Võro.

In a nod to the famous James Bond catchphrase, this year's theme, "Mu nimi om kiil. Võro kiil!" ("My name is Language. The Võro Language!") highlights the role of language as an element of identity.

Organizers say keeping the Võro language alive means not only speaking it, but also adapting it to modern use.

After years of translating Minecraft terminology, the popular game is now playable in Võro. Hipp Saar will lead a group gaming session at Kagukeskus in Võru.

The week will also feature what organizers say is the world's first Võro-language Zumba class. Project manager Kadri Laube said the goal is to attract around 100 participants.

"We want to spread the message that we can do all kinds of activities in our own language too," Laube said, adding that the class will also spotlight music by local artists.

Sign in Võru at a handicraft fair in Võru. Source: Külli Eichenbaum

Trivia, music and kindergarten art

Throughout the week, events will take place at kindergartens, schools, libraries and community centers across the regions, including talks, trivia night, a folk music sing-along, book and album launches and a kindergarten art exhibition at the local Maksimarket.

A film marathon at Varstu Cultural Center in Rõuge Municipality will also bring fans and filmmakers together for nearly 10 hours of screenings showcasing the Võro language and culture, while the Uma Laul song contest will feature new Võro-language music by leading songwriters.

Võro Language Week wraps up Sunday with a concert by Ummamuudu at Mõniste Community Center in Mehka.

Laube encouraged people to take the week as an opportunity to think more consciously about their language and everyday habits.

"Every small step toward remembering the language of our childhood or ancestors is a big step toward keeping our language and culture alive," she added.

World.title: Russian citizen expelled to 'prevent activities' that 'threaten' Estonia
World.content:
A Russian citizen was expelled from Estonia on Monday who had links to the Russian security services, Estonia's Internal Security Service (KAPO) said. The individual was a professor at the now-closed Euroacademy in Tallinn and also worked at ERR for two years.

Kapo said it had recommended that Russian citizen Leonid Karabeshkin (Estonian spelling: Karabeškin) be sent out of Estonia and banned him from entering the Schengen area.

It posted the statement on the social media site X along with a video of a man being escorted by two police officers to the Russian border at Koidula in southern Estonia.

"The aim of the expulsion is to prevent and counter activities that threaten the security of Estonia and Europe more broadly," KAPO wrote.

@Politsei saatis KAPO ettepanekul Eestist välja Venemaa kodaniku Leonid Karabeskini ning kehtestas talle Schengeni sissesõidukeelu. Väljasaatmise eesmärk on ennetada ja tõkestada Eesti ning laiemalt Euroopa julgeolekut ohustavat tegevust. https://t.co/CQDTtZ7Jge — Kaitsepolitseiamet (@kaitsepolitsei) November 2, 2026

Links to Russian intellegence

Kapo spokesperson Marta Tuul told ERR that Karabeshkin had connections with Russian intelligence services and people working on their behalf.

"He regularly traveled to Russia and met with them there. Several of them have been sanctioned by the European Union and Ukraine for carrying out Russia's hostile influence activities. And he is linked to influence networks such as CIRP, RuBaltic and Regnum, as well as individuals associated with them," she said.

"In the case of Regnum, we are talking about Sergei Rekeda and also Sergei Rudnov. The latter is also on the United Kingdom's and Ukraine's sanctions lists. CIRP is the Center for International and Regional Policy of Russia, and he worked there as a project manager, while several people with FSB backgrounds have participated in events organized by the center," Tuul explained.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said Estonia will not turn a blind eye to threats to our security or that of Europe.

"Those with links to Russian intelligence services and hostile influence networks have no place exploiting our openness. One such individual has now been expelled from Estonia and barred from entering the Schengen area. Rightly so. We will not tolerate activities that undermine our security," he said.

Estonia will not turn a blind eye to threats to our security or that of Europe. Those with links to Russian intelligence services and hostile influence networks have no place exploiting our openness. One such individual has now been expelled from Estonia and barred from entering the Schengen area. Rightly so. We will not tolerate activities that undermine our security. — Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) November 2, 2026

Karabeshkin worked at ERR

Karabeshkin worked as a foreign news reporter for Estonian Public Broadcasting's (ERR) Russian-language radio news from 2022 to 2024.

The employment contract was terminated by mutual agreement, although not because of the circumstances that came to light on Monday. Both before and after his employment, he occasionally appeared as a guest to comment on foreign affairs in Russian-language radio and television programs.

ERR Management Board Chairman Erik Roose said that, in light of Monday's news, ERR has conducted an initial rapid assessment, as the news is unpleasant and requires more thorough analysis.

"There were no suspicions concerning Karabeshkin when he was hired. During his employment, the editorial team also saw no signs of such attitudes or influence activities that would have been reflected in the content. Otherwise, we would have acted immediately and terminated his employment contract. We will continue discussing with editorial managers what lessons can be learned from this," Roose said.

Leonid Karabeshkin. Source: Gergey Lukecha/ERR

Asked whether Karabeshkin's influence activities were in any way reflected in his work at ERR, KAPO's Tuul said probably not.

"However, it did give him an opportunity to gain access to people he was interested in," she said.

Tuul said Karabeshkin had contacts with Russian intelligence services and shared information with them about the Russian-speaking population living in Estonia. Asked what specific activities by Karabeshkin led to his expulsion from Estonia, Tuul replied that such matters are assessed as a whole, rather than on the basis of a single incident. "This was systematic activity."

Professor and dean at Euroacademy

Before working with ERR, Karabeshkin was a political scientist and the dean at the now-defunct private university Euroacademy in Tallinn from 2006-2020. His specialization was international relations, Russian foreign policy, and political processes in the former Soviet Union.

According to the Estonian Research Information System (ETIS), Karabeshkin studied at St. Petersburg State University from 1997 to 1999. From 1999 to 2002, he was a doctoral student at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences. From 2002 to 2005, Karabeshkin worked at the Center for International and Regional Policy in St. Petersburg.

He then moved to Estonia, and on February 1, 2006, became an associate professor and dean of the Faculty of International Relations at Euroacademy. In 2012, he was promoted to professor. He remained associated with the institution until it closed operations in 2020.

Karabeshkin then continued writing publications and speaking at conferences. For example, in 2021, he spoke at the Baltic Defense College's annual conference on Russia. In 2022, he published a research article in an Austrian Ministry of Defense publication on the Russian peacekeeping operation in Karabakh.

This article was updated to add comments from Margus Tsahkna, Erik Roose and Marta Tuul. Then again to add additional details about Karabeshkin's career.

World.title: Defense Forces broke law on Ukrainian soldier training background checks
World.content:
The Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) acted illegally when it barred a reservists from taking part in a military exercise due to his criminal record, the Justice Chancellor ruled.

The EDF together with the state Defense Resources Agency (KRA) declined to allow the reservist from taking part in the Legio training mission for Ukrainian military personnel

"The Defense Forces' desire to involve only reservists, including volunteers, with impeccable pasts and backgrounds in training certainly deserves recognition. However, background checks must be carried out on a proper legal basis, and this also applies in the current security situation," wrote Olari Koppel, director of the Office of the Chancellor of Justice, acting in the capacity of Chancellor of Justice.

"A legal analysis of the application submitted to the Chancellor of Justice and the course of events related to it allows us to conclude that the Defense Forces and the Defense Resources Agency erred in this case when they provided the applicant with unclear and inaccurate information about the organization of the selection process and the background check. The Defense Forces' inquiry into the applicant's archived criminal record was also not in accordance with the law," Koppel added.

According to the Chancellor of Justice, the candidate was also not sufficiently informed of the actual basis for the check, and the initial refusal was not adequately justified.

At the same time, the Chancellor of Justice considers that the Defense Forces have the right to decide whom to involve voluntarily in the mission. However, a refusal must be based on specific circumstances and clear legal reasoning, rather than merely general references to the values of the EDF

The Chancellor of Justice asked the Minister of Defense to report within one month on what steps would be taken to ensure that background checks on reservists are lawful in the future. He also proposed clarifying the Defense Forces Organization Act to provide a clear legal basis for checking candidates applying for international training missions.

The KRA also announced on Monday that applications had opened for Legio, an international training initiative taking place in Poland and led by Norway, which aims to support Ukrainian soldiers through military training and strengthen their combat capabilities.

As part of the initiative, the Estonian Defense Forces contribute by providing military training to Ukrainian personnel. According to Rainer Järvela, head of the Reserve Service Bureau at the KRA, Estonia is participating to help maintain and develop the Ukrainian Armed Forces' combat capabilities.

The instructor team, consisting of Estonian active-duty military personnel, reservists and Defense League members, organizes and conducts basic soldier training for Ukrainians in cooperation with representatives of other countries.

Estonia is seeking applications from active-duty military personnel, reservists and Defense League members for the initiative. Estonia joined the training mission in 2025 and will continue contributing in 2027 through both training planning and instructors. Applications for the first rotation can be submitted until November 27.

Koppel is acting Chancellor of Justice following the previous office holder, Ülle Madise, becoming President of Estonia last month. Madise has nominated Justice of the Supreme Court Oliver Kask for the role.

World.title: Iraq’s foreign reserves hit $75.3 billion
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s foreign reserves rose to over 113.99 trillion Iraqi dinars (almost $75.3 billion) as of October 15, 2026, according to data released by the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI).

The country’s foreign reserves increased compared to September, when they stood at approximately 101.718 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $67.17 billion), local news outlet Shafaq News reported.

Director of the CBI’s Statistics and Research Department, Samir Neama, said that the country’s foreign currency reserves can cover Iraq’s imports for a whole year.

Speaking at the MERI 2026 forum in Erbil, Neama clarified that the CBI is in a very comfortable situation in terms of foreign reserves.

While International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports indicate a capability to finance imports for three to six months, Neama confirmed that the reserves are sufficient to cover the country’s needs for more than a year.

A Standard Chartered economist said in early October that Iraq may resort to the IMF if oil revenues continue to fall and the currency’s devaluation fails to boost state finances as intended.

Standard Chartered chief economist for the Middle East and Pakistan Carla Slim said that any potential program with the IMF could entail structural reforms, particularly regarding the public sector wage bill, to enhance fiscal sustainability, Bloomberg reported.

If the current pace of depletion continues, Iraq’s foreign reserves might fall to roughly $60 billion by the end of the year, down from over $100 billion at the beginning of the year, according to Slim.

The economist indicated that the local currency’s exchange rate may be adjusted again in the future months, based on changes in oil earnings and foreign reserves.

World.title: Australians held in Iraq over ISIS connections may face death penalty
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – 13 Australian men and boys detained in Iraqi prisons over alleged connections to ISIS could potentially face trial and the death penalty by hanging.

Between January and February 2026, the US military transferred approximately 5,700 detainees, including around 2,200 foreigners from 65 different countries, from prisons in northeast Syria to al-Karkh Central Prison near Baghdad due to increasing instability in Syria.

The detainees transferred from northeastern Syria to Iraqi custody earlier this year included the 13 Australian men and boys.

After completing their investigations, Iraqi authorities are proceeding with charges under extensive anti-terrorism legislation that carries the death sentence.

The Australian federal government has stated that it will not engage in the repatriation of the detainees and has refused to intervene or assist in their return.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has denounced the transfer, claiming that Australia is outsourcing its duties rather than pursuing its nationals domestically. They have also warned of possible torture-extracted confessions, unjust trials, and execution.

There is disagreement among the public and community over the issue. Human rights supporters say that Australia should bring its nationals back to stand prosecution under domestic law, while others maintain that individuals who travel overseas must deal with the laws and legal systems of the host nation.

World.title: Iraqi PM to visit Kuwait, Bahrain
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is scheduled to visit Kuwait and Bahrain this week as part of a regional diplomatic tour.

Official sources confirmed the trip is set for the current week, with reports noting a visit to Bahrain planned around Wednesday.

Al-Zaidi is expected to hold talks in Kuwait focusing on resolving longstanding bilateral and economic issues, including maritime boundary demarcation, the Mubarak al-Kabeer Port project and its potential impact on Iraq’s al-Faw Grand Port, missing Kuwaiti people and property from the 1990 invasion, and broader regional security cooperation.

The Iraqi prime minister’s agenda in Bahrain is expected to address regional de-escalation, security, strategies to open new economic and investment avenues, and concerns regarding Bahrain’s Shiite community.

As part of the Iraqi government’s effort to foster regional economic integration, handle cross-border security issues, and foster confidence, al-Zaidi has made recent regional visits to Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria, Turkey, and Iran.

World.title: Papa Johns to enter Iraq in 2027, plans 25 restaurants by 2035
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Papa Johns, an American pizza brand, has revealed ambitions to join the Iraqi market, with the first restaurant set to open in spring 2027 and a goal of 25 outlets throughout the nation by 2035.

The expansion follows a ten-year renewal of the company’s franchise deal with PJP Investments Group, which extends their exclusive Middle East collaboration until 2036 and formally adds Iraq as a new market.

PJP, which manages Papa Johns restaurants in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Jordan, intends to increase the brand’s regional footprint from 167 to more than 400 by 2036.

Todd Penegor, President and CEO of Papa Johns, said that the company’s entry into Iraq underlines its trust in the Middle East as a crucial region for worldwide growth.

PJP has worked with Papa Johns for over two decades, and its restaurant network has grown dramatically under the ownership of Levant Capital.

The arrangement marks Papa Johns debut into Iraq’s rapidly expanding restaurant and food service business, bringing another worldwide dining brand to the country.

World.title: Iraq plans to expand oil tanker fleet
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Oil Ministry is planning to purchase large oil tankers to increase its ability to transport and market crude oil internationally.

The strategic move seeks to improve financial returns from crude exports while lowering transportation expenses.

The spokesperson for the Oil Ministry, Salim al-Rikabi, told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) on Monday that the Iraqi tanker fleet currently comprises six small and medium-sized tankers.

Al-Rikabi explained that the ministry is also considering establishing partnerships with specialized firms in the maritime transport sector.

Crude oil can be stored or transported across the Strait of Hormuz by renting tankers from other businesses, according to al-Rikabi.

The Iraqi Ministry of Oil is considering the purchase of 10 oil tankers as part of its efforts to develop its export infrastructure and expand options for delivering shipments to global markets.

The step is part of the government’s efforts to strengthen the role of the Iraqi Oil Tankers Company (IOTC) and leverage the ownership of maritime transport assets, which would provide greater flexibility in marketing crude oil and managing shipments.

The plan is considered crucial given Iraq’s desire to improve the terms of its oil sales and reduce the discounts associated with certain existing marketing and transportation arrangements.

Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair revealed recently that the ministry is considering the purchase of 10 supertankers, with an estimated total cost of $2 billion, according to Attaqa News.

According to Khudair, the projected fleet will have a total capacity of 10 million barrels since each tanker has a capacity of around one million barrels.

Owning these tankers would increase export earnings; estimates indicate that Iraq might save between 30 percent and 40 percent on the losses it presently suffers from price reductions.

World.title: Iraqi British Professor Salman Rawaf criticizes treatment at Baghdad Education Conference
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Prominent Iraqi-British public health academic Professor Salman Rawaf has criticized the organization of the Third Iraq Education Conference at the University of Baghdad after microphones were removed from in front of him during his speech.

A video circulating on social media shows Rawaf expressing frustration over the incident, describing the situation as disgraceful and questioning the organization of an international academic event after travelling approximately 5,000 miles to attend.

Rawaf is a Professor of Public Health at Imperial College London and Director of its World Health Organization (WHO) Collaborating Centre for Public Health Education and Training.

The incident came just days after Rawaf was officially welcomed by University of Baghdad President Professor Alaa Abdulhassan Atiyah Hassan during a meeting focused on strengthening academic cooperation between the University of Baghdad and Imperial College London.

According to the university, the discussions covered joint research, academic exchanges, postgraduate supervision and visiting professor programs aimed at expanding international academic partnerships.

Rawaf is also a graduate of the University of Baghdad’s College of Medicine and has established an international reputation for his contributions to public health.

The removal of microphones during his conference appearance sparked criticism on social media, raising concerns about the treatment of internationally recognized Iraqi academics visiting their home country.

Rawaf subsequently described the incident as an organizational error involving the departure of television channels, rather than attributing it to a deliberate attempt to silence him.

The incident has nevertheless drawn attention to the importance of professional conference management and ensuring that distinguished academic guests are given appropriate opportunities to contribute to Iraq’s educational and scientific development.

World.title: Iraq holds French ISIS suspects accountable for terrorist ties
World.content:
Baghdad – A decade ago, the Islamic State group broadcast its crimes as it recruited radicals from around the world and imposed a brutal system of oppression across swathes of Syria and Iraq.

Years on from the group’s military defeat, accused members are again in the spotlight — this time on trial in Iraq, including French nationals, for atrocities committed against the people trapped in the so-called caliphate.

Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year, charged with belonging to the group that controlled large parts of both countries between 2014 and 2017.

In its first verdicts handed down last week, Baghdad’s Karkh Criminal Court sentenced nine men to jail terms of up to 20 years.

A 24-year-old defendant, taken to Syria by his mother more than 10 years ago, was given 15 years. AFP is withholding his identity for legal reasons.

When the sentence was announced, the man said in Arabic: “I went to Syria, but it was my mother who chose for me. What is my fault?”

– ‘Deceived’ –

Thousands of people travelled from Europe to join IS during the war in Syria, where it declared a caliphate in 2014.

France, while repatriating hundreds of family members of jihadists, has refused to bring back most of the men accused of involvement, leaving them to face justice abroad.

Many French recruits were from disadvantaged suburbs of major cities and faced limited opportunities. They included descendants of immigrants, as well as converts to Islam.

The group imposed an extreme interpretation of sharia, forcing women and girls into sexual slavery, and jailed or killed anyone who dared speak out against its atrocities.

Fear was the group’s instrument of domination over areas where women were hidden from view and where executions were carried out by bearded militants in public squares, for all to see.

Now, the accused are now being brought to court with shaved faces, wearing orange jumpsuits.

About 1,500 French people are believed to have joined IS.

Among them was Kamel Ben Mbarek, 42, who said he had worked as a driver for the group’s Islamic police in Raqqa, in northern Syria.

“I regret it… because I wasn’t young when the organisation deceived me,” he told the court.

Driven by “anger at the abuses of the Syrian regime”, he embraced an ideology “that retained only certain passages of the Quran” — a manipulation he only realised when he read the holy book in prison.

Fewer than half of the French defendants have appeared so far.

“I regret everything I did. I’ve lost everything,” said Adel Bouaoun, 28, accused of taking part in IS operations in Syria’s Aleppo and Palmyra.

He recounted harsh conditions in Kurdish-run prisons in Syria, saying detainees had died, and described “physical and psychological torture”.

IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and then in Syria in 2019 by a US-led coalition.

Thousands of jihadists, along with their families, were left in Syrian prisons and camps under Kurdish command.

Earlier this year, the new Syrian authorities that came to power after the fall of Bashar al-Assad took over the prisons holding the jihadists.

The US army then transferred more than 5,700 detainees of about 60 nationalities to Iraq, including at least five French nationals.

Rights groups have criticised the judicial process, calling it rushed and saying that confessions were extracted under duress.

“This entire procedure is a form of pressure. You have recorded statements that are not mine,” Lakhdar Sebouai, 34, said in court.

Also among those awaiting trial is Adrien Guihal, who claimed responsibility on behalf of IS for the July 2016 attack in Nice, when a truck rammed Bastille Day crowds, killing 86 people.

– ‘Law of the jungle’ –

At one hearing, three defendants were visibly moved when they saw their siblings, who had come from France, for the first time in years.

The judge allowed them to speak together for a few minutes.

In October, French lawyers Matthieu Bagard and Marie Dose, who are defending many of the 47 French nationals, said the Iraqi judiciary had barred them from entering the country to attend the hearings, after they described the detainees’ treatment as “inhumane”.

The two lawyers are calling for the defendants’ repatriation to France so they can be tried there.

Two Iraqi lawyers appointed in their absence refused to speak to AFP.

“Even if his sentence is different, he was tortured like an adult and tried like an adult,” Bagard told AFP, referring to the 24-year-old taken to Syria as a child.

Observers, representatives of the French embassy and journalists are attending the trials.

Rights groups fear death sentences will be handed out.

Before the court, Thomas Barnouin, 45, whose verdict is expected November 18, recalled travelling to Syria at the start of the conflict, convinced that he had a religious duty.

But “the organisation applied the law of the jungle, not the law of God”, he said.

“We did not know that it also wanted to carry out terrorist attacks in our own country, in France,” he added.

“I reject all its crimes.”

World.title: Israel army withdraws after Hebron operation
World.content:
Hebron – Israeli troops withdrew on Monday from an area of the occupied West Bank’s largest city that they had evacuated of its Palestinian residents, following an attack that killed two soldiers in October.

The operation had emptied a neighbourhood in Hebron city where the two gunmen had lived, with soldiers later destroying their homes — a practice commonly carried out by the military as punishment for attacks.

AFP journalists witnessed residents returning to their houses on Monday after the military left, with many in disarray after having been searched by troops.

“This morning, following the completion of all operational activities, the soldiers withdrew from the area of operation in Hebron. Counterterrorism activities throughout Judea and Samaria continue,” an Israeli military official said, using the biblical name for the Palestinian territory.

On October 23, days ahead of close-fought Israeli elections, two Palestinian gunmen attacked an army checkpoint near Hebron, killing two soldiers before being shot dead in a firefight.

The attack sparked the immediate demolition of buildings in the vicinity of the checkpoint, as well as vows of a major retaliatory operation from senior officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

By the following morning, the military had cleared out the residents of the assailants’ neighbourhood, displacing more than 3,000 people, according to the municipality.

The military official said that “soldiers conducted thorough searches of multiple locations, detained and questioned suspects, and located and confiscated four weapons, several vests, and additional military equipment”.

They also demolished the two attackers’ homes and “sealed an underground space located next to” one of them.

– ‘Terrified my children’ –

On Monday morning, an AFP journalist saw that many buildings had been spraypainted with black X’s to indicate they had been cleared and searched.

Mohammad Juaaba, a relative of one of the assailants, said the top floor of the family’s home had been destroyed, adding they planned to move back into the lower floors.

Rubble from the demolition blast was strewn around the house, and other relatives could be seen cleaning up the spaces that were still habitable.

Muhannad al-Tamimi, whose house had been occupied by soldiers since the operation began, returned to a trashed apartment with furniture and clothing littering the floors, mattresses overturned and a child’s bicycle broken.

“On the morning of the operation, I was sleeping in my home. The army stormed my house and blew up the door,” he told AFP.

“They assaulted me, put a gun to my wife’s head, terrified my children, and kicked my little daughter,” he added, also accusing the soldiers of stealing gold and money.

Asked for comment, the military said it was looking into the allegations.

Reem al-Sharif, a Hebron city council member, said the operation had actually covered two neighbourhoods, telling AFP that municipal workers were helping to clean up around the area.

World.title: Row erupts after Scottish govt sends IT contract to Bengaluru to administer welfare payment
World.content:
