World.title: Filipino embalmers – last caretakers of the dead, seldom cared for
World.content:
Part 2: Trainers say a decade of reforms professionalized the embalming industry, but regulation, data, and pay have not kept pace

PART 1 | Inside the world of Filipino embalmers

Last of 2 parts

When Jonnel Cribello received his license to embalm in 2009, one question followed him everywhere.

“The most frequent question people asked me [was] whether I washed my hands before shaking theirs,” he said.

A registered nurse who once dreamed of becoming a surgeon, Cribello turned to embalming after coming across a media feature on an embalming school. “If I wanted to work with the human body, the easiest route for me then was to work in the mortuary industry,” he said.

Today, he helps teach the next generation of embalmers as an accredited trainer and program director at the Philippine College of Advanced Studies (PCAS) in Cebu, one of only four active accredited embalming schools in the country and the only one outside Luzon.

Embalmers disinfect, preserve, and restore a body so families can hold a wake — often for days — before burial or cremation.

But while the industry has made strides in shedding its perception as dirty work, the systems around it — licensing, data, and pay — have been slower to catch up with other medical-adjacent fields.

Changing image

For years, embalmers were seen as untidy and uneducated, said James Patrick Ovejera, president of the Professional Embalmers Association of the Philippines Inc. (PEAP).

“There was an idea that it’s dirty work, the person is untidy, the person is illiterate, and the person is technically a low-class person,” he said. “There were even depictions in the movies wherein it’s a person that works in a dark place… a hunchback.”

That image began to shift around 2010, when the Department of Health (DOH) set out to professionalize the field, Ovejera said.

The rules governing embalming date back to 1975, when then-president Ferdinand E. Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 856, or the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines. Its chapter XXI, on the disposal of dead persons, covers everything from burial grounds to funeral and embalming establishments.

Detailed rules for embalmers came only in 1996, more than two decades later. They called for the DOH to create a Committee of Examiners for Undertakers and Embalmers (DOH-CEUE), which licenses embalmers and accredits training schools.

In 2010, the DOH reinstated the committee with new members, who worked with the University of the Philippines to streamline the curriculum and licensure exam, under Administrative Order No. 2010-0033. The order also, for the first time, mandated minimum wage for all embalmers.

The committee and the five training schools at the time then went region by region to explain the rules to local officials. Feedback led to new measures, including a refresher program for embalmers with long-expired licenses and a Filipino version of the exam, which was previously in English.

“There are a lot of people [who] are very skilled coming from the provinces…but they couldn’t really understand English well,” said Ovejera. At the time, he had been teaching at the Philippine Embalmers and Undertakers Review and Training Center (PEURTC), and enlisted in the roadshow efforts.

In 2018, embalmers like Ovejera formed PEAP as their own professional counterpart to the Philippine Mortuary Association, which represents funeral homeowners.

“At the time, there was no collective body representing us, and we wanted to do something about that,” he said.

In the classroom

LEARNING. Embalming students at PCAS watch an instructor lead a demonstration on a cadaver. Photo courtesy of PCAS

Under current DOH rules, aspiring embalmers need a high school diploma, at least 140 hours of instruction from an accredited institution, and proof that they have embalmed at least 10 cadavers within a year. They then take a licensure exam held twice a year, every March and September.

Under rules revised in 2021, licenses are issued by the DOH’s Health Facilities and Services Regulatory Bureau (HFSRB) after applicants pass the committee’s exam. These are valid for three years and can be revoked if not renewed within five.

Students spend about two months in class and a month embalming real cadavers at partner funeral homes. Tuition ranges from about P27,000 to about P30,000 depending on the training institution.

Over half of Cribello’s students at PCAS have worked in funeral homes or come from families that own one. His oldest student was 75; the average age is around 45.

“It’s such a unique challenge because people [are] going back to school after years of not having a good habit of reading or studying,” he said.

PCAS now runs two cohorts a year of about 60 students each, up from 10 per cohort in 2009. At PEURTC in Manila, where Ovejera still teaches, local classes run 40 to 60 students, plus a separate class of five to eight from neighboring Southeast Asian countries like Singapore, Thailand, and Malaysia who come to the Philippines for mortuary education. Affordability and English as a medium of instruction are the main attractions.

EMBALMING. Tools and chemicals found in an embalming preparation room at Arlington Memorial Chapels in Quezon City, Manila. Jake Gomez/Rappler

Philippine embalmers train on only a handful of tools and chemicals. In the US, Cribello estimated, training incorporates 30 to 35 pieces of equipment.

“There are very simple kinds and sets of tools that have been used in the past and continue to be taught today here. That much has not changed,” he said.

Most local funeral homes rely on formalin, a cheap formaldehyde solution. Other chemicals used abroad, in what is called soft embalming, can make a face look more natural.

But culture and climate shape the practice, Ovejera said. Filipino wakes routinely run around the clock for days, sometimes weeks, and softer chemicals do not hold up in humid weather.

Cost matters too. A 200-liter drum of formalin costs around P11,000 to P15,000, while soft-embalming chemicals can cost 20 times more, according to Ovejera. For that reason, only select funeral homes offer more technical and upscale embalming options.

An industry behind

Demand for an embalmer’s work is guaranteed. Fair pay, Cribello said, is not.

“There is a certain opportunity to review the industry regulations in terms of the kind of salaries imposed within the industry,” Cribello said. “I personally feel that we are behind [compared with] similar professionals like nurses and doctors.”

Entry-level salaries still hover around minimum wage (P401 to P755 per day, depending on the region), according to PCAS and PEAP, and embalmers get no hazard pay despite chronic exposure to chemicals like formaldehyde, which the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies as a Group 1 carcinogen.

The 2010 rules set minimum wage as the entry point, Ovejera said, but smaller funeral homes often pay per body instead, pushing many embalmers to freelance and work between funerary businesses.

Change in any regard would require legislation. “I agree that there must be changes. But how do we do that? It has to be in legislation,” Ovejera said.

Embalmers also have no seat on the body that licenses them. Under the current rules, the DOH-CEUE’s five members are a chairperson, vice chairperson, sanitary engineer, pathologist, and legal officer. No mention of an embalmer sitting on the committee of examiners.

Licensed embalmers take part only as assessors for the oral and practical exam. By contrast, the board that licenses nurses is made up of nurses.

Counting embalmers

The number of active, licensed embalmers in the country is hard to pin down.

The DOH-CEUE has not formally published updated figures in recent years, according to PCAS. The embalmers association recorded about 5,000 licensed embalmers in 2018, though that count includes those who have died, moved abroad, or let their licenses lapse.

Exams were suspended in 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Since resumption, each exam has licensed roughly 100 people, bringing the total to between 6,000 and 6,300, according to the embalmers association. PCAS estimates 200 to 300 new embalmers a year.

In March 2026, 75 aspirants earned their licenses. After the September 2026 written exam, 125 moved on to the oral and practical portion.

Better data would help as Singapore, Malaysia, and employers in the Middle East, Europe, and North America look to hire Filipino embalmers, Ovejera said.

“Without knowing the actual figures…we don’t even know: do we have enough [at home]?” Ovejera said.

The counts also miss a group that’s harder to track: people who embalm without a license, which DOH rules prohibit. Several embalmers we spoke with said the practice persists, particularly in provinces where training is inaccessible.

Room to grow

Both men remain hopeful that the industry will continue to catch up.

For Cribello, the work remains “the ultimate noble cause.” In his classes, he pushes the fundamentals of hygiene and care for grieving families, along with sounder business practices for a new generation of operators.

“While it’s [grim] and tiring, it gives fulfillment that I can have a platform where I can influence not just one student, but operators and embalmers all throughout the country,” he said.

For Ovejera, it became all the more personal in 2023, when his father died. “I wanted to make sure that we do the best for him,” he said. He helped embalm his father himself.

That experience, he said, further strengthened the importance of the work to grieving families. “The picture of an individual lying there inside the casket…will always be in the cognitive footprint of the family members,” he said.

PEAP has also explored ladderized programs through the introduction of embalming into more Filipino universities, Ovejera said. For now, it remains a short certificate course rather than a degree.

“There’s a lot more work to do… We want to be more globally competitive,” he said. – Rappler.com

*Jake Gomez is a 2026-2027 Henry Luce scholar.

World.title: [New Rx] What if the Philippines leased an island for 100 years?
World.content:
Hong Kong can be a model. Singapore and South Korea might bring in long-term capital, drive regional economic growth, and spark broader national governance reforms in the Philippines

The Philippine peso recently reached a record low of ₱64.17 against the US dollar. While currency depreciation alone does not indicate economic weakness, it raises a key question: how can the Philippines strengthen investor confidence and attract long-term capital for economic transformation?

During a visit to the Philippines, my father made an unusual suggestion: why not lease one island to another country for 100 years?

Under this proposal, the partner country would help establish a distinct legal and institutional framework while the Philippines retains sovereignty, national defense, and responsibility for essential public services. After a century, the Philippines would inherit a thriving economic center with modern infrastructure and competitive institutions.

An idea with an unexpected precedent

In January 2016, then-presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte proposed leasing islands to multinational companies with autonomy to develop infrastructure and operating rules. However, my father’s proposal differs: rather than relying on private corporations, it involves a government-to-government institutional partnership.

The historical comparison is Hong Kong. In 1898, China leased the New Territories to Britain for 99 years. Decades later, Hong Kong helped channel international capital, expertise, and commerce into Shenzhen and the Pearl River Delta, illustrating how a jurisdiction with distinct institutions can stimulate development far beyond its borders.

Not another economic zone

The Philippines already offers investment incentives and special economic zones, but these remain subject to the national administrative framework. What if one island operated under a distinct system of civil and commercial laws, an independent judiciary, taxation, and regulatory institutions?

The goal would be to offer investors predictable rules, enforceable contracts, and credible institutions. Like Hong Kong, it could feature separate residency arrangements while preserving Philippine citizenship.

Importantly, the foreign partner would not operate the entire government. The Philippines would continue providing healthcare, education, policing, municipal services, and defense. The partner would supply the institutional architecture: judicial expertise, regulatory standards, and independent oversight.

Such an arrangement would require constitutional changes, particularly to establish an independent judiciary and a distinct immigration system. The experiment would concern institutions, not merely financial incentives.

Why would Singapore be interested?

Singapore’s domestic market is small, land and labor are constrained, and its companies need international expansion. Initiatives like the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone demonstrate its strategy of pairing financial and technological strengths with regional land and workforce capacity.

A Philippine island could offer another variation of that strategy. Singaporean businesses could establish manufacturing facilities, logistics hubs, and research campuses operating under familiar standards. Headquarters and advanced research would remain in Singapore, while land-intensive operations locate on the island.

Unlike conventional industrial parks, the arrangement would feature a separate judicial and regulatory framework supported by Singaporean institutions.

Private investors could finance much of the infrastructure, limiting Singaporean taxpayer exposure while Singapore contributes institutional expertise rather than assuming territorial administration. Singapore has not expressed interest in such an arrangement, and its potential participation would require further examination.

South Korea offers another possibility

Alternatively, South Korea brings strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and digital governance. The partner could be any country with strong institutions, proven administrative capabilities, and no territorial ambitions.

An economic engine for surrounding provinces

Imagine an underdeveloped island transformed into an international commercial center with modern ports, industrial parks, and universities. The benefits would extend to surrounding provinces supplying agriculture, labor, and materials, stimulating investment across the region. Any location would require an independent feasibility study and a credible process for securing the informed consent of affected communities.

Protecting sovereignty — and the foreign partner

To protect Philippine sovereignty, foreign military bases and territorial claims would be prohibited. The Philippines would retain national defense and natural resource rights, while existing residents’ citizenship, property rights, and political representation would be protected. Equally important, foreign partners would need assurances against unilateral termination by future Philippine administrations. A constitutionally authorized bilateral treaty, international arbitration, compensation provisions, and political-risk insurance could reduce these risks, although no legal safeguard could entirely eliminate them.

Could one island change expectations?

Beyond economics, experiencing predictable permits, efficient dispute resolution, and transparent rules could raise public expectations for governance across the Philippines, encouraging broader national reforms. The island’s greatest legacy might be changing what Filipinos expect from the government.

Beyond defending the peso

The Philippines has pursued growth through incentives and economic zones for decades. The next experiment should focus on institutional credibility. By starting with just one island, the Philippines could create a model that delivers capital, infrastructure, and institutional learning for generations to come. After 100 years, the Philippines could inherit not only a thriving economic center but also institutions and practices worth adopting elsewhere.

Speaking in Parliament in 1977 about Singapore’s need to develop its own institutional approach, then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew expressed a philosophy that remains relevant far beyond its original context:

“We have got to find our own style. We have got to be bold enough to experiment.” – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

World.title: [Rappler’s Best] America, your turn
World.content:
TRUMP. United States President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media after disembarking Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, October 10, 2026.

The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as President Donald Trump enters the last two years of his term

The past week thrilled liberals and leftists across the world as elections in three polarized countries stemmed the march of the far-right in Latin America, demonstrated student power in Europe, and humbled Benjamin Netanyahu.

These polls have been hard fought, but the post-election transitions will be doubly harder.

Crying fraud but also facing corruption charges back home, Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate, has fled to the US into the welcoming arms of his patron, US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro can stay in America for as long as he wants, Trump said. His father, Jair, a former president, is in jail in Brazil.

Running on an anti-corruption wave, Serbia’s student protest movement managed to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election, but now comes the hard part of governing. For starters, the student leaders have called for the resignation of top public officials and investigations into alleged corruption under Vucic.

In Israel, the far-right continues to dominate, but did not come out solidly for Netanyahu, whose party lost the majority in parliament. Without any bloc enjoying majority numbers, however, he will likely serve as caretaker prime minister. How could Israel break an election deadlock? Here’s an explainer.

And so we turn to the next logical question: what will America show the rest of the world this week?

The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as Trump enters the last two years of his term. Here are things to know.

If you’re a liberal and listened to pollster Nate Silver’s interview with Ezra Klein (as I did), you’d be expecting a “momentous” turnaround — a more than 70% chance for Democrats in the Senate — that could flip Congress against Trump. If the results reflect what he’s seeing in his polling, Silver said these would effectively end the Trump era.

The Economist has more conservative numbers. While conceding that the “auguries are good for Democrats,” it’s putting the probability of the US Senate going to the Democrats at just 54%. But the White House is already crafting a path to govern without Congress in case Democrats win, according to a Reuters report.

These are the races that will decide control of the US Senate, and the key seats that could shape the next House.

The campaign period has been reminiscent of traditional tactics in Philippine elections, writes Filipino-American Oscar Quiambao in this piece. There have been concerns about Republican efforts to delay the vote counts and intimidate voters. And let’s not forget that Trump himself offered $5,000 to every American if Republicans win.

There are four ways foreign policy could change if Democrats win this week.

This also marks the first elections in the US where voters have been relying on chatbots to guide them. It’s a cautionary tale.

A study showed almost 40% of chatbots’ replies to election-related queries contained at least one factual error. Read more.

The flood of AI-driven disinformation has been unprecedented, according to this story, which cites one instance when the Democrat running for US Senate in Texas (a Republican base), James Talarico, had to take time off from campaigning due to flu. A fake video about him supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio went viral.

Russia is apparently fueling fake reports about Democrats, according to an intelligence briefing that US lawmakers received. Read more.

Outside the US, in Brazil, AI content bypassed election rules — a lesson for the Philippines, writes Alex Culla in this story.

As Trump spent the past days doing his final push for a Republican win, his defense chief Pete Hegseth flew to Cebu for the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting. There, the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro, snubbed the Chinese defense attaché who ranked lower than him. Bea Cupin gives us a recap of the meeting in this report.

On another note, we extend our deepest condolences to the family of Philip Juico, who died on October 31 after years of battling cancer.

Here are some of Rappler’s bests that you shouldn’t miss:

JC Punongbayan spells out what we can do as the peso continues its steep decline. Watch Shay Du’s take on it here.

James Patrick Cruz shows how to track insertions in the House-approved 2027 budget. There’s pork barrel everywhere, writes JC Punongbayan.

Lance Spencer Yu lists the adjustments that businesses need to make to regain customers dealing with high prices and a weak peso.

Isagani de Castro Jr. tells us why 2 Valid IDs is on track to make Philippine film history.

Joey Salgado writes that Dutertismo will be on the ballot in the 2028 elections — even if Sara Duterte is disqualified from running.

Paterno Esmaquel II reminds us how Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla dropped the ball on fugitive Senator Bato dela Rosa.

Rappler’s Best is a weekly Rappler+ exclusive newsletter of our top picks delivered straight to your inbox every Monday. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to subscribe.

The views expressed by the writer are his/her own and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Rappler.

World.title: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
World.content:
STRAIT OF HORMUZ. Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 6, 2026.

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson says the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran

Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday, November 2.

The negotiators departed on Sunday, November 1, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the draft proposal.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran, with Tehran now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal.

The spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha to facilitate the exchange of messages with Washington via Qatari intermediaries.

“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently. These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said.

On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged.

Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump.

The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.”

Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Senate majority united in stripping 2027 budget bill of ‘corruption-prone items’ – Lacson
World.content:
PING LACSON. Senator Ping Lacson speaks during the Senate plenary debates on the 2026 budget on November 18, 2025.

Senator Ping Lacson says no one will be spared in their bid to 'cleanse' the proposed 2027 budget

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate majority bloc is united in removing “corruption-prone” items from the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said.

“The majority of senators are rallying behind Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito’s efforts to cleanse the 2027 budget of unwarranted, whimsical, and corruption-prone items — all means all!” Lacson said in a social media post.

Over the weekend, Lacson said Ejercito had secured the commitment of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) that it will submit all supporting documents for its infrastructure projects by Tuesday, November 3. Projects without the required documents would be removed from the House-approved version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

Budget advocacy groups, including the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, had flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion with no published project attachments in the HGAB.

A separate Senate review also found that the number of DPWH projects had increased from 11,420 in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to 16,244 in the House-approved GAB. Of these, 6,271 were new projects introduced by lawmakers without prior vetting by the executive branch.

Lacson also said Ejercito would invite civil society organizations to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the budget, which would be livestreamed to promote transparency.

The Senate will take up the budget bill when plenary sessions resume on November 9, with plenary debates expected to begin on November 23. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime Ramps Up Civilian Airstrikes as ASEAN Envoy Visits
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime continued bombing civilian targets even as it hosted ASEAN’s special envoy last week, killing more than a dozen people and wounding over 50 across four days.

Special Envoy Maria Theresa Lazaro visited the southern Shan State capital of Taungyi on an October 28-30 humanitarian mission, meeting the regime’s foreign minister during her trip.

Meanwhile, The Irrawaddy recorded nine regime airstrikes from October 29 to November 1, resulting in 16 deaths and 51 injuries. Over half of the attacks occurred in Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the ethnic Arakan Army (AA).

On Sunday, regime warplanes targeted Rakhine’s Kyaukphyu, a hub for China-backed projects and gas pipelines, along with AA-controlled townships of Kyauktaw, Pauktaw, and Mrauk-U.

In Mrauk-U, five people including a baby were killed and nine wounded when cluster bombs shattered a temporary maternity clinic.

The clinic was established after a December 10 bombing raid destroyed Mrauk-U District Hospital, killing at least 33 patients, caregivers and medical staff and injuring around 70.

Sunday’s airstrikes killed at total of 12 civilians and injured 32 others across Rakhine, according to an AA statement.

They came two days after the Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO) and a coalition of 70 local and international Rakhine groups called on the UN Security Council, ASEAN, international governments, and global humanitarian agencies to enforce a no-fly zone over Rakhine State.

In Karenni State’s Loikaw, three children were killed and eight injured when two regime fighter jets and a Y-12 aircraft bombed their school in Wanngawt village as holiday meals were being served on Sunday.

Any hope of a break in the bombing campaign as the regime pushes for regional reintegration was shattered the day Lazaro arrived. As the special envoy touched down on Wednesday, blasts hit Tawkyaunglay village monastery in Sagaing’s Chaung-U Township, where around 60 worshippers were gathered for Patthana chanting. The attack wounded a 57-year-old monk. Bombs struck a former prisoner-of-war camp in Chin State’s Hakha on the same day, but no casualties were reported.

On Saturday, an airstrike on a temporary shelter at Thaezalauk village monastery in Sagaing’s Homalin Township left seven displaced people injured. The attack came shortly after resistance forces captured the local regime outpost. Elsewhere in Sagaing, a woman was killed and three residents injured when a pair of gyrocopters attacked Duhtauk village in Salingyi Township despite the absence of clashes on the ground.

Human rights activists criticized Lazaro’s visit as bid to create an image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded regime to mask the reality of daily civilian atrocities and mass displacement.

According to data collected by the parallel National Unity Government, a total of 6,467 civilians have died in regime airstrikes since the February 2021 coup.

World.title: Regime, Thailand Discuss Russian LNG Supply Route via Dawei
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime and Thailand have discussed importing Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Myanmar and sharing supplies to help meet growing energy demand in both countries, according to regime media.

The proposal emerged during separate meetings in Bangkok on Saturday between junta Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin, Thai Energy Minister Akanat Promphan and Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov.

According to the regime, discussions focused on a trilateral energy cooperation framework under which Russian LNG would be shipped to Myanmar and distributed to Thailand. Officials also examined the possibility of building an LNG terminal in Dawei and utilizing existing gas pipeline infrastructure linking Myanmar and Thailand to transport imported gas.

The latest discussions follow Akanat’s visit to Naypyitaw on October 19, when he met regime chief Min Aung Hlaing and held separate talks with Ko Ko Lwin on expanding bilateral cooperation in the energy and natural gas sectors.

During those meetings, officials reportedly discussed plans for a Myanmar-Thailand-Russia energy trade network centered on the Dawei area.

The proposal has gained momentum in recent months. In August, Ko Ko Lwin met his Thai counterpart in Bangkok alongside prominent Myanmar oil magnate Michael Moe Myint, whose companies cooperate with the regime in the oil and gas sector.

The inclusion of Russia’s economic development minister in the latest round of talks suggests the three sides are moving to advance the Dawei-based energy trade initiative.

Analysts note that the interests of all three parties largely align. Myanmar and Thailand face growing energy needs, while Russia is seeking new markets for its abundant natural gas exports amid Western sanctions.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Russia in August, Myanmar and Russia signed memorandums of understanding covering the power and oil and gas sectors. Russian President Vladimir Putin said energy would remain a key pillar of bilateral cooperation and highlighted significant potential for LNG exports to Myanmar, including possible re-exports to third countries.

The junta has already signed several agreements with Russia covering fuel imports, including LNG, and says it expects to conclude an energy cooperation pact with Thailand in the near future.

The effort is also linked to the junta’s attempt to revive the long-delayed Dawei Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project, which has struggled to attract investment amid political instability and Western sanctions.

During his Russia visit, Min Aung Hlaing described the Dawei deep-sea port, special economic zone, and energy cooperation package including an LNG terminal, oil refinery, power plants and gas-based infrastructure projects as strategic pillars of Myanmar-Russia economic cooperation.

For Russia, closer ties with Myanmar could provide opportunities to expand investment and access new markets in Southeast Asia, which Moscow expects would offset economic restrictions imposed by Western countries.

Min Aung Hlaing has repeatedly portrayed Myanmar as a reliable partner for Russia in Southeast Asia, telling Putin that Myanmar stands ready to support deeper cooperation.

Thailand has long been involved in Myanmar’s energy sector through major offshore gas projects such as Yadana and Zawtika. Since the 2021 military coup, Thai companies have become some of the most significant foreign investors in Myanmar’s oil and gas industry after the withdrawal of several Western firms.

The junta also awarded the Min Ye Thu offshore project, the first new offshore project approved since the coup, to Thailand’s Gulf Petroleum Myanmar Co., Ltd.

Located off the coast of Tanintharyi in southern Myanmar, the Dawei Special Economic Zone is envisioned as a strategic hub incorporating a deep-sea port, industrial estate, power facilities and transport infrastructure, while giving Thailand direct access to the Indian Ocean.

In recent months, both Min Aung Hlaing and his deputy Nyo Saw visited Dawei to inspect “regional development tasks”. Myanmar military Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin also toured military commands in Tanintharyi Region in June, stressing the need to secure strategic projects including the Dawei deep-sea port and key transportation corridors.

However, analysts say ongoing armed conflict and instability in the region remain major obstacles to the realization of the Dawei project and broader energy cooperation plans.

World.title: China Reopens Trade Through Border Crossings Controlled by Armed Groups
World.content:
China has lifted restrictions on the flow of key goods into territories along the border that are controlled by ethnic armed organizations with ties to Beijing, allowing fuel, construction materials, medicines and other previously banned imports to enter Myanmar.

Residents and traders say China has recently relaxed some restrictions imposed when the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) and Kachin forces seized key border trade routes during anti-regime Operation 1027 in 2023–4.

At the military regime’s request at the time, Beijing blocked the flow of construction materials, machinery, electrical goods, fuel, medicines and explosives through those crossings.

“In Muse, previously restricted items can now be imported through Kyin San Kyawt border gate,” a Muse resident told The Irrawaddy. “Restrictions remain in place at the Sinphyushin and Nandaw gates that are still controlled by the regime.”

At the Namhkam border crossing controlled by the TNLA, trade has not yet fully resumed. TNLA spokesman Lway Yay Oo said only food and household goods are being allowed in to help improve living conditions for locals.

“The border gates have not fully reopened yet,” she told The Irrawaddy. “The relaxation benefits people living in border areas, but whether the crossings are fully reopened depends entirely on the Chinese government’s policy decisions.”

She added that a full reopening of border trade would help reduce shortages of fuel and medicine in the region.

The cash-strapped regime is furious that it can no longer tax imports and tries to intercept them elsewhere if they make their way further inland. In a cabinet meeting on Oct. 28, putschist president Min Aung Hlaing warned that smugglers are indirectly financing armed groups by paying them taxes, thereby strengthening their capacity and obstructing his own “peace” efforts.

In northern Shan itself, Chinese products are now plentiful and relatively cheap, but once they pass through Hsipaw, Kyaukme and Nawnghkio and onward to Pyin Oo Lwin, Mandalay and Yangon, it is a different story.

Transport operators say frequent inspections, unofficial payments and cargo checks at checkpoints have increased both delivery times and transportation costs, pushing up prices for consumers.

One transporter cited the example of a car tire that sells for around 380,000–400,000 kyats in the northern Shan capital of Lashio but can cost as much as 850,000–900,000 kyats in Mandalay.

“If the regime genuinely wants to reduce prices for consumers, it can establish a customs checkpoint in Lashio and allow legal imports with proper tax payments,” he said. “That would improve the flow of goods and bring prices down.”

Instead, Min Aung Hlaing has urged his ministers to intensify the crackdown on “smuggling” and ensure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through regime-controlled channels.

World.title: ASEAN Envoy’s Farce: Humanitarian Aid as Smokescreen for Regime Atrocities
World.content:
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Special Envoy and Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro has staged a farcical “humanitarian mission” in Taunggyi, a safe city in a military-controlled part of Shan State, where there has been no fighting or war-related destruction since the military coup in 2021.

Meanwhile, her hosts, the Myanmar military junta, continue to send paramotors, gyrocopters and fighter jets to bomb villages, schools, hospitals, markets, Buddhist monasteries and residential houses, killing and maiming women, schoolchildren, babies and displaced civilians.

What Lazaro has done is a grotesque spectacle, a cynical manipulation of humanitarian aid and a shameful betrayal of the people of Myanmar.

Let me be absolutely clear: Lazaro is not an innocent diplomat who has been deceived or manipulated by the junta. She knows perfectly well what is happening in Myanmar. She knows about the daily airstrikes, the massacres of civilians and the deliberate obstruction of humanitarian assistance to communities most desperately in need.

She knows what she is doing. She has willingly played her part in this cynical, carefully choreographed farce.

The purpose of this theatrical humanitarian performance is to manufacture a false image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded military regime and provide ASEAN with another opportunity to rehabilitate Min Aung Hlaing and lift its ban on the criminal junta’s political representatives attending the bloc’s summits.

The junta decided where Lazaro could go, what she could see and whom she could meet. She was not allowed to meet Aung San Suu Kyi, despite repeated requests from the Philippines. She did not meet representatives of the National Unity Government, ethnic revolutionary organizations, local administrations or the civil society networks delivering humanitarian assistance in areas beyond junta control.

The military controlled the stage. Lazaro knowingly played her assigned role. She happily posed for photographs. And the junta collected the political dividends.

Her photographs from peaceful, junta-controlled Taunggyi are part of a carefully constructed smokescreen intended to conceal the reality of Myanmar: daily atrocities against civilians, relentless aerial bombardment, mass displacement and the systematic obstruction of humanitarian assistance precisely where it is needed most.

I do not object to food reaching people displaced by the junta’s deliberate burning of villages and bombing of towns and cities. Every bag of rice matters to those who receive it.

What is outrageous is that ASEAN’s special envoy has played along with this farce, allowing humanitarian aid to be used as a propaganda instrument to whitewash the very military responsible for creating Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe.

What did Lazaro achieve?

No meaningful breakthrough in humanitarian access to resistance-controlled areas, where atrocities continue, hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced, and millions of internally displaced people remain beyond the reach of international aid. No access to Aung San Suu Kyi. No genuine engagement with all relevant stakeholders. No commitment by the military to stop bombing civilians.

Instead, the junta proudly announced that its foreign minister had discussed with Lazaro the restoration of Myanmar’s “original role and rights” within ASEAN.

There it is. The real political dividend of this entire farce.

ASEAN’s own Five-Point Consensus requires an end to violence and engagement with all concerned parties. Yet Lazaro allowed the junta to dictate the terms of her mission, select her interlocutors and exploit humanitarian assistance for its campaign of international rehabilitation.

We should refuse to pretend that this was merely another unsuccessful diplomatic initiative undertaken with good intentions. Lazaro was not simply a spectator in this shameful performance. She was an informed and willing participant. She chose to cooperate in a spectacle that served the junta’s political interests.

She cannot hide behind diplomatic language about dialogue, humanitarian assistance and constructive engagement.

While Min Aung Hlaing’s forces continue their campaign of aerial terror against the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s special envoy has knowingly helped project an image of his regime as a legitimate and cooperative partner deserving renewed international acceptance.

Instead of exposing and confronting the perpetrators of Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe, Lazaro has willingly participated in a performance that helps polish their bloodstained image.

The people of Myanmar do not need ASEAN’s humanitarian theater. They need humanitarian assistance that actually reaches those most in need. They need protection from the military’s relentless airstrikes. They need ASEAN to stop providing diplomatic cover and opportunities for international rehabilitation to those responsible for their suffering.

Igor Blazevic is a senior adviser at the Prague Civil Society Centre. Between 2011 and 2016 he worked in Myanmar as the head lecturer of the Educational Initiatives Program.

World.title: Rakhine Civil Society Urges UN No-Fly Zone as Civilian Deaths Soar
World.content:
Rakhine civil society organizations have urged the United Nations and international actors to declare a no-fly zone over the western state as civilian deaths from regime airstrikes surge to unprecedented levels.

The regime has bombed dozens of civilian targets in the month since a Sept. 28 aerial attack on a busy market killed at least 50 people and drew widespread international condemnation.

The Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO), an umbrella group of 70 local and international Rakhine groups, is urgently calling on the UN Security Council (UNSC), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), international governments, and global humanitarian organizations to back their statements with immediate action to prevent further loss of civilian life.

Along with a no-fly-zone, the ASCO is demanding international sanctions to cut off the supply of aviation fuel, weapons and other military equipment that sustain the regime’s aerial campaign.

The appeal follows an escalation in deadly strikes on civilian areas since the market massacre.

“Our local humanitarian workers were on hand to witness the slaughter of children and pregnant women in the Kyauktaw bombing,” an ACSO official told the Irrawaddy, explaining the urgency behind the appeal.

Requesting anonymity for safety reasons, he stated the regime had conducted over 600 airstrikes across Rakhine over the past six months, targeting markets, displacement camps, and monasteries in Thandwe, Ponnagyun, Mrauk-U and Sittwe, and in neighboring Chin State’s Paletwa Township.

Data from the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute, a research body founded by military defectors, shows the regime launched 136 aerial attacks across Rakhine in September alone, leaving 144 civilian casualties — 62 dead and 82 injured. Rakhine logged the highest civilian casualty count in the country, followed by Sagaing with 101 and Magwe (61).

Additionally, the ACSO urged the international community to establish cross-border channels to deliver food, medicine, and basic necessities directly to displaced populations facing severe hardship in war-torn Rakhine.

It also called on the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar to document human rights violations and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable through national and international justice mechanisms.

The regime ramped up airstrikes in Rakhine after the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) seized 14 of its 17 townships along with Paletwa during its 2023-2024 offensive. Intense battles continue around the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone, as AA forces push to capture the regime’s last remaining Rakhine strongholds.

On Tuesday, the regime’s key allies — China, Russia, and Belarus — blocked international condemnation over its human rights record at the UN General Assembly.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic push for legitimacy since installing himself as president in April after a widely derided election, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and India. Critics have condemned the diplomatic thaw as normalizing a regime that is deploying military force to subdue its own population.

“If the international community continues to turn a blind eye to the suffering public, we can only conclude that it lacks any empathy,” the ACSO official said.

World.title: Regime Threatens Migrant Workers in Thailand Over Document Boycott
World.content:
Myanmar regime Labor Minister Maung Myint on Thursday warned that migrant workers who boycott the Certificate of Identity (CI) process in Thailand would be banned from returning home if they failed to apply for the document.

With its CI-issuing centers in Thailand seeing very few applicants, the junta’s Labor Ministry has intensified its threats. Before the regime began enforcing remittance requirements as part of the CI application process, the facilities were regularly overcrowded with thousands of Myanmar migrants eagerly seeking the documents.

Migrants are boycotting the CI process as the cash-strapped junta attempts to wring more money out of them. Workers applying for the document must now prove that they remit at least 25 percent of their wages to Myanmar through official channels, as well as a 2 percent income tax payment. Official channels offer far less favorable exchange rates than unofficial channels.

Fearing their hard-earned wages will fund the regime’s military campaigns against civilians, workers have launched an online campaign demanding the Thai government grant legal stay and work permits without requiring a CI, which serves as an alternative document to the Myanmar passport.

The Thailand Migration Reform group urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the framework based on the Pink Card, an identity card issued by Thailand for undocumented foreigners residing in the country.

Maung Myint said the CI process was “a project implemented in cooperation with the Thai authorities,” adding that migrant workers without a CI or a passport and an Overseas Worker Identification Card (OWIC) “would be undocumented.” He added that they would not be allowed to travel back to Myanmar during their time off.

The regime started operating five CI centers across Thailand on October 14, but they have seen few applicants. Those who have attended have paid the extra cost for the application, while most are holding off to monitor the situation.

The boycott campaign has derailed Maung Myint’s goal of matching last year’s total of US$5.6 billion in remittance inflows in 2026. Thailand hosts Myanmar’s largest migrant population, estimated at approximately 4 million.

Since he was appointed labor minister earlier this month, Maung Myint has been pushing for enforcement of the remittance and tax rules in order to squeeze foreign currency from overseas workers, who have emerged as a major source of foreign currency for the regime amid shortages and international isolation.

On Tuesday, he said that by trying to cut off foreign currency inflows to the regime, the campaign was only “driving the people of Myanmar and migrant workers into ruin, instead of damaging the government.” He said the funds were to be used for fuel and gas imports, a claim he has often made.

He accused the campaign organizers of being “gaslighters,” claiming they themselves hold CIs or passports while urging workers not to apply for them.

“He is just acting like a psycho,” Khin Soe, a board member of the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT), which is organizing the campaign, told The Irrawaddy in response to the minister’s claim. “He may not even understand what he said. He just seems to follow orders from above.”

He added that there would be no reason to oppose the regime, or campaign against the CI process, if its policy benefited workers. “I don’t take [his accusation] seriously,” he said.

An ultranationalist with a military background, Maung Myint is known for spreading hate speech against the Muslim community and slandering the National League for Democracy.

During his election campaign in 2020, when he represented the Union Solidarity and Development Party, a lawsuit was filed against him over his use of an inflammatory song that urged voters to choose the party “to protect race and religion and to drive out a group that destroys the race.”

Winning seats in elections in 2010, 2015 and 2025-26, he has served as a minister and deputy minister in various ministries—including labor and foreign affairs—under successive regimes since 2004.

In his new role as labor minister, Maung Myint has become the face of the regime’s efforts to extract funds from Myanmar workers and their families amid the country’s political and economic crises.

World.title: Big Brother Defends Myanmar Regime at UN, Chinese Aid Shortfall, and More
World.content:
China defends Myanmar regime at UN

The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee devoted its 29th plenary session Tuesday to Myanmar’s human rights crisis, hearing reports from Special Envoy Julie Bishop, Independent Investigative Mechanism head Nicholas Koumjian, and Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie. All three highlighted the war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the military regime.

Of the 23 countries whose delegates spoke, only Belarus, Russia and China defended the regime. Finding nothing good to say about it either, Beijing instead urged the international community to say fewer bad things. “The international community should focus on helping bridge differences and resolving problems rather than intensifying tensions and aggravating turbulence,” China’s representative said.

Myanmar, after all, is “an important member of the ASEAN family and an equal member of the international community,” he added, voicing support for the regime’s pursuit of a development path “suited to its national conditions and supported by its people.”

Beijing bristled when Currie noted that during Min Aung Hlaing’s first 100 days after declaring himself president, he deployed new coercive surveillance technologies “gifted” by China and Russia to suppress dissent.

China’s representative rejected the allegation, calling it “false information,” and urged Currie to carry out her mandate “objectively and impartially” and avoid spreading “unverified” claims that could mislead the public.

Currie hit back directly: “Countries that are most loudly complaining about interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs are ones that are most actively interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs. Those that are talking most loudly about peace are the ones selling the weapons to Min Aung Hlaing that he uses against his own people.”

She challenged Beijing’s denial, saying she would welcome any evidence refuting that China was selling arms or providing political and economic support to the regime. Currie reminded delegates that under UN procedures, China, Russia and Belarus had been given five days to respond before her October report was published—and none of them had.

She cited the 2023 report “The Billion Dollar Death Trade” by her predecessor Tom Andrews as the proof of her claim. The report found Myanmar’s military imported over US$1 billion in arms and dual use goods since the 2021 coup, with China and Russia identified as top suppliers. Chinese state-linked firms provided raw materials and equipment for Myanmar’s ordnance factories including aircraft parts and explosives precursors used in attacks on civilians.

A milestone for China’s cross-Myanmar pipeline

The Myanmar–China crude oil pipeline has transported more than 100 million metric tons of crude oil since it began operations in 2017, PipeChina announced earlier this week. Stretching 771 km from embattled Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State through northern Shan State to Yunnan Province, the twin oil and gas pipelines are strategic lifelines that reduce Beijing’s dependence on the congested and vulnerable Malacca Strait.

One of China’s four major energy import corridors, the pipelines traverse 22 townships across Rakhine, Magwe, Mandalay and Shan, and today ethnic armed organizations such as the Arakan Army (AA), Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) control substantial sections there.

Myanmar is projected to receive around $1.5 billion annually from the pipelines, though the exact profit structure is unclear. It certainly receives a fixed, annual right-of-way payment of $13.81 million for both pipelines plus $1 per ton of crude transiting through the country—PipeChina reckons at an average rate of 35,000 tons a day, most of it disgorged at Kyaukphyu from the Middle East. PipeChina and CNPC own 51 percent, while state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) holds 49 percent.

The gas pipeline, meanwhile, started operation in 2013 and carries output from the offshore Shwe fields, with a a design capacity of 12 billion cubic meters per year. China National Petroleum Corporation holds a controlling 50.9 percent stake and MOGE just 7.365 percent. Sales of natural gas from Shwe to China are estimated to generate around $1 billion annually.

To finance its stakes, MOGE borrowed around $1.5 billion from the China Development Bank at an interest rate of 4.5 percent, according to Sandhi Governance Institute. Nobody knows how much of that has been paid back or ever will be.

Chinese aid bottleneck throttles Myanmar regime’s budget

Myanmar’s military regime faced severe fiscal strain in the 2025–2026 fiscal year when China withheld approval for multiple projects under the Lancang–Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Special Fund. Naypyitaw’s budget deficit shot up amid overspending by ministries and loss‑making state enterprises.

Deputy Planning and Finance Minister Kyaw Htin admitted that the deficit was exacerbated by failure to secure expected grants, project approvals, and technical resources from Beijing. The Ministry of Cooperatives and Rural Development did submit proposals for LMC financing in 2025, but the response was deafening silence. Likewise, the Industry Ministry budgeted for computer hardware and technical equipment for Chinese experts who were to come to Myanmar for a technology transfer, but they never turned up and the equipment was not delivered.

The reasons are shrouded in mystery. In a recent article in regime newspapers, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia claimed China had backed 140 development projects in Myanmar through the LMC Special Fund. In March, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said the country benefited from 132—worth $38.6 million—since 2017.

Either way it would be the biggest handout to any Mekong country.

Some older Chinese projects are already falling to pieces. Kyaw Htin admitted that power transmission lines from two China‑backed hydropower plants—the 240 MW Dapein Hydropower Station in Bhamo, Kachin State and the 600 MW Shweli 1 Dam in Namhkam Township, northern Shan State—were damaged and could not be repaired due to “security conditions,” depriving the regime of projected electricity revenues.

Russian grant money that had been promised was also not forthcoming, Kyaw Htin said. The rest of the world has suspended official development aid since the 2021 coup.

More trouble in Shan over Kokang ‘Sinicization’

The past two weeks have seen growing tensions between Shan communities and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) that is consolidating its control in territories it has seized over the past three years.

The Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—comprising the armed Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the civilian Shan Nationalities League for Democracy, and other Shan opposition groups—issued a statement accusing the MNDAA of undermining ethnic rights, erasing Shan cultural heritage, and imposing Chinese language and governance systems there.

The MNDAA rejected the allegations as “baseless” and “politically motivated” and accused the SSJAC in turn of stirring the ethnic pot.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations also released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and stability on the Chinese border. And in April, Ta’ang civil society groups condemned the MNDAA after it seized Kutkai, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

Founded in 1989 from the remnants of the Communist Party of Burma, the MNDAA is rooted in Kokang, an enclave that is 90 percent ethnic Chinese. Once limited to Laukkai and Kongyan townships, the group has expanded its territory west of the Salween River since Operation 1027, and locals report a great deal of painting over of signboards and other attempts to suppress their languages and identities by their brash new masters.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Hosts Russian Mining Billionaire After Approving Gold Ventures
World.content:
Russian mining billionaire Vladislav Sviblov — head of Russia’s Areal Group — met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Wednesday to discuss cooperation in mineral exploration and mining between the two Western-sanctioned actors.

According to regime media, both sides spoke of “mutual trust and friendly relations” between Myanmar and Russia and discussed cooperation in education, science, and technology.

Formerly known as Highland Gold Mining Limited, Areal Group rebranded after expanding beyond precious metals into base, rare, and strategic minerals. Areal and its owner have been under U.S. and EU sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Similarly isolated by international sanctions after the 2021 coup, Min Aung Hlaing and his regime have been courting economic and diplomatic support from Russia.

On the day that Sviblov arrived in Naypyitaw, Myanmar’s Investment Commission approved 16 new investment proposals — including large‑scale gold mining ventures. The green lights came just weeks after Min Aung Hlaing invited investment in Myanmar’s mineral sector at the Russia–Myanmar Economic Forum in August, touting “value‑added mineral products” as a new export base.

Russia’s sanctions‑hit companies have leaned toward Asian markets since 2022, while Myanmar’s regime, starved of foreign currency, is eager to attract Russian capital.

Regime insiders suggest rare earths may have been on the agenda of Wednesday’s meeting, given the presence of natural resources minister Khin Maung Yi, while Sviblov himself spoke on on rare earths at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.

Myanmar boasts rich deposits of the critical minerals, exporting roughly half of the world’s heavy rare earth elements over the border to China.

Meanwhile, the U.S.’s recent reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that a global scramble for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. Regime supporters now boast that the junta has a “rare earth card” to play, pointing to parallel interest from India.

However, almost all of Myanmar’s estimated 600 rare earth mines lie beyond the regime’s control in territory overseen by ethnic armed groups. Despite repeated invitations by the regime and talk of “strategic partnerships,” Russian [mining?] businesses have yet to make any substantial investments in Myanmar.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Coal-Chemical Complex Planned by 2028 at Qarmet as Tokayev Hails Industrial Progress
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s steelmaker Qarmet is building new coke batteries scheduled to enter service in 2027, a project that will form part of the country’s first coal-chemical complex, as the company advances a $3.5 billion modernization program reviewed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev during his visit to Temirtau on Nov. 2.

The new coke batteries are among four major industrial projects planned at the steelworks through 2028. The program also includes a new long-products rolling mill, a galvanizing and polymer-coating line, and a casting and rolling complex.

During the visit, Tokayev praised Qarmet’s investment plans and progress, saying the plant could become “a symbol of progress, success and even prosperity.”

The company plans to produce 4 million tons of steel in 2026, alongside 3.6 million tons of coal concentrate and 3.9 million tons of iron ore concentrate. Since Qarmet began operating, investments have reached $2.7 billion, while the modernization program through 2028 is valued at $3.5 billion.

New coke batteries and steel production

The new coke batteries, Nos. 8 and 9, will have a combined designed capacity of 1.5 million tons of dry coke annually. Each battery will comprise 54 ovens, with chambers measuring 7.6 meters in height.

The facilities are expected to replace ageing production capacity dating to the 1960s and 1970s. Their development will also support the establishment of Kazakhstan’s first coal-chemical complex, designed to enable deeper processing of coking products.

Another major project is a new long-products rolling mill being built with Chinese technology partner CERI. With an annual capacity exceeding 540,000 tons, the mill will produce A600 and A1000 reinforcing steel, angles and channels.

The facility’s furnace will have a capacity of 100 tons per hour, and commissioning is planned for the end of 2026. The project is expected to reduce reliance on imported construction materials and supply steel for major infrastructure projects, including nuclear power plants.

Qarmet is also modernizing its converter shop. In 2024, converters No. 1 and No. 2 underwent major overhauls to increase production capacity and improve operational reliability. The modernization also includes a transition to natural gas.

By 2028, the company aims to increase annual steel production to 5 million tons, coal production to 9 million tons and iron ore concentrate output to 5 million tons.

Restored tram network in Temirtau

Tokayev also reviewed the restoration of Temirtau’s tram network, which Qarmet restored in 2024. More than 30 kilometers of tram tracks were restored or replaced, and eight new trams were introduced. The system also features electronic payment, while Qarmet employees and veterans can use the service free of charge. The network has recorded more than 1 million passenger trips.

“Indeed, the tram is a link between the past and the present for Temirtau. It was right that residents demanded the restoration of tram services and that you responded to their request,” Tokayev said.

He also emphasized the importance of improving living conditions in Temirtau, including expanding access to gas, and welcomed positive changes in the city. He called on the company to continue its modernization efforts and contribute to the city’s development.

Industrial growth and employment

During a meeting with employees and trade union representatives, Tokayev described the Karagandy Region as the “land of hardworking people,” highlighting its contribution to Kazakhstan’s industrial output.

Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product is expected to reach $398 billion by the end of 2026, while manufacturing accounts for more than 14% of the economy, according to figures cited during the visit. Tokayev also highlighted Qarmet’s contribution to workforce development through the “Bolashakka Zhol” (“Path to the Future”) initiative. The program aims to train and employ approximately 500 young specialists, with a particular focus on skilled trades.

He called for continued support for small businesses, referring to a previously announced three-year exemption from inspections, and stressed the need to make loans more affordable for entrepreneurs.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Trade With CAREC Countries Rises 14.4% to $8.8 Billion in 2025, Economy Minister Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with countries participating in the Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation (CAREC) program reached $8.8 billion in 2025, up 14.4% from the previous year, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said at the opening of the second Tien Shan Forum on Economic Cooperation in Central Asia in Almaty on Nov. 2.

According to him, foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan’s economy has exceeded $30 billion since 2005. He identified expanding regional trade, strengthening transport and logistics links, and attracting high-quality investment as key priorities under the CAREC program.

“Our common task is not only to increase trade volumes, but also to consistently remove barriers, simplify trade procedures, develop e-commerce and expand entrepreneurs’ access to the markets of neighbouring countries,” Zhumangarin said.

He also mentioned that Kazakhstan is expanding the capacity of transport corridors, modernising its railway and road infrastructure, and developing multimodal transport. Improving cross-border freight movement will also require greater compatibility between transport systems, digitalised border procedures and shorter cargo processing times.

Kazakhstan’s investments in CAREC countries have exceeded $4 billion. More than 28,000 companies from countries in the region are registered in Kazakhstan, alongside more than 2,500 joint ventures, according to the figures presented at the forum.

Zhumangarin said investment should support the establishment of new production facilities, the introduction of modern technologies, higher labour productivity and the production of goods with greater added value. Kazakhstan is also interested in expanding cooperation with international financial institutions in transport and logistics, industry, agriculture, energy and digital infrastructure.

Other priorities on the regional agenda that Zhumangarin mentioned include the digitalization of trade and logistics, climate change and the sustainable use of water resources.

The second Tien Shan Forum is taking place in Almaty on Nov. 2-3 under the topic Strengthening Sustainable Connectivity and Quality Investments in Central Asia. The forum is organized by the CAREC Institute and Kazakhstan’s Ministry of National Economy, with the Asian Development Bank serving as a strategic partner.

Around 400 participants are attending the event, including government representatives from CAREC countries, international financial institutions, development organisations, businesses and experts.

World.title: Kazakhstan Releases Second Tiger Into Wild as Reintroduction Program Advances
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan released a second Amur tiger into the wild on Oct. 31, marking another milestone in the country’s efforts to restore tigers to their historical habitat after more than 70 years of absence.

The male tiger, named Amur, was released in the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve as part of Kazakhstan’s tiger reintroduction program. The first tiger, a female named Umit, was released on July 31.

The release was attended by Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Alibek Kuantyrov, Chairman of the Forestry and Wildlife Committee Daniyar Turgambayev, Director General of the Amur Tiger Centre Sergei Aramilev, Freedom Shapagat Corporate Foundation Managing Director Ruslan Dzhumashev, and reserve staff and specialists, including members of the anti-conflict team.

“Today, we are taking another important step towards bringing tigers back to Kazakhstan. On July 31 this year, the tigress Umit was released into the wild, and today we have released the second tiger, a male named Amur,” Kuantyrov said.

He thanked the Amur Tiger Center and its specialists, as well as the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) and other partners for supporting the program and helping restore natural ecosystems.

“Our main goal is not simply to return these predators to their historical habitat, but to establish a sustainable population capable of living and reproducing independently in the wild,” he said.

Preparing Amur for life in the wild

After arriving in Kazakhstan, Amur was kept in a specially equipped acclimatisation enclosure in the Ile-Balkhash reserve under continuous specialist supervision. Before his release, the tiger underwent veterinary examinations and behavioural assessments. Specialists evaluated his health, hunting skills, ability to obtain food independently and response to human presence. The results confirmed that he was ready to live in the wild.

Amur was fitted with a satellite collar to help specialists monitor his movements and adaptation to the natural environment.

“Every tiger release carries significant responsibility. We must be certain that the animal is ready to live independently in the wild. That is why the decision is made only after a thorough assessment of its health, behaviour and hunting skills,” Turgambayev said.

He added that specialists would continue tracking the tigers’ movements and monitoring their adaptation.

Umit, the first tiger released into the reserve, continues to explore the territory and hunt independently. Her movements are also monitored using a satellite collar, and specialists report that her adaptation is progressing successfully.

Two tiger cubs that arrived in Kazakhstan alongside the adult animals remain under specialist supervision. A decision on their release will be made after they reach the appropriate age and complete the necessary assessments.

Restoring tigers’ historical habitat

The Balkhash region and the Ili River valley were historically home to the Caspian, or Turanian, tiger. The subspecies disappeared from Kazakhstan in the mid-20th century as a result of habitat loss, declining numbers of wild ungulates and poaching.

Kazakhstan established the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve in 2018, beginning efforts to restore natural habitats, rebuild the prey base and develop conservation infrastructure. A key part of the program is increasing populations of wild ungulates, which provide food for tigers. Bukhara deer and kulans have been relocated to the reserve, alongside other measures to protect species that form the basis of the predators’ food supply.

In September 2026, 30 kulans were relocated from Altyn-Emel State National Nature Park to the Ile-Balkhash reserve. Restoring habitats and prey populations has laid the groundwork for the next stage of the program: returning tigers to the region. The effort involves government agencies, researchers and international partners.

International cooperation supports the program

The reintroduction program is being implemented through cooperation between Kazakhstan and Russia, with the participation of international conservation organisations and researchers.

In May 2026, four Amur tigers captured in the wild in Russia’s Khabarovsk Territory, two adults and two cubs, were brought to Kazakhstan. They were placed in specially equipped acclimatisation enclosures in the Ile-Balkhash reserve.

“The cooperation between Russia and Kazakhstan under the tiger reintroduction program is particularly important for the conservation of this rare species. The transfer of the animals represents a practical contribution to the joint initiative,” Aramilev said.

He described the program as an example of cooperation between the two countries in protecting natural heritage and restoring tiger populations. WWF has also supported Kazakhstan’s efforts to restore ecosystems in the Balkhash region, including work on tugai forests, prey populations and reserve infrastructure. In 2024, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources and WWF International signed a memorandum on further cooperation under the tiger reintroduction program.

Protecting local communities and wildlife

Alongside the release of tigers, the program places emphasis on public safety and preventing conflicts between people and predators. A dedicated anti-conflict team monitors the animals’ movements, communicates with local residents and responds to potential incidents.

“The return of tigers is not just about the moment they are released. It also requires the daily work of reserve staff. We continue to monitor the animals, study their behaviour, protect the territory and work with local residents,” said Kanat Kozhabekov, director of the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve.

He said the priority was to ensure that the tigers adapt successfully while local communities feel safe. The reintroduction program is intended to restore not only a predator that disappeared from Kazakhstan, but also the ecological balance of the southern Balkhash region. As an apex predator, the tiger plays an important role in maintaining the natural balance of its ecosystem.

The program’s long-term goal is to establish a sustainable tiger population in the Ili River delta and southern Balkhash region that can reproduce independently in the wild. Achieving that goal will require continued monitoring, habitat restoration, protection of prey species and the gradual release of additional tigers.

Background

The Turanian tiger historically inhabited tugai forests and river floodplains across Central Asia, including the Ili River basin, Balkhash and the Syr Darya River.

Molecular genetic research has confirmed a close genetic relationship between the Turanian and Amur tigers. The Amur tiger was therefore selected for the restoration program in Central Asia. The long-term initiative combines ecosystem restoration, increases in prey populations, phased tiger releases and continuous scientific monitoring.

World.title: Almaty Museum Opens Exhibition About Mountaineering Legends
World.content:
ASTANA – The Museum of Almaty has opened “Peaks Reaching for the Sky,” an exhibition on the history of mountaineering in Kazakhstan from the 1930s to the present day.

Visitors can learn how mountain camps helped train generations of athletes and explore the life stories of the climbers who shaped the sport. The display brings together archival photographs, documents, personal belongings, and the equipment climbers carried to the summits. It traces how mountaineering took root in Kazakhstan, from the first ascents and landmark expeditions to the achievements of today’s athletes, reported Kazinform news agency.

From the first ascents to today’s climbers

One of the key milestones in the history of Kazakh mountaineering came on July 17, 1930. That day, Ivan Mysovsky, Vladimir Gorbunov, and Alexander Berggrin, led by Grigory Beloglazov, made the first organized ascent of the mountains around Almaty.

In the years that followed, climbing clubs began to appear in the city. In 1935, around 250 climbers from across the country gathered in Almaty and climbed the surrounding peaks, including Talgar Peak.

A separate part of the exhibition is devoted to World War II. A school near Gorelnik trained instructors for the Soviet Union’s mountain rifle units, and around 15,000 service members passed through it.

The stands also display archival photographs of expedition members, materials on how climbers prepared for their ascents, and the stories behind famous summits, including Khan Tengri, the best-known peak in Kazakhstan.

The exhibition pays tribute to the climbers who built the reputation of the Kazakh school. Among them are Kazbek Valiev, Valery Shevtsov, renowned coach and expedition leader Ervand Ilyinsky, and Maksut Zhumayev, who has climbed all 14 of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks. It also honors the legendary Anatoli Boukreev, who held the Snow Leopard title, and Denis Urubko, who also summited all 14 eight-thousanders.

A separate section of the exhibition is dedicated to women climbers and their contribution to the sport.

Kazbek Valiev, one of Kazakhstan’s best-known climbers and the first Kazakh to summit Everest, attended the opening.

“I want to congratulate everyone on the opening of the mountaineering department of the Museum of Almaty. I think it is well deserved, because the history of mountaineering in Kazakhstan is vast. Most of its achievements are tied to Almaty climbers. The Almaty Mountaineering Federation is doing a lot to popularize the sport among city residents,” he said.

Lyazzat Sagyndikova, director of the Association of Almaty Museums, said the exhibition is meant not only to tell the history of the sport but also to show the contribution of people who devoted their lives to the mountains. She added that their stories “inspire the younger generation to strive for new heights.”

The exhibition is open from Oct. 28 through the end of November 2026.

World.title: TikTok Becomes Business Tool for Kazakhstan’s Entrepreneurs, Survey Finds
World.content:
ASTANA — A new survey by TikTok and the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs found that more than 70% of surveyed companies use the platform for business at least once a month, while 88.3% reported a positive effect on attracting new customers. The study also found that more businesses associate TikTok activity with a share of their revenue.

The findings were presented at the TikTok Impact Forum in Almaty on Oct. 28, ahead of Entrepreneur’s Day, as the platform and Atameken released the second annual edition of their study, The TikTok Effect: The Platform’s Impact on Small and Medium-Sized Businesses in Kazakhstan.

From visibility to revenue

The survey, conducted in September and October this year, covered 206 companies across all 20 regions of Kazakhstan and seven industry groups: culture, entertainment and tourism; health, beauty and sports; food and nonfood products; catering; education; and real estate services. Among respondents, 43.7% said they used TikTok for business monthly, up from 29.5% in the previous survey, an increase of 14.2 percentage points. Another 27.2% reported using the platform weekly or more often.

Regular use is not limited to recently established companies. Among businesses operating for more than 10 years, 31% said they use TikTok for marketing weekly or more frequently.
