World.title: Abkhaz outraged by remarks about them in Russian-published encyclopaedia on Black Sea Armenians
World.content:
Abkhazians outraged by Russian-published book on Armenians

Authorities in Abkhazia are calling for the authors of the Armenians of the Black Sea Region encyclopaedia to face criminal charges. The local Armenian community funded the publication in Russia. Abkhazia’s Prosecutor General’s Office has launched a preliminary inquiry after finding material in the book that contains offensive remarks about the Abkhaz and Abaza peoples.

The controversy centres on a short entry in the encyclopaedia about the term “Abaza”. In Turkey, people use this word to refer to Abkhazians and Abazins. Many members of these communities moved to the Ottoman Empire in the second half of the 19th century as a result of the Caucasian War.

The entry says that Hamshen Armenians, who moved from Turkey to the Black Sea coast of the Caucasus following the genocide, used the term “Abaza” as a euphemism for “masturbating”.

“The publication in the Armenians of the Black Sea Region encyclopaedia is neither an academic debate nor an accidental mistake. All indications suggest that it was intended as an outright provocation,” the influential Abkhaz veterans’ organisation Aruaa said in a statement.

The organisation called for tough measures against the authors and others involved in publishing the book. These could range from declaring them persona non grata to opening criminal cases against them.

Several other political and civic organisations in the republic, including pro-government groups, backed the demand.

“There is an urgent need for a clear and principled legal assessment of the contents of the Armenians of the Black Sea Region book, as well as the actions of its authors, publishers and others involved in preparing and distributing it. Several statements in the book raise legitimate concerns and harm inter-ethnic relations,” their joint appeal said.

The Union of Armenians of Russia responded to the outrage in Abkhazia. Its representative, Agasi Arabyan, said that almost the entire print run of the encyclopaedia had been withdrawn and immediately returned to the printing house for corrections, despite the significant additional costs. The author resumed promoting the book only after the disputed passage had been removed.

However, the publishers could not locate and retrieve several copies that they had distributed immediately after receiving them from the printing house. They therefore announced that they would buy back the remaining copies and destroy them. They managed to find some, but not all.

Armenians are the second-largest ethnic group in Abkhazia. In the latest presidential election, held in March 2025, most local Armenians supported incumbent President Badra Gunba. In all previous elections, however, their votes had been distributed fairly evenly among the main presidential candidates. Support from the Armenian community proved to be one of the decisive factors in Gunba’s victory, but it also triggered several inter-ethnic conflicts.

World.title: Azerbaijan's investment advantages: from manufacturing to regional exports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. Azerbaijan’s investment potential is vast. One of the country’s main advantages is that, by bringing together its manufacturing, logistics, and trade capabilities on a single platform, it provides investors with the opportunity to access not only the local market but also broader regional markets. From this perspective, the country’s geographic location, industrial zones, and export capabilities serve as elements of a unified investment model.

When an investor decides to establish a manufacturing operation, one of the key considerations is not only where the products will be manufactured, but also where they will be shipped and at what cost. From this perspective, it would be incorrect to view Azerbaijan solely as a domestic market. The country’s advantage lies in the fact that the production capacity being established there, in addition to meeting domestic demand, can be used to enter neighboring and regional markets. In particular, the development of transportation links with Central Asia, Türkiye, Russia, Georgia, and other nearby markets could make production in Azerbaijan more attractive for an export-oriented investment model. Thus, for an investor, the Azerbaijani market is not only a final destination for consumption but also a gateway to regional markets.

The expansion of production in industrial zones managed by the Agency for the Development of Economic Zones is crucial for the development of the country’s non-oil and gas industry and for increasing its export potential. The main advantage of industrial zones is that the infrastructure and institutional capabilities related to an investor’s manufacturing activities are concentrated in one place. In other words, by manufacturing products in Azerbaijan, an investor can direct them to both domestic and regional markets.

Azerbaijan's transformation into a regional manufacturing and export hub also creates additional opportunities for the development of non-oil and gas industries. In particular, the production capacities being developed in the chemical, processing, and food industries, as well as in the production of construction materials, mechanical engineering, logistics equipment, agricultural processing, and other sectors, can be aligned with regional demand.

Institutional Support for the Implementation of Strategic Investment Projects

Institutional mechanisms that accelerate the implementation of investment projects, ensure coordination among government agencies, and assist in resolving administrative issues faced by investors are of great importance. To this end, the Cabinet of Ministers issued a resolution on the establishment of a Commission to ensure the expedited implementation of strategic investment projects and to strengthen interagency coordination. The essence of the document lies in coordinating the activities of government agencies during the implementation of strategic investment projects and organizing the project implementation process more efficiently.

The time required to obtain project approvals, complete the necessary procedures, coordinate with relevant agencies, and make decisions also affects the economic efficiency of investments.

Therefore, accelerating strategic investment projects and strengthening interagency coordination can be viewed as institutional factors that help transform Azerbaijan’s investment potential into tangible production and export results.

International Investment Forum: Turning Opportunities into Concrete Projects

The Azerbaijan International Investment Forum serves as an important platform for showcasing Azerbaijan’s investment potential on the international stage and strengthening the country’s role in regional economic ties.

One of the main topics of discussion at the 2nd Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, held on September 25–26, 2026, in Baku, was an assessment of Azerbaijan’s role in the South Caucasus in terms of global connectivity and investment stability. The forum’s theme, “Restoring Trust in a Fragmented World: The South Caucasus as a Pillar of Global Connectivity and Investment Stability,” reflects an approach to the country’s investment opportunities within the context of regional and international economic ties.

In order to develop the forum as a regular international platform, the Organizing Committee of the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum was established by decree of President Ilham Aliyev on August 7, 2026. The forum’s significance in terms of investment strategy extends beyond simply bringing together international investors. Such platforms create conditions for presenting Azerbaijan’s economic opportunities, infrastructure projects, industrial potential, and regional connections as a unified investment proposition. This, in turn, can help promote the country not only as a market that attracts capital but also as a favorable location for establishing production and accessing various markets. The international platform presents opportunities to investors, while an effective institutional environment supports the transformation of these opportunities into concrete projects.

During the 2nd Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, 23 documents were signed with international investors and partner companies, covering investment projects with a total value of $10.8 billion. The agreements provide for cooperation in the energy, industrial, digital economy, agriculture, pharmaceutical, and other sectors. These agreements demonstrate that Azerbaijan’s investment opportunities span various sectors of the economy, and cooperation with international partners is expanding at the level of specific projects.

Main Objective: Creating Economic Value Added

Thus, the strategic objective of Azerbaijan’s investment policy is to attract more investors to the country and to transform Azerbaijan into an economic hub where production is well-established, value added is created, and access to regional markets is ensured.

World.title: Azerbaijan, US discuss expanding cooperation in military education (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. Delegation led by Rector of the National Defense University of the Azerbaijan Ministry of Defense, Major General Gunduz Abdulov has paid a visit to the United States of America.

This was reported by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense.

As part of the visit, the delegation held meetings at the U.S. National Defense University and the Near East South Asia Center for Strategic Studies (NESA).

During the meetings held, a comprehensive exchange of views took place on the current status and future prospects of bilateral cooperation in military education, the adaptation of professional military education to modern challenges, strategic leadership, and the development of human capital in the defense sector.

Major General Gunduz Abdulov provided detailed information on the reforms implemented at Azerbaijan NDU, including the application of the competency-based education model, the enhancement of the modern officer training system, Continuous Professional Military Education (CPME), and ongoing efforts to develop military education based on international best practices.

The meetings reviewed joint academic initiatives, including the professional development and exchange of faculty members.

Furthermore, the analysis of academic course curricula and the development of the professional non-commissioned officer (NCO) system were a central focus of the discussions.

During the meeting, the sides held extensive discussions on opportunities for mutual cooperation in developing AI-enabled wargaming, as well as other issues of common interest.

In conclusion, an agreement was reached on the implementation of the planned activities.

It is noteworthy that such meetings are of high significance in terms of expanding international partnerships in professional military education and learning best practices.

World.title: Addo-Carr's future in Parramatta's hands as B-sample returns negative
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr's immediate playing future is in the hands of the Parramatta hierarchy after police advised the winger his second result from a roadside drugs test had come back negative.

Addo-Carr met Eels officials at a board meeting on Monday afternoon to respond to a breach notice after it was widely presumed the former Test and State of Origin star would be sacked.

The Eels released a statement afterwards.

Eels star Addo-Carr allegedly returns positive test for cocaine NRL player Josh Addo-Carr is being investigated by police after allegedly returning a positive test for cocaine.

"Josh and his legal team were given the opportunity to respond to the notice," the Eels said.

"The club will consider their submission and make a decision in due course."

The 31-year-old allegedly tested positive to cocaine at a random roadside test in September.

But police have confirmed to AAP that no further action will be taken, leaving Addo-Carr to potentially earn a stay of execution.

"About 11.10pm on Friday [11 September 2026], officers attached to Inner West Police Area Command were patrolling Enmore Road, Newtown, when they stopped the driver of a vehicle for random testing," a NSW Police spokeswoman said on Monday: "The driver — a 31-year-old man — was subjected to a roadside breath test, which returned a negative result. "The driver underwent a preliminary drug wipe, which allegedly returned a positive indication for cocaine. An oral fluid sample was obtained and sent away for forensic testing. Following the testing the result has returned a negative result. No further police action is expected."

Addo-Carr has scored 27 tries in two seasons with the Parramatta Eels. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Addo-Carr was sacked by Canterbury almost two years ago to the day for testing positive to cocaine.

He declined to talk to media after leaving the club's headquarters at Belmore about 6pm.

But his lawyer, Elias Tabchouri, thanked the club for being "generous with their time".

"The club were able to allow us to express our thoughts in relation to this situation," Tabchouri said.

"We remain positive in relation to the negative finding for the B test, and we remain committed to the club."

Pressed on whether Addo-Carr would remain with the Eels in 2027, after bagging 27 tries in his first two seasons in blue and gold, Tabchouri said: "That's a matter for the club right now. We're waiting for the outcome".

"Josh has always maintained — and still maintains — a commitment to the Parramatta club."

World.content:
Hello! Welcome back to the US midterms daily briefing.

Today is the big day! Americans will head to the polls to vote for the next US House of Representatives and US Senate.

We'll launch our live coverage of the elections later today, but in the meantime, let's dive into what happened overnight.

Click here to see how popular Trump is today, and click here for a quick breakdown on what the midterms are all about.

Here's what you need to know today

Final midterm pitches: Politicians across the country are finishing their push for voters on the eve of election day. Trump ditched the campaign trail and gave a speech in Washington, DC. Standing in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he announced he was officially reopening the monument and joked that he wanted to name it after himself. Meanwhile, Democratic candidates are hoping to capitalise on frustrations over the cost of living and the Iran war.

Standing in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he announced he was officially reopening the monument and joked that he wanted to name it after himself. Meanwhile, Democratic candidates are hoping to capitalise on frustrations over the cost of living and the Iran war. California ballot stoush: I mentioned yesterday that the Trump administration has said California may have thousands of non-citizens on its voter rolls. A federal judge tossed a Department of Justice (DOJ) request to block the counting of more than 20,000 on those grounds. Now, the DOJ has filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court of the US (SCOTUS), asking it to take up the matter. If SCOTUS decides to overrule the lower courts' decisions, the federal government's role in elections (usually state matters) could change radically.

Now, the DOJ has filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court of the US (SCOTUS), asking it to take up the matter. If SCOTUS decides to overrule the lower courts' decisions, the federal government's role in elections (usually state matters) could change radically. What the polls say: Election forecasters are publishing their final midterm race ratings. Sabato's Crystal Ball has made calls on every race, and predicts a 239-196 Democratic House and a 53-47 Democratic Senate. The Silver Bulletin tips a 241-194 Democratic House and 53-47 Democratic Senate, and FiftyPlusOne puts Democrats at a strong likelihood to claim both chambers.

Let's dive deeper

North America correspondent Lauren Day is in Michigan this week. It's one of a handful of states tipped to decide who will end up with a Senate majority. I messaged with her about what issues voters are weighing ahead of casting their ballots.

E Elissa Fitzgerald You're in Detroit, known as "Motor City", the heart of America's car-making industry. What's a common thread you heard from voters there? L Lauren Day The common thread everywhere I’ve been in this election cycle is really the increasing cost of living and the Trump administration policies people are blaming that on: tariffs and the Iran war. Here in Detroit, it's even worse, though. The car-making industry has been really impacted by the tariffs. Everyone drives, so the price of fuel is causing a lot of pain. The average income in Michigan is significantly lower than the national average, and it's right on the border with Canada, so that trade war has really upset people. I went to an auto repair shop today, and the owner said a lot of people were really struggling to make ends meet, but he has no choice but to put prices up. E Elissa Fitzgerald There has been a bit of infighting among Democrats in Michigan this week, too. What's the latest? L Lauren Day It's been a wild weekend here in Detroit after Haley Stevens — who lost the primary to Abdul El-Sayed back in August — made a shock endorsement of Republican candidate Mike Rogers. Some people think it might actually boost support for El-Sayed but others are quite worried that this could, at best, distract and, at worst, derail the Democrats in this crucial Senate race. The feud centred around El-Sayed's criticism of Israel, of which Stevens is a staunch supporter. It's also exposed a wider rift within the Democratic Party over its policies on Israel, which will no doubt continue to be a major issue beyond the midterms and into the 2028 presidential race (yes we're already thinking about the next election before this one is even over).

Want to hear more from Lauren? She spoke about Stevens's surprise endorsement here and about former president Barack Obama campaigning for El-Sayed here.

How popular is Donald Trump today?

US President Donald Trump might not be up for election at the midterms, but his popularity will strongly influence the outcome.

The president's party almost always loses House seats in midterm elections, and that trend gets steeper when the president is unpopular.

Historic polling data collated by analytics firm Gallup shows presidents with approval ratings below 50 per cent have seen their party lose an average of 37 House seats.

Presidents with approval ratings above 50 per cent have netted smaller losses, with an average of 14 seats.

World.title: Another SA council scraps Acknowledgement of Country
World.content:
A South Australian council's decision to scrap the Acknowledgement of Country from its meetings without consultation is "confronting" and "sad", First Nations people say.

Lower Eyre Council voted 4-2 in favour of councillor Neville Tresize's motion, which said the acknowledgement was "ceremonial" and "no longer" carried "the significance or impact intended".

About 6,000 people live in the council area, which covers the traditional lands of the Nauo and Barngarla people on southern tip of the Eyre Peninsula.

Emmalene Richards says Indigenous people are "being used as a political tool". (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jenae Madden)

Barngarla woman Emmalene Richards said it was "confronting" that the motion was passed without warning.

"It shouldn't be up for debate for people to cast their own perspectives and options," she said.

"Where's it going to end? We are constantly, as Aboriginal people, being used as a political tool, which is really sad.

"It will create a bit of a ripple effect, negatively, for Aboriginal people because we've worked really, really hard for many generations to have [the acknowledgement] put in place."

Elder Jody Miller, a Nauo, Wirangu and Kokatha descendant and vice-chairperson for the Nauo Aboriginal Corporation, said it was "sad" the decision was made without consultation.

"[The Acknowledgement of Country] is about letting people know that Aboriginal people were here, they are still here and they will be here in the future," he said.

Mr Miller said it was "a big thing," to be acknowledged "especially because so much of our history has been lost".

But he said he was open to a discussion with the council.

"We can have a cup of tea and start a conversation so we can all live together," Mr Miller said.

'Broader reflection of Australian politics'

Lower Eyre Council is the latest in the state to remove the Acknowledgement of Country since 2024. It follows the Northern Areas Council, the City of Playford Council and the Naracoorte Lucindale Council.

Jo-Anne Quigley says the council "respects the diversity of perspectives" in the community. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Adam Sheldon)

Lower Eyre Mayor Jo-Anne Quigley said the council remained committed to reconciliation, respect and recognising the contribution of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples within the Lower Eyre community and was open to feedback.

"Council understands that members of the community will hold a range of views on this matter, and respects the diversity of perspectives that exist across the community," she said.

Councillor Isaac Taylor, who voted to keep the acknowledgement, said the dominant discussion in the chamber was about the significance of the practice.

He planned to introduce a motion next month to reverse the decision.

Isaac Taylor says the decision is reflective of a broader trend. (Supplied)

"There's an attitude that it doesn't reflect any benefit to First Nations people to acknowledge country," Cr Taylor said.

"I disagree with that viewpoint, but it's a viewpoint people have."

He said there were "no issues locally" over the past twelve months that led to the motion.

"I think it's a broader reflection of Australian politics at the moment," Cr Taylor said.

"We've seen the rise of One Nation and other resistance politics. I think that's given a voice for people to be more open about things they might've disagreed with behind closed doors."

He said there was a discussion during the meeting about the acknowledgement being replaced by something that would provide a "tangible benefit" to First Nations people, such as a scholarship program or the changing of place names.

Ms Richards was supportive of that idea but said it was a confusing way to go about it.

"Why would you remove something to improve it when you could just have engaged community to work with council?" she said.

Emmalene Richards says making changes to benefit Indigenous people is a nice idea, but consultation in the first place would have preferable. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jenae Madden)

Local Government Association of SA president Heather Holmes-Ross said cultural protocol choices were determined by councils.

One Nation SA president Carlos Quaremba said the party had "always opposed racially divisive rituals like acknowledgements of country" and that he suspected Lower Eyre Council would not "be the last" to drop the acknowledgement.

"One Nation expects that elected members of Lower Eyre Council have consulted with their constituents on this matter, listened to their views, and acted accordingly," he said in a statement.

Barngarla Determination Aboriginal Corporation has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Molecular traces from 'blood cells' found in 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones
World.content:
Coastal microbes you would find at the beach may have helped preserve red blood cells in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

An international team of scientists, led by Kliti Grice at Curtin University, report they have found traces of heme, in the hind limb bones of a Brazilian feathered dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali.

Heme is a molecule in haemoglobin, which is a protein red blood cells use to carry oxygen.

The molecules were found inside ellipsoid structures in the vascular canals — tiny channels for blood transport — in the dinosaur bone, the researchers reported today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Loading...

"No-one's actually found heme inside a fossil blood cell ever," Professor Grice said.

"It gives us a complete new type of evidence for studying dinosaur physiology, so how red blood cells connected with oxygen transport and metabolism."

The new study adds to research about preservation of dinosaur soft tissues, something once thought impossible over time periods of millions of years.

But some experts were yet to be convinced the ellipsoid shapes seen in the study were definitively blood cells.

'No idea there would be blood'

Bones from the Aratasaurus sampled in the study were discovered in a mine in the north-east of Brazil in 2008.

The dinosaur was estimated to be about four years old, weigh 34 kilograms and measure 3.1 metres long from head to tail.

The dinosaur died on microbial mats, colonies of bacteria and archaea often found in coastal locations.

The Brazilian scientists who sent the bones to Professor Grice had no indication of what would be found inside.

Professor Grice and her team analysed small pieces of the bones using a number of tests including light scanning electron microscopy, pyrolysis and mass spectrometry.

The samples were also tested for ancient DNA but came up negative (so no-one is cloning dinosaurs anytime soon).

"They had no idea that there was going to be blood cells or heme inside," she said.

"It didn't look too special.

"What we found is that the bone was almost 80 per cent heme."

"The fact that this [fossil] was engulfed in a microbial mat probably helped enormously with this preservation," Professor Grice said.

Conditions such as oxidation as micro organisms fed on the carcass, combined with mineralisation at the same time would have preserved its soft tissue.

The Aratasaurus fossil comes from a dinosaur that died on a microbial mat which may have helped preserve mineralised red blood cells. (Supplied: Victor O. Leshyk)

Blood cell status debated

Mauricio Barbi, from University of Regina, who was not involved in the study, said the authors had provided convincing evidence of mineralised structures consistent with red blood cells.

But he noted caution was still necessary.

"Their identification [of red blood cells] still involves some interpretation," Professor Barbi said.

"We are not talking about intact blood cells or preserved haemoglobin, but rather chemical remnants and mineralised structures that may retain information about the original tissues.

"Still, that is quite remarkable considering the age of the fossil."

Bones from the femur, tibia and foot of an Aratasaurus which were used in the study. (Supplied: Curtin University)

North Carolina State University emeritus Professor Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved in the study, said she did not think the red blood cell data was convincing.

"However, I have no problem with the presence of heme and collagen in the bone matrix," she said.

"These authors are to be commended for employing multiple methods to support their contention of endogenous 'cell-like' structures."

Professor Schweitzer said one of the images of the "cells" in the study appeared to be about 15 or so microns in size.

"This is smaller than almost all non-mammalian red blood cells, which are larger because of the retained nucleus," she said.

Soft tissue knowledge growing

While soft tissue scientists debate how to interpret the results of chemical analysis of different specimens, they agree advanced imaging techniques combined with sensitive chemical analyses are revealing hidden information in fossils.

Professor Barbi said the field was moving beyond simply asking whether biological structures could survive fossilisation to better understanding of the physiology of animals that disappeared millions of years ago.

"Ultimately, I think studies like this are opening a rather exciting window into the biology of extinct animals, even if we are still learning how to interpret what we find," he said.

Professor Schweitzer said the conventional wisdom that organic material disappeared after a million years or less was now being routinely challenged.

"There is much the past can teach us about the molecular make up of ancient organisms, their molecular evolution, and factors contributing to molecular preservation," she said.

Curtin University geochemist Kliti Grice with an Aratasaurus bone. (Supplied: Curtin University)

There are hopes among researchers like Professor Grice that more museums will offer up fossils to aid this kind of research into the future.

"We'll be able to completely ask new questions of these fossils that have been in museums for decades," she said.

Curtin University researchers are also trying to understand more about the process of blood mineralising in microbial mats.

They are currently running tests on whether they can mineralise human blood with mat samples from Shark Bay.

World.title: Step one: Survive. Step two: Protect the planet
World.content:
Loading...

These three scientists are conducting vital research at the Earth's poles that will help us understand how our planet is changing — and they're pushing the boundaries of exploration in the process.

Human instinct would drive most people from a gaping hole in an ice sheet.

Especially as ferocious meltwater gushes into the seemingly bottomless cavity.

But for Professor Alun Hubbard, it's an irresistible invitation.

Originally from Wales, the glaciologist at Finland's University of Oulu has been studying Greenland's icy interior for three decades.

He's used to conducting research in "surreal and absurd" places to help us understand how our polar regions are changing — and therefore how the rest of the planet and the way we live on it is, too.

Loading...

The Greenland ice sheet is one of Earth's two, continent-scale ice masses (the other being Antarctica). It's a powerful system that simultaneously reflects heat and stores water, helping keep the world's climate in balance.

Every summer, it sheds billions of tonnes of ice.

But, in recent years, that rate of loss has been accelerating to "unprecedented" levels.

Professor Hubbard believes there's a fossilised ancient forest inside the vast sinkhole that might offer clues as to why.

"As the base of the ice sheet thaws and more meltwater accesses it, [the forest is] starting to break down that organic matter and it's starting to leak methane," he says.

It's an educated guess that Professor Hubbard doesn't want to wait to test.

Not when he has a background in climbing and mountaineering, some rope, carabiners, and a team he trusts supporting him.

Loading...

A short while later, the scientist dangles above the meltwater thundering down the shaft — which is called a moulin — equipped with a sensor that reveals the truth.

It is, indeed, expelling excess methane.

This discovery matters, because methane is a powerful accelerator in the climate system, capable of reducing the strength of even the most stable layers of ice.

If more of it's leaking from ice sheets like this one than previously thought, the climate models we use need to be updated to reflect that.

That's why Professor Hubbard decides to volunteer himself.

Again.

This time, he wants to feed a fibre optic cable through the rushing meltwater that will record temperature shifts in the depths of the ice below.

Loading...

The findings are stark: the ice is apparently sitting at –4°C, when it should be between –18°C and –20°C.

According to Professor Hubbard, this has massive implications for projected sea-level rise.

The scientist knows his research matters, but it's also the "thrill" that keeps him coming back to work at the poles of the Earth.

"I feel far more comfortable on the Greenland ice sheet hanging off a rope than I would at a party," he says.

This isn't to say Professor Hubbard is unaware of what's ultimately at stake.

"If you screw up in that position, there is no chance of survival whatsoever … At least I know that if something goes badly awry, it'll be a quick one," he laughs.

Professor Hubbard admits he's "actually probably pretty depressed about the global situation at the moment". ( )

He tries his best to keep things "fun" in the field given the tendency to be "very serious and gloomy about climate change". ( )

Spontaneity is a big part of that. He didn't plan to abseil into the moulin ahead of time — "it was just, 'Hey, we're in this place, we've got the kit, let's do it." ( )

The glaciologist is one of 15 researchers from across the world whose vital work is featured in the new documentary series, Ages of Ice.

Narrated by the dulcet tones of acclaimed Scottish actor David Tennant (Doctor Who, The Hack), Ages of Ice is a three-part program that follows a range of scientists including oceanographers and climatologists as they work on a diverse mix of projects in brutal conditions across the polar regions.

It would be remiss of the series not to feature stunning landscapes from Greenland to Antarctica, as well as the animals who call these places home.

But Ages of Ice isn't sanitised escapism masquerading as a nature documentary.

Ages of Ice was filmed over three years, with the team flitting to the likes of Austria's Natur Eis Palast (pictured) and Nunavut in the Canadian Arctic. ( )

Loading...

It was so cold at times that the Ages of Ice crew had to take their camera batteries with them to bed in their sleeping bags. ( )

Camera operators and subjects alike experienced frostbite on their hands and faces. ( )

But for all weathered by the small team — there were only two or three of them in the field at a time — they got to see things like the musk ox of the Arctic (pictured). ( )

The penguins of Antarctica, speaking in a language we'll never truly grasp. ( )

Loading...

A bearded seal in Svalbard whose expression demanded to be immortalised on film. ( )

This year alone, we've seen devastating floods in Nepal, reports it might be too late to save places from Venice to Cocos (Keeling) Islands from rising sea levels, as well as a record El Niño forecast.

And it would be hard to forget the warning that the world is on track to breach the 1.5C global warming benchmark by 2030.

Writer, director and producer Karina Holden feels it's too late for "distracting forms of storytelling".

She wouldn't call Ages of Ice a "doomsday series", though.

An acclaimed natural history documentarian who brought us the likes of 2017's Blue, Karina Holden (pictured left), also has a background in science. ( )

"[Ages of Ice isn't] trying to make people feel scared or hopeless or depressed," Holden explains. "But we have to be realistic about what we are learning about the planet.

" We're now having to make decisions, vote policies in and find leadership as to how we're going to work based on the science recording these changes. "

This sense of urgency is part of the reason Professor Hubbard allowed Holden and her crew to capture his descent into a nightmare-inducing moulin in Greenland in search of answers.

It's also why Dr Adrian McCallum agreed to have his arduous 600-kilometre data-collecting journey documented.

He may be working on the same ice sheet, but the geotechnical engineer and polar explorer from the University of the Sunshine Coast in Queensland is embarking on a very different project to Professor Hubbard.

Dr McCallum has just 30 days to trek across one of the most hostile environments on Earth with his crew of four other adventurers and scientists.

As if that wasn't enough, they must each pull 100-kilogram sleds behind them.

Dr Adrian McCallum has to write journal articles as an academic. "But ... a documentary that potentially reaches millions is arguably more impactful," he says. ( )

Hailing from Australia, Germany, Denmark, Greenland and Sweden, this team met for the first time mere days before their trek began. ( )

Skiing 20 kilometres per day takes the group a minimum of 10 hours. ( )

Behind Dr McCallum's sled is a ground-penetrating radar, collecting data.

"It projects energy into the ice sheet, which bounces off reflections within the ice sheet, [and] comes back to the surface. We can then work out how deep snow ice interfaces are," he explains.

From there, the hope is the team will be able to project what that might mean for sea-level rise.

But collecting the data involves a relentless month-long cycle of ice, wind and round-the-clock filming.

Every night, they must set up camp in a new stretch of the barren landscape and fall asleep with only a tent to protect them from the elements.

Loading...

There's no turning back.

Only trudging onwards.

And in an extreme environment like this one, big weather events pose a serious risk.

With just 50 kilometres left to trek, Dr McCallum and his team face a storm — right when they're also about to run out of food.

To make it out before conditions turn deadly, they have to complete the final stretch of the journey in two days instead of the three they'd ordinarily allow for such a distance.

It's a close call.

Loading...

"I was very aware that if we did something wrong here, it could be the end of us," Dr McCallum says from the other side. "The winds were such that the helicopter couldn't get in.

"There were some very honest expressions shared amongst us."

Stream Ages of Ice on ABC iview From Antarctica to the Arctic, Ages of Ice is a high-stakes journey into the heart of our planet's frozen wilderness, following researchers as they push the boundaries of exploration.

Dr McCallum started training for the expedition a year out, running, cycling and pulling tyres behind himself twice a week. He was in the military for 20 years and has completed 10 polar expeditions in his lifetime.

He still wasn't ready for the reality of this trek.

"We're really surviving first, travelling second, and then thirdly, gathering data," Dr McCallum considers.

"You do need to like to suffer a little bit, or at least be prepared to suffer, because you will suffer.

"And you need to have something that's pulling you through that, that's driving you to do your work beyond the harshness of the environment."

For Dr Susanne Lockhart, the promise that her research has the power to help protect some of the most vulnerable life on Earth is what keeps her going.

Every summer, the independent marine biologist from Melbourne straps herself into a small submersible to find out what's living beneath the ice on the bottom of the seafloor in Antarctica.

The sub she's using to explore the depths of the Bellingshausen Sea this time is built to endure more than a tonne of force pressing on it.

Loading...

"I've never been in a space capsule, but I can imagine that being in the submersible is very similar," Dr Lockhart says.

" It's a little claustrophobic. There's not a lot of room. You're very aware that you're completely reliant on the technology around you to keep you alive. "

Teeming with starfish whose delicate arms stretch out in conversation with each other, sponges believed to be over 1,000 years old, and delicately rippled Nudibranchs, much of the Benthic zone where Dr Lockhart works feels like an alien world.

But this is Earth.

Loading...

For almost three decades, the marine biologist has been trying to prove how vital these poorly understood Antarctic worlds are to our planet; we now know fragile ecosystems like this one help maintain the balance of the entire Southern Ocean, on which 10,000 known species depend.

"The invertebrates on the sea floor take carbon that falls from krill and other organisms, and put it back into the sediment, which is what we want," Dr Lockhart explains.

"We need it to go back into the earth to balance things out."

Because of Dr Lockhart's work, more than 500 square kilometres of the Antarctic seafloor have been declared permanently off limits to commercial trawlers fishing for krill, whose activity threatens the existence of these fragile worlds.

Loading...

Once she's returned to the surface, Dr Lockhart must face what scares her far more than travelling so far below the ice: the possibility she won't be able to make as much of a difference as she'd like before it's too late.

The state of the planet frequently induces feelings of depression and fears of futility in many of the scientists featured in Ages of Ice.

So do the global politics that constrain their research and the implementation of their many and varied recommendations.

And yet, they each still ultimately have hope.

"I still think we have to try and make our voices heard," Professor Hubbard begins.

"People may think there's no point. But every tonne of CO2 that we can stop from going into the atmosphere, if we can really focus on getting to carbon neutral within 10, 20 years, we really do avoid a major catastrophe."

To Dr Lockhart, it's simple.

" It's way beyond time to get serious," she says. "We're at a geopolitical crossroads. Public pressure is the only thing that's going to [make a difference]. "

Loading...

We've got a story for you. Stream Ages of Ice on ABC iview or watch on Tuesdays at 8:00pm from November 3 on ABC TV.

Tim Wilson has pushed back on a Liberal backbenchers attempt to prevent his party from adopting a policy of allowing first home buyers to access their super early to buy a home.

World.title: High Court to hear challenge to under-16s social media ban
World.content:
Australia's world-first social media ban for users under 16 will face its first major legal challenge in the High Court today, nearly a year after taking effect.

Online giant Reddit and advocacy group the Digital Freedom Project argue the ban is unconstitutional because it excludes young people from civic engagement.

The policy, which came into effect in December last year, requires social media platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent Australians under 16 from creating or keeping an account.

Since then, nearly 5 million social media accounts have been blocked from the 10 affected platforms: Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Snapchat, X (formerly Twitter), TikTok, YouTube, Kick, Reddit and Twitch.

And there lies the heart of the plaintiffs' legal contest — that the ban places an unreasonable burden on Australia's implied freedom of political communication.

The Digital Freedom Project is also suing the eSafety commissioner.

While Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project's legal bids are separate, they are challenging the law on the same constitutional ground and have been joined by the High Court into a single special case.

Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project will tell the High Court the ban is unconstitutional because it excludes young people from civic engagement. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

In written submissions to the High Court, Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project argued there was a "fundamental disconnect" between the law's intention and its reality.

They said many children under 16 had found ways to dodge age-assurance technologies to keep their accounts or create new ones, and that potentially harmful content was still available even without an account.

The plaintiffs also argued there were "obvious and compelling alternatives" that would have achieved parliament's purpose with a lesser burden.

Reddit, which is also suing the minister for communications, is further seeking a declaration that it is not captured in the legislation as an "age-restricted social media platform".

Its lawyers have argued the law deprives young people of the ability to "speak, interact, organise and reach domestic and global audiences quickly and inexpensively".

"The deprivation is profound where it is inflicted on a group that does not have the avenue of the ballot box."

Commonwealth argues rules consultative, targeted, and changeable

The Commonwealth says the burden on political communication is justified because it protects children from the risks of harm associated with the engagement-promoting features on social media. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

For its part, the government has long maintained the purpose of the ban is to protect children from the risks of harm associated with some social media features.

Lawyers for the Commonwealth will tell the court about the risk of harm created by social media platforms which are motivated by advertising profits to prioritise user engagement and retention.

They argue the rules that accompany the policy are consultative, targeted and will be able to change over time.

The Commonwealth also claims political communication freedoms only apply to "electors" — people who are eligible to vote — and therefore any burden is indirect, modest and justified.

For their challenge to succeed, Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project will need to convince the High Court that the way the law seeks to achieve that goes too far.

Monash University constitutional law professor Luke Beck said the government had a strong case.

Luke Beck says even if the challenge is successful, the ban may not be completely abandoned. (Supplied)

"It's very clear that the Commonwealth can regulate social media and online spaces," he said.

"So this case is going to be useful in clarifying the extent to which the government can regulate."

Professor Beck said even if the government lost the case, it may not see the policy abandoned altogether.

"It may just be a technical breach that can be fixed with some tweaks in the legislation," he said.

In a statement, the government said it was on the side of Australian parents and kids.

"We will stand firm to protect young Australians from experiencing harm on social media," a government spokesperson said.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further while this matter is before the courts."

Reddit says it will continue to comply with the ban as it challenges the law in the High Court. (Pexels)

Reddit said it shared the government's goal of protecting young people online, "but there are better, more effective ways to achieve it than the social media minimum age legislation".

"As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Adam Collins, the company's chief communications officer.

The case has drawn international attention from the British-based Free Speech Union, US-founded internet company trade association NetChoice and US non-profit Electric Frontier Foundation, who have all sought to appear as an amicus curia or "friend of the court".

State and territory attorneys-general have also made submissions in support of the Commonwealth.

Hearings will continue across Tuesday and Wednesday.

World.title: US midterms 2026 LIVE updates: Trump jokes about renaming Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in final pitch to voters; Republican control of House and Senate under threat from Democrats
World.content:
Welcome to our live coverage of the US midterm elections.

Americans head to the polls tonight (AEDT) in elections that could have big ramifications for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency.

All seats in the US House of Representatives and a third of those in the Senate come up for grabs.

The midterms could have big ramifications for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency. AP

The results will determine whether the Democrats can neuter Trump’s agenda or if he will maintain his grip on America until the presidential election in November 2028.

The elections, which are on track to be America’s most expensive ever, are being fought on issues including the cost of living, the war on Iran, artificial intelligence and data centres, abortion rights, the immigration crackdown, and, of course, the president himself.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan says Australia is desperate for a change in government, close to 18 months from an election where he will seek to change his seat in parliament.

The senator will contest the central Queensland seat of Capricornia following the retirement of long-serving MP Michelle Landry. The election is due by May 20, 2028.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan will attempt a move to the lower house at the next election. Alex Ellinghausen

Canavan said the threat of another rate rise this afternoon showed “we desperately need a change of government”.

“I’ve got to do my job as part of a team to do that because to get that change, we need 76 seats in the lower house,” Canavan told Nine’s Today program this morning.

World.title: Henry’s soccer dream had just begun. Tragedy on the way home means his dad won’t be able to watch on
World.content:
NationalVictoriaRoad Toll Henry’s soccer dream had just begun. Tragedy on the way home means his dad won’t be able to watch on Shelby Brooks and Eleanor Campbell Updated November 3, 2026 — 6:55am ,first published November 2, 2026 — 7:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A father who shared a love of Arsenal Football Club with his seven-year-old son has been killed after a motorcycle collided with the family’s SUV on Sunday evening. Ivan Harrison, 43, was driving his son, Henry in Brighton East about 6.30pm when the SUV they were in flipped after colliding with a motorcycle at the intersection of South Road and Olive Street. Ivan Harrison was driving his son Henry home when he died in car crash. The motorcyclist, 19-year-old Zac Keinan, and Harrison died at the scene. Keinan’s father, Jacob, remembered his son as “an amazing human and free spirit living his best life and did it all his way”.



“He was so happy and proud of his achievements,” he wrote in a social media post, “[Zac was] loved and adored by everyone”. 19-year-old motorcyclist Zac Keinan, with his father Jacob. Instagram Henry, who suffered an upper body injury, was pulled from the car by bystanders after he was found dangling upside down by his seatbelt, a witness told The Age. Tania Benbow, Henry’s mother, said both she and Henry were traumatised and devastated by the loss of Harrison. She said Harrison, who moved to Australia from the UK, was an “amazing, positive and social father who adored his son”.



Henry and his father shared a special bond through their passion for soccer and spent hours watching the FIFA World Cup together this year, Benbow said. Ivan Harrison has been remembered as an amazing father. Henry had just been selected to play for a local football academy. “It’s heartbreaking that his dad is now not there to practice with and watch him this upcoming season in the team,” she told The Age. Benbow thanked the community for rallying behind her and Henry in the aftermath of the tragedy and urged other parents to take car safety seriously, even during short trips.



“If there is one message I want other parents to take from this tragedy, it is to always ensure your child is safely secured in an appropriate booster seat and to keep them in the back seat for as long as possible, even for the shortest trips. I truly believe this saved Henry’s life,” she said. Emergency services were called to reports a car and motorcycle had collided at the intersection of South Road and Olive Street about 6.30pm. Nine News Pipe Vergara was driving home on Sunday evening when two motorcycles loudly accelerated past his window. Seconds later, a massive bang echoed through the street. As he slowed down and stopped to help at the sight of a black SUV flipped over on the road, bystanders were already reaching in to rescue Henry, who was hanging upside down by his seatbelt inside. “The little boy was taken out by a member of the public and given to two ladies who were looking after him. He was fine, but shocked, and calling for his mum,” Vergara said.



The double fatality tops a horror road toll for the Melbourne Cup long weekend so far, with nine people killed since Friday night, four of them riding motorcycles. Several others are in hospital with life-threatening injuries. Vergara recalls that a second motorcycle carrying two people who had been travelling with the destroyed Honda circled back and arrived at the scene of devastation. “Five seconds later, the other motorcycle came up with the other passenger. They took their helmets off and threw them to the floor and started screaming and yelling.” “I moved a little bit closer and could see the body of the rider in a very bad condition, I saw the splash of blood everywhere.” Locals have said the intersection of South Road and Olive Street was known for having dangerous turns.



Brenda Maloney, who saw the police cars down the road from her daughter’s block of units after the crash, said her daughter had avoided a collision at the same spot a week earlier. “There’s a little gap there where you can do a U-turn, and it’s very dangerous there,” she said. The rider of the motorcycle and driver of the car, who are yet to be formally identified, died at the scene in Brighton East. Nine News Horror long weekend on Victoria’s roads The latest deaths cap off a horror Melbourne Cup weekend of nine fatalities on Victoria’s roads, with a public holiday still to come tomorrow.



On Friday afternoon, a 25-year-old died after his motorcycle collided with a car in Footscray. The driver of the car was arrested and interviewed at the scene before being released. Later that night, another motorcyclist died when he collided with a car in Healesville about 64km north-east of Melbourne’s CBD. The 21-year-old died at the scene. An elderly woman died after she was hit by a car in the state’s south-west on Saturday afternoon. The driver, a 52-year-old man, stopped at the scene and provided immediate assistance. He will be interviewed by detectives.



On Saturday night, a 26-year-old man was killed when his motorcycle lost control and crashed into a tree in the Mornington Peninsula suburb of Blairgowrie. The motorcycle’s passenger was airlifted to hospital with critical injuries. Images from a fatal crash in Werribee on Saturday show a ute flipped on its roof. Nine News Police were called to another fatal car crash, north of Ballarat, at roughly the same time, after two cars collided just before 6.30pm. A male driver died at the scene while his female passenger was seriously injured.



About an hour and a half later, a driver died in a separate incident after his ute crashed into a tree in Melbourne’s west. An investigation into the incident in Werribee is ongoing. Anyone who witnessed the crashes or with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. World.title: Albanese warns world leaders of growing threat to democracy after Haines attack
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalAnthony Albanese Albanese warns world leaders of growing threat to democracy after Haines attack David Crowe Updated November 3, 2026 — 6:37am ,first published 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Antigua and Barbuda: Democracies are under increasing danger from violent threats and political polarisation, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has warned in a speech to political leaders at a Commonwealth summit of 56 nations. Albanese cited the attack on independent MP Helen Haines as an example of the risks to democracies as he prepared to meet leaders to discuss issues ranging from climate change to social media regulation and artificial intelligence. Dancers perform at a ceremony attended by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and King Charles at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda. Getty Images He will meet UK counterpart Andy Burnham on Tuesday (AEDT) for talks tipped to focus on fuel security, defence and rules for young British visitors to Australia on working holidays. Another key objective for the prime minister is to gain support from dozens of Commonwealth countries for Australia’s bid for a place on the United Nations Security Council.



The opening day of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda in the Caribbean, featured social gatherings with King Charles and Queen Camilla as guests of honour. A sudden downpour sent royal aides racing for umbrellas. AP “Across the world, political polarisation is reducing social cohesion, placing additional pressures on democratic processes,” Albanese said in an address to leaders at a forum before formal talks on Tuesday. “Workers in all jobs are feeling this as the emotional temperature of our societies rise. “Threats against elected representatives are also increasing, especially against women. And inevitably, some of these threats have been followed through.



Anthony Albanese attends the cricket in Antigua and Barbuda. POOL “Serving and former parliamentarians have been injured and even murdered. Just a fortnight ago, an Australian member of the House of Representatives, Dr Helen Haines, was attacked, suffering grievous injuries. She remains in a serious condition.” Albanese offered to help smaller states in the Commonwealth bolster their democracies, saying he wanted to amplify their voices and work to resolve conflicts. “This is the approach Australia would bring to the United Nations Security Council, should our candidacy for a seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2029-30 be successful,” he said. The remarks outlined the agenda for Albanese’s participation to CHOGM over five days this week, two years after the Commonwealth last met in Samoa.



The Australian government hopes the Commonwealth can be a united force in calling for an end to wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, although the last CHOGM did not mention Ukraine in its final statement. “The conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East are not only taking a tragic toll in human life, they are also having a devastating impact on the global economy,” Albanese said. “Returning our nations and our world to the path of prosperity and rising living standards requires an end to those wars. “Australia has been consistent in our calls for Russia to end its illegal invasion of Ukraine, for a Middle East ceasefire, and for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen and restore the freedom of navigation and trade. “Free and fair trade provides the stability all nations need to flourish. It matters to

every one of our economies. And Australia will always strongly support it.”



A debate about slavery has dominated the meeting for Britain, with King Charles expected to address the issue in his speech and Burnham signalling he is open to issuing a formal apology. The Australian agenda is focused on seeking common positions on climate change, social media and artificial intelligence. Retired cricketer Sir Viv Richards attended the celebrations. Getty Images “Australia understands that for many member countries, climate change is an existential threat,” Albanese said. “We are playing our part in tackling climate change domestically. Our domestic emissions targets are ambitious, but achievable.” Albanese joined the King and Queen and other Commonwealth leaders at a cricket match that pitted Caribbean leaders against counterparts from other Commonwealth nations.



Related Article Analysis

King Charles III The King and the colonies: Why Charles will have to confront slavery Australia was represented by Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade assistant secretary James Buttigieg, who opened the bowling. A sudden downpour sent royal aides racing for umbrellas at an earlier function, an independence day ceremony for Antigua and Barbuda, but other social events went smoothly. Charles made light of the soaking when speaking later to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne. “I think I’m about to grow watercress on my suit,” he joked. The Caribbean team, with legendary West Indies captain Sir Vivian Richards as its honorary manager, played a team with former England captain David Gower as honorary manager.



Anthony Albanese and his wife, Jodie Haydon, arriving in Antigua and Barbuda. ABC Australian borrowers are expected to be hit with another interest rate hike on Tuesday, heaping more pressure on Albanese’s economic credentials as polling continues to show lacklustre support for his government. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor suggested on Monday that Albanese shouldn’t be overseas while having “lost control of the economy”. “The prime minister doesn’t get this. He needs to get control of our borders here in this country and going and having a talk with the UK prime minister to get him to fix the problem for us, I don’t know where that’s going to land,” Taylor said. Albanese has targeted backpackers as part of his move to lower Australia’s annual intake of migrants.



Working holidaymaker numbers have risen to record highs under the terms of a Coalition-era free trade agreement, which allowed British backpackers to live in Australia for up to three years without working in the regions. The influx of British temporary visa holders in the past three years far outnumbers the corresponding flow of Australians to the UK. World.title: AI is coming for office workers. How vulnerable is Brisbane?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAI AI is coming for office workers. How vulnerable is Brisbane? Marissa Calligeros and Matt Wade November 3, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

More than 40 per cent of the tasks performed by workers across Brisbane are vulnerable to AI automation, new analysis shows. But researchers say that figure would rise to about 45 per cent with closer analysis of Brisbane’s CBD and inner suburbs, including South Brisbane, Fortitude Valley, Newstead, Milton and Spring Hill, where knowledge-intensive services such as finance, professional services, and information technology are concentrated. One expert says Brisbane (pictured before the completion of Star Casino at Queens Wharf) has more ‘breathing space’ to prepare for AI disruption than the southern capitals. Getty The Gold Coast is the second most vulnerable area to AI automation in Queensland, the report by consultancy SGS Economics and Planning reveals, despite the city’s prevalence of jobs in tourism, hospitality and construction, which require a physical presence. At least 37 per cent of tasks performed by workers on the Gold Coast are exposed to AI disruption, according to the report.



In Logan and Ipswich council areas, where a high share of workers are employed in retail, hospitality services and transport, the figure falls to 35 per cent. That correlates with data showing that the most common job in the Logan suburbs of Kingston, Marsden and Park Ridge is a storeperson (someone who receives and sorts goods in a warehouse), while the inner suburbs of Bulimba and Newstead are dominated by sales and marketing managers. It reflects a broader trend that the share of tasks vulnerable to AI automation declines with distance from capital city centres, and in the case of Queensland, also illustrates how connected the economies of Brisbane, the Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast are. This is a departure from previous waves of economic disruption, especially the automation and outsourcing of manufacturing activities in the 1980s and 1990s, which hit employment in outer suburbs and regional areas hardest.



Alison Holloway, a partner at SGS Economics and Planning and the report’s co-author, noted the data for south-east Queensland was skewed by the size of the Brisbane City Council area. Council areas in Sydney and Melbourne are much smaller by comparison, enabling a more granular analysis of inner-city suburbs with a high concentration of knowledge-economy jobs. But Holloway said Brisbane’s professional heartland in the CBD was no less vulnerable to AI disruption than the city centres of Sydney and Melbourne, where 45 and 44.5 per cent of work tasks are at risk of automation, respectively. “What we’re seeing in other capital cities is that city-based professionals in finance, technology and business services are most likely to see their jobs change, and these jobs in Brisbane are typically located in the inner parts of the local government area,” she said.



But AI innovation expert and the director of Griffith University’s Data Trust, Professor Dian Tjondronegoro, said the infrastructure demand and economic momentum ahead of the 2032 Olympic Games was creating some “breathing space” for Brisbane. “I would say Sydney and Melbourne will have arguably higher exposure to AI disruption, because of the nature of the knowledge-based industries there,” he said. Professor Dian Tjondronegoro from the Griffith Data Centre says Brisbane businesses have a unique opportunity in the coming years to review what every role in their organisation means in the era of AI. Griffith University “In Brisbane, we’re not that far behind, but our saving grace, if I may use that word, is the infrastructure work leading up to Brisbane ’32.” He said Brisbane should seize upon the years before the Olympics to prepare for the ways AI automation will change work patterns.



“We need to remember that it is not about us being replaced by AI, but how people can work smarter and more efficiently with AI,” he said. “To rehire is a lot more expensive than to reimagine a new way of doing things with AI,” he added, noting that last year Google rehired a swathe of software engineers it had made redundant two years earlier. Research by the Department of Industry’s Office of the Chief Economist published in July found no evidence of broad labour market upheaval from AI in Australia, although employment in occupations more exposed to generative AI has grown more slowly than others. Holloway said the effects of AI automation would have a “different spatial pattern” to previous economic transitions caused by technological change.



“Earlier waves of automation took on routine, manual tasks, so their effects were felt most in manufacturing suburbs and farming regions,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

University An arts degree or a trade: How to futureproof your career “AI can now take on parts of the cognitive work done in offices, and those jobs are concentrated in the professional heart of our cities.” The analysis measured the exposure to AI automation of work tasks, not the probability of jobs disappearing altogether. “In the past we’ve seen the closure of mines and things like car manufacturing, which has impacted whole communities, but this is now a different part of the economy and different locations that will be more affected,” Holloway said.



“There is a lot we can learn from those previous economic transitions to think more strategically about what’s coming with AI automation.” The SGS Economics and Planning analysis used estimates of how exposed each occupation is to AI automation made by federal agency Jobs and Skills Australia, along with census employment data, to map exposure both where people work and where they live. Fox chief executive officer Lachlan Murdoch acknowledged a steep decline in viewership on Fox News ahead of midterm elections and attributed it to “viewer fatigue.” The cable news network had seen similar trends during the 2006 midterms, which also fell during a president’s second term — George W. Bush’s, Murdoch said on a call with analysts on Monday (US time) to discuss financial results. Fox chief Lachlan Murdoch says viewers are watching less television overall. Getty Fox News notched strong viewership last year because of coverage on events like massive floods and the assassination of right-wing political activist Charlie Kirk, which could account for the unfavorable comparison this year, Murdoch said. The network is still the most-watched on cable and is expected to have more daily viewers on average than in any other midterm year going back to 1998. Fox News experienced a 28 per cent drop in its prime-time audience to an average of 2 million viewers from September 28 to October 25, according to Nielsen data.



“Those viewers are not going to any other channel,” Murdoch said. “They’re not switching to CNN or MS NOW. They’re just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.” Related Article Media & marketing The inside story of the downfall of a Trump-loving host at Fox News Versant Media Group’s MS NOW experienced a 15 per cent increase to 1.16 million viewers, while Skydance’s CNN averaged 644,000 viewers, a 16 per cent increase over the same period, Nielsen data showed. Some media observers attribute the decline to President Donald Trump’s slipping approval ratings, suggesting disengagement from Fox’s traditional Republican audience. The Democrats are currently favoured by both traditional polls and prediction market odds to win the House of Representatives and Senate, as voters grapple with issues around affordability, a controversial war in Iran and tariffs.



Fox reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $US4.57 billion ($6.5 billion), exceeding Wall Street’s estimates of $US4.31 billion. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation were $US1.64 billion, beating analysts’ expectations of $US1.37 billion. The network also reported record political advertising for midterms of more than $US350 million. Fox saw $US250 million spent on political ads on local stations, $US50 million on the Tubi streaming platform and another $US50 million for national political ads. US President Donald Trump’s sliding approval ratings have been cited as a factor driving the fall. AP Overall, ad revenue jumped 47 per cent to $US2.08 billion in the quarter, mainly from broadcasting the men’s FIFA World Cup over the summer. Murdoch said the network is interested in pursuing the US media rights for the next two tournaments. FIFA began the bidding process for those last month. The rights are expected to fetch as much as $US4 billion. “We were obviously happy with the performance of the World Cup this past year and we’ll be looking at the rights for 2030 and 2034 in a disciplined manner as we would with all sports rights,” Murdoch said.

World.title: ‘Like a runaway train’: Private girls’ schools lead 2027 fee hikes
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPrivate schools ‘Like a runaway train’: Private girls’ schools lead 2027 fee hikes Alex Crowe November 3, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Parents with children attending Victoria’s high-fee schools can expect to pay thousands of dollars more next year, as independent and Catholic schools point to payroll tax and teacher wages to justify fee hikes well above inflation. Families with students at all-girls schools will be among the hardest hit, with several raising year 12 fees well above the 6.3 per cent average for Melbourne’s high-fee schools. Deakin University education policy expert Emma Rowe said private school parents were “locked in” to uncapped fee hikes each year, describing it “like a runaway train at the moment, and it’s really unsustainable”. Ivanhoe Girls’ Grammar School has built a four-storey facility at a cost of about $37 million. Ivanhoe Girls’ Grammar School has raised its fees 15.1 per cent to $41,900 for years 11 and 12 next year, the largest increase of any school included in The Age’s analysis.



In 2025, the independent school in Melbourne’s north-east began construction of a $37 million four-storey building, which will have a cafe and specialist tech facilities including audio recording and studio spaces when it opens. The price tag exceeded the school’s entire yearly expenditure of $34.63 million, according to its 2025 annual report, of which the majority – $24 million – went to staff salaries. Ivanhoe Girls’ Grammar School will open its state-of-the-art facility next year. Eddie Jim Some families have expressed frustration online with the school’s “entirely unnecessary empowerED building and program”, accusing it of hiking fees to pay for its development. The school did not respond to a request for comment when contacted by The Age. Rowe said tying fees to government funding – where the more a school charged, the less taxpayer funding it would receive – would limit the “problematic” year-on-year hikes.



This would encourage schools to maintain low fees and keep independent education more affordable for financially struggling families, Rowe said. “You can’t expect public funding but no public regulation,” she said. “It’s not OK to have publicly funded schools that keep raising their tuition fees.” Rowe noted that while high-fee schools weren’t uncommon internationally, Australia was an outlier in the extent taxpayers propped them up. Genazzano FCJ College in Kew has raised its fees 9.6 per cent to $45,500 for year 12 in 2027, the second-largest increase in the schools analysed by The Age.



The Catholic all-girls school sold prime real estate for $1.98 million in April to pay down debt, as enrolments plummeted 35 per cent since 2020, from 834 students to 609 students this year. Principal Loretta Wholley said Genazzano fees remained below those of other independent schools in Kew. “Like all schools, we are managing significant cost pressures, and the 2027 fee reflects our continued investment in teaching and learning,” she said. “Genazzano has educated students in Kew since 1889 and is planning confidently for the future.” Mentone Girls Grammar School, whose enrolments have declined 25 per cent over the same period, had the third-biggest hike – 8.2 per cent – charging $43,000 for years 11 and 12.



Camberwell Girls’ Grammar School, where enrolments have grown by 3.6 per cent, had the fourth-highest rise of 7.9 per cent, with fees reaching $45,595 for years 11 and 12. Principal Debbie Dunwoody said school council had considered economic conditions, educational priorities and the “investment required to maintain the quality of our education and student experience” when reviewing fees. Related Article Education The most and least popular schools with parents – see how your school ranks “We recognise that families make a significant financial investment in their children’s education,” she said. “Our responsibility is to ensure that investment continues to deliver the quality of teaching, breadth of educational opportunities and strong academic outcomes that families have come to expect from Camberwell Girls.”



Several other high-fee schools, including Xavier College, Melbourne and Camberwell grammar schools, Strathcona Girls, Geelong College and the Jewish schools had not published their 2027 fees with just weeks left in the school year, creating uncertainty for families. Australia’s most expensive school, Geelong Grammar, will charge $58,320 per year for years 10 to 12 students attending its Corio campus next year. The future King Charles III with Geelong Grammar students in 2005 when he returned to the campus he attended as a teen. Wayne Taylor Its flagship campus, Timbertop, where year 9 students board for four terms near Merrijig to experience Victoria’s high country, will cost $99,756. When extras, including up to $1300 in skiing costs and $30 for a birthday cake, are added, most families will see that fee soar past six figures.



The combined cost of a student attending from prep to year 12 will be $606,700 at Geelong Grammar in 2027. If fees continue to rise at 5 per cent, the combined cost will be $702,331 by 2030. Independent Schools Victoria has pointed out that schools face cost pressures beyond general inflation of 4.3 per cent, including rising staff costs, which account for about 70 per cent of school operating costs, plus insurance, utilities and Victoria’s payroll tax. The Liberal Party has vowed if it wins government later this month, it will repeal the payroll tax for government and non-government schools. Independent Schools Victoria chief executive Rachel Holthouse said Victoria was the only state that charged the tax on independent schools, and it affected schools serving everyday families, adding to costs for parents. Independent Schools Victoria chief executive Rachel Holthouse. Joe Armao



Holthouse said more than half of all new independent school enrolments since 2019 hade been in schools charging less than $7500 a year. “We know cost-of-living pressures are real, and many families are working hard to afford the school that best suits their child’s needs,” she said. However, those with children at mid-fee schools will also see increases in 2027, including those at one of the almost 300 Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools. A spokesperson said fees would be capped at 5 to 9 per cent – with some exceptions – in line with recent years. Catholic schools, whose teachers have had pay parity with public colleagues since the 1990s, have warned families that matching Victorian public school teachers’ historic 28 per cent pay increase could result in fee hikes and program cuts.



De La Salle College has increased its fees by 9 per cent – to $17,593 for year 12 – in 2027. The all-boys Catholic school in Malvern has had enrolments drop 22.5 per cent from 2020 to 2026. But principal Michael Ilot said De La Salle had more students moving from higher-fee schools because they recognised the college’s academic value. De La Salle principal Michael Ilot says the Catholic school has families which have turned away from high-fee schools. Ilot, who previously held a senior position at Xavier, said families reported valuing the academic opportunity, quality teaching and strong school community at De La Salle’s accessible cost.



“That’s why we have kept our fees capped at 9 per cent, without compromising on the educational quality and pastoral care our students receive,” he said. “You don’t need to pay the highest fees to achieve the best results.” University of NSW economist Richard Holden said it wasn’t unreasonable for private schools to claim public school wages were driving up staff costs. “They’re competing for teachers in a general teacher labour market, so if one part of a sector gives a large pay rise, then it’s hard not to give the same large pay rise to your own teachers,” he said. Editor's pick CBD Hollywood star’s generosity leaves diners stunned In addition to wages, Holden said schools had a range of costs, including inputs like energy, education costs such as AI subscriptions, and ensuring facilities met families’ expectations.

World.title: ASX set to jump on RBA day, Wall Street rises as oil prices tumble
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump on RBA day, Wall Street rises as oil prices tumble Stan Choe November 3, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
