World.title: Solomon Islands government moves to end 'unstable coalitions, party defections'
World.content:
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale's coalition is preparing to undertake a major constitutional reform initiative, including introducing "anti-defection measures" to create a "more predicable political environment," the government has announced.

Wale, who leads the Government for Reform, Empowerment, Accountability and Transformation (GREAT), is currently recovering in an Australian hospital after departing Honiara for emergency medical treatment for an undisclosed condition last week.

The Solomon Islands Prime Minister's Office has not confirmed when Wale would return home.

However, in a statement on Monday, the government said it was advancing a reform package aimed at strengthening political stability and governance.

"The proposed amendments seek to address longstanding challenges in the country's political system, including unstable coalitions, party defections, recurring motions of no confidence and short parliamentary terms that can disrupt policy continuity and national development," the statement read.

It said the constitutional reforms would be built around six key pillars.

These include the responsible use of motions of no confidence; stronger political party integrity and anti-defection measures; transparent and rules-based government formation; a stable, continuous parliamentary term; stronger institutional independence and integrity, including safeguards for Parliament and the Judiciary and support for the Opposition front bench; and constitutional recognition of Solomon Islands' Christian identity.

"For ordinary Solomon Islanders, the intended benefits include greater continuity in government policies and development programmes," the government said.

World.title: Household hot water savings 'could be bigger than solar'
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2305616%2Fhousehold-hot-water-savings-could-be-bigger-than-solar

New Zealanders have an opportunity to save money on their power that's equal to the potential of solar, but they may not even be aware of it, one market commentator says.

Powerswitch head Paul Fuge said hot water controls had the potential to benefit households significantly, if they were used well.

He said New Zealand had had "ripple control" on hot water cylinders since the 1950s, which allowed lines companies to reduce hot water demand to stop lines overloading.

New technology and smart meters were replacing that, and providing the benefit to households instead.

Audio player for " NZers could save money on power bills " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2305616%2Fhousehold-hot-water-savings-could-be-bigger-than-solar

NZers could save money on power bills Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"There are a lot of plans that reward you for having hot water control,' Fuge said. "If you allow the network to control your hot water through ripple control, you can get a lower tariff on your hot water, or they might call it night rates or control rates.

"You can get a benefit there, but this [smart control] gives you more. It's significant, because if you look at hot water, it's about 30 percent of a household's costs.

"It's a really big area for people to save money."

Power represents a significant cost to NZ households. Boris Zhitkov

He said the technology would allow consumers with time-of-use plans to heat their hot water overnight, when their power was cheaper.

"Your hot water cylinder only comes on during low-cost periods. If that's 30 percent of your cost and you're doing that at much lower electricity rates, that saves you heaps of money."

People could install devices on existing hot water cylinders, he said, while newer hot water cylinders might have the functionality built in. Some power companies were also offering it for customers, via their smart meter connections.

Fuge said his own hot water cylinder came on at 10pm and the water would stay hot.

"There is no downside to heating up at night.

"If people are looking to save money, buying a hot water heat pump and controlling it for low-cost electricity rates... you can really make a big dent in your household electricity costs.

"I always say, for a lot of people, for a lot of large households, it's probably more than solar.

"It's a more surefire way of saving money, I believe, for many households, large households with kids, who are using a lot of hot water. It could make a bigger impact than putting solar on."

New Zealanders have an opportunity to save money on their power that's equal to the potential of solar, market commentator Paul Fuge says. DmitryMo

He said having solar as well would be ideal, because the water could be used as a type of battery for the solar system.

"You can use the technology to make sure you're heating up your hot water with any excess solar, rather than putting it back into the grid at a lower rate."

EECA research, evaluation and insights lead adviser Gareth Gretton said his organisation had looked at hot water as part of wider research into demand flexibility.

"With smart devices for controlling loads in houses and businesses, there's more opportunity to do smart things," he said. "You could have a situation where, if the wind is blowing and the sun is shining, you could be turning hot water cylinders on and potentially warming them a bit hotter than they normally would sit, because at times when renewable energy is plentiful, it's a bit of a case of use it or lose it.

"It's a really big opportunity. Hot water is a surprisingly large amount of our residential demand, indeed our electricity demand as a whole.

"Simply heating hot water in houses is something like 10 percent of New Zealand's electricity use."

Smart meter provider Bluecurrent said - on 7 August, winter's coldest day this year - 100,000 hot water cylinders with smart meters shifted 81.2MWh of power away from the evening peaks, saving an estimated $77,000 to $100,000 in wholesale costs.

It conducted a survey that found 85 percent of people did not know the technology existed. Most were open to more hot water control, but wanted assurance there would be a real saving.

Bluecurrent chief customer officer Matt Bostwick said households with their hot water controlled by power companies used 10 percent less power than those without.

"There are lots of ways that the dynamic control of hot water heating can save households money. We've done some research looking at the drivers for New Zealand power consumers - what would motivate them to participate in hot water load control.

"Of course, the N o.1 thing was, 'If it saved me some money, I'd be up for it'.

"Really interestingly, nearly 20 percent - one in five - said, 'If I knew I was contributing to making the energy system more sustainable, I'd be up for participating in that as well'."

He said many more households could start making better use of their hot water control.

"Some 1.4-1.8 million homes today have a hot water cylinder, and it doesn't matter whether you're the home owner or a renter, you still get the opportunity to participate in that, because the key element - the hot water cylinder - is already there.

"We just have to get them connected and activated and turned on."

World.title: The top 10 things to watch for in the US midterm elections
World.content:
Audio player for " CNN's Karin Caifa on the final day of US midterm campaigning " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/world/2305415%2Fthe-top-10-things-to-watch-for-in-the-us-midterm-elections

CNN's Karin Caifa on the final day of US midterm campaigning Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Analysis - We know, you're sick of elections. But while everyone is gearing up for our general election Saturday, first we've got the US midterms to cope with.

The midterm election results will come starting about Wednesday midday NZ time, and Americans will vote on who will serve in Congress in the House of Representatives and Senate.

Currently Congress is held by Republicans, which has mostly accepted Republican President Donald Trump's agenda. But margins are tight and control of the House and possibly Senate could flip.

Read a full explainer here about how they work: What are the US midterms and why are they a big deal?

Here are 10 things to keep an eye on Wednesday:

1. The early races will tell us if there's a "blue wave."

The phrase "blue wave" means a strong result for the opposition Democrats. Traditionally, the party in the White House almost always does badly in midterm elections, which are seen as a referendum on the party in power.

American poll watchers seem to be almost unanimous in believing the Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives, while the smaller Senate is less certain.

There are so many congressional races for the lower House - 435 of them - that it may not be immediately clear who's ahead, but many congressional seats are considered noncompetitive and only a few dozen to be "swing" seats. All it will take is a couple of seats picked up for the House to swing to Democratic control. There are 35 of 100 Senate seats also up for election.

The first results will start rolling in on the US East Coast, which is 17 hours behind us, about 7pm Tuesday their time or 1pm Wednesday our time. Key states will be South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews faces Sen. Darline Graham; North Carolina, where Democrat Governor Roy Cooper is poised to flip a Senate seat, and Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown, a former senator, and incumbent Sen. Jon Husted are nearly tied in polls.

By 8pm ET (2pm NZT) polls will be closed in almost half the country, including another key Senate race in Maine, and by 9pm (3pm NZT) Texas and Michigan will be closed (more on them in a second). Polls will then start to close in far western states like California, Montana and Oregon on into the evening our time.

The final poll to close will be Alaska at 1am ET (7pm NZT), where another key Senate race is being held.

In an aerial view, voters wait in line on the last day of early in-person voting at the Franklin County Board of Elections on November 01, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. Voters in battleground state Ohio are deciding House and Senate contests, as well as the race for governor that is considered a toss-up. JON CHERRY / AFP

2. Be ready for 'stolen election' talk and legal challenges

That Alaska race has already been plagued by legal battles after a New York Times report found Democratic involvement in getting a Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot as a 'spoiler' candidate against sitting Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan. Some claim the similar names could intentionally mislead voters.

There have been a flurry of pre-emptive lawsuits filed around the country by the Trump administration, which has targeted both California and Washington state in attempts to set aside ballots over unproven allegations of noncitizen voting.

Donald Trump has never conceded his loss to Joe Biden in the 2020 election and has made countless claims of voter fraud made against Republicans.

Whatever the actual results are in the midterms, expect the debate and rhetoric to continue for weeks and possibly months to come. It's even possible that some candidates could be refused to be seated when the new Congress begins in January if things really heat up.

3. Could Democratic wins affect New Zealand?

It's possible we may see ripple effects here. Trump's unpopular Iran war and global tariffs, including against New Zealand, have largely been pushed through by a compliant Republican Congress. If Democrats assume control of the House and Senate, there will be considerably more pushback against them.

However, more than many presidents, Trump flexes executive power, and many of his decisions have been made by executive orders and emergency declarations and he could also simply veto any legislation Democrats put through. A two-thirds congressional majority is required to overturn a presidential veto.

If the Republicans are thoroughly humbled on midterms day, it's possible the Iran war may be quickly wound up, although its impact on petrol prices in New Zealand is likely to linger.

A voter dressed as Lady Liberty waits to cast their ballot on the final day of early voting ahead of the November 3 midterm elections in Charlotte, North Carolina, on October 31, 2026. AM STEWART / AFP

4. Will negative campaigning backfire?

Political races have been dirty since time immemorial, but this year has seen several low points. Name-calling and racial and gender attacks have become commonplace.

Many voters say they are tired of negative campaigning. There have been attacks by both Republicans and Democrats, but the Republican attacks have received far more attention this year.

Audio player for " Michigan Senate race thrown open by Democrat's endorsement " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/world/2305415%2Fthe-top-10-things-to-watch-for-in-the-us-midterm-elections

Michigan Senate race thrown open by Democrat's endorsement Morning Report Download MP3 5m

In Ohio, Republican governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy put out an ad that featured Democrat Amy Acton's long-estranged elderly mother calling her a liar. Acton was the victim of childhood sexual abuse by her late stepfather, and had not spoken to her mother since 1978, when she and her brother were removed from her custody. Ramaswamy's controversial ad drew condemnation from both Republicans and Democrats and polls indicate his support has rapidly fallen since.

Trump himself has launched many attacks such as repeatedly using an anti-transgender slur against South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who is cisgender.

The results on election day in some of these races may determine if voters have had enough of gutter tactics, or if they're just an accepted part of politics in 2026.

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a campaign rally on November 01, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. SPENCER PLATT

5. The Michigan Senate Race

One of the most combative races is between Republican Mike Rogers and progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim US senator. El-Sayed has increasingly become the focus of anti-Muslim attacks - Trump has called him a 'jihadist' and said metal detectors would be required at the Senate if he's elected. Polls have shown El-Sayed with a small lead.

The race got even more bizarre in the past day when his Democratic primary opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, shocked watchers by endorsing Republican Rogers.

6. California tries to tax billionaires

California is pushing a referendum on a one-time 5 percent tax on all billionaires living in the state, the money from which would fund healthcare programs. Proposition 40 has drawn heavy coverage and a massive effort by super-rich Californians against it, while progressives like Senator Bernie Sanders have rallied for it. Polling has shown support for passing the tax may be slipping.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico with supporters at the conclusion of a campaign rally in Kerrville, Texas. BRANDON BELL / AFP

7. The Texas Senate race

Democrat James Talarico is facing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Normally Texas is deep Republican red, but Paxton has been dogged by a series of scandals in his career including a fraud indictment and impeachment. The polls have shown a close race but Talarico has a bit of an edge. If he wins, he'll be the first Democrat senator elected in Texas since 1988.

8. Reports of suppression or possible violence

American politics has become increasingly charged with violence with incidents like the assassination of Republican activist Charlie Kirk and the murder of a Minnesota Democratic state representative and her husband.

If there are any attacks on voting places or protests over results that turn violent, it could turn into a grim situation that escalates quickly, much like the attack on the US Capitol in 2021.

Sean Kessler directs traffic as voters wait in line on the last day of early in-person voting at the Franklin County Board of Elections on November 01, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. JON CHERRY / AFP

9. Could it have ripples in global politics?

Worldwide, there seems to be a tug-of-war between the right and left which shows Trump's heavy influence on how politics is done. Recent elections in Brazil and Serbia showed a push back from the left and progressive activists, and while Israel's election last week remains too close to call, far-right leader Benjamin Netanyahu has seemingly lost much of his power in the results.

Academics and political deep thinkers will be spinning out reams of copy over what the midterms mean if Trumpism is rebuked - or if Republicans do far better than expected.

Donald Trump's reaction to midterm results could affect politics for some time to come. AFP / BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI

10. Most importantly, what will Trump do?

There's never quite been a president as unpredictable as Donald Trump, and it's hard to know how he may react to a major Democratic victory, or if he'll accept it.

Even if the Republicans suffer catastrophic losses, Trump will still be president. But his power may be curtailed, and it's possible there could be more investigations into alleged misconduct by his administration.

He also will inevitably suffer "lame duck" status in the final two years of his administration, as the 2028 presidential race basically begins the day after midterms.

World.title: 'Most New Zealanders would be appalled': Abusive parents blocking children from therapy
World.content:
Audio player for " Children blocked from therapy by parental consent rules " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2305773%2Fmost-new-zealanders-would-be-appalled-abusive-parents-blocking-children-from-therapy

Children blocked from therapy by parental consent rules Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A survivor of domestic violence says the law makes it too easy for her abusive ex-partner to block their children from accessing counselling despite their pleas for therapy.

A new report by Backbone Collective details how abusive legal guardians are preventing their tamariki from accessing therapy and healthcare, because consent of both parents is needed.

The organisation advocates for survivors of domestic violence and is calling for changes to the law that would prioritise children's safety.

Sarah* has the police reports and criminal court file to show her ex-partner was physically abusive - she left him when he started hurting their children and is their main caregiver.

But when her children needed counselling and were keen to get help through therapy, their dad refused consent.

"It's devastating to see your child in a traumatic state, them crying themselves to sleep, even self-harming, and as a mother, all you want to do is help them and to have to say to them, we can't get help because your father says no ... it's ridiculous."

But the law states that both guardians' consent is needed for a child's non-routine treatment, including mental health treatments, until they turn 16.

In New Zealand, both parents are afforded guardianship status even if one of those parents is abusive - it is uncommon for a parent to lose guardianship.

"If you are split up, any time you need to seek assistance for your child, you have to get consent from both parents. That's the law and so most of the time I've gone through my lawyer and he's come back through his lawyer and just said, nope, that's it," Sarah said.

It wasn't just one instance.

"He has blocked everything really from GP visits, school counsellor, therapy, pediatrician, any sort of specialist visits, anything to do with medical health and mental health, he has a say and has refused consent," she said.

"For him, I believe it's control. It's not about what's best for the children. It's mostly about punishing me. He knows that the best way to punish me is to hurt the children."

A survivor of domestic violence says the law makes it too easy for her ex-partner to block their children from accessing counselling despite their pleas for therapy. 123RF

Backbone Collective surveyed women who experienced family violence and heard from 63 mothers of 113 children from around the country. They described how abusive legal guardians had blocked or compromised their children's access to therapy, after their children had experienced violence.

Its report released on Tuesday, Daddy says No, detailed how the abusive parents had refused consent through legal proceedings in the Family Court or directly with the therapeutic service, often threatening.

Co-founder Deborah Mackenzie said all but one were fathers and some had compromised their children's access to counselling by demanding records.

"What these mothers told us is that the system and people working in the system currently enable abusive parents to block children's access to therapeutic support."

She said the mothers wanted their children to access the help they needed after experiencing domestic violence.

A quarter reported at least one of their chldren was sexually assaulted, 57 percent said their children had been physically assaulted and 76 percent said their children had been verbally assaulted.

"I think most New Zealanders would be appalled to learn that the person who has used violence against a child is the very same person who gets to block that child getting support to recover and heal."

Mackenzie said it was a coercive control tactic that the law was enabling.

"Every attempt by the abuser is to stop the child talking about the violence and abuse but it's also about being able to continue control over the child and also over the protective mum long after they've separated."

She said over the last two years, specialist family violence and sexual violence therapeutic service providers had told Backbone that they were increasingly being forced to stop providing sessions to children due to legal demands from abusers' lawyers, in the form of cease and desist letters.

Mackenzie said providers were not all equipped or resourced to respond despite there being no doubt the children needed therapeutic help, many urgently.

The mothers in the survey described how they had sought therapy for their children because they had serious concerns for their children's mental health due to self-harming or suicidal thoughts, anxiety or depression impacting their daily life.

"It's really important in supporting children's recovery from the abuse because we know that when a parent uses family violence or sexual violence against a child that has a huge negative impact on children," Mackenzie said.

"It's protective mums that are left coping with these impacts on their children, so they're seeing very distressed children, children having troubles at school, children having trouble regulating their emotions and their relationships with others."

Almost half of the mothers who responded to the survey told Backbone one of their children had difficulty with learning, concentrating or remembering and 44 percent indicated at least one of their children had difficulty communicating or socialising.

Mackenzie also said many mothers described parenting orders which forced their children to have ongoing unsupervised or sometimes supervised contact with the abusive father and that this resulted in further emotional distress for the children.

Calling for change

University of Auckland associate professor Carrie Leonetti is an expert in family law and said in New Zealand, the guardianship rights of parents appeared to be prioritised over children's rights to access support.

Associate Professor Carrie Leonetti at University of Auckland says the institution should apologise and reassure it would not retaliate against whistle blowers. Supplied

"I think we need to separate the question of residence, of care, of contact with children from the question of legal decision making. There are cases in New Zealand where perpetrators who are imprisoned for criminal acts of family violence retain guardianship over their children, that's just insane."

She said children with capacity to decide for themselves should be able to access therapy such as counselling.

"Maybe the questions should just be why should any parent for any reason be able to stop their child getting psychological treatment that's helpful to them, that's necessary for their health and that they made an informed decision to get."

Leonetti said New Zealand was out of step internationally in its commitment to co-guardianship even when there was domestic abuse.

"What's common in most countries is that the court will designate a residential parent and guardian and they have to advise but not get consent from the other person in order to do things like enrol children in school, get children medical treatment," she said.

"Just because these women have children with the men who abused them, that they have to be chained to these men until their youngest child hits at least 16 or even 18 is just shockingly outdated and really out of step with global norms."

Backbone Collective is calling for changes to the law, including the Care of Children Act, that would stop known abusers being able to block their children's access to therapy and prioritise children's safety.

This included removing any right of Protection Order respondents to have decision-making power over their children's access to therapeutic services and child safety programmes or access the case notes.

Mackenzie said such change was urgently needed.

"We are saying that the system needs to make safety, wellbeing and the best interest of tamariki it's highest priority. Whatever the policy tools are used, policymakers must be successful in stopping abusers from interferring with children's access to therapeutic services and healthcare."

Sarah said the impact of her ex-partner blocking their children's access to therapy had been extensive because they did not receive help when they needed it.

"It's absolutely devastating. I think that as a mother what you want to do is protect your children and I think I find from what I've seen women in my situation, a mother's first instinct is to protect the children. We go to court, we come at it as this is what's best for the child."

She said the children had accessed therapy through their school counsellor on their own terms but not without her ex-partner trying to stop it.

"Basically most women in my situation, our option is either to fight a lengthy battle in court, spend money on legal fees. The court waiting time is absolutely horrendous ... when a child has an immediate problem and you can't get a court date for six months, it's just so frustrating," Sarah said.

"The other option is waiting until the child is old enough to consent for themselves, which is frustrating. It's crazy that you should have to wait for a child to be a certain age to be able to consent for themselves."

She would like children's health needs given priority over guardianship law.

"If you have an abusive parent, then the children should have immediate access to help. It should be mandatory. I feel that it's incredibly important and very urgent. It's incredibly traumatic," she said.

"My children saw me be abused and they were abused themselves. It's physical violence, it's emotional trauma, and it shapes a child's life. And for them to not be able to have the proper counselling and therapy services, it affects them into their adult life."

World.title: Manhunt underway after two people seriously injured during aggravated robbery in Auckland's Avondale
World.content:
Two people have been seriously injured following an aggravated burglary in Auckland's Avondale overnight.

Detective Senior Sergeant Rebecca Kirk said those involved were still being sought by police.

At 3.20am on Tuesday a group was socialising at a house on Ahiriri Ave when two unknown men approached the house, Kirk said.

A fight broke out and two people were injured by a weapon one of the men had with him.

The men then attempted to steal from the home, Kirk said, but were unsuccessful and fled in a car before police arrived.

The two injured people were taken to hospital in serious conditions, she said, and police were trying to find those involved.

Anyone with information was asked to contact police on 105 online or by phone, referencing file number 261103/2286.

World.title: All Blacks 'heartbroken' by sudden death of security chief, says assistant coach Jason Ryan
World.content:
Assistant coach Jason Ryan has made an emotional tribute to Logan Cadwallader, saying the All Blacks were "heartbroken" at the sudden death of a man who has been the team's head of security for a decade.

A New Zealand Rugby statement on Tuesday morning said Cadwallader, a married father of three, had been found dead in his hotel room in Edinburgh on Sunday night NZT after a medical event.

Cadwallader was a former New Zealand SAS soldier who went into the security business after leaving the army and was at the forefront of the All Blacks' security arrangements at home and around the world.

Ryan, wiping away tears during his online address to New Zealand media, described Cadwallader as a "quiet hero" and a "great team member".

Logan Cadwallader. SPECTRE

The All Blacks are in Edinburgh preparing for their Nations Championship test against Scotland at Murrayfield on Sunday morning NZT.

"This is something you don't really prepare for, losing a team member," said Ryan, who has worked alongside Cadwallader since joining the All Blacks as a forwards coach in 2022.

"I just want to, on behalf of the All Blacks, pass on our sincere condolences to Logan's family, particularly his wife Nannette and three kids Trey, Brooke and Mia.

"I can tell you that the team is heartbroken. He had a massive influence on a lot of people in the All Blacks in the last decade. Loges was our quiet hero. He was always looking ahead for us and always looking out for us and our families.

"The country has lost a great soldier and we've lost a great team member. And we love him."

World.title: US Air Force plans expanded training at Northern Marianas airports
World.content:
The United States Air Force is proposing expanded military training at airports on Saipan, Tinian and Rota in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), prompting calls for greater public consultation and scrutiny of potential environmental impacts.

In a notice published in the Federal Register on 28 October, the Air Force announced plans to prepare an environmental impact statement for aircraft training and exercises at four airfields across the three islands.

Under the proposal, each airfield could accommodate up to 1200 fixed-wing aircraft operations and 320 helicopter operations annually, along with up to 1000 military personnel and 550,000 gallons of fuel.

Aircraft operations refer to takeoffs and landings rather than individual aircraft.

The Saipan-based community group Our Common Wealth 670 is calling for the initial 30-day public consultation period to be extended to at least 60 days.

The group said the review must consider aircraft noise, environmental contamination, civilian airport operations, cultural resources and public safety, as well as the cumulative impacts of military activities across the Marianas.

It also urged greater participation by Indigenous Chamorro and Refaluwasch communities, citing the islands' history of military land acquisition, displacement and environmental contamination.

"The timing of this scoping period raises serious concerns," the group said, noting that the review coincides with the approaching holiday season.

However, Commonwealth Ports Authority board chair Bart Jackson said the proposed military activities would not disrupt commercial aviation, airport capacity or civilian access.

"No. Absolutely not. No impact," Jackson said.

"We are working cooperatively with them. They will be a paying tenant."

Northern Marianas congressional delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds welcomed the territory's contribution to US military readiness but encouraged residents to participate in the environmental review.

"These are decisions that can have lasting implications for our communities. Your participation matters, and the federal government needs to hear directly from the people who live, work, and raise their families on these islands," she said.

The Air Force said the proposed activities would strengthen military readiness and its ability to operate from multiple locations in the Indo-Pacific.

Another option under consideration would allow up to 1400 fixed-wing and 384 helicopter operations annually at each airfield.

The proposal remains subject to environmental review, and no final decision has been made.

Public meetings are scheduled for Saipan on 18 November, Tinian on 19 November and Rota on 21 November.

World.title: National's voters are walking. Here's where they're going
World.content:
Audio player for " Jo Moir discusses the latest election polling and campaigning " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2305619%2Fnational-s-voters-are-walking-here-s-where-they-re-going

Jo Moir discusses the latest election polling and campaigning Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Analysis: Almost one in five people who voted National in 2023 now back ACT or New Zealand First, according to a breakdown of the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll.

But Labour is still the biggest single beneficiary of National's reduced support.

The poll's headline numbers - released on Thursday - showed National's overall vote falling to 24.8 percent and Labour on 30.6 percent.

Closer analysis shows just 56.9 percent of those who said they voted National in 2023 still back the party.

Labour has picked up 14 percent of National's previous voters.

Audio player for " National faces party vote challenge as campaign winds up " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2305619%2Fnational-s-voters-are-walking-here-s-where-they-re-going

National faces party vote challenge as campaign winds up Morning Report Download MP3 8m

ACT takes 10.6 percent and New Zealand First 7.8 percent, giving National's coalition partners a combined 18.4 percent of its 2023 voters.

The findings come as National pushes back against a right-wing strategic voting campaign calling for National supporters to give just their electorate vote to National, and their party vote to ACT or NZ First.

The strategy relies on National winning more MPs in electorates than its party vote would normally allow, thereby creating an overhang and boosting the coalition's combined numbers.

Listen to Caucus: Top political commentators unpick and make sense of New Zealand's election campaigns with frank and forthright discussion.

Former prime minister Sir John Key has warned against the tactic, calling it "the opposite of clever". On Monday, he told Morning Report that National needed to remain a "strong core" of any resulting government.

The RNZ-Reid Research figures do not establish whether voters have switched teams for tactical reasons or who they intend to back with their electorate vote.

National's losses also extend well beyond its coalition partners.

Roughly a quarter of National's 2023 voters now favour a party outside the coalition, are undecided or say they would not vote.

Alongside Labour's 14 percent, Opportunity attracts 4.9 percent of National's previous voters and the Greens take 3.6 percent.

The movement between National and Labour is heavily in Labour's favour, with just 3.3 percent of Labour's 2023 voters now backing National.

Labour also retains more of its previous supporters, with 71.5 percent of its 2023 voters still backing the party.

Its biggest losses are to the Greens, which attract 9.9 percent of Labour's previous voters, followed by Opportunity on 5.6 percent and NZ First on 5.1 percent.

Reid Research surveyed 1000 eligible voters online between 20-26 October, with the results weighted to reflect the population.

World.title: Cats' rise well overdue as AFLW finals loom
World.content:
Co-captain Nina Morrison has always felt Geelong had the potential to be among the AFLW's best teams.

And she is not surprised by teammate Georgie Prespakis's rise to super stardom that has helped remove Geelong's underachievers tag and catapult the Cats to new heights.

Geelong has thrived under former Melbourne mentor Mick Stinear this year and will face the Demons in Saturday's qualifying final at Princes Park.

The Cats (11-1) are the highest-scoring regular-season AFLW team of all time and only finished second behind North Melbourne on percentage.

"We've been disappointed the last couple of seasons, to be honest, about where our performance has been," Morrison said.

"I feel like I've always looked at the group that we've had and the list profile and thought that we could be playing better footy.

"So in that sense, I would look at our performance and it doesn't feel like it's come out of the blue.

"We've probably just unlocked a few things that were already there and it's just about being able to do that all together and at the right time."

Georgie Prespakis is one of the superstars of the AFLW. (Getty Images: AFL Photo/Michael Willson)

Explosive midfielder Prespakis, the runner-up in the 2025 AFLW best and fairest, has gone to another level.

The 23-year-old has averaged 30.6 disposals, 8.1 clearances and eight score involvements.

"She's put in a body of work off-field as well to get herself in the right mindset coming into games to be able to perform well," Morrison said.

"She's obviously a star of the competition and I stand back in awe sometimes at the things she's doing on-field.

"She's an amazing player but her ability to bring her teammates into a game has always been a strength, but [she's] riding the ebbs and flows of that a bit better this season.

"To be someone that can do such incredible things but then also be such a great teammate has been her real growth this year."

Saturday will be the first time Stinear leads Geelong against Melbourne.

Tyla Hanks and Melbourne's impressive midfield will pose a tough test for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Wiltshire)

Morrison, who will play her 75th game, played down how much his inside knowledge could help against a star-studded midfield led by Kate Hore, Tyla Hanks and Olivia Purcell.

"We haven't played them, clearly, this year so I'm looking forward to the challenge of going up against one of the best mids in the comp, just seeing how we stack up against them," Morrison said.

"Obviously they're a pretty well-rounded team and Mick will know them pretty well as well.

"I'm sure he'll have some little things that we can draw on but I think a big focus for us over the course of the year has been how we focus on us and do us well. I'm sure that'll be no different this week."

Morrison insisted having to play at Princes Park instead of home ground Kardinia Park — booked out for a dirt bike event — was not on players' minds.

AAP

World.title: Usyk's path to global dominance goes through Gatton
World.content:
Oleksandr Usyk has earned a tongue-in-cheek invite to resume his cruiserweight career in Gatton after the boxing great's plan to return to the division set him on a path for David Nyika.

The Ukrainian (25-0) unified the cruiserweight division before wiping the floor of his heavyweight rivals, beating Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury and Daniel Dubois twice in the last five years.

The 39-year-old now wants to return to the cruiserweight ranks and sweep the belts again in one final act, with the vacant IBF title his first target before a date with current WBO and WBA champion David Benavidez (32-0).

Benavidez will fight Michal Cieslak for the WBC belt next month.

New Zealand Olympian David Nyika, based in the rural Queensland town of Gatton under trainer Noel Thornberry, is the IBF's number one-ranked fighter.

A potential title fight has been put on hold until the organisation's legal dispute with fellow Queensland-based champion Jai Opetaia is resolved.

Opetaia, who brutally knocked out Nyika to retain the IBF and The Ring belts in January last year, had his IBF status stripped when he debuted for rebel league Zuffa Boxing this year.

Jai Opetaia knocked David Nyika out when they met in January, 2025. (AAP Image: Dave Hunt)

Usyk's plans have put a spanner in the works for Opetaia, who is eyeing off a heavyweight cameo against Deontay Wilder next month before a potential unification clash with Benavidez next May.

Opetaia could still win back his IBF strap in the courtroom and earn a date with Usyk he has coveted since they competed at the 2012 London Olympics when the Australian was barely 17.

Opetaia exacts brutal toll in knockout, with heavyweight domination in his sight Jai Opetaia is the only man who can challenge heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk says promoter Eddie Hearn, after the IBF and Ring champion exacted the toll of trying to match it with boxing's best from David Nyika.

But even then Nyika remains the mandatory opponent and would command step-aside money for the Opetaia-Usyk fight to proceed.

"We'd have to sit down and come to an agreement, but we'd enforce his mandatory for sure if we were to stand aside," Thornberry told AAP on Monday.

Thornberry trained and managed former world champion contender Alex Leapai out of his Gatton boxing shed and has regularly held fight nights at the town's Shire Hall.

With Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh backing Usyk, Thornberry joked that he could pencil in an upgrade to the venue as part of the fight contract.

Oleksandr Usyk (right) won the undisputed IBF, IBO, WBA, WBC and WBO world heavyweight titles. (Getty Images: Richard Pelham)

"I've reached out to Usyk's management, they know we're certainly interested," Thornberry said.

"I'm sure they see David as a good way back in, but it's a great opportunity for David and he said he'd take it in a heartbeat.

"And, historically, no-one goes well when they come back in weight."

Oscar De Le Hoya lost to Manny Pacquiao, who went up two classes, when he dropped down in weight for their 2008 clash, while Antonio Tarver got the better of Roy Jones Jnr in a three-fight saga between 2003–2005.

Usyk showed off his slimmed-down physique at Canelo Alvarez's Saudi Arabia win on the weekend, but Thornberry reckons the jury is out.

"They come back down and go, 'Oh shit, this is a different algorithm to what I was accustomed to,'" he said.

"So let's see."

AAP

World.title: Wanderers' chair calls out 'totally unacceptable' fan treatment by police
World.content:
Western Sydney chairman Paul Lederer has slammed the "totally unacceptable" treatment and over-policing of Wanderers' supporters this season and vowed to seek answers from police.

The Red and Black Bloc (RBB), Western Sydney's active supporter group, staged a silent protest against over-policing in the opening 20 minutes of Saturday's goalless draw between the Wanderers and Macarthur at Campbelltown Sports Stadium.

The RBB, who also held banners that read "Stand Up For Fans. Not Police Demands" as a message to the Australian Professional Leagues (APL), said they had been directed by NSW Police to surrender their drums, megaphone and banners two hours before kick-off.

Macarthur coach and former Socceroo Sasa Ognenovski and his Wanderers' counterpart Ufuk Talay backed the fans, and Lederer joined them on Monday, releasing a lengthy statement.

Ufuk Talay (right) and Sasa Ognenovski were both sympathetic to the fans' cause. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

"Since the beginning of the season, we have witnessed repeated issues surrounding the treatment of our supporters. The events of this weekend have brought those frustrations to a tipping point," Lederer said.

"The treatment of our members and fans has been totally unacceptable. Enough is enough.

"The RBB are an integral part of our club which we are extremely proud of. That will never change, and we will continue to stand behind the positive contribution they make to the Wanderers and football in this country.

The fans who care the most The Red and Black Bloc are the most controversial sports fans in Australia, but the game they love is struggling.

"Our supporters should never be made to feel like second-class citizens simply because they choose to support a football club.

"We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for equal treatment and common sense.

"For too long, our supporters have faced excessive policing, policing that you as members and fans pay for."

Lederer pointed to hundreds of fans being withheld from entering the Sydney derby for up to 30 minutes and the presence of up to 20 public order and riot squad officers behind the Wanderers' supporter bays in Campbelltown.

"This only adds to the feeling of intimidation experienced by the families that largely make up our supporter base," he said.

"This level of treatment is neither reasonable nor proportionate, and there is no justification for a riot squad presence at our football matches."

Wanderers' fans, pictured here in round one's Sydney derby, have been backed by their chairman. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Lederer stressed the club did not condone anti-social behaviour, but said most of Western Sydney's fan base were not a problem and should be treated with "the utmost respect".

"As chairman, I have a responsibility to protect the future of the Western Sydney Wanderers. That means standing up for the people who give this club life," he said.

"I will not accept our members and fans being treated as though their passion makes them any less deserving of respect. Neither will this club.

"We will continue to raise our concerns directly with NSW Police, the A-Leagues and relevant stakeholders, seek clear answers and push for fair, consistent and respectful treatment."

Lederer also thanked the Wanderers' fans.

"You have never stopped standing up for this club," he said.

"And as your chairman, I want you to know that we will never stop standing up for you."

AAP has contacted the APL and NSW Police for comment.

AAP

World.title: Big is beautiful as Australia's first UFC champion finally comes home
World.content:
It has taken more than a decade, but Rob Whittaker, Australia's first-ever UFC champion, is finally coming home.

The UFC light-heavyweight has been confirmed for the promotion's next card in Sydney on February 7, where he will face Uzbekistan's Bogdan Guskov in his first hometown fight in over 12 years.

Whittaker can barely recall his last effort in the Harbour City, when he knocked out American Clint Hester in 2014.

It came so early in his career it was closer to his Padstow products days as a Railcorp electrician than a world champion.

"It's hard to remember, to be honest. So much has happened since. I've ridden the rollercoaster," said Whittaker.

Rob Whittaker last fought in Sydney in 2014. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Josh Hedges )

"My friends and family can all be there. They can be a part of the whole journey without having to spend a billion bucks to be there.

"But I hope things settle down. I'm going to have to stop replying (to people asking for tickets).

"It'll be good to be home after so long. You normally have to travel so far to put on a show."

Putting on a show far and wide has been second nature for Whittaker during his long career with the UFC.

Since that night in Sydney, all but one of his UFC losses have come against future or reigning world champions, confirming his status as one of Australia's top combat sport exports.

The 35-year-old snuck in a few fights on home soil, but the last was in 2019 when he lost the middleweight title against Israel Adesanya in Melbourne in front of over 57,000 fans, still the biggest crowd in UFC history.

The crowd won't quite be the same at the Sydney SuperDome for this card, headlined by rising Perth lightweight Quillin Salkilld's bout with Benoit St Denis, but Whittaker — a father of three sons and three daughters — is just happy he can take his kids to work.

Rob Whittaker recently broke a two-fight losing streak. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"Last fight, my two eldest could come. This time it might be my three eldest. They loved it last time, and I loved having them be a part of it," said Whittaker.

"They get to see their old man work for a living. I'm sure half the time they think I'm unemployed.

"I love fighting. I don't think there's a cooler way to earn money if we want to keep it real basic, and I'm good at it as well. I'm earning a trade, and I'm going to keep doing it."

The fight will be Whittaker's second since moving from middleweight (83.91kg) to light-heavyweight (92.99kg).

After a third-round knockout win in his division debut over Nikita Krylov in July, he has plenty of confidence after snapping a two-fight losing streak.

Whittaker was wary of the power difference against bigger fighters, but after a strong start, where he left Krylov with a broken jaw, bigger has become beautiful.

Rob Whittaker has bulked up from middleweight to light-heavyweight. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"I'm definitely more confident in my ability to zip and zag and my ability to land power, to be faster, to have the confidence to shoot when I feel it, to have confidence in my instincts again," said Whittaker.

"I can eat for fuel, I don't need to starve myself, and that makes living — especially with a family and heaps of kids — much more enjoyable.

"But it's a slippery slope, because after a fight I can get really stuck in.

"Light-heavyweight eating is different to middleweight eating, let me tell you."

Guskov has a strong track record with 15 knockouts from his 18 wins, but Whittaker is confident he has the experience to outpoint the 34-year-old.

"He's a big, rangy guy. He hits hard, he's finished a lot of people, but there's nothing he brings to the table that I haven't seen in my years in the game," said Whittaker.

"There's nothing he brings to the table that I think I can't beat."

World.title: Australian batting 'stronger' despite repeat South Africa collapses
World.content:
Coach Andrew McDonald says Australia's batting is in a better place now than before the South Africa tour, despite admitting the team underperformed in the 2-1 series loss.

Players began flying out of South Africa on Sunday and Monday, with Australia to now turn its focus to a home series against New Zealand and a tour of India that starts in January.

There remains an ongoing sense of frustration about the way the South Africa tour ended, with McDonald lamenting several missed opportunities to clinch the series.

That includes letting South Africa off the hook with the ball in Gqeberha and Cape Town, while nightmare collapses in both those Tests also hurt.

Australia has been 4-95 or worse in 14 of its past 25 Test innings, with that brittleness exposed again as the team slumped to 8-62 on the series-deciding day five in Cape Town.

But Australia's coach pointed to the performances of Cameron Green, Matt Renshaw and Josh Inglis as reasons for legitimate positivity, with the latter two scoring centuries.

Josh Inglis scored a superb century in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

"If you look at the batting unit, I think we walk away in a stronger position," McDonald said.

"For Josh Inglis to step up at late notice [in Cape Town] … he's been a batter that's been carried around with us for a while; it's exciting.

"Albeit there's a lot of negativity floating around at the moment, it's exciting to see him and Cameron Green and even Matthew Renshaw."

McDonald also admitted selectors would have some decisions to make "around the age profile of that team", with 23-year-old Cooper Connolly playing his second Test in Cape Town and Sam Konstas firing in the Sheffield Shield.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

"It's still a very good cricket team with a lot of very good players in there, and down the path they will be acknowledged as legends of the game," McDonald said of the current side.

"So we've got to balance that out with who comes in, what the next decisions are.''

Beyond the obvious turning points, McDonald pointed to Australia's inability to build a big first-innings lead in Cape Town after starting day three at close to parity with four wickets down as a big moment in the series.

But he stressed that not all fault lay with the batters, after the bowlers failed to put a final nail in South Africa on day four in Cape Town.

Australia has now lost three of its past five Tests, with the back-to-back defeats in Gqeberha and Cape Town the first successive failures since the 2023 Border-Gavaskar Trophy.

The defeats have cost Australia the number one spot in the rankings, ahead of a nine-month period that includes the away Border-Gavaskar Trophy and Ashes series.

Still, McDonald pointed to Pat Cummins's 60 per cent win rate as skipper and the fact it was one of the highest among all Australian captains.

"We've underachieved here," McDonald said.

"It feels as though it's hard to win on the road. That's the greatest challenge, and that's where we will be critiqued.

"And we're incredibly frustrated that we weren't able to execute this tour after being 1-0 up."

AAP

World.title: West Coast Eagles star suffers brutal injury news
World.content:
West Coast could be without midfielder Ella Roberts for the entire 2027 AFLW season after scans confirmed the superstar had ruptured her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Roberts, 21, suffered the right knee injury when she planted her leg in an attempt to change direction in the first quarter of Saturday's loss to Hawthorn, the Eagles' final game of the campaign after failing to make finals.

The midfielder immediately went down and had to be assisted from the field.

The Eagles confirmed on Monday that Roberts had torn her ACL and would need a knee reconstruction.

Given the typical 12-month recovery from that surgery, Roberts will be racing the clock to feature at all next year.

"We are all saddened by the injury sustained by Ella," West Coast AFLW boss Michelle Cowan said.

"Our priority is to arrange surgery as soon as possible and ensure she receives the very best care and we will wrap our arms around her throughout this journey.

"She is a true professional and we have every confidence she will approach her recovery with the same diligence and determination, fully supported by our medical team."

Roberts, who can play both midfield and forward, is one of the most talented players in the game and has kicked 20 goals in 55 games since her 2022 debut.

She is a two-time All-Australian and won the Eagles' best and fairest award in 2024 and 2025.

Roberts averaged 21.7 disposals and five clearances this year as West Coast finished 13th.

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: NZ duo on brink of history as Lebanon goes into folklore
World.content:
The group stage of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books after a remarkable double-header to finish things off.

Lebanon's golden-point win over France and Tonga and Samoa's epic showdown were both classics, giving the tournament the close finishes that have been in short supply.

With Australia, New Zealand, Tonga and Samoa progressing to the semifinals, here are the quick hits from the final round of matches.

1. Was this the last World Cup for the old Kumuls?

Gairo Voro is one of several Papua New Guinea players with a big future. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

No country in rugby league will see the sport transform in their nation from this World Cup to the next like Papua New Guinea.

The entry of the PNG Chiefs to the NRL in 2028, with their near-limitless resources and game-bending salary cap concessions, will change the game in the land where they love it most.

So long as the Chiefs fulfil their promise of creating strong pathways for local talent to make it to the top level, it has the potential to change the national side forever.

England's World Cup fate is resting on a miracle After a scratchy win over Papua New Guinea, England's Rugby League World Cup needs a miracle to stay alive.

The prospect of talents like five-eighth Gairo Voro, who scored a sharp solo try, or winger Dudley Dutoi, who got the better of England star Dom Young, getting regular NRL football is a tantalising one.

The two were among Papua New Guinea's best in a spirited defeat, and from the Highlands to the islands of New Britain there can be so many more like them.

PNG's improvement over the past decade has been steady, but it is about to hit overdrive. This game against England might be the last dance for the Kumuls as we've come to know them.

2. The New Zealand duo closing in on history

Casey McLean seemingly cannot stop scoring tries for New Zealand. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It was another Kiwi romp as New Zealand punished a Fiji side that struggled to backup from last week's fine performance against Australia, but amid the near-endless tries and ill-tempered flare-ups, Casey McLean and Jamayne Isaako continued their march towards history.

Isaako scored 26 points from a try and 13 goals from as many attempts to go with his 38 points against the Cook Islands the weeks before, and the winger is closing in on Shaun Johnson's all-time Kiwi pointscoring record.

The former Dolphin has 215 points from his 17 Tests, just 10 shy of Johnson's mark, and could claim top spot as early as the World Cup final if the points continue to flow for Stacey Jones's side.

McLean has more work to do to run down Manu Vatuvei as the nation's highest-ever try-scorer, but he is making a cracking pace.

In just seven Tests, McLean has scored 15 tries to sit in equal-eighth spot on the all-time list. Every other player around him had at least 20 caps, and Vatuvei took 29 to collect his 23 tries.

The second four-try haul of his budding career means that at just 20, McLean is odds on to become New Zealand's Test try-scoring king sooner rather than later.

3. Are Australia still the favourites?

Australia has done enough to qualify for the semifinals. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

The Kangaroos are one of only two unbeaten sides heading into the knockout phase, but their hold on favouritism is shaky at best.

Their brilliant win over New Zealand in the tournament opener had more than a few elements of fortune in their favour, especially the two length-of-the-field intercept tries that kept them in the game early on.

They scratched their way past Fiji and romped home against the Cook Islands since, looking short of their best in both performances.

While they are always a threat, it feels as though all four nations in the semifinals are in with a chance of lifting the trophy rather than it being Australia's birthright.

Kevin Walters has a big decision to make at halfback between Tom Dearden and Sam Walker but seems to have settled on Reece Walsh as his custodian, and after the Broncos playmaker laid on five tries in this 66-6 mauling to go with his game-changing plays against the Kiwis, it's hard to argue.

4. Lebanon-France is what the World Cup can be

Abbas Miski's miracle try was one of the moments of the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

After a tournament filled with blowouts, the epic finish between France and Lebanon shows what's possible when things line up right at the World Cup, as two winless teams desperate to restore some pride played out a classic.

This was two teams of similar skill levels in front of a rowdy and emotionally invested crowd at a venue that accentuated at least one of the fan bases.

That's a simple recipe to follow, and while you won't always be rewarded with the epic finish of this golden point thriller, a new format that keeps teams like this together and therefore produces more of these match-ups is a must for 2030.

When that next tournament rolls around, plenty of tales from this game will be told, from Cesar Rouge's game-winning field goal controversially chalked off the board to Lebanon's remarkable extra-time try to Abbas Miski.

That score put the tragedy of French fullback Arthur Mourgue, a mad genius who doesn't always nail the genius part, into World Cup folklore after his remarkable field goal sent the game to extra time before a maniac kick inside his own 20 fell for the Cedars's winning try.

5. The veteran Tonga cannot do without

Tui Lolohea had another role to play in another epic win for Tonga. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Amid a match with a galaxy of stars that promised a glorious future for Samoa and Tonga, Tui Lolohea seemed the odd man out.

The Tongan veteran was the only player in the game who doesn't ply his trade in the NRL, and given his mercurial career, he might have seemed a weak link for the Mate Ma'a.

But after 12 seasons in the red jersey, Lolohea has proven himself an invaluable part of their rise to the top of Test football, and while they have more talent at their disposal than ever before, they always come back to him when it counts.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only man to have played in each of Tonga's most important wins over the past decade and always seems to defy critics when it matters most.

He is older and slower, but he always gives Tonga what they need — the 31-year-old, who currently doesn't have a club for next season, set up a try for Jojo Fifita with a clever floating pass and held up well in defence under heavy pressure from Samoa, who clearly targeted the former Huddersfield Giant.

With Latu Fainu fit and Talatau Amone in the squad, Tonga are not short of options in the halves, but Lolohea rewarded coach Kristian Woolf's faith yet again, as he always seems to do when it matters most.

World.title: Large crocodile spotted near future Olympic rowing course
World.content:
The sighting of a saltwater crocodile near the proposed 2032 Olympic rowing precinct in Rockhampton is under investigation, while Rowing Australia says it is a "shock" and a wake-up call.

North Rockhampton Golf Club alerted members at the weekend when the crocodile, estimated to be up to 3 metres long, was spotted near the 11th hole.

The sighting was within a few kilometres of the Fitzroy River precinct earmarked for rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The selection of Rockhampton as the home of the Games' rowing has been questioned by some. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

On Monday, a spokesperson for the Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI) said the sighting was not reported to the department, but was now under investigation.

Speaking in Hervey Bay on Monday morning, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli played down concerns about the crocodile and expressed confidence in Rockhampton's ability to host the Olympic rowing events.

"Many, many decades of success prove that it's a world-class venue," he said.

"It's a magnificent community and they'll do it very, very well."

David Crisafulli has backed Rockhampton's rowing venue amid renewed crocodile concerns. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Rowing Australia life member Ray Ebert said the sighting was a wake-up call for those involved in planning the 2032 Olympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River.

"It's a bit of a shock to me," Mr Ebert told ABC News Breakfast on Monday.

"I've been saying that the crocodiles are the least of our problems. I'm going to admit to something that none of the politicians have admitted to: maybe I was wrong."

Mr Ebert pointed to previous crocodile sightings in the area, including two reported in December 2024, involving animals measuring about 2.5 metres and 1 metre.

Loading...

He said the latest sighting raised questions about how authorities would manage crocodile risks around the proposed rowing venue.

"It's not the crocodiles that you can see that I would be worried about. It's the ones that I can't see," he said.

Mr Ebert questioned whether the Queensland government was taking the issue seriously enough and said the sighting could prompt further questions about the venue's suitability and safety.

Rowing venue scrutiny

State and national rowing regattas have been held on the Fitzroy River and the venue has also been used by Australian rowing teams for pre-Olympic training camps over the years.

In September, Mr Crisafulli announced the Rockhampton venue had passed an independent technical assessment "with flying colours" to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

It came after months of fierce debate over the Fitzroy River's suitability, including its status as a crocodile habitat.

The Rockhampton rowing facility has hosted multiple events. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

International sporting bodies are now awaiting the next phase of venue planning, which include technical details and confirmation of service levels and facilities needed for Olympic and Paralympic competitions.

Queensland Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the sighting highlighted the need for the Crisafulli government to release the technical report underpinning Rockhampton's selection as an Olympic rowing venue.

Mr Miles said the report should outline how crocodile risks would be managed during the Games, arguing its release would help address concerns about the Fitzroy River.

A sign at the North Rockhampton Golf Club warns visitors of crocodiles on the course. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

University of Queensland crocodile expert and emeritus professor Craig Franklin was more critical of the decision to hold Olympic rowing on the Fitzroy River.

He described it as a political decision rather than one based on common sense, saying he would go so far as to call it "foolish".

On September 19, a saltwater croc was spotted upstream from the Rockhampton rowing course, according to the Queensland government's official sightings dashboard.

There have been two further sightings since that were reported closer to the proposed venue.

Croc expert supports removal

Reptile expert John Lever, who owns Koorana Crocodile Farm near Rockhampton, said the animal was likely to be a male saltwater crocodile and estimated it was "up to three metres" long based on the photograph of the sighting.

Mr Lever said wildlife rangers would likely need to assess the animal's behaviour before a decision was made about whether it should be removed.

Koorana Crocodile Farm owner John Lever. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

The area is not currently classified as a Category A zone, where crocodiles are automatically targeted for removal.

However, Mr Lever said he believed crocodiles spotted in the vicinity of the planned Olympic venue should be dealt with.

"With the Olympics coming up, my take on this would be that any crocodile seen in that area should be removed," he said.

"But that's not up to me to do that, it's up to the government."

A DETSI spokesperson said the Queensland Crocodile Management Plan was reviewed every year.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since its selection as an Olympic venue. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Mr Lever said heavy rainfall in central Queensland last week may have stimulated the animal's activity.

"There's crocodiles, of course, in the Fitzroy [River], we all know that, so a sighting is not uncommon," he said.

"This is the mating season. Males and females are both moving around looking for mates."

Tech.title: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

BMW says that it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow.

The new system can help steer, speed up, and slow down the vehicle on both highways and city streets using its built-in GPS navigation. While driving in town, it can assist with changing lanes, making turns, yielding to other cars, and driving through roundabouts. But as a Level 2 driver assist system, it still requires drivers to keep their eyes on the road and stay ready to take over at any moment. On the highway, BMW will allow drivers to remove their hands from the steering wheel — but on local roads, they’ll need to keep their hands on the wheel.

BMW is the latest automaker to commit to releasing a partially autonomous city driving feature to its customers, as the industry races to keep up with Tesla and its Full Self-Driving (FSD) system. BMW, in particular, recently introduced its next-generation Neue Klasse platform, which includes a driver assist system partly powered by Qualcomm’s technology. And with hands-free highway driving now widely available in many mass-market vehicles, the next frontier is a safe and capable city driving feature that rivals FSD.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Image: BMW

BMW says its system works cooperatively with drivers rather than fighting their control, which means they can steer, brake, or speed up at any point to adjust their driving without shutting the system off. At the same time, the car shows what it sees and what the assistance system is doing right in your line of sight through the heads-up display and in a clear 3D map on the main dashboard screen.

The necessary cameras and sensors already come built into models like BMW’s 3 Series, 7 Series, X5, iX3, and iX4. BMW can activate the feature through an over-the-air software update. The system follows new European safety rules that let cars suggest and make automated driving moves on city streets for the first time. BMW says that outside experts have already road-tested the setup and confirmed it meets the technical standards, with final official government approval expected in early 2027.

With more cars equipped with partial automation hitting the road, safety researchers are growing increasingly worried about driver attention and the potential for these systems to cause crashes. There is compelling evidence that, regardless of the company, most driver-assist systems are less safe than normal human driving. Drivers tend to develop an overreliance on these systems to drive the car for them — even after a short period of use. And when it’s time to take back control of the vehicle, their reaction times are slower than what’s considered safe.

BMW is entering risky territory with the adoption of a Level 2 driving feature. Much like Tesla, the company is emphasizing that drivers remain responsible for the vehicle even while using the partially autonomous system in urban environments. Tesla does the same for its FSD feature, but some customers have successfully argued in court that the company bears some responsibility for crashes when they occur.

Tech.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.

In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”

“We know that trust is earned.” — Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer

The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.

Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.

Previous Next





1 / 4

To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.

It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.
